en: Preface to the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, composed by Shi Huize.
Regarding the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, it is also known as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. It originally consisted of five hundred verses [composed by] Nāgārjuna.
This is the work of a bodhisattva.
To borrow "lamp" as its name signifies that non-conceptual wisdom possesses the merit of both quiescence and illumination.
To cite this as the central heading indicates that the mirror-like wisdom is free from conditions and observations, equally transcending the two extremes.

Thus, the lamp is fundamentally without mind, and wisdom is devoid of illumination; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal, and the meaning of the Middle Way lies herein. Therefore, I have relied upon this discourse to clarify it.

Now, as for those who pursue the expressions while stagnating in their meaning, or cling to the conventional while deluding themselves about the truth—tumbling between the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and floundering within the realm of existence and non-existence; those who guard the name while losing the reality, and clutch at the leaves while discarding the root—how could they have intended such a thing?

There is indeed a reason for this! Allow me to set it forth. If one constructs the causes of discrimination and invites the fruits of delusion, then afflictions and karma perfume the internal consciousness while evil associates form external conditions.

This leads to pride as lofty as a towering mountain, views as deep as the vast ocean, the fire of anger difficult to touch, and verbal sharpness rarely met. Hearing talk of existence, they rejoice; listening to discourse on emptiness, they give rise to slander. Among the six types of biased attachments, each claims their own view is not biased; five hundred masters of treatises vie to produce divergent arguments. Some use the heterodox to confuse the orthodox, others use the false to equate with the true. Their consciousness appears to awaken but instead falls further into delusion; though the teachings seem to penetrate, they become even more obstructed. This may be called discarding pearls to play with stones, abandoning treasure to carry firewood, fearing dragons upon seeing a painting, or shrinking from an elephant when following its tracks.
To cherish such [worldly things] is truly lamentable. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna appeared as a preeminent savior for the world;

he resolved his mind upon awakening by reviling sensual desires and humbled himself by reading the profound sutras. Having received the prophetic prediction of the Sole Honored One, he lit the torch of the Dharma upon Jambudvīpa. His realization surpassed the initial stages of reliance, and his merit exceeded the positions of subjugation. He exhausted the single reality and investigated the two capacities; wearing the two seals, he settled the hundred schools, and blending the three emptinesses, he brought all things into equilibrium. Having endured various hardships throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, he felt pity for those who were deluded and thus composed this treatise. Its phrasing is profound and its purport subtle; it refutes with skill and establishes its arguments with artistry. Yet, when applied to those of dull faculties, it often engenders timidity and retreat.

There was the Bodhisattva Vidyākaraprabha, a general of the Mahāyāna Dharma, who embodied the Way within his heart and extensively surveyed the mantras. He composed commentaries upon them to reveal the secret treasury and bestow the wish-fulfilling jewel; thus, the concise and the extensive complement one another, and teacher and disciple mutually illuminate each other.

As for the diverse tenets of our own vehicle arising in a thousand ways, and the divergent calculations of non-Buddhists proliferating in myriad strands—wherein those of donkey-like vehicles gallop in competition with four-horse chariots, and fireflies vying to outshine the dragon-torch—it is impossible not to categorize their respective types and reveal the lineages of their masters.

Once the jade and stone were separated and the dark and yellow were distinguished, there arose several schools in the Western Regions that took up the brush; yet, in examining facts and analyzing subtleties, this [work] is the most refined and profound.
If one includes both the fundamental and the derivative [aspects], there are six thousand verses. Such is the Sanskrit original; when translated, it is reduced accordingly.

Our Emperor’s divine way surpasses that of Fuxi and Shennong, and his transformative molding is equal to that of the Creator. He unifies the Six Directions and penetrates the Three Powers of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity; he encompasses the four types of living beings and propagates the Ten Wholesome Deeds. By honoring the root and extinguishing the derivative, he achieves non-action and Great Peace; by guarding the Mother and preserving the Child, he governs through non-speech. Furthermore, he has set his heart upon the Buddhist scriptures and contemplated the Ultimate Truth with profound vision. He considered that since the Holy Teaching reached the East several hundred years ago, much remains lacking among the myriad phenomena it bears; thus, he longed to hear what had not yet been heard, laboring over it both in waking and in sleep.

The Tripitaka Master Prajñāmitra of Central India—translated into Chinese as Mingyou (Bright Friend)—was one whose learning encompassed both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, who broadly mastered all systems of exposition, who had cast aside the self to delight the spirit and sought the profound to nurture his nature. With a mind ever intent on traveling afar and a heart devoted to benefiting sentient beings, he was able to sustain his life by leaning against wooden pegs and summon companions by raising smoke; thus he braved frost and ice to cross the Pamir Mountains and endured wind and heat to traverse the River of Sands.

Five years having passed and forty thousand *li* traversed, on the twentieth day of the eleventh month of the year Juezi, the first year of the Zhenguan era of the Great Tang, he arrived at the imperial capital carrying the Sanskrit texts upon his head.
In the past, the Qin dynasty summoned Kumārajīva, exerting great effort with military force;
the Han dynasty invited Kāśyapa Mātanga, toiling the envoys from distant lands.
How can these be compared to the present, where spiritual resonance occurs and the Way accords with the hidden signs?

Auspicious signs appeared throughout the empire and the state, and this man of virtue descended among us; when the officials reported his arrival, the Emperor’s heart was filled with extraordinary joy.
In that year, an imperial edict was issued to establish him at Daxingshan Temple, and he was further requested to translate one section of the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra*.

In the sixth month of the fourth year, he moved to Shengguang Monastery and summoned the śramaṇas specializing in scholastic learning—Huìchéng, Huìlǎng, Fǎcháng, Tánzàng, Zhìshǒu, Huìmíng, Dàoyuè, Sēngqié, Sēngzhēn, Zhìjiě, Wénshùn, Fǎlín, Língjiā, Huìzé, and Huìjìng—to act as translators. The śramaṇas Xuānmó and Saṃgha, along with the Tripiṭaka master’s fellow student, the Vinaya Master Jùduō, and others served as witnesses and co-translators for this treatise.

Fang Xuanling, Duke of Bin and Left Vice Director of the Secretariat; Du Zhenglun, Grand Master of the Household to the Crown Prince; and Li Xiaogong, Prince of Zhaojun and Minister of Rites, were all sagacious and worthy ministers who assisted the state and provided salvation for their times. They served their sovereign with utmost loyalty and integrity, and cast aside their physical forms in their quest for the Dharma.

From the time the Sage Ruler first conceived this intention until its ultimate and far-reaching proclamation, the benefits have been profound and the advantages substantial; indeed, these were made possible through [the Emperor’s] inspired development.

The Imperial Commissioner for Supervising Translation, Right Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and Minister of the Court of Palace Revenues, Lanling Xiao Jing, possessed the roots of faith from the very beginning and the power of wisdom to sustain it to the end. With tranquil contemplation he sought the Truth, and with an open mind he admired the Way; he assisted and promoted [this work] as a shadow follows a form, providing encouragement and support without ceasing.

Those virtuous monks rose early and never grew weary; they investigated the profound essence, discarding the ornamental to preserve the substantial. They rejoiced when encountering the underlying principle through direct observation, and scrutinized right and wrong within the teacher’s presence. Though the texts were already established, they examined them again with care; though the meanings were clear, they reviewed them repeatedly.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month, under the year of the Shouxing (Longevity Star) cycle, this examination was completed.

As for this treatise: while contemplating the illumination of the Middle Way, one preserves the Middle but loses contemplation; while the Emptiness reveals the Supreme Truth, one attains the Truth but deviates from Emptiness.
Thus, the south-pointing chariot is fundamentally intended for those who are lost, and the mirror that reflects the gallbladder is for the purpose of examining the depraved.
If one is not depraved, there is no application for the mirror; if one is not lost, the chariot serves no purpose.
This treatise refutes and establishes precisely through this means.

Although it repudiates internal views and excludes external ones, exhausting the false and reaching the ultimate truth, that which remains subtle is preserved, and that which may be refuted is indeed refuted.
Vast and expansive! Immense and boundless! To encounter it, one cannot fathom its source;

to follow it, one knows no end to its ramifications. Truly, it is a whetstone for polishing the spirit, a boat and carriage for crossing the perilous oceans, a thunderclap that startles the benighted consciousness, and the sun and moon that illuminate the dark paths.

In this land, there previously existed a four-fascicle version of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*; while its root verses were largely identical [to the current edition], Piṇḍola served as its commentator, obscuring the specific tenets of the school, whereby students remained ignorant of them.
Now that this treatise has appeared, it may serve as a clear mirror.
May those gentlemen who seek to awaken to the profound examine and savor it with care.
It universally severs all conceptual discrimination and extinguishes all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Able to uproot the very source of existence, You skillfully expound the Dharma of ultimate truth.
Regarding that which transcends the realm of speech, You skillfully establish it through words and letters.
You shatter the deluded mind of evil wisdom; Therefore, I prostrate in homage to you.
The commentary states: What is the meaning of these verses?

My teacher, the Noble One, having realized it for himself within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, has examined the ultimate truth and revealed its true meaning in order to sever the net of all evil and false views.
Although those with evil views may practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), because they are deluded, all their actions become unwholesome.
Now, desiring to cause them to awaken to and understand the Right Path, I have composed this *Madhyamaka-śāstra* based on the pure Āgamas to proclaim and disseminate the Buddha’s word.
Regarding the purpose for which this treatise is composed, what are its characteristics?

It is said that the Bhagavat, seeing those sentient beings shrouded by ignorance and destroyed by the dense forest of the net of various conceptual proliferations—such as arising and ceasing, permanence and annihilation, unity and difference, coming and going—gave rise to supreme compassion and exerted courageous wisdom. For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of eons, he sacrificed his own body and life for the benefit of others, never experiencing weariness or fatigue.

They are able to bear the burden of the immeasurable accumulation of merit and wisdom; they drill into the ocean of the realm of *prajñā*, severing the net of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); being independent of other conditions and free from discrimination, they attain the true nectar of all phenomena.

Regarding the realms of rebirth, the duration of life, the nature, the location, the time, and so forth, he gathers and benefits beings in a manner unique to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists;

solely for the sake of those who aspire to the Supreme Vehicle, he establishes names, phrases, and expressions such as "non-arising" based upon both conventional truth and ultimate truth—this is the most excellent among the true teachings on dependent origination.

My own ācārya likewise, regarding such textual passages as "non-arising" and so forth, revealed the Tathāgata’s true principle, attained a realization in accordance with reality, and gave rise to supreme vigor.
Having realized [the truth] as it is, I praise the Bhagavat and have therefore composed this treatise.
Furthermore, with a mind moistened by the water of compassion, having verified what I myself have understood, I utter these words so that the world may likewise attain understanding.
As a verse says:
“Neither ceasing nor arising, Neither annihilated nor eternal,
Neither one nor manifold, Neither coming nor going.”
"Dependent origination stills conceptual proliferation;
because the Teacher has skillfully extinguished it, I pay homage to that Bhagavān, the most supreme among all teachers.
Commentary:

Because the meanings of those phrases are understood in immediate succession, one understands the meaning of this treatise; therefore, these phrase-meanings are explained first. Because it is destroyed, it is "ceased"; because it arises, it is "originated";

because the continuity of death ceases, it is "cut off"; because it abides at all times, it is "permanent"; because there is no distinction or difference in meaning, it is "one"; because there is the meaning of differentiation and diversity, it is "various"; because it moves toward this meaning, it is "coming"; because it moves toward that meaning, it is "going"; because this cessation does not exist, it is "not ceased," and so on, up to: because this going does not exist, it is "not going."
Their arising and ceasing, as well as their identity and difference, are negated from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Their annihilation and permanence are negated within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).
As for their coming and going, some say they are negated by both [truths].
Some may say that all such things are negated in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because [the Buddha] is the one who does so; "he" refers to the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).
As for "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is called dependent origination because various causes and conditions combine to give rise to phenomena.
Because the grasping at the intrinsic nature of speech never occurs again, it is called the "cessation of conceptual proliferation.
Because all calamities and obstructions are absent, or because its intrinsic nature is empty at times, it is called "well-extinguished."
Because he expounds and unfolds the meaning, his teaching is correct and not inverted.
Having thoroughly realized the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—he is therefore called the Buddha Bhagavān.
For this reason, I pay homage.
What is meant by the phrase "the most supreme among all teachings"?

It is because it reveals the path for gods and humans to gain faith and joy in nirvāṇa through non-erroneous dependent origination, and because it provides instruction that is most excellent for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
What has been expounded is precisely non-erroneous, because it is superior due to its being dependent origination.
Question: You yourself just now stated that you were teaching the dharma of dependent origination.
If you say it is dependently originated, how can it not arise?
If you say it does not arise, how can it be dependently originated?
These words are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, because the understanding [of the meaning] would regress, both the words and their meaning would be destroyed, as in the statement: "All speech is false.
The response is:
If all dependently arisen phenomena were non-arising, then that person would indeed form such an understanding, and I would incur this fault.
I have never said that all dependent origination is non-arising; therefore, there is no fault as described above.
How is this so? It is because dependent origination exists within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but it does not exist even conventionally in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
As for that which they call a cause, this meaning is not established.

Just as with generosity (*dāna*) and so forth, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) they are not said to be wholesome; rather, they are called wholesome because they include [the cycle of] birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, as it is said that consciousness is the self, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), consciousness is truly not the self.
Understanding it in this way, there is no fault.

Likewise, when a conjured man arises, the self-nature of that man does not actually arise; similarly, the arising of the internal sense-bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) and so forth are like illusions or mirages—they are spoken of from a conventional standpoint (saṃvṛti), not from the ultimate standpoint, and therefore there is no error.
Question: It is appropriate for phenomena (dharma) that arising is followed by cessation;
because the former exists, it is like that which is not severed.
Answer:

Since birth and death are beginningless, the objection that "the cessation must come first and the arising later" is likewise refuted; this is not a fault of a non-conclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*), for one observes the sequence of the meaning rather than their difference.
If you first offer a refutation, it incurs the same fault as [the argument regarding] arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, the Dharmaguptakas say:

"In the beginning of your treatise, you state that this unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma), which is not subject to arising, ceasing, and so forth, is a distinct dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)."
This argument is not correct.
Why? Because it exists within our own system.
Regarding your initial statement that [dependent origination] is not shared with the Śrāvakas and others, the meaning is inconsistent.
The proponent says:
It is in order to negate intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that I speak of specific dharmas of dependent origination, such as "non-arising" and so forth, so that you may attain understanding.
If you claim that there exists such an unconditioned dependent origination (asaṃskṛta-pratītyasamutpāda) in order to convince others,
this argument is not tenable, because it lacks any verifiable essence.
If your intention is to maintain that dependent origination is definitive and thus termed "unconditioned dependent origination," [that too is incorrect].
This interpretation is flawed. Why?
Because it negates arising.
Since that arising has no intrinsic nature, it should not be called "common.
This is because there is no cause for the arising of what is non-existent, just as with [the case of] abiding.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
The meaning of "non-arising" and so forth is not exclusive to the Śrāvakas.
What is the meaning of this?
That which lacks the essence of arising differently is called "non-arising," just as [the self] lacks sovereignty.
The extinction understood by those non-Buddhists is an extinction that lacks substantiality; therefore, it is called "non-extinction.
For example, the doctrine of no-self is neither discontinuous because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions, nor is it eternal because the cause perishes when the fruit arises.
When that mani jewel, powdered dried cow dung, and sunlight come together, fire is thus produced.
One cannot say it is not one because of its nature, nor can one say it is manifold because of its distinct nature.
Since it perishes at the very moment it arises, the meaning of neither coming nor going is precisely as such.
As for what you stated at the beginning of your treatise—that this dependent origination is not shared with the śrāvakas and is distinct—[it is as follows].
This interpretation is not correct.
The proponent of the treatise says:
Although you have spoken these words, they contradict right principle.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because that which arises does not arise.

Desiring to enable others to understand the distinct meaning of dependent origination as non-arising and so forth—since this is the uncommon, specific dependent origination—I have placed it at the beginning and praised the Buddha Bhagavān before composing this treatise. First, by causing one to realize that what arises does not arise, the other points, such as non-ceasing and so on, will be easily understood.
How is it that one causes the understanding that those [phenomena] do not arise and so forth?

It is because those who give rise to conceptual constructions perceive them as being manifest before them. Regarding all such assertions—whether they claim that the essence arises from itself, from another, from both, or without cause—all these explanations are incorrect.
Based upon the Āgamas and correct reasoning, when one observes reality as it truly is, arising is found to be without meaning.
Therefore, the author of this treatise, having reached a definitive conclusion through his own authority, spoke this verse:
"At no time and in no place Does there exist even a single entity."
"Neither from self, nor from another, nor from both, nor without cause do they arise.
The commentary states:
"Not from self" means that those aggregates established as the phenomena that arise ultimately lack any intrinsic nature.
Just as with each successive stage, one should understand that "self" (*ātman*) carries the sense of "one's own.
For what reason is the substantiality of all those things negated?
It is because such negation pertains to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), and furthermore, because it negates the entire web of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Free from the net of all conceptual proliferation" means that there are no remaining objects of cognition.
"The absence of objects" is intended to establish non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, as for "negation," it is because it negates the existence of any remaining sensation.
It employs alternative skillful means to teach that all phenomena do not arise and that skillful means themselves do not arise, so as to bring about understanding in others.
This is not the *siddhānta* of the Mahāyāna.
How is this known?
As it is said in the Āgamas:
Form does not give rise to activity, because it does not practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, "not arising by itself" means that such an essence does not arise of its own accord; this is the correct understanding.
If one understands this differently and asserts that [cognition] does not arise from its own essence, this position is flawed.
What is the flaw? It is the fault of [the cognition] being produced by another.

Furthermore, regarding your statement that [things] do not arise from themselves: it is not merely that there is the fault of arising from another, but also the fault of arising from both self and other.
This is not what we intend, as it contradicts our established tenet (*siddhānta*); therefore, this was said as a provisional teaching (*upāya-vacana*).
Within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth lack the meaning of self-arising; this is not practiced in the world because they exist.
It is, for example, like the shifting of different schools of thought, which does not lead to understanding.
As for the reason "because it exists," it is identical to the fallacy of being a non-reason (*ahetu*), because the supporting example lacks an essential nature (*abhāva*).
Thus, that reason fails to apply universally, due to the fault of lacking an example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva-doṣa*).
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
Regarding that which you have established, what meaning do you intend to establish?
Is it that the effect is designated as "self" (sva)?
Is that which is called the "cause" itself?
What fault is there in this?
If you establish the substance of the effect as being "self," then my own tenet (*siddhānta*) is established.
If one posits that the essence of the cause is itself [the effect], it contradicts the meaning, because the essence already exists within the cause.
In this way, all instances of existence arising should be termed "arising."
As for your statement that "it does not arise," is this not indeed the case?
The proponent says:
These words are meaningless.
Do you not know?
Because [arising] from self-nature and arising from other-nature are both refuted by the analysis of the process of origination (*utpādāṅga*), all such positions are negated.
You speak these words due to improper reflection and delusion; thus, there is no fault, only a difference [in perspective].
The commentary states:
No phenomena arise from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because such arising would be purposeless and because it would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, that [position] is untenable.
What is the meaning of this?
Because [the opponent] has failed to state a reason and an example, and because they have been unable to avoid the faults pointed out by others,
this refutation demonstrates the fault of establishing a perversion.
What is this perversion?
This is because it would entail the fault that entities arise from another, the fault that existence-in-becoming (bhava) has a cause, and the fault that existence-in-becoming would be finite;
furthermore, it would contradict the established tenets (siddhānta). Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya might say:
"It is not the case that entities do not arise from themselves."
Why is this? Because that which one intends to produce is, in turn, eliminated by oneself; it is as when it is said that rabbit horns arise within the three realms.

Furthermore, you wish to set aside your own position in this manner, yet the causal relationship I have established is capable of being understood, for there is no difference in their essential nature.
"Just as the self arises from that causal substance as its own resultant dharma, therefore the meaning is established.
The proponent says:
"This is a false conceptualization; it does not accord with reason."
Having first refuted that position, there is thus no fault.
In this way, the essence of these phenomena does not arise from itself;
nor is it the case that they arise from another.
Why is this? Because at no time and in no place does any entity whatsoever arise from another.
What is the meaning of this?
The claim that they arise from other factors is a conventional expression.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the internal sense bases do not arise from those various conditions. Why is this?
Because they are "other," just like a jar and so forth.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), other conditions cannot give rise to the sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as the eye.
Why is this? Because it is other, just as in the case of a sūtra and so forth.
Question:
Your statement regarding "the other" does not establish the logical reason (*hetu*). Why is this so?
Because it is a part of the thesis (*pakṣaikadeśa*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is sound."
The answer is:
You have spoken poorly.
The sound of impermanence is the sound of the Vedas.
Regarding the phrase "because it is a sound," it is like the sound of a drum.
This is because one part of the proposition (*pratijñā*) serves as the reason (*hetu*) for its establishment;
it does not mean that [the reason] is merely one side [of the proposition]. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
With atoms as the cause, the fruits of all phenomena arise.
Taking those two atoms as the beginning, the aggregates of earth, water, fire, and wind successively emerge and form in this manner.
When you speak of "the other," do you mean that it is the quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*) that functions as the cause?
Or do you mean that it is something distinct [from the self]?
If you mean that the quality of the self is the cause, then the status of being a cause is not established.
Why is this? Because there are no distinct qualities (guṇa) apart from the substance of the self (ātman).
If one were to differentiate them based on the principle of their being distinct entities, that position would be refuted by worldly understanding.
The proponent says:
That explanation is incorrect because it speaks of the cause in general; for it is the collection of those factors that can produce another's cognition.
Such a cause of cognition is generally designated as "other," not because there is a conceptual distinction between the self (*ātman*) and the qualities (*guṇa*).
That which is understood by the world is not thereby destroyed, because the propositions established are distinct.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the initial arising of earth-atoms is not called "earth-substance," because they are merely atoms.
It is like a particle of fire.
Thus, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), when a minute particle of fire first arises, it is not called "actual fire," because it is merely a minute particle.
It is like a particle of water.
These points should be explained in this sequence.
Furthermore, the Abhidharmika says:
When you speak of "the other," do you mean that it is called "the other" because its causal capacity is empty?
Is it that he is able to speak non-emptiness for the sake of others?
Both positions entail faults. Why is this so?
If the effect is said to be "other" because its functional capacity is empty, then the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is not established.
If that capacity were not empty, then the dharma which is the capacity would be empty, and thus the analogy would be destroyed.
The proponent says:

Because it refers to the collection of phenomena in general, because it is observed from the perspective of things, and because it gives rise to cognition in others, your claim that the meaning of the reason is unestablished, that the proving property is empty, and that the example is destroyed, does not apply; these are merely like shadows and reflections.
Furthermore, there are those of our own school who say:

"If, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), those internal and external bases (*āyatana*) do not arise at all, then the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not established, and that which serves as their support is destroyed."
Because you incur the fault that the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The proponent says:
Because conventional discourse is real, and because internal and external things such as the jar and the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) are perceivable.
What you have said regarding "that which has passed" is inconsistent.
Furthermore, the master Buddhapālita explains:
"That which is produced by another is also not so."
Why is this? Because it would give rise to errors in all respects.
The commentator says:

If he were to speak in this manner, there would be a perversion between the probandum and the probans; that is, because the fallacy arises that the essence [of the entity] originates from both its own cause and [other causes].
Alternatively, since at some time or in some place a single entity might arise [independently], his previous statement is contradictory.
Furthermore, if it were otherwise, there would be the fallacy that [the effect] arises everywhere at all times.
To claim that this statement can establish the fallacy of arising from another is inconsistent.
As the verse says:
“Cyperus and Pueraria lobata remove heat; the *āmala* fruit dispels fever.
A barren woman has no child; bamboo shoots have a bitter taste.
The hare-mark adorns the moon; in the springtime, one makes merry.”
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The earth and other elements, as seeds, produce sprouts and other fruits, being both distinct and non-distinct from them."
Based on this meaning, it is said that they arise simultaneously as a single entity.
That assertion is incorrect. Why is this?
As for "non-common," it does not mean that it belongs neither to self nor to others; rather, there is never, at no time or place, a single entity that arises from what is common.
Therefore, their explanation is erroneous.
Furthermore, what does this mean?
If it is claimed that [the two] arise simultaneously in order to convince others, this argument fails because the probandum lacks an essential nature (*asvabhāva*).
Moreover, within this context, the doctrine of the Nirgrantha school is also refuted by stating that [the two] do not arise together.
What is the meaning of this?
That [opponent] claims that gold and non-gold, human effort, fire, and so forth—through the power of both self and other—give rise to bracelets, armlets, and the like.
To refute such a claim, it is said that they do not arise independently; this is how it should be understood.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "there is no such thing as causelessness," what does this mean?
It means that at no time and in no place does a single entity arise without a cause.
Why is there no causelessness?
Because it is examined as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
If one asserts that there is such an examination, it is immediately refuted by what is examined and understood in the world;
since this fault exists, what are the characteristics of this worldly examination?
The worldly convention intends for the internal sense bases to be produced as substantial entities.
Why? Because they exist both collectively and individually.
It is, for example, like a sprout and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding what is understood by the world as being "excessive": if such a thing exists in the world, it is known to arise from causes—such as silk produced from thread, a basket made from bamboo strips, or a jar formed from clay—and it is because of that [understanding] that it is considered excessive.
Furthermore, that which is an evil cause is also called "no-cause," just as [the term] "no-wife" and so forth.
What is an evil cause?

It refers to such things as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), the Person (*puruṣa*), the Womb (*yoni*), Time (*kāla*), and Nārāyaṇa; because these are not real, they are no-causes and cannot give rise to an entity.
If it is claimed that [the self-nature] causes understanding by arising from that very self-nature, this is not so, as it can be proven otherwise.
Even if one were to state a proof, that too would be flawed.
Furthermore, those who cling to self-nature say this:
I establish this thesis: those internal sense bases and so forth arise by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why? Because they adorn the self-substance (*ātma-bhāva*).

Just as the roots, filaments, stems, and leaves of water-born flowers possess beautiful colors and forms, like great blue pearls, indranīla, and abhinīla gems, or like the various variegated, radiant, and lovely patterns on the neck of a peacock—all these are such by their very nature.
The proponent says:
That which establishes this doctrine—that there is an agent who acts by way of intrinsic nature—fails to observe that there is no agent apart from the causes and conditions of karma.

If that were so, then the causes and conditions for the arising of the internal sense bases, which are determined by worldly cognition and established through common linguistic convention, would again fall into error.
If it concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the analogy lacks a real entity. Why?
Because within the ultimate truth, lotuses, jewels, and so forth are fundamentally without arising.
Furthermore, you wish to establish with me the doctrine that all phenomena are established through the absence of causes;
I shall now demonstrate to you that because of the absence of causes, nothing at all is established.
Furthermore, they establish the absence of a cause; for if one were to speak of a cause, their prior position would be refuted.

Moreover, if it is argued that because my establishment of the absence of a cause cannot bring understanding to those who assert a cause, one must provide a reason [for this], I shall now explain the absence of a cause.
For example, it is like speaking the language of a barbarian to that very barbarian.
For this reason, one employs skillful means to state the logical reason (*hetu*), yet this is not a refutation of the previous statement.
This argument is incorrect.
Why is this? That which functions at the limit of speech is also like the characteristic that has been attained.
By means of this meaning of the characteristic, one causes others to attain understanding.
To speak as one would to a barbarian: "Where there is smoke, there is fire," this is intended to cause them to understand by giving rise to a cognition of the mark (*liṅga*).
Since the words used here differ from those [used for] them, it does not constitute a valid proof.
Furthermore, there are others among the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas who say:
"The *kalala* and sprouts arise without conditions, whereas jars,
garments, and the like arise because they possess conditions."
Because it does not arise from the intrinsic nature of all entities,
that which I have sought to establish is established.
The proponent says:
Since the arising of all things at all times is entirely negated,
what you have stated is inconsistent with this.
By such reasoning, there is no arising from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, there are outsiders who maintain that Īśvara is the cause, who speak as follows:
"Sentient beings lack wisdom and possess no autonomy regarding suffering and pleasure; both the good and evil realms are entirely under the command of Īśvara."
The proponent says:
He establishes this thesis that Īśvara is the cause of the world's arising;
yet even within the conventional realm, this should not be so.
Why is this? Because there may be causes for sorrow or joy,
as in the case of a cowherd.
If one maintains that Īśvara is the cause of all things who creates the world, this argument is not tenable.
It should be understood thus: because he is an object of cognition, just like Īśvara himself.
Therefore, you should know that even according to that conventional perspective, Īśvara is not capable of independently producing all phenomena.
If you insist that Īśvara is the cause that produces all phenomena, then is this cause and its effect identical in nature?
Is it of the nature of another,
or is it of both natures?
These various conceptual distinctions have already been refuted previously.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of origination, this shall be refuted in detail later.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), Īśvara cannot originate all phenomena.

Some may say that the various karmic causes of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) serve as the basis for Īśvara’s abiding, arising, and destruction, as well as for the increase and decrease of suffering and pleasure.
One who speaks thus establishes what I have established as conventional discourse, not as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
because in the ultimate truth, karma does not arise.
Furthermore, those who maintain that the "Person" (*puruṣa*) is the cause of birth say this:
Because he is the cause for all beings in the world, what is the meaning of this?
It is like threads woven together to form a net, like water emerging from a moonstone, or like a tree producing branches and leaves; in these ways, all sentient beings take him as their cause.
It is likewise so.
That is to say, whether past or future, moving or unmoving, distant or near, internal or external—all such things have the Puruṣa as their cause.
The proponent says:
This view was already refuted previously when the position that Īśvara is the cause was examined;
it shall now be further discussed.
Just as I am not the cause for the aggregate of the body-faculty of Devadatta, why is this?
Because of my [nature].
For example, Yaśodatta’s self, and furthermore,
the collection of Yaśodatta’s body, sense-faculties, and so forth, are not created by Yaśodatta’s self.
Why is this? Because that pleasure and pain arise from the cognition of their causes.

For example, regarding the collection of the sense-faculties such as the body-faculty of Devadatta, if one were to claim that the "bound self" is the cause of the three realms and not the [cognition of] all [causes], this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because, due to the self, just as the self is understood to be liberated, that [proponent's] attachment is not established, as it involves a fault in the thesis (*siddhānta-doṣa*).
Question:

Regarding your statement that "the self" is the reason (*hetu*), since this is merely one part of the thesis (*pakṣa*) you have yourself established, the reason you have put forward fails to prove the point; it is therefore fallacious.
Answer: The meaning of being without fault has already been explained previously.
Why is there no fault?
As stated above, sound is impermanent because it is sound, just like the sound of a drum.

If someone were to say, "The thesis I establish is that there is only one self; just as with the distinctions made regarding space, jars, and so forth, all are merely conventional designations, and because they are conventional designations, they are infinite," [then...]
For this reason, the analogy lacks substance; the refutation by means of proof is not established, because there is no fault in the thesis being set forth.
The proponent says:
that is poorly stated.
What is the meaning of this?
Because space is unarisen, its essence is unobtainable, like a flower in the sky.
To speak in this way, the proposition that "space is one" is not established; it is merely a verbal expression.
In worldly conventions, the general designation of a "self" is intended to indicate a provisional conceptualization for the sake of cognition.
Your attempt to establish a single self to convince others fails because it lacks any essential reality; thus, your thesis is untenable.
Question:
The bound self and the liberated self do not possess distinct natures. Why is this?
If it is because of the self, then it would be like the liberated self.
The response is:
within the realm of nirvana without remainder, a single liberated self does not exist.
As previously stated, this cannot be avoided.
This shall be explained in detail in the "Examination of the Self" (*Ātmaparīkṣā*).
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya says:

According to my established thesis, that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the cause; that is to say, beginning with Brahmā and extending down to the limit of the world's maintenance, the arising of all phenomena as effects is entirely due to intrinsic nature.
Just as those internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) are the determinative causes for suffering, pleasure, and delusion because they possess them;
if worldly objects possess them, I know them to be the cause.
Just as with sandalwood chips, shards of pottery, or gold ornaments— due to such general and specific causes—
the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) are said to be the causes of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because those internal sense bases possess pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Thus it should be understood that the aggregates of form, perception, mental formations, and consciousness all have pleasure, suffering, and delusion as their intrinsic nature. Why?
Because they are aggregates.
It is, for example, like the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Therefore, both the logical reason (*hetu*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are established.
The proponent says:
For this reason, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the analogies such as sandalwood are not established because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), because [the self] is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) by the deluded, the analogy is not established.
Those two—pleasure and suffering—are distinct from external phenomena and do not have the intrinsic nature of pleasure and suffering; this is how they should be understood.
Why? Because they are objects of cognition.
For example, it is like a cognition that does not correspond to its object of verification.
The opponent asks:
"In your ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no illustrative example."
Answer: Because it refers to awakening in general, the world commonly understands and takes it as a metaphor; furthermore, a metaphor is not something that lacks an essence.
For this reason, those elements (dhātus) do not serve as the cause for the Great Truths and so forth, because they are not understood [as such].
For example, O Great Being, if you wish to assert that "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) is the cause, it is refuted by its own logical test. The opponent says:

"I establish that the 'Great Being' (*puruṣa*) is associated with cognition (*cetanā*), whereby it becomes manifest; therefore, your statement that it is due to a lack of manifestation is an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*). Furthermore, because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is not present [in the subject], and because there is a fault in the analogy (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*)."
The proponent says:
That statement is meaningless. How so?
Because this is a general statement of causes and establishes specific meanings, it remains unintelligible in various places, and as a whole, it does not hold. Furthermore,

regarding those who claim that phenomena do not arise without a cause, but rather that their nature (*svabhāva*), time (*kāla*), or Nārāyaṇa serve as the cause— this should be understood as already explained in the refutation of Īśvara.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
You state that [an entity] does not arise from itself, from another, from both, or without a cause;
yet you claim that there is a locus and a substance capable of producing a single thing. While it is true as you say that such a thing does not actually arise, [your argument fails].
Although in reality there is no arising, it is so because of the understanding of its activity.
The proponent asks:
"What kind of thing is this?"
What is meant by "manifesting through action"?
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:
it is like a lamp [revealing] a jar and so forth.
The proponent says: Since the two things—the lamp and the jar—have from the very beginning never arisen, how can one seek to perceive them by means of a lamp that has not arisen?
Just as with a non-arisen jar or the like, which is like a horse's horn, how could it possibly be perceived?
Since all phenomena are unarisen in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), this question is posed based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*): "What function does that lamp perform with respect to the jar?
The opponent says:
"It performs the function of receiving [the light]."
The proponent says:
Feeling did not exist previously and only comes into being later.
Since it was non-existent before and exists afterward, feeling is itself a conditioned production.

If it is argued that visual consciousness in the dark is devoid of sensation at that time because the obstruction of darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp, this has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, since this is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), is the dispelling of the obstruction of darkness not itself a conditioned action?
If you maintain that perception exists prior to seeing,
then if it already exists, what further use is there for a lamp?
Furthermore, what is meant by the term "vase"?
In my teaching, the combination of the four great elements and their derivatives is called a "vase.
When that lamp exists, it arises simultaneously with its illumination.
For this reason, within the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are causes of production; each individual entity arises from its own cause through a continuous succession.
Why is this so? For example, just as light arises simultaneously with an object, it serves as its efficient cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena that arise are non-existent, and there is likewise no cessation; for things that are not themselves understood—such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and other such truths—cannot cause another thing to be understood.
Why is this? Because it is due to a lack of understanding, like a flower in the sky.
Therefore, your statement that "that which is not yet understood is being understood" is incorrect.
Furthermore, the master Buddhapālita explains this passage as follows:
"Nor does that entity arise without a cause. Why is this?"
If there were no cause, then everything would constantly arise from all places and from all things.
Such a fault would follow; therefore, this position is not tenable. Why is this so?
The meaning of these words of yours clearly contradicts what is to be established and that which establishes it. How so?

Because those entities arise from causes, or because an entity arises at a certain time, or because a single entity arises in a certain place, there is an initial arising; thus, this contradicts your previous statement.
Such an incongruity has already been refuted previously.
If there were any other sense of incongruity, it would likewise be as explained before.
Furthermore, in this context, nothing arises without a cause, for no treatise whatsoever asserts such a thing.
There is no time or place—whether within one's own school or another school—in which a single thing, whether defiled or pure, arises without a cause.

This should be stated for each case accordingly; for this reason, the meaning of dependent origination as distinct from non-arising is established, such that it is not shared with the non-Buddhists and others.
Furthermore, the Abhidharmikas say:
"There are four kinds of conditions that can give rise to all phenomena.
How can you say that dependent origination does not arise?"
As it is said of me,
the verse states:
"Conditioned cause (hetu-pratyaya) and object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), Successive condition (anantara-pratyaya) and dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)."
"All phenomena arise from four conditions; there is no fifth condition.
The commentary states:

"The causal condition" refers to the five types of causes: the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to all phenomena (*dharma*).
The immediate-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), with the exception of the final mind and mental factors arising in an Arhat.
The dominant-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Regarding the absence of a fifth [condition]: whether within one's own school or another school, whether among gods or humans, whether in the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, or other treatises, the Buddha has never taught that there exists a fifth condition.
Furthermore, as the Mahāsāṃghika school also states: "The various conditions, such as 'prior non-existence' (prāg-abhāva) and so forth, are all subsumed within the four conditions.
For this reason, these four kinds of conditions are able to produce all phenomena."
As for your statement that the substance of things does not arise from others, this meaning is not tenable.
The author of the treatise says in verse:
"All entities whatsoever, as well as external conditions,"
"Speech, sounds, and so forth—these all lack intrinsic nature.
The commentary states:
"The various entities" refers to those such as the eye and so on.
"External conditions" refers to the *kalala* and so forth.
"The sound of speech" refers to the time of their conjunction.
"Lacking intrinsic nature" negates their own essence.
What is the meaning of this?
Those various entities and so forth all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor do they exist in another place or by means of an *īśvara* (Lord) and the like.
Therefore, it is said that "those others lack substance."
Furthermore, as for what constitutes its own-nature (svabhāva) while asserting that the various conditions constitute an other-nature (parabhāva) which exists—
this has already been refuted through logical proof in the previous discussion on the meaning of non-arising.
For this reason, you are unable to refute my position herein.
Furthermore, there are those who, through their own minds' false conceptualization, speak as follows:
"If there is that which can give rise to the essence of phenomena, it is said to be 'arisen from another,' and not from its own essence."
If there were no other conditions, then [a phenomenon] could not arise.
Because there are other conditions, all phenomena attain their arising; this is because conditions are determinate.
My interpretation of this is incorrect.
Why is this? If one speaks thus to negate self-arising, it serves to support my own position.
However, if one claims that when various entities have not yet arisen, another can cause them to arise, such a statement is untenable, for it is subject to the same refutation as before.
Furthermore, if it is said that the essence does not arise from another, thereby precluding the possibility of its arising from something distinct external to that essence, this supports my analogy.
For this reason, within the conditions of the red and white [semen and blood], there is no eye or other faculties, because the phenomenon of the eye is empty within the assembly of conditions.
Why is this so? Because the various conditions lack intrinsic nature, as they themselves lack "otherness.

Furthermore, there are two types of discourse here: from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), those sense-bases such as the eye do not arise from the conditions of the red and white [semen and blood].
Why is this? Because the eye and so forth do not exist,
just like a jar.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the various conditions such as the red and white [semen and blood] lack the functional capacity to produce the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and so forth. Why is this?
Because that eye is empty (*śūnya*).
It is like a weaving knife.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), causes and various conditions cannot produce the eye. One should understand it thus:

out of compassion for those in the world who dwell in confused wisdom and engage in disputes regarding non-causation or false causes, the Buddha, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), spoke of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
For this reason, my thesis is not undermined; it should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, there are others who differentiate by asserting that the essence arises from another.
The proponent says: they share this same [fallacy] here.
Furthermore, one should reflect: among these four conditions, how can they give rise to the various entities such as the eye?
Moreover, what are their distinct names and differences, as distinguished by the Mahāsāṃghika, the Vaiśeṣika, and others?
Are those [other conditions] also subsumed within this by way of their respective characteristics?
Therefore, it is certain that there is no fifth condition.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is not appropriate for the eye and so forth, nor for anything else, to function in such a manner.
Why is this not so? As the verse says:
"The self and other such entities, The internal sense bases and various conditions—"
"Each and every one does not exist, because they lack intrinsic nature.
The commentary states:
Whether considered collectively or individually among the various conditions, the essence of those [factors] such as the eye is entirely unapprehendable.
These sounds do not exist within their individual causes, nor do they exist within their combination, nor do they exist elsewhere.

Whether from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) or ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there has never been a time when an entity possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arose first, nor has there ever been an entity devoid of intrinsic nature.
All conditions that depend on another entity arise in the future.
How can these various meanings of "other" be established?
They cannot, because there is absolutely no "other," as the cause of "otherness" lacks any intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, if you arbitrarily posit that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which will arise in the future because it depends upon this nature,
then your claim that "a condition is other" by virtue of the power of mutual dependence is merely empty words.
Why is this? Because those various conditions lack any other-nature (*parabhāva*), one should not conceive attachment toward them.

While "other" is conventionally designated within the realm of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) such an "other" does not arise, as has already been explained previously.
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:

According to my view, there exists a subtle essence of the self (*ātman*); at a later time, that [essence] causes [the effect] to become manifest. Thus, by taking the non-manifestation of the effect as the condition for another [state], it is established.
"How can you refute it?
The proponent replies:
"Your statement is incorrect."
The foolish people of the world do not understand this; it is difficult to establish the meaning of a subtle self within jars and other such objects.
As for what you say regarding "cognition," that has already been refuted.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle One.
2. *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Two.
Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāvarman of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Chapter on the Examination of Conditions (Pratyaya-parīkṣā), Part Two. Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
If the capacity for the various effects is absent within the conditions, then the conditions do not produce an effect.
Such a proposition establishes what I have already established. Why is this?
If you claim that the essence of the effect does not arise, then it would be permanent; thus, your initial thesis is self-contradictory.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect.
Because it is entirely precluded from arising at all times.
Furthermore, that which does not arise is not said to be permanent. Why is this?
Because things that do not arise are not intended to exist even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas speak as follows:

"Although those various conditions cannot produce an effect, consciousness arises because there is activity among the conditions—namely, the eye, form, space, light, and attention; therefore, we maintain that there must be arising and activity."
I shall now explain that activity and arising.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there exists the activity of that consciousness which produces its own fruit as it arises. Why is this?
Because there are conditions.
For example, when the various conditions—such as water, rice, fire, and fuel—are assembled and brought together with a concentrated mind, they are able to produce cooked rice.
By this evidence, my thesis is established.
The proponent states in verse:
"Within conditions, there is no agent.
The commentary explains:
I do not intend for that which is ultimately real (paramārtha) to act as the agent that cooks rice, because it is devoid of activity;
thus, your analogy is invalid. Since the analogy is invalid, you are at fault.
Why is this? Because the factors that could establish it do not exist.
Since there is no establishment, there is certainly no activity of consciousness arising within the conditions.
Whether [the effect] exists or does not exist, it does not arise; this shall be refuted later.
Since the agent does not arise, the meaning of "cause" is not established.
This should be stated thus in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, if you maintain that the agent is spoken of in a general sense, it contradicts the meaning.
That which depends on conditions is the object of worldly cognition; the activity of producing consciousness is inseparable from the essence of those various conditions.
In the *Buddhapālita-vyākhyā*, there is another opponent who offers this explanation:
"What is the meaning of these statements regarding 'arising from self' or 'arising from another'?
This point is of no use to me."
Although the conditions such as the eye give rise to visual consciousness— just as a potter and other factors bring about the cooking of rice—
the opponent establishes this by asserting that there is an entity that arises.
In order to refute that [position], the Master Buddhapālita cites the root verse, saying:
"The agent does not exist within the conditions. Why is this?
That consciousness has an agent during its past arising, its future arising, or its present arising—this too is not so.
The proponent says:
those [positions] are inconsistent.
"Your two statements, the former and the latter, merely establish a thesis (*pratijñā*).
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya says:

'You have attributed this fault to me to refute my position that there is no sense of "action" (*kriyā*) within the causal conditions (*pratyaya*), on the grounds that action does not arise; thus, your analogy is invalid. This argument is not correct."
There exists a present activity.
How is this known through inference?
Because activity produces its own results, such as consciousness and so forth, by virtue of that activity; it is like the activity that can cook rice.
The proponent states in verse:
"Apart from conditions, there is no action.
The commentary explains:
Because conditions do not exist, there is no agent that exists independently without being conjoined with conditions.
This is because, as previously stated, the faults of an agent existing within the conditions have been explained in succession.
Furthermore, there is a master of treatises who explains this verse as follows:
"The very arising of the nature of consciousness is itself the act.
The proponent says:
As stated in the preceding verse, there is no agent within conditions, nor is there an agent apart from conditions.
If one were to claim that there exists an agent that produces consciousness, this meaning is not tenable.
Why is this? Just as consciousness does not exist, its agent likewise does not exist.
If one were to say that there is no separate agent, but that this very [consciousness] is the agent by virtue of being the condition, that too is not correct.
If it is argued that while the conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the action (*kriyā*) possesses intrinsic nature, the master Buddhapālita states:
"In that case as well, there would be the fault of [the action] existing without conditions.
The proponent says:
If it is claimed that an agent can exist without conditions, this meaning is not tenable. Why?
Because if action were to exist spontaneously without those conditions, such a principle does not obtain.
Buddhapālita says:
How can there be "action" within the conventional truth?
Because self, other, and various conditions depend upon one another, action exists; for instance, when a subsequent moment can produce the essence of an effect, this is called "action."

Just as the nature of those dharmas that are about to arise in the future is produced through activity within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and it is not the case that there is no such activity—unlike your own position which asserts that activity exists within the conditions—this statement is without fault.
The proponent says:
"If you now fail to state reasons, causes, and similes, but merely establish a thesis and attribute faults to another, this explanation is not established.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
There are other phenomena that arise, such as visual consciousness and so forth.
Why is this? Because they are produced through volitional activity.
For example, when the conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind combine with a seed, a sprout emerges.
Since this is the answer, your previous proof has been refuted.
The proponent says:
As stated in the preceding verse, there is no activity within conditions.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), their arising is negated.
That agent is without intrinsic nature; it is not tenable that an agent exists through the conjunction of conditions such as seeds and so forth.
Your claim that an agent definitely exists within the conditions is unestablished, because there is no supporting example.
What you previously replied was unable to refute me.
Furthermore, an opponent says:
"Just as rice seeds and the like truly exist."
Why is this? Because of the existence of volitional action (*abhisaṃskāra*).
Within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one wishes to conform to conventional truth in accordance with what is desired.
It is likewise in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), just like the horns of a rabbit.
Since the meaning is established by means of this analogy, the intended point is proven.
The proponent says:

If you establish the meaning of "action" in this way—claiming that there is an agent within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), as in the case of rice seeds and so forth—this is not correct. Why is that?
As the verse says:
"Whether existence or non-existence acts, / The action of conditions is not established.
The commentary states:
Since a rabbit’s horn does not exist within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), its existence is likewise not established in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The same applies to "action" (*kriyā*), as it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for your claim that your desired thesis is established because it is proven by analogy, these two faults you have identified instead revert back to you.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The non-existence of a rabbit's horn is itself its essence.
How is this known?"
As it is stated in the sixth chapter of the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra: "Because there is a distinction;
for example, the blue utpala lotus is distinct from its color."
The proponent says:
What you have said is incorrect. Why is this so?
Regarding the distinct substantial entities of the flower and its color and so forth, these are all unestablished within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because there is no supporting analogy.
If you think that, just as I establish the existence of the substance of form and so forth, I am unable to cause you to understand [this point].
In this way, your establishment that form and so forth lack intrinsic nature cannot lead me to understanding, because you and I share the same fault.
Now I shall answer you: there is no such shared fault.

Why is this? Since the existence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in produced phenomena has already been refuted in this manner, how much more so should the existence of an intrinsic nature in that which is unproduced be refuted?
Whether there is an intrinsic nature or no intrinsic nature is merely what you intend to demonstrate as a distinct characteristic.
I now refute your interpretation that existence and non-existence fall into the two extremes.
Since I do not adhere to the views of existence or non-existence as you do, I do not fall into these two extremes.
What is the meaning of this?
You establish the existence and non-existence of an entity in order to cause others to accept it; however, because you provide no proof for its non-existence, this is not what I intend.
Therefore, since your position is illogical, my thesis is established.
As for your claim that we share the same fault, this too is incorrect.
Furthermore, regarding those who assert that things arise, one should ask this:
before the effect has arisen, do those conditions and so forth lack causal efficacy?
Is there an agent?
If the various conditions are without agency and cannot produce a fruit, how can they be called "producing a fruit without agency"?
Because their functional capacity is empty within the conditions, they are said to be "without agency."
If functional capacity were empty, then that [cause] would not be the condition for, nor could it give rise to, that fruit.
For example, a barley seed does not produce a rice sprout; this [case you propose] should not be so.
If there were an agent, one could verify the existence of this agency;
however, since it does not exist within the conditions (*pratyaya*), and because an effect arises [only when those conditions are met], we speak of "agency" in that regard.
When the effect has not yet arisen, that agent performs no action.
Based on this evidence, the meaning of "cause" is not established.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
"When that fruit arises, the various conditions perform an action."
For this reason, they mutually support and encompass one another, and the arising of the fruit is thereby sustained.
It is not that the cause fails to establish itself; thus, the response and the proof are also established.
The proponent says:
You Sautrāntika masters, do you intend to maintain that, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), an effect arises from the gathering and aggregation of conditions such as grain?
If this were indeed the case, then these causes and conditions would remain [ineffective] until the fruit had actually arisen.
Prior to this point, why would these rice grains and so forth not be called "non-conditions"?
Such a thing is impossible.
Because they function as conditions in this way—for example, until one has received instruction from another, why would one not be called an "ignorant person"?
This argument is not established.
It is asked:
If this were so, then before the fruit has arisen, the various conditions would not be conditions.
"I intended it thus, therefore there is no fault.
He replied,
"You are greatly at fault."

Why is this? Your mind understands only that before the fruit has arisen, the various conditions are not conditions; yet you do not realize that at the very moment the fruit arises, those conditions are likewise not conditions.
For this reason, why is it that when the sprout arises, those rice seeds and so forth are not its causal conditions by their own nature?
Because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they cannot be described as being either identical or different.

If it is asserted that at the moment prior to those grains and so forth, there exists no entity arising from itself, from another, or from both, then this establishes exactly what I have set out to prove.
Why is this? Because the two dharmas of cause and effect cannot be said to be either identical or different.
Although they cannot be so described, it is nonetheless necessary to depend upon those conditions for an effect to be able to arise.
To speak in this manner is likewise refuted by the same arguments as before; that is to say, how could a sprout arise, even down to the moment immediately preceding its birth?
Furthermore, regarding those who claim there is arising, they say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), those conditions such as the sense-bases (*āyatana*) are able to give rise to the internal bases."
Why is this? Because it is a condition, like a sprout from grain and so forth.
If something cannot arise, it is not a condition, just as, for example, a rabbit's horn.
The proponent says:
According to what you have stated, regarding that which exists as a condition within the ultimate sense, does this condition exist, not exist, or both exist and not exist with respect to its effect?
In all cases, it should not be so.
As the verse says:
"It is neither definitively existent nor definitively non-existent; such is the meaning of all conditions."
The commentary states:
This condition does not exist.
Since it cannot be as it is grasped, this meaning shall now be demonstrated.
Regarding the verse’s statement that “conditions are non-existent,” what does this mean?
What is this non-existence like, being comparable to flowers in the sky and so forth?
It can be understood by means of the *māyā* (illusion) analogy.
In this way, since that [object] does not exist as even a single thing, is it a condition for a flower in the sky or for a rabbit’s horn?
Regarding this explanation that there is no such condition, what is the meaning of these words?
This examination of the conditions for rice grains and so forth shows that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why?
Because the effect does not exist.

Just as flowers in the sky do not exist and space has no substantial entity, so too the sprout and other such things do not exist, because conditions such as rice seeds and so forth do not exist, being like flowers in the sky.
Someone may say:
"I do not wish for that existent phenomenon (*bhāva*) to arise; rather, I wish for that phenomenon which is capable of arising to arise, because it previously lacked an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The proponent replies:
When you say that conditions do not exist, what do you mean by that?
For instance, in the case of things such as a jar, before they have arisen, they possess no substantial nature or characteristics.
Since they lack an intrinsic nature, what further conditions could there be for those jars, garments, rice grains, and so forth, which would cause the phenomena intended to arise to actually arise?
In this way, there would be no single condition.
One should understand this meaning: from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), rice seeds and the like are not conditions for sprouts and the like. Why is this?
Because that which has not yet arisen lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), like a jar or other such objects.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon already exists, conditions would be useless. Why is this?
Because they possess intrinsic nature.
Thus, within the context of conventional truth, those rice seeds and so forth are likewise not conditions for the sprouts and so forth. Why is this?
Because it does not observe [the cause] as being produced, just like a sprout that has already arisen, or other things such as a jar or a garment.
By this proof, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is not established.
The Sāṃkhya says:
Substantial entities exist and are produced by depending upon conditions.
At times, a subtle effect already exists within the conditions; subsequently, it awaits those conditions, which cause the subtle to become coarse.
Your claim that since [the effect] already exists, what use are conditions, is incorrect.
The proponent says:
That which understands the agent has already been refuted.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence from the subtle to the coarse, whether it be existent or non-existent, the faults previously mentioned apply; thus, your statement is incorrect.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
In reality, all conditions are neither existent nor non-existent.
To speak of them as being either existent or non-existent is logically incorrect.
What, then, does this mean?

It means that within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), when an effect arises and manifests, the various conditions (*pratyaya*) harmonize, mutually supporting and encompassing one another so as to attain their own intrinsic nature, because these conditions exist.
At that time, that fruit cannot be said to be non-existent because it arises;
nor can it be said to be existent because it has not yet manifested.
Desiring it to be thus through these causes and conditions, there is no fault as previously stated.
The proponent says:
This too is merely one's own conceptual construction.
Whether there is existence or non-existence, such should be the meaning of conditions.
Because both existence and non-existence are absent in two ways, neither can be predicated.
For example, as with other things, whether they exist or do not exist, both are not conditions.
This is the intention of the proponent.
Furthermore, in this context, it is simply that both existence and non-existence are inexpressible. Why is this so?
Because it exists and because it does not exist, and because it is not non-existent.
Such a thing is a "non-thing.
That is to say, whether it be visual consciousness or a sprout, its conditions—namely the eye and so forth, or the various seeds and so forth—cannot be said to be real.
Why is this? Because those fruits cannot be described as either existent or non-existent, just like other things;
thus, the Sautrāntikas cannot avoid this fault.
Furthermore, the self-nature of existence is empty in its essence, for the meaning of "arising" is established within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Again, there are those who speak of both [existence and non-existence], namely the Nirgranthas, who say:
"That fruit is both existent and non-existent, because it arises through conditions."
It is my intention that this be so; therefore, the aforementioned faults do not apply.
The proponent says:
As for those Nirgranthas and others who employ the expedient means of speaking of both existence and non-existence, this is not a secure position, and their thesis is unestablished.
Thus, having already explained the general refutation of all conditions, we shall now provide a specific refutation.
Herein, because one observes conditions in their totality: if something can produce a distinct condition, it is called a cause.
In this way, phenomena arise from a combination produced by mastery; it is not that a single factor can produce them, and furthermore, because such production is negated.
I intend it thus, establishing the meaning of "cause" within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one should speak thus because causes are not causes.
If you think that this cause—whether it be an existent thing, a non-existent thing, or both existent and non-existent—is able to produce an effect, this is not the case.
The verse says:
"Neither existent nor non-existent, / Neither existent nor non-existent, phenomena arise.
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are thus; how can it be said that causes are able to produce?
Therefore, they are not causes.
Likewise, those [causes] cannot produce, whether [the effect] exists or does not exist.
Just as the cases of self and other have already been refuted through examination,
