if both existence and non-existence were present, there would be two faults. Therefore,
the nature of the reason is not established.
If it is argued that the arising of produced phenomena must be explained by means of causes, this is also not the case.
This is because [characteristics] such as "existence" do not arise.
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is an effect due to a cause; the cause is likewise so, because the arising of the effect is established.
Furthermore, the proponents of our own school say:
There exists a cause capable of giving rise to those internal sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth; this meaning of dependent origination was taught by the Tathāgata.
Just as it was taught by the Tathāgata, it cannot be altered, just like the quiescent state of *nirvāṇa*.
This "ability to cause arising" is the meaning of the condition as cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That which is the object of mind and mental factors is the meaning of the condition as object (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Those mind and mental factors that have just ceased—excluding the final mind of an Arhat—is the meaning of the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
If this dharma exists, that dharma arises; this constitutes the meaning of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because it was taught by the Buddha, the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth serve as the very essence of conditions.
As for your statement that [the reason] does not exist, this reason is unestablished because it contradicts your own thesis.
The proponent says:
Your proposed thesis may be so in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because the analogy is flawed, what you have said is not correct.
How do you establish the meaning of this reason?
Is it that the Buddha spoke thus within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
Is this spoken by the Buddha from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
If it is spoken thus from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), your own position is undermined.

If it is spoken thus from the perspective of the ultimate truth, then in that ultimate truth, there is neither existence nor non-existence, because no phenomenon arises as either existent or non-existent.

Since that which exists, that which does not exist, and that which both exists and does not exist lack an intrinsic nature as an effect, and because conditions cannot be apprehended, causes are unable to produce them.
If this is so, how can you definitively claim that those causes are able to produce them?
For this reason, your logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is contradictory (*viruddha*).
Furthermore, some say:
"The means of negation is accepted."
This *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* elucidates that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
That phenomena lack intrinsic nature is because both [aspects] are negated.
The "two" refers to the designator (*nāman*) and the designated (*abhidheya*).
That which is designated has already been refuted as previously explained.
Now, the designation itself shall be successively negated.
To state the meaning in general: it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent, and so forth.

Worldly people all desire that an effect arises from a cause; yet, whether that cause exists, does not exist, or both exists and does not exist, it is in every case impossible for an effect to arise through its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is only because the verbal designation "cause" is applied that one cognizes the substance of that cause.
Because of such causes, they are not associated.
Or, as some say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is the arising of various entities."
Why is this? Regarding the claim that "there is a cause," as previously explained in its refutation, that cause is not established.
Furthermore, another proponent of a divergent theory says:

Whether it be existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent, because it does not arise from its own essence, it does not possess the characteristic of a cause; thus, the meaning of "cause" is not established.
To explain it in this way is incorrect.
Furthermore, we shall now examine the meaning of that object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for its nature as an object-condition, it is likewise not like those conceptual constructions and discriminations.
As the verse says:
“The Dharma taught by the Bhagavat Is the reality of the dharma that is without conditions;
Since the essence of this dharma is thus, Where could there be an object-condition?”
The commentary states:
Those visual consciousnesses and so forth are not called "conditions. Why is this?

Because there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is merely the false conceptualization of one's own mind; in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the arising of that phenomenon is negated.
Even when it seeks to arise, it is not a capable object-condition.
Why is this? Because they arise from desire, just like material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

For this reason, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has no intrinsic nature; it is only within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that the eye and so forth are established as "dharmas" by virtue of their mutual support through causal characteristics.
Just as consciousness arises only after depending upon light, it is therefore called an "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya), unlike the case where wealth and its owner exist simultaneously.
If that were so, there would be no dharma capable of being the object of cognition.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the consciousness that acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka*) is not established; for just as the perceived object (*ālambana*) does not exist, the perceiver likewise does not exist, because the perceived object is a non-entity.
The meaning is as follows:
For example, one who commits the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) never perceives the Truths; therefore, that cause is not established, and it also contradicts the meaning of conditions (pratyaya).
Furthermore, another person said:
"If that which is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) cannot take form as its object, this principle is consistent.
The masters of various schools (nikāya-ācāryas) also speak thus:
What are the phenomena that lack an object of perception?
They are form (*rūpa*) and nirvāṇa.
If you intend that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) lack an object of perception, then what you previously asserted is self-contradicted.
What are the dharmas that possess an object?
They are the mind and mental factors.
The commentator says:
Your words are unskillful; the analogy I have established is now even more evident.
The opponent says:
"The mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) necessarily possess an object of perception (ālambana), unlike derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), because [otherwise] there would be no analogy."
Furthermore, that which is grasped serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*).
The proponent says:
as for that [notion] that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have something grasped, this shall be further refuted later.
As it is taught according to the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), I do not intend for consciousness to possess the capacity to cognize.
As the Buddha said:
"Furthermore, O Valiant Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!"
One should practice in this manner: form is not an object of perception.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack objects of perception; there is not even the slightest dharma that can be grasped.
If that is graspable, then this is the object of perception.
Thus, O valiant one!
One does not practice form within form, nor even practice consciousness within consciousness.
"O Courageous One!
Because all dharmas do not proceed, they are not seen by form (*rūpa*), nor are they seen by consciousness (*vijñāna*); even up to being neither known by consciousness nor visible.
If from form through to consciousness they are neither known nor seen, this is called the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The examination of the object-condition is complete.
Furthermore, regarding the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as you have analyzed it, one should carefully examine its characteristics:
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all categories and all phenomena are negated as having no arising, for this reason.
As the verse says:
"If phenomena do not arise, their cessation is not tenable;
if phenomena have already ceased, they are not conditions. What, then, could their sequence be?"
The commentary states:
What is the meaning of this?
It is because there is no arising.
Just as a second head cannot be said to perish, so too,
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the concept of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is untenable.
Thus, that position is not established, because it is contradictory.

Regarding that explanation: if you wish to establish that these successively extinguished minds and mental factors constitute the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*), this is not tenable. Why is this so?
Because that substance has ceased, it is like consciousness that has long since ceased.
It is also like material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), because [the mind] is not their condition (*pratyaya*).
When these mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are about to arise, since that object has ceased, what can serve as their condition?
Because it is not this condition, and because that which has ceased and the dharma about to arise cannot be mutually encompassed; the meaning is as follows:
it is neither an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor a universal condition (*sarvatraga-pratyaya*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because such a mind arises due to specific determinative causes and conditions, each existing in its own place to bring about the entity [of the mind], because it provides benefit when the object of desire ceases, and because the subsequent past moments form a continuous sequence that constitutes the condition of immediate contiguity (*samanantarapratyaya*), this argument is incorrect.
Because non-material phenomena have no place of abiding, the six consciousnesses cease in succession; this is called the "mind" (manas).
Thus, to claim that the ceasing mind serves as the immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is not free from logical error.
If you intend for that which is about to cease to be the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), your establishment of this condition is merely words. Why?
Because being simultaneous, it cannot be an immediately preceding condition.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "the dharma that has ceased is not a condition" and the question of its sequence, another interpretation states:
the word "and" (*ca*) here should be understood as including "results that have not yet arisen."
What is the meaning of this?

Since both that cessation and the unarisen seed, sprout, and so forth lack any intrinsic nature, they are both without cause; thus, the two cases of the cessation and arising of the seed and sprout fall into this error.
The proponent says:

He establishes this thesis, namely that "cessation" lacks both intrinsic nature and duration; yet one must still conceptualize its arising and its activity. Because it would lack a cause, both cessation and arising incur such faults.
This statement is not incorrect, for it is free from fault; the relationship between the probandum and the probans is clearly established.
Since this is merely a reversal [of conventional order], what fault could there be?
Now an argument shall be established: that cessation is not conditioned. Why?
Because it exists due to causes, just like the unceased collection of mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, the claim that things arise without cause is inconsistent with the existence of causes;
these two statements are incompatible.
What is the meaning of this?
If [the cause] is stated first, the meaning is not established;
if it is stated later, it contradicts one's own position.
This is because the arising of all phenomena has been refuted, and this verse likewise refutes the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*).
He incurs two faults: namely, the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha-hetu*) and the fault of contradicting one's own position (*svārtha-viruddha*).
Having thus analyzed the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), what, furthermore, is the characteristic of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
If these dharmas exist, then because those dharmas arise, they are called dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Such is your position.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), conditioned dharmas do not arise; rather, they cause others to understand that all dharmas are like illusions, for their own-being is fundamentally empty and unapprehendable.
As the verse says:
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature, because their own characteristics do not exist.
The commentary states:

For this reason, within the Mahāyāna itself, it is not only in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) that all phenomena lack arising; even in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), it is impossible for an effect to arise from a cause.
The verse says:
"That this exists when that dharma arises—this meaning is not so.
The commentary says:
For this reason, you cannot avoid the fault of that [logical] cause.

Furthermore, the Blessed Buddha, through his non-conceptual wisdom, skillfully establishes and teaches those in the world who do not believe in the profound Dharma; for the sake of providing them with consolation, he extols in various ways the supreme merits of nirvana, such as its tranquility and cessation.
Because these are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), they are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Within the ultimate truth, since that nirvana and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), the analogy lacks substance and the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.

Should there be those who wish to maintain that, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because they are like the quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), these individuals are subject to the same faults as previously mentioned regarding the analogies. By explaining the various defects such as impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth, one censures conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in order to prevent attachment to them and to lead such persons toward the truth.
For them, he explains the merits of the quiescence of nirvāṇa;
because it is subsumed within conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), he says that it has an essence.
However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it truly lacks any essence.
Your intended meaning cannot be established because it is logically untenable.
Having thus refuted these various conditions,
another opponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there exist conditions that can give rise to the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) such as the eye. Why is this?
Because their effects arise, just like the sprouts of grain and so forth.
If it were non-existent, the effect could not arise, just as, for example, tortoise hair cannot be made into clothing.
The proponent says:
When you say it exists, do you mean that the self-nature of the effect exists within each individual condition?
Does the self-nature of the fruit exist through the conjunction of various conditions,
or does it not exist even within each individual condition when they are not conjoined?
One should inquire in this manner.
The opponent says:
"Why do you ask this question?
The proponent replies:
If [the effect] exists, it has already been refuted as before; if the effect exists, what further use are conditions?
If it does not exist, that too has already been refuted; if the effect does not exist, what further use are conditions?
As a verse says:
"Neither individually nor in combination do effects exist within the various conditions;
if they are thus not conditions, how could an effect arise?"
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), such and such effects and so forth do not arise, because they do not exist within their conditions; this is the meaning.
It is like there being no curd in clay, from which curd cannot be produced, because it is not the cause.
If the essence of the sprout were not present within the rice seed and so forth, it could arise in this way;
however, this is so from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), because it accords with the views of the wisdom of ordinary beings.
To claim that the internal sense bases, such as the eye, arise within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is incorrect.
As the verse says:
"If the effect does not exist within the conditions, yet that effect arises from those conditions;
And it likewise does not exist outside the conditions, how could the effect not arise?"
The commentary states:
He speaks thus because faults would arise.
Just as there is no effect in that which is not a condition, there is likewise none among the conditions.
For example, that sound is impermanent because it is produced.
For what reason would a jar, being produced, not be impermanent?
As has already been stated previously, sound is impermanent.
Why is this? Because it is produced, just like a jar;
this meaning should be understood.

If, by this expedient means, sprouts and so forth were to manifest as empty within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) while arising from seeds and so forth, then the nature of those sprouts and so forth would not be as it is. Why is this?
Because it is an effect, it is like curd;
therefore, it does not exist, because one cannot avoid the faults previously stated.
Furthermore, some say:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), those internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) exist; I accept this because their conditions evolve and change, just as clay becomes a jar.
The commentator’s verse says:
"The conditions and the intrinsic nature of the fruit."
The commentary states:
This means that it is because those conditions undergo transformation.
The verse says:
"Conditions have no intrinsic nature.
The commentary states:
This means that conditions lack self-nature; such is the meaning of the verse.
For example, when clarified butter is transformed into the mind of a Brahmin, its own substance cannot be apprehended as an object, as has already been explained.
The verse says:
"If that which is conditioned lacks intrinsic nature, How can it be transformed into a result?"
The commentary states:
This clarifies that, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the causal condition does not transform into the essence of its effect; such is the meaning of the verse.
For example, if Devadatta is a youth practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), how could he be the son of Yajñadatta?
Furthermore, it is like a magician who creates a lump of clay; that lump is empty of intrinsic nature, yet it can produce jars and other objects through transformation.
Such a process cannot be believed by any omniscient one within the context of conventional truth (saṃvṛti); therefore, conditions do not transform into effects.
Thus, these analogies lack substance, because the phenomena of the "proven" (sādhya) and the "prover" (sādhana) do not exist.
As previously stated, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, and there is also the fault of contradiction.
The opponent says:
If that which takes itself as its object does not function as a result, then the object-entity may be absent while the result is not lost, because it does not obstruct the self-entity of the result.
According to my established thesis, the internal sense-bases exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because it is an effect, just like a sprout and so forth.
The author of the treatise says in verse:
“There is no fruit without an object.
The commentary states:

That there could be a transformation resulting in a fruit without an object cannot even be believed within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), let alone be credible within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
This argument is not established.
The opponent says:
If, in the ultimate sense, the nature of a condition were empty, then that which is not a condition would have a non-empty intrinsic nature.
Moreover, this "non-condition" is precisely what I intend; therefore, the meaning of "non-condition" is established.
The proponent says:
"If one merely negates the entity of a condition, there is no 'non-condition' [remaining]. How could you expect me to make you understand by means of a 'non-condition'?"
Furthermore, the verse on opening and closing states:
"How can there be that which is both a condition and not a condition?
The commentary explains:
The entities of conditions and non-conditions do not exist; such is the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, I have already previously refuted both existence and non-existence as being devoid of the arising of an effect; for this reason, the effect has no intrinsic nature.
Since the fruit has no essence, conditions are not conditions; where, then, could the essence of those conditions be found?

Thus, the meaning of these words is fundamentally non-existent; it arises merely through the mutual dependence of mind and sound, stating that the fruit lacks intrinsic nature because the essence of conditions is empty.

Furthermore, from what has been stated above, the four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) asserted by the non-Buddhists—namely, causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), and dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—differ according to their respective intrinsic natures.
By refuting what has been established by others, the meaning of non-arising is clarified; therefore, in this chapter examining dependent origination, the meaning of non-arising is established.
As it is said in a verse within the Mahāyāna sūtras:
"If that which arises through conditions does not arise, then its arising as a self-essence cannot be found."
If one speaks of that emptiness by relying on mastery, understanding emptiness is called non-negligence.
If a person knows that not a single thing arises, and likewise knows that not a single thing ceases—
since it is neither existent nor non-existent— they see this world as entirely empty and quiescent.
Primordially quiescent and free from all arising, With such a nature, already in nirvāṇa,
He acts as our protector and turns the wheel of Dharma, Proclaiming the emptiness of all phenomena to reveal it to them.
Neither existence nor non-existence arise, nor do they both; Neither non-existent nor existent, there is no place for arising.
The causes and conditions of the world are all like this; It is only those ordinary beings who engage in false conceptualization.
The eternally unarisen dharma is the Tathāgata; All those dharmas are like the Sugata.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "Mañjuśrī,
you should know it thus."
"All those dharmas neither arise nor cease; this is what is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Because all craving has been extinguished therein, it is called 'non-arising'."
If there is no arising for that, it is itself bodhi.
The world is inverted, giving rise to false attachments.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Buddha neither appears in the world nor enters parinirvāṇa, because from the very beginning there has been neither arising nor cessation.
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"Having understood those aggregates, They neither arise nor cease;
Though they move within this world, The worldly dharmas cannot defile them."
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail herein.
The commentary on the "Examination of Conditions" chapter is concluded.

Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.

Chapter Two: An Analysis of Going and Coming. Furthermore, the first chapter has already explained that the essence of all phenomena is without arising, thereby causing people to gain faith and understanding as an antidote.

Now, furthermore, the second chapter is commenced to clarify the distinctions of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) regarding neither coming nor going, so that beings may recognize them and thereby refute opposing doctrines. What is the meaning of this?
Within worldly dharmas, one possesses mastery over verbal expression and develops deep attachment to the activities performed therein.
Now, in order to extract the arrow of such clinging, I shall negate this single mode of appearance; once this is done, other external forms of activity will be easily refuted.
Regarding what was said, the outsider says:
There must be such an arising of the substance of the internal bases. Why is this so?
Because the distinctions among those objects can be expressed in speech;
if these distinctions among objects did not exist, they could not be expressed.
For example, one cannot say that the son of a barren woman comes or goes, whereas it is not so in the case of Devadatta or Yajñadatta.
By means of this analogy, the meaning that all phenomena arise from both self and other is established.
The proponent says:

If it were established that [phenomena] arise from their own nature due to the repeated cultivation of generosity, morality, meditation, and so forth, or if they were established as being understood by the world in terms of their activity or duration, then this would involve the fallacy of establishing what has already been established.

Just as one who is in meditative concentration observes with the eye of wisdom, the practices of giving, ethical discipline, and so forth, as well as their non-practice, cannot be found as substantial entities within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although the distinctions between those objects may be described, the logical reason (*hetu*) for such a claim is not established.
Just as the arising of formations is refuted, formations themselves are likewise demolished.
Furthermore, if you claim that the causal seeds I establish are understood by us both in the same way such that our respective analyses are equally valid, this argument is not tenable.
Why is this? Because those reasons for establishing [the existence of] both are proven to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Such heterodox positions are contradicted by the evidence, as they conflict with the meaning of those reasons.
Furthermore, if one asserts that there is a "goer" within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then three things—the already gone, the not-yet-gone, and the place of going—should be perceivable.
As the verse says:
"That which has already been gone over should not be apprehended."
The commentary states:
This refers to the fact that the phenomenon of going has already ceased.
This meaning is understood by both oneself and others, and thus need not be further established.
The verse says:
"That which has not yet departed is likewise not received.
The commentary says:
Because of the goer.
This is the intended meaning, just as in the case of one who has already gone.
Furthermore, how is it that there is no "not yet gone"?

This means that for that goer, there is as yet no act of going, because that phenomenon has not yet gone; thus, both the proving factor (*sādhana*) and the proven factor (*sādhya*) are established with ease.
This is because the entity of the phenomenon and its characteristic of "about to go" are established by means of an analogy and a logical proof.
Furthermore, how is this so?
Because that which has not yet gone is also not received; thus the meaning is established. Why is this?
Because it has not yet gone, just like other persons who are about to go.
Furthermore, a disciple of Ulūka says:
What is "not yet gone"?
Is it as with Devadatta, that he who has not yet departed is said to be departing, and thus [the teaching] is not accepted?
Or is it as with Devadatta, that he who is departing is made to appear as not departing, so as to cause others to understand?
The proponent asks:
For what reason and by what causal conditions is such a question posed?
The opponent replies:
If you intend to accept the former alternative, then my position is established.
If you intend to accept the latter alternative, then it contradicts the meaning of your own reason (*hetu*).
Therefore, it is not the case that the former reason is unestablished.
Furthermore, I establish that there exists a distinct dharma of "going" (gati) apart from substance (dravya).
Your statement that this is not the case is incorrect; there is indeed going apart from substance.
How is this established?
That is to say, outside of the self-entity, there is the conjunction of the referent and the term "Devadatta" as an object, and thus there is the going of Devadatta.
Such is my intention; because it proceeds by way of conditions, one should understand it to be like the conjunction with Devadatta.
The proponent says:

If, within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there were a "going" conjoined with Devadatta such that—by manifesting a syntactical meaning external to his own substance and conjoining it with that object—one produced the cognition of "going" to cause another to understand, then this would be established within conventional truth; yet, having already been established, it would further incur the fault [of redundancy].
Why is this? Merely having distinctions of before and after at every moment within a spatial limit is what is called "conjunction.
Since the name "Devadatta" is merely an aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and lacks intrinsic substance itself, how could there be a separate "going" that conjoins with it?
Such wisdom is what I intend.

Furthermore, when names and phrases are associated with Devadatta, they cannot be established as real entities because no analogy exists within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, their substance is unattainable.
Thus, even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this contradicts reason;
how much more so within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)! You cannot avoid these faults.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:

Motivated by desire, that wind-element and the four great elements (mahābhūta) which constitute the body arise; this collection of the body, occurring in immediate succession at its boundaries, arising and ceasing in front and behind, is called "going."
If it is claimed that there exists a separate external phenomenon of "going," this is not correct. Why?
Because wherever it arises, that which arises immediately ceases.
It is like a flame: those who are deluded say it moves, but in reality this is not so.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is likewise no time of going.
To negate that "goer" within the ultimate truth constitutes the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
The proponent says:
Because you negate arising, your statement regarding the skillful means does not establish its meaning. Why is this so?
Because the one who has abandoned delusion regarding fire and so forth is identical in nature to the one who is deluded, we also wish to negate the distinction between the goer and the act of going.
Furthermore, wise people of the world do not approve of what you maintain.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
In our system, when the quality of motion (*calana*) increases predominantly, the effect becomes manifest; for that which has not yet moved is designated as "moving."
The proponent says:

Since that adherence to [the notions of] "cognition" (*vijñapti*) and so forth has already been refuted, the meaning of "going" (*gati*) is not established; this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, those who advocate for going, having heard the aforementioned faults, feel fear in their hearts and together establish this doctrinal position:
Since that which has already gone is gone, it does not incur the aforementioned fault; this principle is certain.
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"Distinct from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, The present going is likewise not apprehended."
The commentary says:
What is the meaning of this?
It is because that "time of going" cannot be apprehended.
If there is a time of going, is it that which has already gone,
or that which has not yet gone?
If it were half-gone and half-not-yet-gone, both positions would entail logical fallacies.
The opponent says:
Your statement that "the time of going is also not apprehended" is incorrect. Why is this so?
This must be accepted.
How is this known?
The manner of lifting and lowering the foot at that location is what is called "the time of going."
As the verse says:
"Neither in what has already gone nor in what has not yet gone does going occur; rather, going occurs at the time of going.
The commentary states:
What I intend [to establish] is that because there is a reason for departing, the meaning of "departing" is established.
Furthermore, some say: if there is a place of departure, then one can speak of "departing" existing there.
Such verbal expressions possess substantiality as sound, because the act [of speaking] and its basis are not separate.
To say that "what has already gone" and "what has not yet gone" do not negate going is inconsistent.
Since your assertion that "going" is not perceived during the time of going fails to establish its meaning, your refutations of what has already gone and what has not yet gone are likewise invalid.
The commentator states in verse:
"If it were the case that there is 'going' during the time of going, how could such a principle be possible?"
The commentary states:
As you intend, that there is a "goer" who goes while in the process of going—
this proposition is not established.
Why is this? Because it is a "goer.
This is because the "one who has already gone" has already been refuted.
Furthermore, if one definitively distinguishes between the act of going and the goer, does the act of going exist within that which has already gone?
Does it exist within that which has not yet gone?
Or does it exist in a place other than these two?
As previously explained,
furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both the act of going (*gati*) and the goer (*gantṛ*) are proven to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How so?
The verse says:
"Because the time of going is empty of going, it is not tenable that there is going at the time of going.
The commentary says:
It is like asking about a horse stall: "Whose horse stall is this?
and answering, "It belongs to that person who has the horse.
Then one asks again, "Whose horse is it?"
To those who hold that there is a "wooden frame" [of motion], one asks: "What is meant by the time of going?
They reply: "Going occurs at that place."
Question: Where did he go?
Answer: At the time he went.
Both [answers] are unclear.

Some may claim that, regarding the "time of going" as understood within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) since beginningless time, one wishes to establish "going" within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
This is not correct. Why?
Since this single act of going belongs to that very time of going, where else could there be a separate act of going such that one could say "one goes at that time of going"?

Therefore, your statement regarding the arising of the internal sense-bases and the conventional designation of their distinct objects within the ultimate sense, as well as your citation of Devadatta and others as examples, fails in all three respects—thesis, reason, and example—because they lack intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense.
Or it may be argued: "In this way, the activity of going does not belong to the time of going; because it does not belong [to that time], the name 'going' is applied to it.
Since that [activity] has substantial existence, the reason is not unestablished."
As the verse says:
"It is said that the goer goes while going.
The commentary explains:
If it were the case that going occurs simultaneously with the goer, this principle would indeed be so;
yet, to claim that there is no going is a flawed position.
Therefore, the verse says:
"There is no going in the time of going.
The commentary states:
If there is no going within the time of going, then it cannot be designated as "the time of going."
If there were no goer at the time of going, the world would not believe or accept it.
Therefore, the action of going is subsumed under the time of going; its conjunction with that time is necessarily so.
Your claim that there is no going, yet there is a goer distinct from going, is incorrect because it entails logical fallacies.
If you wish to avoid the aforementioned fault and maintain that going and the time of going are conjoined, and that the goer likewise proceeds in this manner, this position is also untenable.
As the verse says:
"When going is conjoined with the time of going, the goer is merely a conceptual construction.
The commentary explains:
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), going, conjunction, and so forth are all unfindable, existing only as conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
If this were definitively the case, what fault would there be?
The verse says:
"If that which is in the process of going were to go, and if it were further reached by this act of going, then one would fall into the error of two goings; this principle is not so."
The commentary states:
This means that, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), such a meaning is untenable.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If there were two acts of going, then there would be two goers.
The commentary asks:
For what reason is this negation made?
If there were two dharmas, then there would be two [entities].
The verse says:
"To say that going exists apart from the goer—this meaning is not tenable."
The commentary states:
For this reason, it should not be so;
for it must be purified of the faults previously mentioned.
What, then, is this? Just as in this way, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), when one observes that goer, the act of going is established;

in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is the opposite of this. Thus, because such distinctions of objects, verbal expressions, and metaphors are verified to lack intrinsic nature, the internal sense bases do not arise, and there is neither coming nor going; thus dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established.
Furthermore, the Vaiyākaraṇa says:
"The thesis I have established is free from the aforementioned faults. Why is this so?"
Because there is only a single entity of motion itself as it proceeds,
when that [entity] moves at that place, it is called "going.
That which performs the action of moving is called the "goer."
Therefore, your claim that there are two goers and two acts of going does not avoid this fault.
The proponent says:
because the act of going is negated within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), time lacks intrinsic substance.
Because there is no substance at that time, going is also not established.
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the continuous succession of a collection of movements occurring without interval across spatial locations is termed "the goer.
When one examines the time of going, it lacks any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, [your position] is inconsistent.
Furthermore, some say:
"It should be understood that going definitely exists.
What is the meaning of this?
Because that exists in dependence upon this;
if this basis were absent, that would not exist,
just like the son of a barren woman or the act of walking backward.
What is the characteristic of "going" in dependence upon a "goer"?
It is, for example, Devadatta.
Therefore, if there is a substratum, then that going exists, because it is established by means of its cause.
In this way, the arising, going, and not-yet-going of all these internal sense-bases (āyatana) are also established.
The author of the treatise says in verse:
"Apart from the goer, there is no going."
The commentary states:
Your claim that the "goer" is the basis for going, and that because this basis exists it serves as the cause of going, is incorrect.
Why is this? If the cause has not yet been stated, then "going" is not established.
This fault you cannot avoid.
As the verse says:
"That there is going apart from the goer—this meaning is not so.
The commentary explains:
If one is separated from the goer, going is not established.
The meaning of this statement has already been analyzed above.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If that going does not exist, where could there be a goer?
The commentary states:
Because the cause of that goer is proven to lack intrinsic nature, such is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "from where does sound [arise]":
this means that for one who does not believe in a "goer," the meaning of the statement is established.
This has already been explained at length previously, because the goer lacks intrinsic nature.
Thus, there is the fault that the reason is unestablished due to its dependence [on that basis],
as well as the fault of contradicting the intended meaning.
Furthermore, some say:
Since going has empirical verification, there is no fault in my prior position.
You should listen attentively: I definitively establish that such going exists. How is this so?
If this possesses conjunction, then that can be pointed out;
if this lacks conjunction, then that cannot be pointed out.
It is like a rabbit, which has no horns and thus cannot be pointed out as having horns.
Now, there exists going and conjunction that can be pointed out, such as saying, "That Devadatta is going.
Because going exists, my thesis is established.
The proponent says:
If you insist that there is a "going" of Devadatta which can be pointed out, do you intend for there to be a goer in the ultimate sense, or not?
As the verse says:
"That which has already gone does not go.
The commentary states:
Now, this meaning shall be established through skillful exposition.
That is to say, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that which goes does not go. Why is this?
Because action exists, it is like one who abides.
Therefore, it should be known that the goer does not go.
Furthermore, some say:
I have now established that the one who has not yet gone moves.
By this expedient means, you are unable to refute me.
The proponent says:

Just as the act of going is already untenable when one speaks of a "goer" in conjunction with going within the context of conventional truth, how can it now be said that "one who has not yet gone goes"?
As the verse says:
"One who has not yet gone does not go."
The commentary states:
"That which has not yet gone" [is so called] because there is no going; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, if it has not yet gone, how can it be "going"?
If at some time one has already departed, how can one be called a "non-departed person"?
This is self-contradictory.
Furthermore, to speak by way of expedient means: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which is a non-departed person is not called "departing."
Why is this? Because "going" is empty, just like that "otherness.
The preceding negations should be stated in this manner for the sake of the various masters of our own school as well as for non-Buddhist practitioners such as the *Kukkurika* (Grain-Eaters).
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
According to what you have stated, that which has not yet gone is called "not going.
By establishing this point, you prove what I already maintain.
The proponent asks:
What is meant by "one who has not yet gone"?
The opponent replies:
Because the act of going is not yet completed, one is called "one who has not yet gone";
if the act of going were already completed, one would be called "one who goes.
The proponent says:
What you have explained is subject to error, as has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, if you say that "that which has not yet performed the act of going" is called "the non-goer," this is not tenable.
Why is this? Because you contradict yourself.
That is to say, according to your position, the goer possesses the intrinsic nature of going even prior to having gone.
Furthermore, you claim that because staying and so forth belong to one who has not yet gone, the goer lacks an intrinsic nature.
Such an intention is incorrect. Why is this?
Because you refute your own established thesis;
that is to say, since the entity of the "goer" cannot be found when one speaks of "going" prior to its having been performed.
Furthermore, another person says:
Because there is a different perspective, one is called a "goer";
because there is another perspective, one is called a "non-goer.
By virtue of this principle, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The proponent says:
Your claim that, apart from the goer and the non-goer, there exists a distinct third entity that joins with that motion is incorrect. Why is this so?
As the verse says:
"Apart from that which has gone and that which has not yet gone, there is no third goer.
The commentary explains:
What does this clarify?
It means that apart from the goer and the non-goer, there is no third [category], because such a thing would be either a goer or a non-goer.
To claim that such a person exists makes it difficult for others to understand.
Furthermore, since the "goer" and the "non-goer" have already been refuted,
your claim that there is a goer by virtue of a particular perspective and a non-goer by virtue of another perspective is not established.

If you argue that because the goer possesses activity, this activity is not pervasive, and thus the meaning of your proposed reason is unestablished on account of its lack of activity, this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? You claim that the goer is conjoined with the act of going; such an act of going is precisely what I refute.
For example, sound produced through effort is impermanent.
Although the act of going is not omnipresent, it is nonetheless impermanent because it is an act; thus, the logical reason is established.
Likewise, since the goer is conjoined with the act of going, and I have refuted this, the reason is not unestablished.
If there were anyone who could establish the meaning of "not yet gone," they too should answer by using this very reason of "not yet gone.
If it is claimed that there is a goer, [it must be acknowledged that] there is no goer and no one who stays.
The proponent’s position is that the analogy lacks substance because it fails to possess one part of the property to be proven;
this argument is not tenable. Why is this so?
Since both parties understand the composite entity that is being analyzed,
what fault could there possibly be in my citing "one who remains" as an analogy?
Likewise, the claim that a single person is called "the goer" is not tenable.

As previously stated, if it is argued that "that [object] can be pointed out because of its conjunction with motion," then this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks substance. This is because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is present [in the example], which contradicts the intended meaning of the reason.
The opponent says:
In the world, one sees with the eye that "that goer goes," and having seen it, one gives rise to the verbal expression.
Although hearing and other [senses] exist, they do not surpass seeing with the eye.
For this reason, the [logical] reasons and so forth are not unestablished.
The proponent says:
Such a view is held by wisdom within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which regards this as real.
When one observes according to principle within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), what is called "seeing"?
If that which is seen through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) were taken as the ultimate truth, it could not be trusted.
How is this known?
As the verse says:
"If one claims that 'the goer goes,' how can this meaning be established?"
The commentary states:
The act of going by one who is already a goer does not establish the meaning of "going.
It is like a person who claims to be brave and strong, yet flees at the mere sight of the enemy when facing the battlefield.
If this "valiant one" were established, your thesis would be proven.
How could it not be established?
As the verse says:
"Because that which has departed does not have departing, the meaning is not established in this way.
The commentary states:
As I have previously explained for the sake of leading others to understanding, going has no intrinsic nature.
Wherein is understanding brought about?
As stated in the preceding verse, because that which has already gone does not go, and the arising of that going has also been previously refuted.
"That which has already gone does not go" is the formal proposition (pratijñā) intended to bring about understanding in others.
How is this to be understood?
As stated in the verse above: "If it is said that the goer goes.
What is the meaning of this?
The establishment [of these] is as previously analyzed.

Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither going nor a goer; because going is not real, it is merely through false conceptualization that one designates a "goer" by the name of "going."
The proponent of that argument establishes a thesis in this manner and incurs the following fault.
What is the fault?
The verse says:
"Since the act of going is already empty for one who goes, how can there be a goer who goes?
The commentary states:
If it is claimed that going is established because the goer and that going are conjoined, this meaning is not tenable.

Why is this? If you wish to avoid the aforementioned fault by establishing, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that there is a single "going" which, when conjoined with a "goer," is designated as "going"—this position then falls into the error of two goings.
As the verse says:
"If the goer were conjoined with going, then one would fall into the error of two goings. Why is this so?
The verse says:
"First, the going of the goer; second, the goer's going.
The commentary states:
For this reason, there is a further fault.
Specifically, it results in the fallacy of two goers. How so?
The verse says:
"It is not tenable that there is going for one who has already departed.
The commentary states:
If the basis does not exist, the dependent cannot exist; such is the meaning, and thus it follows that there must be no going.
Because there is a goer, there must be two acts of going.
Because there are two acts of going, it follows logically that there must be a goer, who is designated as such.
Furthermore, because one would desire the act of going and the goer to be one, this is established according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), analogies lack intrinsic nature; as has been stated, the logical proof [adduced] by the opponent is not established.
The outsider says:
"Going definitely exists."
Why is this? Because that initial setting forth exists.
If there were no things in the world, there would be no initial arising, just like a flower in the sky.
Because there is a thing in the world that moves away from a certain location, this is called "initial departure" and is described as having the characteristic of motion; therefore, going exists.
The proponent says:
It is like dyeing a chicken; although its color later becomes different, the substance of the chicken remains one and the same.
You are also like this; although your words differ from the former, their meaning is no different.
Regarding what was previously asked, I now ask you in return:
Is that which has already been traversed called "the initial setting out"?
Is it called "initial setting forth" when one has not yet set out?
Or is it called "initial setting forth" at the very moment of setting out?
Neither of these three cases is correct.
As the verse says:
"In that which has already gone there is no setting forth; in that which has not yet gone there is also no setting forth;
in the process of going there is no setting forth— where, then, could there be setting forth?"
The commentary states:
There is no initiation of motion within that which has already gone, because the activity of going has already ceased there.
Likewise, there is no initiation of motion within that which has not yet gone, because where there is no movement, there is no going; such is not the case for the former.

In the "time of going" (*gamyamāna*), there is no initiation of motion; that is to say, since the already-gone (*gata*) and the not-yet-gone (*agata*) both lack the meaning of "going," how can it be said that there is going in the time of going?
Since none of these three possess an initial initiation of motion, the verse says: "Where could there be an initiation?"
For this reason, your logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished and your thesis (*pratijñā*) is also refuted.

Thus, the initial departure of that which has already moved, that which has not yet moved, and that which is moving is unestablished; this is intended to lead others to faith and understanding, and such is the meaning of the statement.
How is this verified?
It is said that there is no initial departure in what has already gone, because it is [already] gone.
For example, as with one who has gone, there is likewise no departure in what has not yet gone, because it is [still] ungone.

For example, in the case of one who intends to go, there is no "setting out" within the state of not yet having gone or while in the process of going, because they are [still] a "goer," just like one who has already gone or one who has not yet gone.
Thus, the initial setting out lacks intrinsic nature; the logical reason is unestablished, for there is a fallacy in taking that which is itself unestablished as a reason.
The opponent says:

I have a different argument; namely, because there is the linguistic expression "that going," by this means going possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because its own state is distinct, and furthermore, because it serves as the cause for the arising of a distinct verbal expression through the combination of words.

If this [self-position] did not exist, then the cause for the arising of distinct expressions regarding the synthesis of the categories of meaning within their respective positions could not exist. This is like one born blind; because visual consciousness can never be synthesized with him, it cannot be said that such a blind person has seen, is seeing, or will see.

Now, there exist composite conceptual entities such as the "dharma of going" (*gati-dharma*) and its own state (*sva-sthiti*), which serve as the causes for the arising of distinct linguistic expressions; therefore, it can be said that the cessation of that motion is called "already gone," the actual commencement of the dharma of motion is called "the time of going," and the non-occurrence of the activity of motion is called "not yet gone."
Therefore, I say that because the cause possesses power, the phenomenon of motion is not empty;
thus, the intended meaning is established, and the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The proponent says:
If there were a phenomenon of going that could be described as "the time of going," then the same logic would apply to "that which has already gone" and "that which has not yet gone.
It has already been explained at length that such going lacks intrinsic nature;
yet you persist in maintaining its existence, so it shall now be further refuted.
As the verse says:
"When motion has not yet begun, there is no time of going; Nor is there any [time] when it has already gone.
Since that initial arising of going is empty, From where could that which has not yet gone set forth?"
The commentary states:
Since going does not arise when it is conjoined with that which has not yet gone, such is the meaning of the verse.
It first explains the emptiness of going so that others may attain understanding, thereby refuting the propositions established by the opponent through logical proof.
Furthermore, as for the question of where that which has not yet departed originates, this clarifies that there is no departing.
Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), conceptual construction does not arise.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
"There is no that which has gone, nor that which has not yet gone, nor is there that time of going;
within the absence of the phenomenon of going, why do you engage in false conceptualization?"
The commentary states:
"False discrimination is like a person with cataracts who sees hairs, mosquitoes, gnats, flies, and the like in empty space; these all lack intrinsic reality."
As the verse says:
"In this way, at all times, one has never seen the initial departure;
yet you speak of 'going' and so forth— the faults are thus exceedingly many."
The commentary states:
For example, just as Nārāyaṇa pursued the Asura King Kūṭadantaka, so too do the fallacies of going and so forth constantly pursue you.
Furthermore, some say:
"The dharma of going exists in the ultimate sense (paramārtha). Why is this so?"
Because they are mutually contradictory.
That is to say, in various instances they are found to be contradictory and exist in mutual dependence, just as light and darkness.
Thus, since going is found to exist in contradiction with staying, to claim that there is no going is logically untenable.
The proponent says:
One who establishes this position should also be questioned: "In your view, whom do you intend to cause to abide?
Is it the one who is going?"
Is it for that which has not yet departed?
If that which is departing were to abide, this would be logically untenable.
As the verse says:
"The goer does not abide.
The commentary states:
This means that within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the establishment of an abiding goer cannot be found through logical proof.
Why is this? Because that which has departed is characterized by motion; for example, it is like Devadatta walking while his movement has not yet ceased.
If one were to claim that that which has not yet departed abides, this too is not correct.
As the verse says:
"That which has not yet departed does not abide.
The commentary explains:
That which has not yet departed is called "staying" because it lacks departure and because, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), its departure has ceased.
This argument is untenable, because departure has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, those possessed by evil views and dominated by false attachments speak thus, desiring to establish a distinct state of "abiding.
As the verse says:
"Other than that which has gone and that which has not yet gone, who could there be as a third who abides?"
The commentary says:
To speak of "abiding" when there is no one who abides is a logically tenable position; such is the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If that which goes were to abide, how could this principle be established?
Since the goer is empty of going, both going and abiding are unattainable.
Commentary:
Going and staying are mutually exclusive; they cannot coexist at the same time—such is the meaning of the verse.
The statement that "going is empty" is intended to bring about understanding, for there is no substantial entity to be demonstrated in the case of a goer who stays.
The opponent says:
For example, just as a potter is called a "potter" because he is capable of producing [pots] throughout the three times without failure,
so too one who is going, even though he is not currently in the act of going, is still called a "goer."
Since this meaning is established, there is no fault.
The proponent says:
By your acceptance of conventional phenomena, that which was previously established as the ultimate truth is now entirely lost and destroyed.
For this reason, the reasons and examples previously set forth are flawed.
Furthermore, there is another principle that reveals those flaws.
Regarding this "abiding" you have established, what is its meaning?
Is it that the one who is going, having already gone, comes to rest and this is called abiding?
Or is it that the one who is going, while not yet having gone or while in the process of going, comes to rest and this is called abiding?
All three [positions] are incorrect. Why?
The verse says:
"When there is going, there is no staying.
The commentary states:
If "staying" were defined as the union of the act of going with the goer, such a meaning would not hold true.
The opponent says:
"What I previously stated—that 'the already-gone' is called 'abiding'—is established, for it can be verified through valid cognition.
The proponent states in verse:
"Because that which has already gone does not exist.
The commentary states:
The notion that what has already gone abides is logically untenable.
Why is this? Because that which has already gone has its going ceased; therefore, to speak of it as "abiding" would be to designate something that does not exist.
If you intend to say that the time before one has gone is called "abiding," that too is not correct.
Why is this? Because it is logically untenable for there to be cessation before one has gone.
For these reasons, that which has not yet gone cannot be called "staying"; thus, the logical reason is unestablished and the proof lacks substance.
What is the meaning of this?
Those things such as light and darkness cannot be established in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), because they are mutually contradictory and because they also contradict your own formal proposition.
Furthermore, some say:
"I establish the meaning of 'abiding' because it is characterized by contradiction, since there is an initial commencement;
moreover, that [abiding] can be removed, because its essence possesses arising."
This interpretation is not correct, as it entails the following fault.
As the verse says:
"The faults regarding going, arising, acting, and ceasing Are identical to those explained regarding going."
The commentary states:
Just as it is illogical for a goer to go, for one who has not yet gone to go, or for a going that is distinct from these two,
so too is it illogical for there to be an initial departure in what has already been gone over, what has not yet been gone over, or in the process of going.
Thus, since that which has already gone, that which has not yet gone, the process of going, and the cessation of going are all unestablished,
it is likewise not the case that there is one who abides, one who has not yet abided, or one who abides apart from those two.
Because abiding does not exist, that which has already abided, that which has not yet abided, the time of abiding, and the initial commencement of abiding are likewise unattainable.
Since the initial commencement does not exist, the meanings of that which has already abided, that which has not yet abided, the time of abiding, and the cessation of abiding are all untenable.
As explained extensively above,
because the text is cumbersome, I shall now provide a brief demonstration.
What is the meaning of this?
That which abides does not abide. Why?
Because going is empty.
Just as that which has already abided—whether its abiding has not yet ceased or has long since been established—has no initial commencement of abiding. Why is this?
Because it has already abided, just like that which has long since been established.
Furthermore, for that which has already abided, there is no abiding to be removed.
Why? Because going has no intrinsic nature, just as in the case of one who has not yet ceased abiding.

As has been demonstrated by the three propositions concerning that which is already abiding, the same applies to that which is not yet abiding and that which is in the process of abiding; these should be refuted through the aforementioned method of analysis.
Thus, the meaning of "abiding" is not established, as it is subject to logical fallacies.
The opponent says:
Your claim that there is neither going nor a goer is not tenable. Why is this so?
Because you subvert worldly conventions,
people of the world will all say, "It is Devadatta who has gone," or "It is Yajñadatta who has gone.
Your claim that this is not so contradicts the common understanding of the world.
Just as everyone in the world knows that the moon is the moon, yet someone might say, "This is a rabbit, not the moon," so too is it with you.
The proponent says:
What further meaning do you intend by establishing this reason?
Is it because it contradicts what is understood by the world,
or is it because it contradicts what is understood by your own treatise?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it were contrary to what is understood in the world, the meaning of the reason would not be established. Why is this?
Because that "going" and the "goer" cannot be found within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Since I do not negate the existence of "going" and a "goer" as they are understood in the world within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
is your intention to refute my position by claiming that it contradicts what is understood in your own treatise?
In making this statement, you do not understand the underlying principles.
It should be stated thus: "The refutation you have received incurs this fault;
such is not the case."
Why is this? Even regarding the explanations provided by our own treatise, I do not adhere to them.
This is because, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both "going" and the "goer"—the natures of these two—are not accepted, as has already been refuted previously.

Furthermore, if within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) both "going" and the "goer" were definitively existent, they would necessarily be either identical or distinct, and thus could be found upon investigation.
Yet, when examined in this way, neither case is tenable.
As the verse says:
"The act of going is the goer—this is not so;
The act of going is different from the goer—this meaning is also not so."
Why are these two positions untenable?
The verse says:
"If it is claimed that the action of going is identical to the goer,"
"The agent and the action would then be one and the same; this is the fault.
The commentary states:
Such a meaning is the fault of perversion.
If sound were eternal, then a jar would also be eternal because it is a product.
This argument is not established. Why is that?
If a jar were produced, it would not be called eternal.
For this reason, sound is impermanent because it is produced, just like that jar.
These words are trustworthy.
Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), going and the goer—these two are not one. Why is this?
Because there is an agent and an action, just as there is that which cuts and that which is cut;
these two manifestations cannot be distinct. Why is this?
Because both "going" and the "goer" are mutually empty, they are like any other entity.
Some may raise this objection:
"If going and the goer are mutually empty, then since emptiness has no distinct characteristics, their essential nature cannot be apprehended."
As for your citation of the "cutter" and the "cut" as an analogy, this argument is not established.
The proponent of the treatise says:
You have not explained it well, because you merely negate oneness.
The distinction between these two characteristics is understood by all in the world.
Thus, the mutual emptiness of that which cuts and that which is cut is established;
this principle is just like the mutual emptiness of the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived.
Because the two characteristics are distinct within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are cited as an analogy; thus, the analogy is not unestablished.
If it is argued that the "cutter" and the "object cut" are non-different in their essence within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), [we reply: [they are indeed so].
Why is this? Because it possesses measure, just like the very substance that is being cut.
Therefore, the position that establishes [the self] as a single entity is incorrect.
Why is this? Because it is not established that the entity being cut is not distinct [from the act of cutting].
Why is it not established?
Because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not grasp at the two extremes of identity or difference;
whereas in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), although subject and object are distinct, to speak of them as "one" is to refute worldly understanding.
Furthermore, if you think that because I negate the identity of the goer and the going, I therefore accept the extreme of difference, that is also not the case.
As has already been stated, in the ultimate sense, I do not adopt either of the two extremes of identity or difference; therefore, there is no fault of accepting difference.
Furthermore, some say:

"According to the thesis I establish, there is no such fault as previously mentioned. This is because, from time immemorial, the seeds of habitual tendencies produced by the conceptual proliferation of names and expressions serve as the cause; thus, through the sovereign power of false discrimination, specific causes and conditions give rise to their respective effects."
This position intends to establish that the act of going and the goer are definitively distinct; in order to refute this, as the verse says:
"If it is claimed that the act of going Is definitively distinct from the goer."
The commentary states:
From the perspective of conventional conceptualization, there is nothing that can negate [the self].
However, when observed according to reality, this is not the case.
Why is this not so? As the verse says:
"Without going, there would be a goer; without a goer, there would be going."
The commentary states:
How could these two exist separately?
Because they are distinct, just like a jar and a garment.

Those who maintain a distinction between them do not, however, intend for the act of going to exist apart from the goer, nor for the goer to exist apart from the act of going; for they hold that these exist through their mutual dependence as the supported and the support.

Regarding the teaching by means of skillful methods: within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not intend for there to be a distinction between "going" and the "goer," because language involving distinctions arises only through mutual dependence and opposition, just as in the case of the intrinsic nature of going itself.
Thus, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not intend to differentiate a dharma of going as something existing apart from the goer.
Why? Because distinct designations arise only through dependence upon their counterparts, just like the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the goer itself.
The opponent says:
"Since you employ a circular argument that fails to bring understanding to others, you incur this fault.
The proponent replies:
Since those distinct categories lack intrinsic nature, the meaning of "reversal" (parāvṛtti) is established.
The opponent says:
In the world, there naturally exist both the supported and the support; it is not necessarily the case that they are conjoined.
As for your statement that there is dependence upon a counterpart, this reason is unestablished. Why?
Because it does not pervade one part of the object to be proven.
The proponent says:

Those various entities also possess this and that, because they are distinct through mutual observation; thus, there is no fault in their being correlative counterparts, and the reason is not unestablished.
Your proposed proof ultimately establishes only difference.
Because difference has been previously refuted, non-difference is established.
Since the various schools lack intrinsic nature, they do not fall into the two extremes;
nor is the understanding of the world thereby destroyed.
How is it not refuted?

In this treatise, we have observed with ultimate truth that the union of the dependent and the supported, as previously explained, is not an object of observation for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Furthermore, some may say:
"The self is distinct from going, because that goer can be pointed out—
just as Devadatta and his horse are distinct, since the supported and the support possess two different characteristics."
The proponent says:
You have not stated it well, because the meaning of the "goer" as a self-entity is not established.
Since Devadatta, the horse, and so forth are distinct, this point is not established; for in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the analogy lacks any real entity.
If there are those with false wisdom who differentiate the various characteristics of causes and so forth, they should also be answered by means of this same principle.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"The wise and intelligent person understands it thus: regarding the word 'goer,' there is a motion external to its own substance, which is conjoined with and integrated into the meaning of the term."
It is like Devadatta being the object of cognition, depending on whether [the action] occurs or does not occur;
it is like saying "blue-clad," where other [qualities] are not applicable.
If it were not so, the term "goer" would have no distinction between occurrence and non-occurrence, just as in the case of "Great Existence" (mahāsattā).
The proponent says:
Your establishment of this distinction as a proof is incorrect. Why is this so?

The relationship between the basis and that which depends upon it lacks substantial reality; since the conjunction of these two—the act of going and the goer—has already been refuted, the logical proof is also invalid. How is this known?
This refers to multiple individuals sharing the same name; apart from their own individual substances, no external referent (padārtha) corresponds to them.

Whether there be two, three, or even an infinite number of such persons, such as Devadatta and others, this serves as a proof that the reason for the application or non-application of a term is not invariably certain.
The opponent says:
Because there is a distinction, although they share the same name, the sound "Devadatta who is black, tall, and departing" applies to that [specific individual] and does not apply to others.
For this reason, my logical ground (hetu) is established and is not non-conclusive.
The proponent says:
As you have stated, "Devadatta is black and tall," because he lacks intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), the meaning of the logical ground is not established.
Regarding the analogies of the blue-clad servant and objective spheres, neither can be found within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
If someone were to say that the act of going is distinct from the goer because their difference is perceived, [that too would be untenable].
Establishing a proof in this manner is refuted by the same reasons and examples as before.

Furthermore, if you argue that because my establishment of the negation of difference based on unity and the establishment of unity based on the negation of difference never departs from difference, the negation of difference cannot be established—this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because the negation of both identity and difference has already been explained previously.
By the power of this reasoning, one destroys attachment to the two extremes; how, then, could the cognition of such an object arise?
Since the wise have already understood this, I am without fault.

Therefore, regarding your statement that I negate the non-difference between the goer and the act of going, and your subsequent establishment of a distinction while claiming to accept their non-difference—I do not possess such a fault.
Furthermore, if you were to examine this carefully and take up my previous statement— that because the goer’s own essence is not distinct [from the act of going],
the thesis is unestablished— then your claim that the analogy lacks substance and thus constitutes a fault on my part is incorrect.

Why is this? Apart from the essence of the goer, there is no other distinct phenomenon; because there is no other distinct phenomenon, the essence of the goer is established, and because its essence is established, the analogy is without fault.

Thus, the Vaiśeṣikas and those who consume husks and the like, concealing their own faults and seeking to subvert correct reasoning, find that all the proofs they previously asserted are unestablished.
Furthermore, some may say:

"You previously refuted 'going,' yet now you abandon that and instead discuss other matters—whether identity or difference; since both 'going' and the 'goer' are unestablished, this is not a sound argument. This is not so.
As the verse says:
"The goer and the going, these two, are established as being either identical or different.
The commentary states:
Are the goer and the act of going one and the same, or are they different?
Since those two exist, can they be apprehended?
If it is explained through skillful means that they are either one or different, as the verse says:
"Since those two are not established, how could there be going?
Commentary: Since "going" has already been refuted, it is not because one wishes to abandon it.
By this same principle, the position of identity is likewise refuted, for both [identity and difference] exist within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
You should understand that, according to your own view, whether as identical or different, the act of going would be established for the goer in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There is no such principle as this: that one might cause others to understand by asserting the existence of a unity or diversity that does not exist. This argument is incorrect.
Or perhaps some person, clever and arrogant, might say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no goer who goes, because of the act of moving, just like other objects."
One who abides in this manner does not abide, because they engage in activity and motion, just like Devadatta.
Regarding the phrase "that which has not yet ceased its departure," what do these two preceding proofs demonstrate?
Regarding the agent who performs an action: is it the external agent who acts, and does this act or not act?
Or is it the bodily agent who acts, and does this act or not act?
If one says that external action is non-action, then the analogy is not established, because it is produced by something else acting.
If one says that bodily action is non-action, then it contradicts the meaning, because the speaker speaks and the cutter cuts.
The same applies to his departure; since the body is already in motion, how can it be called "non-action"?
Thus, the proof previously stated is invalid, as it contains a logical fallacy.
The proponent says:
Since that distinct agent does not perform the action of going, for this reason, the analogies regarding that agent and so forth are established.
As for the fault you previously alleged, it now returns to you.
The analogy having been established, it does not contradict the meaning.
How does it not contradict?
As the verse says:
"Because the goer has departed, that going does not go. Commentary:
"That going does not go" means that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that going is not produced.
