Why is this? Because there is no difference, just as in the case of the self-nature of "going.
This means that those who assert non-difference are refuted by their own logic, and they also contradict what is commonly understood in the world.
Why is this? As the verse says:
"Just as one sees such a person, / Because they go toward a village and so forth."
The commentary states:
It is universally understood in the world that for such a person, villages and so forth exist externally as distinct entities.
Furthermore, because the act of going depends upon the goer, that going does not go.
What is the meaning of this?
For this reason, as the verse says:
"Since there is no act of going prior [to the goer], therefore there is no going by a goer."
The commentary states:
Just as the self-essence of one who stands can serve as the cause for going and perform the act of going, [in this case] there is no such goer.

Although there is no goer, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the intention serves as the cause, which subsequently gives rise to functional activity. Through the sovereign power of the wind element, at the boundaries of space without interval, the aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise; they are differentiated by time, with each moment (*kṣaṇa*) differing from the preceding and succeeding moments.
Because these [actions] arise, one is called a "goer.

Within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is certainly not intended that such an agent serves as the cause for being an agent; therefore, the verse says: "Just as one sees this person going to a village and so forth, it is not by means of its own essence (*svabhāva*) that it acts as the cause for itself."
In this way, for those of our own schools who hold that the act of going ceases when the goer is eliminated, it should be understood that such going does not go.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas say:
"The body is a distinct name for the collection of earth and the other elements; because those particles increase, it is called 'going'."
Thus, it is held that the goer is the person who possesses the action of going (gati) based upon a collection of causes (hetu-sāmagrī) as its support for the result of going.
This position is incorrect. Why?
Because there is no goer when one has not yet gone.
If that which has not yet gone were called a "goer," then likewise, that which is stationary should also be called a "goer"; however, this is not actually the case.
If it is claimed that that which has already gone is the cause of that going, this too is not so. Why?
As stated in the previous verse: "Just as one sees such a person going to that village and so forth."
What is the meaning of this?
It should be understood in this way: that going cannot perform the act of going.
An opponent says:
To claim that because there is an act of arising, one speaks of "the sprout arises," is like saying a wise person "produces" wisdom for themselves;
such a position is incorrect and is merely a false conceptualization.
Since no act of arising occurs at the time when the sprout has not yet arisen, to speak of an "act of arising" is logically untenable.
Thus, that the goer himself goes, the speaker himself speaks, or the cutter himself cuts—none of these are tenable. Why?
Because the principle of self acting upon itself is untenable.

With that intention as the cause, there subsequently arise the causes such as effort, the basis, and the act of articulation; the collection of formations consisting of those syllables, phrases, and sounds is what is called "speech. To maintain that there exists a separate, intrinsic substance of speech is incorrect.
Regarding the statement that "one who speaks is first called a speaker," such a meaning does not exist.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
As previously stated, by means of going one knows the goer; that going, however, does not go.
Although you have refuted it, the meaning is still not correct.
Why? Because apart from that goer, there exists a separate dharma of going; for this reason, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
What is the distinction between these two meanings?
They are the cognition of reality and the cognition of karma.
These two differ because their objects are distinct.
For example, the cognition of a cow and that of a water buffalo are distinct from one another.
If they were not distinct, there would be no difference between their respective objects, just as there is none within the intrinsic nature of the cognition of a cow itself.
The proponent says:
If one goes by means of a going, then that goer does not go; this fault has been explained previously.
Now, to negate that [notion of] difference, as the verse says:
"Because the goer has already gone, that which is other than the goer does not go either.
The commentary states:
That [proponent] posits "otherness" in order to lead others to understanding, yet it is proven to be without intrinsic nature.
As the verse says:
"The existence of this thing as distinct from that thing is not established.
The commentary explains:
In the ultimate sense, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that my analogy is established.
Furthermore, because the act of going (*gati*) is negated by the goer (*gantṛ*), that which is distinct from the act of going does not go either.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
"Since the goer is one, it is not possible for there to be two acts of going."
The commentary states:
Why is this not so? Because it is known through the establishment of a proof (sādhana).
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no distinct act of going apart from the entity that goes. Why?
Because two acts of going cannot coexist, just as in the case of one who stands still.
Furthermore, the Proponent of the Consumption of Chaff (*Tuṣaka*) says:
According to my established doctrine, there is only a single act of going (*gati*). When this act of going conjoins with that which goes, it is called the "goer" (*gantṛ*).
Because of this distinction, [the goer] can serve as the cause for the act of going, since it performs that very going.
It is like someone saying,
"That Devadatta is going.
Or again, it is like a lamp being the cause of its light, which is then called "lamp-light."
As you previously stated, because the goer is one, it is not possible for the act of going to be two; this interpretation is incorrect.
The proponent says:
You have not explained it well.

As previously stated, since both "going" and "that which has not yet arisen" have already been refuted by the various arguments such as the force of the reasons (*hetubala*), etc., in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, that which goes is not the cause for the conjunction with going, because it is the distinct cause for the arising of the cognition of sound, just like that [other] action (*karman*).
By this proof it is known that your claim that "going" and the "goer" are conjoined is merely a false assertion. Why is this?
Because when a person has not yet been conjoined with going, they are not a goer, just like one who is standing still.
To claim that there is a conjunction between "going" and the "goer" is incorrect.
Furthermore, when one examines the matter according to reason, neither "going" nor the "goer" can be found.
As the verse says:
"Whether existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent—
these three types of goers each do not employ the three kinds of going."
The commentary states:
There is a real goer, who, because of being conjoined with going, is said to "possess going.
What is the meaning of this?
If there were a real act of going, it would not involve three kinds of going— namely,

that which has a real act of going does not go, that which lacks a real act of going does not go, and that which possesses both does not go— because it constitutes a movement, just like any other object.
If there is no real goer, there are likewise no three kinds of going, because going is empty, just like the one who stays.
Both the simultaneous going and the goer are refuted by the same previous argument.
As with the refutation of the goer, so it is with the act of going (*gati*).
One should understand this through the application of formal propositions (*pratijñā*), logical reasons (*hetu*), and illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This is because, when examined through both reason (*yukti*) and scripture (*āgama*), the three types of going are not established at any time.
As the verse says:
"Therefore, going has no intrinsic nature, and the goer is likewise so;
the time of going and all phenomena— all these are non-existent."
The commentary states:
Just as the previously established proof refuted the "goer" and the act of "going," all other functional phenomena (*dharmas*) should likewise be excluded by this same principle.

This chapter clarifies that going lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in order to lead one to believe and understand the distinct meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—that there is neither coming nor going—and thus it is established.
As it is said in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
"That which has neither going nor coming is called the noble going and coming.
Furthermore, as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
“Good son! The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Avacanopama-sūtra*:
"Coming and going have no reality; all phenomena are like space.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Those atoms and so forth likewise come from nowhere and go nowhere, because such coming and going cannot be perceived."
Furthermore, as the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Paramavikrāmin: "Good son,
because the coming and going of form cannot be seen, it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"That which cannot be seen as the coming or going of the five aggregates is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
Such sūtras as these should be explained extensively here.
The commentary on the "Examination of Going and Coming" is finished.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Three.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Four.
Verse Text by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Three: Examination of the Six Faculties. Furthermore, regarding the establishment of this chapter, what are its characteristics?
This chapter is taught in order to prevent the arising [of such views] and to cause people to recognize that the six internal bases (*āyatana*) and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Furthermore, this chapter follows immediately after the previous one because it seeks to negate the attachment to "going" and to bring about a thorough understanding of the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the bases and other phenomena.
Regarding the first analysis, the opponent says:
"The arising of internal sense bases exists; this should be accepted as such within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is that?"
Because the object is determined:
if this arising did not exist, that determined object could not exist, just like the son of a barren woman.
For this reason, it is known that there is the arising of internal sense-bases, because their objects are determined.
As the verse says: "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, The body, and mind— these six faculties,
And their objects, such as form and the rest, Are the respective spheres corresponding to their number."
The commentary states:
For this reason, the stated reason is established, and the thesis regarding the arising of entry is set forth.
Next, as for the analysis, the opponent definitively asserts:
There is such a going.
Why? Because it produces an effect, just as one perceives form and so forth.
The proponent says:
These two types of conceptualization are now refuted in succession.
Those sense organs, such as the eye, each exercise predominance; when they assemble, they perform the function of apprehending form and so forth. Therefore, they are called "organs" (indriya).

Within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), forms and other objects are also perceivable outside the sense faculties, because the essential nature of the agent can be demonstrated; that is to say, it is called the "eye" because it sees, and so on, up to the "mind" because it cognizes.
Furthermore, these faculties and so forth are so called because they manifest the various objects that are visible, audible, olfactory, gustatory, tangible, and cognizable.
What is the meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*)?
It means that the faculty possesses the power to apprehend the sense-field; therefore, it is called an object.
The claim that the subject and the object exist within conventional truth,
yet are definitively existent within the ultimate sense, is an untenable position, for it contradicts the true meaning.
How is it demonstrated so that they may understand?
It is like the contemplation of the eye-faculty.
The verse says:
"Thus, that eye-faculty cannot see its own self;
since it does not see its own self, how can it see another?
Explanation:
Why is it not seen?
Such a visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) cannot be established as a grasper from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Why is this so?
The verse states that the eye does not see its own substance because it possesses resistance and is likewise derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), just like the ear and other sense organs.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the eye does not see form.
Why is this? Because those material phenomena arise from causes, just like the nose and so forth;
furthermore, because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), just like the tongue and so forth.
Thus, in the ultimate sense, form is not the object of the eye. Why?
Because it is an accumulation, like the nature of the eye itself.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, form is not the object of the eye. Why?
Because it possesses resistance.
Furthermore, because it is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), like the ear and so forth.
Moreover, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), visible form is not the object of the eye. Why is this?
Because it arises from causes, like the nose and so forth;
and because it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), like the tongue and so forth.
Furthermore, some say:
"That the eye does not see" means that it does not see its own substance;
because form is visible, the eye is therefore able to see form.
The proponent says:
Regarding what you have said—that the eye does not see—this merely assists me by providing the power of my reasons and analogies; how could it possibly refute the thesis I have established?
Furthermore, the Abhidharmikas say:
If there were no qualification, then such a statement as "the eye does not see form" would actually establish my own position.
Why is this? Because it pertains to a single door.
In my established thesis, that which lacks a portion does not see form because of the eye.
If the eye, as a constituent part (*sāvayava*), were unable to see forms, the meaning of the *Āgama* you accept would be undermined.
As it is said in a verse from my *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
"The eye, as a constituent part, sees forms; It is not the consciousness that depends upon it."
"In the Abhidharma, it is stated in this way; does this not contradict the meaning of the Āgamas you have accepted?
The proponent replies:
"According to your thesis, if you wish for this 'part-possessing eye' to see visible forms, that is not correct."
Why is this? Because there are no two faults; that is to say, it is not the case that what has already been established is established again, nor is the intended meaning undermined.
How so? It is not undermined.
As a verse in the sutra says:
"The eye does not see the objects of form, The mind does not know all phenomena;
This is called the supreme reality, Which worldly people cannot transcend."
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not intend for that eye to see forms; thus, as extensively refuted previously, this point is established.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, that composite eye (*sāvayava-cakṣus*) cannot see forms.
Why is this? Because it is the eye-faculty; for example, like an eye without parts.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that eye with parts cannot see forms.
Why is this? Because it is a material sense-faculty (*rūpīndriya*), just like the ear and so forth.
Furthermore, this does not contradict what is commonly understood in the world.
Why is this? Because the propositions established are distinct; that is to say, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no one who can charge [us] with error.
Furthermore, in the Kāśmīra-vibhāṣā, the proposition is established as follows:
That is to say, that eye sees various forms because it performs the function of seeing.
The proponent says:

Your stated reason [hetu] is invalid because it is a part of the very thesis [pakṣa] you intend to establish, because the corroborative instance [dṛṣṭānta] lacks substance, and because you have already refuted it; therefore, this argument is not established.

Furthermore, if there were an agent, it would contradict the meaning established by those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*), and it would also differ from the position of those who deny momentariness.
Neither of these cases is tenable; therefore, the doctrine maintained by the Kāśmīrīs is inconsistent.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without agency (*nirvyāpāra*), the eye cannot see, nor does anything else see.
Nevertheless, with the eye and visible form as conditions, visual consciousness arises.
In the Sūtras it is stated thus: your claim that "the eye does not see" constitutes the fallacy of proving what has already been established.
The proponent replies:
Since arising has already been refuted, visual consciousness cannot be apprehended; therefore, there is no fallacy of proving what has already been established.
Furthermore, the meaning thus received is not undermined, because one accepts the meaning of the sūtras in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), however, it is established that they lack intrinsic nature, as the seeing and the visible of both the eye and form have already been refuted.
As for those various distinctions, their meanings are all untenable.
Thus, in order to cause students to give rise to various insights, this brief exposition has been made.
As stated in the preceding verse: "In this way, that visual faculty cannot see its own self."
If one does not see one's own nature, how can one see another?
For, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the eye does not see form. Why is this?
Because its own substance is not perceived, just like the ear and other [senses].
Or, as some say:
the eye can apprehend form without reaching the object.
Why is this? Because the sense-faculty of the eye possesses the capacity for apprehension; it is, for example, like when a person performs an act of seeing, yet it is said that "the king sees.
The proponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no such principle as the eye being able to apprehend a visible object without reaching it. Why?
Because the eye cannot apprehend its own self-substance (*svabhāva*), just like the ear and other [senses].

Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the objective form-objects (*rūpa-viṣaya*) that are apprehended are not such that they do not reach the range of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Why is this?
Because they are derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), just like fragrance and so forth.

Because it is obstructive, because it arises from causes, because it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and because it is a composite accumulation—by these various reasons, the view that the eye does not reach its object and that form is not apprehended is refuted.
The formal proposition and the illustrative example have been explained in detail as before; one should examine and understand the erroneous attachments regarding these two gates.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the eye does not fail to reach its object.
Why is this? Because it is an object of the present, just like the nose and so forth. Or, as some say:
The eye does not reach its object.
Why? Because it apprehends form with an interval, just as the mind does.
Furthermore, because it apprehends form during moments that are effortless (*anābhoga*), and because it apprehends it in excess,
the formal proposition and the illustrative example should be understood as before.
The proponent says:
This statement is not correct.
Your claim that [the sense organ] does not reach the object implies that it apprehends form with an interval.
Since "apprehending form with an interval" is merely one part of your own thesis and possesses no further distinct meaning, this argument is untenable.
Furthermore, if there were no distinction in time, the meaning of the "grasper" would be undermined.
Even if it were established through real causes, it would lack substantiality upon examination.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the intention [of the grasper] does not reach its object; thus, this attachment to a "grasper" is untenable, as it contradicts the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
Your statement that the eye does not apprehend an object without reaching it establishes what I already maintain. Why is this?
I wish to show that the eye reaches the object in order to apprehend it.
The proponent says:
"Apprehension without reaching" is intended to lead one to believe and know that the nature of the eye is empty.
Since the eye and its objects are empty, how could the process of reaching the object and grasping it be established?
You are falsely generating joy where there is no basis for it.
Furthermore, why would it not be the case that the eye reaches the object and grasps it?
Because it is by way of the faculties (*indriya*), it is analogous to the mind (*manas*).
Furthermore, one does not apprehend the nose and other faculties; thus, there is no fallacy of being non-exclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Why is there no fallacy of being non-exclusive?
The same applies to the olfactory faculty and the others, as will be explained later.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the eye reaches its object," what is the meaning of this?
Does it intend to imply that the support [of consciousness] reaches the perceived object in this manner?
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
Because that eye-consciousness does not actually go outward to its support.
Why is this? Because it is a consciousness, like the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth;
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), visual consciousness cannot apprehend that object.
Why is this? Because it exists due to causes, just like sound and so forth.
The opponent says:
"You rely on two propositions that mutually refute one another; by relying on this to negate that, neither is established.
The proponent says:
"Because both lack intrinsic nature, I do not accept them. Because I do not accept them, the intended meaning is established."
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The visual faculty reaches the object and is therefore able to apprehend form.
Such a view is also incorrect.
That light of the eye-faculty cannot exist even within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
Why? Because it is the cause of the cognition of form (rūpa-vijñāna), just like that form itself.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The visual faculty possesses light, because it is a visual faculty, just like the eyes of bats, cats, and mongooses.
The proponent of the treatise replies:
Regarding the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) as being material form (*rūpa*), it is because it is invisible.
Even if its basis were actually possessed of light, the analogy would still fail.
Furthermore, some say:
As previously stated, regarding the fact that the visual faculty cannot see its own self-nature, what is the meaning of this?
If phenomena possessed a visible self-nature, then when they were in combination, others could also see it, just as, for example, one can smell the fragrance of flowers.
By this principle, the eye does not see itself, nor does it see others.
As stated in a verse from Āryadeva Bodhisattva’s *Śataśāstra*:
“If all those phenomena Had a self-nature existing prior [to conditions];”
"Thus, possessing the faculty of sight, why does it not see itself?
The proponent asks:
"What is the meaning of 'seeing'?"
This means that form is apprehended, and that form is apprehended.
If the eye did not exist and form were likewise non-existent, there would be the fault of what has already been established being established again.
As the verse says:
"Consciousness does not reside in the eye or in forms; it does not abide in the interval between the two.
It is neither existent nor non-existent; where, then, does that consciousness abide?
Furthermore, if you claim that one does not see because the seed of vision is absent within the eye-faculty, then the analogy of the *sumana* flower is incorrect.
Why is this not the case?

Because that flower arises with fragrance due to the sovereign power of the harmony of its causes and conditions; it is like sesame oil, which acquires fragrance because of its combination with *kusuma* flowers.
No one establishes the meaning of "visible" as being an act of seeing; thus, that refutation is unestablished.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that because it does not see itself, it also does not see others, then the analogies of fire and sparks are both ineffective, since fire and sparks do not apprehend themselves or others; therefore, this is inconsistent.

Thus, since the meaning of visual perception is not established, both its arising and its departure are likewise unestablished; this is because the analogy lacks substantiality and because it contradicts the meaning of the logical reason (*hetu*).
The opponent says:
Your statement that the eye does not see form because it does not see its own self is what is being clarified by this principle.
If it lacks power with respect to its own self, it likewise lacks power with respect to others.
Since this principle is not absolute— just as fire lacks the power to burn its own substance but is capable with respect to other things, so it is with the eye—
the author of the treatise states in verse:
“The analogy of fire cannot establish the proposition that the eye sees.”
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which burns is not established; in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), fire does not have the nature of seeing.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that fire is not established as having the property of burning within the conventional sense.
What is meant by "burning"?
It refers to the transformation of fuel through fire.
Therefore, one knows that the intrinsic nature of fire itself is not burning.
Furthermore, regarding the argument that the analogy of fire does not establish the fact of seeing with the eye: that analogy of seeing fire with the eye has already been explained previously.
How was it explained?
The verse says:
"Because the 'gone,' the 'not-yet-gone,' and the 'present-going' have all already been refuted in their entirety.
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no going in the gone, the not-yet-gone, or the present-going, as has already been explained previously.
Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which has been burned, that which has not yet been burned, and the process of burning do not burn.
Why? Because they are, respectively, the time of burning, that which has already been burned, and that which has not yet been burned.
For example, regarding that which is burning, that which has already burned, and that which has not yet burned: as for the state of "burning," it entails two logical fallacies;
as for that which "has already burned," it is like something that has long since finished burning.
That which has not yet been burned is fundamentally without burning.
Thus, it is not seen in what has already been seen, nor in what has not yet been seen, nor at the time of seeing. Why is this?
Because of that which has already been seen, that which has not yet been seen, and that which is being seen.
Just as with that which has already been seen, that which has not yet been seen, and that which is being seen, these should be examined and refuted in their respective order.
Some say: The eye possesses the activity of seeing. Why is this?
Since this is stated in all the treatises of the various schools, it is, for example, like the eye seeing various forms.
The proponent of the treatise says:
This "seeing by the eye" is spoken of as a conventional designation within the realm of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and not from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
How is this known?
Because within this treatise, both seeing by the eye and its arising are negated, that eye is therefore empty.
As the verse says:
"When the eye has not yet seen, it cannot be said that it sees;
to claim that the eye can see is logically untenable. Commentary:
Seeing that this is not the case, the meaning of the verse is as follows.
For this reason, the verse says:
"When there is seeing, there is no 'that seeing'; when there is no seeing, there is likewise no seeing."
The commentary states:
Because one is able to see emptiness, it is like earth, stones, and so forth; such is the meaning of the verse.

Thus, the notion that there are two kinds of seeing and an agent of seeing is incorrect. Therefore, the verse says: "If there is seeing, that seeing does not exist; if there is no seeing, seeing also does not exist. Both possibilities are negated.
For example, if something both exists and does not exist, conditions would all be useless.
Likewise, if something both exists and does not exist, causes are similarly negated.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others say:
Because this eye is the instrument by which one sees, that which possesses the eye is called the "seer.
Since it is the seer who sees with his own eye, it is like a woodcutter who cuts; it is not the axe that cuts.
Therefore, the claim that "it is not seen by the eye" establishes what I already maintain.

That is to say, that agent possesses various instruments of action; because they possess instruments of action, there must necessarily be one who wields them, just as an axe and such tools must have a woodcutter.
The proponent says:
That false discrimination which claims there is a seer—this adherence is not correct.
As the verse says:
"If seeing has already been refuted, one should know that the refuter of seeing is likewise refuted. Commentary:
Just as the eye does not see itself, so too is it with that [refuter].
The claim that the self-nature of a person perceives the person itself is incorrect, because it contradicts worldly conventions of action, just as a sword cannot cut itself and so forth.
How is this known through verification?
It means that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that person has no capacity for seeing. Why is this so?
Because its own essence is not perceived, it is like the ear and so forth.

Nor is the meaning of the reason unestablished; when that sutra states, "I see myself," it merely designates the name "self" upon the mind for the sake of conventional truth, and is not spoken from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Because it is such an object, because it is an object of cognition, and because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Just as with sound and the ear, these various reasons and their corresponding analogies should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), form is not seen by the self. Why?
Because it is a thing (*bhāva*); just as the self's own essence cannot see itself.
The objects of cognition and so forth should be explained in detail in this manner.
An opponent says:
"In the Buddha's Dharma, there is no self."
As for your statement that "the self cannot see itself," this contradicts the teachings.
The proponent of the treatise says:
In the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the analogy of the self is used as a provisional designation; thus, it does not contradict the teachings.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), since both the axe and the analogy lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not the case that what has already been established is established again.
Some say: "Your statement that 'the seer does not see' is self-contradictory."
Why is this? If one says they are a "seer," how can one say they do not see?
If one says they do not see, how can they be called a "seer"?
This is a fault in the formal proposition (*pratijñā-doṣa*).
The proponent says:
"Dependent origination does not arise," as has already been answered previously and need not be stated again.
Furthermore, regarding what you say concerning the "seer": does it see its own self-nature, or does it not?
If it sees its own self-nature, then it would be as the Sāṃkhyas claim: that volition (*cetanā*) is the self-nature of the person (*puruṣa*).
If that which sees were the very essence of seeing, and if that essence were not something produced, then one should be able to see even apart from the eye-faculty.
Furthermore, just as a woodcutter cannot chop without an axe, how could a person possibly see apart from the eyes?
I speak of the seer and the one who cuts within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Because of this distinction, the verse says:
"Neither separate from the eye nor not separate from the eye, A seer cannot be found."
The commentary states:
When the eyes and other faculties have not yet arisen, or when they are abandoned, this is precisely the absence of eyes.
If there are no eyes, then both the seer and the seen are empty.
To claim that there is a seer who exists apart from the grasping at the seen and the seeing is not correct.
Since seeing has no intrinsic nature, the seer likewise does not exist; such is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, if it is argued that the seer is like the self-nature of fire, this argument is also incorrect.
Why is this? Because when there is no fuel, fire has no substance.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
If this visible form could be apprehended without being separated from the eye, it would be proven that there exists a seer who can see.
This position is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because there is no seer.
That form is obtainable means that because the eye, form, space, light, and attention exist, form is obtainable.
Furthermore, when these various conditions are fully assembled, that Devadatta is said to be the "seer"; it is not as the Sāṃkhyas reckon, that a "puruṣa" (spiritual self) is the seer.
Why is this? Because there is no blind person who can see forms.
It is that eye which is able to see that is called the "seer. Just as a lamp, though lacking thought, serves as the cause for illumination, so too is it with the seeing by the eye.
For this reason, even within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no seer.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
the seer has no intrinsic nature; it is called "the seer sees" because visual consciousness arises from the fourfold conjunction [of the eye, form, light, and attention].
The proponent says:

That is subject to the same fault as before; that there exists a distinct seer apart from the fourfold combination of elements is something the world does not know, yet you claim it exists—this argument is untenable.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Apart from the eye, there is no seer, because it lacks an intrinsic nature.
For apart from the seeing of the eye, there is no capacity for seeing that can be collectively designated as a "seer"; this is merely stated according to your own intention.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika position— that in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) the seer sees form—
is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because the eyes are distinct [from the seer], like a jar and so forth, since a seer cannot be established through the first two gates.
Furthermore, if one analyzes the person (*puruṣa*) as the seer, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As a verse says:
"Whether apart from the eye or not apart from the eye, a seer cannot be found;
for that very essence of a seer cannot be seen, whether it possesses eyes or lacks them."
If it is claimed that the seer possesses eyes and is thus able to see, this is also not the case.
Why? Because it is by virtue of the eye having substantial existence that the seeing of forms is established, just as fire is able to burn.
The same applies to seeing with the eye; this should be understood as being spoken of within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If there were a seer distinct from that eye, then even a blind person who lacks eyes would be able to see; however, this is not the case.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"The seer acts together [with the instrument] to be able to see form; it should be known thus, because that [seer] possesses the instrument of action (*karmakaraṇa*).
If this [seer] were without action, then those instruments of action would not exist, just like space."
Because the eye exists, its function is the seeing of forms; thus, one knows there is a seer and that act of seeing.
The proponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), since the eye does not exist at any time, it is incorrect to establish a seer.
As the verse says:
"Because the seer does not exist, both the subject and the object are empty.
The commentary states:
If the seer has no intrinsic nature, then there is nothing to be grasped.
To say that the eye is the instrument for that [seer] and that "one sees with this eye" is logically untenable.
Therefore, your argument that the instrument exists because of its activity is unestablished as a reason; furthermore, it contradicts the actual meaning. Such is the fault.
Furthermore, the followers of our own vehicle (svayānīya) say:

"All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are empty because they depend on causes and conditions and rely upon others; thus, neither the eye nor that self can perceive them, and this principle must be so."
To claim that both the object seen and the subject that sees are entirely without essence is incorrect.
Why? Because those four kinds of effects, such as consciousness and so forth, do exist.
If this [seeing] were non-existent, then that consciousness, contact, sensation, and craving could not be called results, just as in the case of one born blind.
The proponent says:
The objects seen and the act of seeing—this meaning is not established, as has already been refuted previously.
What is now being stated is as the verse says:
"Because the seen and the seer do not exist, the four [factors] beginning with consciousness do not exist.
The commentary states:
Why is it non-existent?
Because its conditions are non-existent.
For this reason, consciousness and the other factors are not established.
Since both the subject and the object are not established, the analogy likewise lacks substantial reality. Some say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), these consciousnesses and so forth do exist, because their effects, such as grasping, possess substantial reality."
The proponent says:
This should be answered as follows.
The verse states:
"Where could that appropriation, which depends on conditions and so forth, ever be found?
The commentary states:
Since consciousness and the other [aggregates] do not exist, appropriation is also not established; such is the meaning of the verse.
"Appropriation" (upādāna) means grasping. How many kinds of it are there? They are:
the appropriation of sensual desire, the appropriation of precepts and vows, the appropriation of the doctrine of self, and the appropriation of views.
With these appropriations as conditions, there arise existence, birth, old age, and death; such faults constantly pursue you."
The opponent’s initial attempt to establish that the eye sees by means of analogies and so forth has already been refuted.
Their arguments regarding the ear, sound, and so on are likewise subject to the same refutation as before.
As the verse says:
"The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as the hearer and that which is heard—
know that these meanings are all likewise excluded, just as in the case of seeing with the eye. Furthermore,
at the beginning of the chapter on the opponent, it was stated that there is going because it produces an effect.
This is also not the case, as stated in the preceding verse.
Therefore, going has no intrinsic nature, and the goer is likewise so; the time of going and all phenomena are entirely non-existent.
For this reason, the externalist's conceptualization that there exists the arising and departing of those entrances (*āyatanas*) is entirely untenable, as previously stated in the refutation.
By means of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the entrances and so forth, faith and understanding are produced; such is the meaning of this chapter, and thus it is established.
As stated in a verse from the *Anabhilāpya-sūtra*:
“The internal and external earth elements have no dual meaning; The Tathāgata’s wisdom is able to awaken to this.
That which is without dual characteristics and non-dual— One should know it thus: as a single characteristic that is without characteristic.”
Furthermore, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottamā-sūtra*:
"Mañjuśrī said to that young girl:
'You should contemplate the elements (*dhātu*).'"
The young girl replied:
"Mañjuśrī! For example, it is just as when the kalpa-fire burns; the three realms and all else are likewise."
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"The eye cannot see forms, The mind does not know phenomena;
This is the unsurpassed truth, Which the world cannot comprehend."
Furthermore, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Regarding all those phenomena (*dharma*), there is no knower and no seer; even that teacher who expounds them cannot be apprehended."
"It cannot be conceptualized by the mind, nor can it be known by the intellect.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Bhagavatī Sūtra*:
"O Sister!..."
The eye does not see forms, and so on, up to the mind not cognizing phenomena.
Thus, because awakening is detached, the eye is detached from forms, and so on, up to because awakening is detached, the mind is detached from phenomena, and so forth.
Furthermore, as the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra: "Good son!
Form does not constitute the object of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not constitute the objects of consciousness and so forth, because objects do not exist."
O Paramavīra!
Form does not know form; form does not see form.
If form neither knows nor sees, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Even so it is for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they are neither known nor seen.
This concludes the commentary on the "Examination of the Faculties" (*Indriya-parīkṣā*).

**Chapter Four: Examination of the Five Aggregates (*Pañca-skandha-parīkṣā*)** Furthermore, this chapter is presented in order to cause [the reader] to understand that the aggregates (*skandha*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Some say: Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there exist the sense-bases (āyatana) and so forth. Why is this?
Because they are subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*).
If they did not exist, those bases of cognition (*āyatana*), such as form, would not be subsumed under the aggregates, like a flower in the sky.
Since the various bases do exist, they are subsumed under those aggregates; for example, the ten types of bases of form are subsumed under the single aggregate of form.
The dharma-āyatana comprises three aggregates—namely, feeling, perception, and formations—as well as that portion of the form aggregate to which it belongs;
the mind-āyatana is subsumed within the consciousness aggregate.
For these reasons, the āyatanas and so forth exist in the ultimate sense.
The proponent says:
That which is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is, briefly stated, of two kinds:
the four great elements (mahābhūta) and that which is derived from them (upādāya-rūpa).
If all distinctions, such as those of the three periods of time, are collectively termed the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),

and if an opponent wishes to take that which is subsumed under the aggregates of the eye and so forth as the cause, then because form is coarse and easy to understand, it shall be analyzed and explained first.
As the verse says:
"If one is separated from the cause of form, then form cannot be apprehended.
The commentary explains:
What is the cause of that form?
It refers to the four great elements, such as earth and so forth.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), form cannot be found apart from these.
Yet, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), form is provisionally designated based on the four great elements as its cause.

However, when analyzed from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), form is found to lack reality because it does not admit its own cause and because the cognition thereof lacks substantiality.
If the cause itself is not apprehended and the cognition lacks intrinsic nature, then that [object] is truly non-existent, like an army or similar constructs.
That the cause of form cannot be grasped and the cognition of form lacks intrinsic nature is likewise the case.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the essence of the object of cognition regarding form (*rūpa*) does not truly exist. Why?
Because it is a cognition;
for example, like the cognition of a forest and so forth.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the objects of the words "form" and "sound" lack reality. Why?
Because they are heard, just like the sound of an army or similar things.
If it is argued that the aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*) are not "exclusive" (*ekāntika*), this argument is incorrect. Why?
Because mental factors (*caitasika*) such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise excluded; thus, they are not non-exclusive.
Some may claim that in the ultimate sense (paramārtha) there exists that real form (rūpa). Why?
Because the cognition of that form remains unchanged despite its transformation.

If the object undergoes change and the cognition is likewise distinct, then this exists conventionally, such as a jar; however, when the color blue changes over time, that cognition remains without difference.
For this reason, one knows that there is substantial form (*rūpa*).
The proponent says:
because it is proven to be without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Having already examined the cause of form, one next refutes the four great elements.
As the verse says:
"If one were to depart from form, The cause of form would likewise not be seen."
The commentary states:
Since these various causes—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth—are all mutually distinct, that form cannot be perceived or grasped within its causes, such as the earth element and others.
For this reason, the author of this treatise first negates that stage at the outset.
What is the purpose of negating that stage and so forth?
It is because there is a great significance [to doing so].
What is the great meaning?
That which arises from causes within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) has, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), no real production.
This lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is as stated in a verse of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"Devoid of accumulation, it has no intrinsic nature;
since that cognition is ungraspable, one knows that dependent origination is empty. Therefore, I teach that there is no self-nature.
No thing arises from conditions, and no thing ceases from conditions."
"Arising is merely the arising of conditions; cessation is merely the cessation of conditions.
The commentary states:
By this expedient means, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), earth is not substantially existent. Thus it is determined that its cause cannot be perceived, because it is not seen.
If one does not perceive something because it is invisible, then in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) that thing does not truly exist, just like an army or similar constructs.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, the objective referent of the cognition of "earth" does not have a real existence as its essence.
Why is this? Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of a forest and so forth.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the referential object of the word "earth" has no reality.
Why is this? Because it is heard, just like the sound of an army or similar things.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no distinct color apart from its own composite parts.
Why is this? Because that [object] cannot be apprehended, as its cognition lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like the intrinsic nature of earth and so forth.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya says:
As for your statement that "form and so forth are not different from earth and so forth," this establishes what I have already established.
The proponent of the treatise says:
It is because difference is negated; it is not by means of non-difference that you are led to understanding.
As for your erroneous distinction that they are not different, I do not accept it.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"The reason you have put forward does not suffer from the fallacy of being non-conclusive (anaikāntika)."
Why is this? Just as if one does not take up a lamp, there is no cognition of a jar, because that [lamp] is also distinct [from the jar].
The proponent says:
You have spoken incorrectly; I merely negate that cognition has no reality because its constituent parts, when combined, cannot be apprehended, and I do not discuss other matters.
Although the lamp itself lacks intrinsic reality, the cognition of the jar arises due to the light of jewels, medicinal herbs, the sun, the moon, and so forth.
Apart from the constituent parts of its own synthesis, no other distinct color can be found.
For this reason, your analogy is incorrect; for the lamp is not a constituent part of the synthesis of that jar itself.
There is no separate entity [of difference], yet this is not the fallacy of non-universality (*anaikāntika*).
As the verse says:
"It is not the case that this thing and that thing are different."
The commentary states:
This meaning will be explained later.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the claim that the lamp is distinct from the jar is also not established.
For this reason, there is no fault of being non-exclusive.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"That army and its constituents are a collective reality, because they exist from the very beginning."
Regarding your statement that earth and the other elements lack substantial reality, and that you establish a proof to bring about understanding, your analogy is unestablished.
The proponent says:
the various components of an army are not the primary cause for the initial arising of that army as a whole.
Why is this? Because it is a totality, like the various parts of a tree—its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves.
Those constituent parts, such as the elephants and so forth within an army, are not the primary cause for the initial arising of that army.
Why is this? Because it is not applicable, just like the sūtras and so forth.
Nor is the analogy devoid of substance, as the verse says:
If one were to be separated from form (*rūpa*), the cause of form would also not be perceived.

As established previously through the thesis, the reason, and the example, it is verified that those [elements] such as form are no different from those such as earth, and that those such as earth are no different from those such as form.
If they were different, it would contradict what was previously refuted;

if they were not different, it would be sublated by what follows later. For if they were not different, milk would be identical to curd, and curd would likewise be identical to milk, because they are not different.
For this reason, this proof is established.
As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"No entity exists apart from [its parts], Like bundles of reeds or in a separate location."
"Whether as one or as different, these are the false discriminations of ordinary beings.
The commentary states:
Just as with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth, they [the opponents] seek to establish them by asserting that they exist because of a cause.
To regard this as a cause is untenable, for such a cause is not established and it contradicts the meaning [of the doctrine].
Furthermore, if you distinguish that form exists apart from its causes, this too is not so.
Why is this? Because it entails faults.
As a verse states:
"If there were form apart from the cause of form, then form would fall into being causeless.
Commentary:
Those who propound the absence of causes claim that they wish for form to exist without a cause.
He should ask as follows:
"Even if what you say were consistent with reason, of which things would those 'uncaused seeds' you speak be?
We do not wish for it to be so," as the verse says:
“There is no such case where a thing exists without a cause.
The commentary asks:
What is the meaning of this?
Because its essence cannot be manifested through any analogy, to deny its cause would entail a grave error.
This position is untenable, as it has already been refuted in the "Examination of Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*) chapter.
The Sāṃkhya says:

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), earth and the other elements truly exist, because their qualities such as color (*rūpa*) are not different [from them], just like the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of color itself.
The proponent (*vādī*) says:
Your reason is unestablished, and your example likewise lacks substance.
This is because the non-difference of form and so forth, as well as the intrinsic nature of form, have already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, some say:
In the ultimate sense, those elements such as earth exist. Why?
Because their effects exist.
If these [elements] did not exist, their effects would not exist, like flowers in the sky.
Since the color of the effect now exists, earth and the other elements are not non-existent.
This position is incorrect, as the verse says:
"If there were a cause apart from form, this cause would have no effect;
how could it be logical for there to be a cause without an effect?
The commentary states:
If there were a cause for form that existed apart from its effects such as form itself, this would constitute a cause existing without an effect. Why?
Because they would be distinct, just like bamboo splinters and the like.
Furthermore, that cause is also a collection of form and so forth.
For this reason, cause and effect are not established.
Since the existence of an effect as you describe it serves as a cause, it contradicts the logical meaning; therefore, this position is untenable.
Furthermore, if one analyzes whether this form exists or does not exist, both positions are untenable because the cause would be rendered useless.
As the verse says:
"If form already existed, It would not depend on the causes of form."
"If form did not exist previously, it would also not depend on the cause of form.
The commentary states:
"If form existed previously, it would have no need for a cause."
Why is this? Because it exists, just like that jar or cloth.
If form did not exist previously, it would be non-existent, like other such things; the meaning is as follows.
Furthermore, those who maintain that there is no cause claim that the cause has no substantiality.
This position is incorrect, as the verse says:
"If form exists without a cause, This principle is not tenable."
The commentary states:
Within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the claim that form (*rūpa*) is without cause is likewise incorrect.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
Regarding the existence of future form (*rūpa*), the answer is the same as in the preceding verse.
Furthermore, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), since the cause has not yet grasped its fruit, form lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
To say that it exists is not logically tenable.
For this reason, to maintain at all times that the four great elements and the derived matter exist is contrary to the meaning.
As the verse says:
"Therefore, regarding the object of form, one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination."
The commentary says:
How is it distinguished?

It means that there is substantial form (*rūpa*), or because the causes—such as earth and so forth—are not different from the effect, and the effect is not different from the cause, there are such distinctions of form, color, and shape.
One should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding this object, for it does not avoid the faults previously mentioned.
Those with keen wisdom who wish to attain true non-conceptual gnosis should observe it with careful attention: just as what is seen in a dream is not so upon waking, that gnosis is likewise.
Furthermore, some say:

When a subsequent fruit arises from the successive continuity of the functional capacity of a prior cause, the characteristic of that causal power is also visible; it is like white cotton cloth dyed with the juice of purple lacquer, which, through the process of perfuming (vāsanā), continues in succession until the color becomes perceptible at the time of the subsequent fruit.
To refute this attachment, it is said in verse:
"If the effect were similar to the cause, this principle would not be so.
The commentary states:
This proves that it is not the cause of its effect; such is the meaning of the statement. Why is this?

Because, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one does not intend for a thread of blue color and so forth to be the cause of a cloth of blue color and so forth on the grounds of their similarity, just as in the case of other blue cloths and the like.
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:
Your claim that the other causes for that blue cloth are likewise non-existent is not correct. Why is this so?
Since the analogy you have established lacks a real entity,
the proponent says:
"You have not stated it well."
When that cloth arises, this cause is not applicable, because it does not constitute that cloth; thus, the analogy is established.
Furthermore, those of our own school say:

there are similar causes and effects and dissimilar causes and effects. Although there is a difference in time between preceding and succeeding moments, within the category of things—just as the flame of a lamp flickers and ceases moment by moment—this is called similar cause and effect.
Just as burning wood produces ash or transforming milk into curd, these are called dissimilar causes and effects.
The proponent says:
those similar causes and effects have already been refuted previously.
Regarding those that are dissimilar, this is refuted as follows now.
The verse says:
"If the effect were not similar to the cause, then the principle would likewise not hold."
The commentary states:
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is established that this grain seed is not the cause of the sprout. Why is this so?
Because they are dissimilar, it is like broken shards of pottery.

Or, it may be argued that the rice grain is the cause of its sprout, because the sprout exists only when the grain exists and can thus be pointed out, just as in the case of the sound of a large drum or a barley sprout.
The proponent says:
You have not stated it well,
because all things that arise are negated.
Because the analogy lacks a substantial basis, it is insufficient to establish the point;
since this fault exists, the objection—that the production of effects such as consciousness by causes such as the eye-faculties is not analogous and thus not invariably uniform—is likewise untenable.

Why is this? Just as all phenomena have been refuted, so too are the visual consciousness and the others likewise negated; since there is no other alternative way [to establish them], it is not the fault of being non-conclusive.
As previously stated, the claim that "because there are real entities such as earth and so forth, their effects exist" is unestablished in both cases, for it contradicts the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas say:
"Because the efficient cause exists"—meaning that when conditioned phenomena arise, all similar and dissimilar dharmas serve as their causes—this [opponent's] analogy lacks substance.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect because there is a distinction [to be made].
For we have already refuted the notion that the causes—such as those arising from their own nature (*svabhāva*), the non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), and so forth—are capable of producing [an effect].

From the beginning of this chapter, these various passages have already refuted the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivative matter (*upādāyarūpa*), enabling others to understand that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) lacks intrinsic substance.
As for the remaining aggregates, such as the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) and so forth, it is as the verse says:
"The aggregate of sensation and the mental aggregate, as well as perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and all other kinds [of phenomena],"
"All such dharmas as these are likewise obscured by the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The commentary states:
"Just as the aggregate of form is negated, so too are sensation (*vedanā*) and the others."

It has already been stated that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), form (*rūpa*) is not substantially real because it does not apprehend its own causes and because the cognition thereof lacks intrinsic nature, like an army and so forth.

Likewise, from the perspective of ultimate truth, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and so on, are all not substantially real because they do not apprehend their own causes and they themselves are not apprehended, like an army and so forth.
All other cases should also be understood in this same manner.
Furthermore, the causes of sensation and so forth—namely contact, as well as visible form, light, space, and mental attention—should be refuted accordingly, as appropriate.
Furthermore, as it has already been made understood by others that the causes such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not distinct,

so too, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the causes such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are likewise without distinction, because their own constituent parts cannot be apprehended through internal conjunction.
He should not accept [the argument] as being like its own cause or its own nature; the fault in this case should also be addressed as previously explained.
If the opponent were to raise such a fault, it should be avoided as before.

Furthermore, regarding these aforementioned phenomena, it refers to the conceptual distinctions—such as those of jars, clothing, and so forth—pertaining to all conditioned phenomena external to the aggregates (*skandha*), which are [asserted by others] to be substantially existent and distinct.

If one argues that [the self] is excluded from form (*rūpa*) by virtue of being included within the aggregates (*skandha*), such as form and so forth—just as it is appropriately excluded from those forms—then this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks substance, because the meaning of the aggregates would be destroyed.

That which is subsumed under the aggregates (skandhas) is subsumed within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and not within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), because it contradicts the meaning of causality.
These various principles should be understood in this way.

Furthermore, there may be those who engage in false conceptualization and discrimination, asserting that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whatever entity possesses a non-empty intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or undergoes arising and ceasing; all such points of contention are incorrect.
Why is this? Because when one observes those marks as they truly are, they are empty.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the various bases (*āyatana*) do not arise, for their substance is not truly existent; observing in this way causes people to gain such knowledge.
If one maintains that the non-empty creates a logical fault for the empty, this too is not the case.
Why? Because it is refuted in the same manner as before.
Nothing whatsoever can invalidate emptiness, as the verse says:
"If one contemplates the nature of a single entity, One sees the nature of all entities;
In this way, if one entity is empty, All are empty."
The commentary states:

Since the preceding passages have refuted the arising of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and clarified for the practitioner that the aggregates (*skandha*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the meaning of this chapter is thus established.
As the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Paramavīrya:
"Good son! Because form has neither arising nor ceasing, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have neither arising nor ceasing."
If those five aggregates neither arise nor cease, this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Son of good family!
Form is detached from the intrinsic nature of form; likewise, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
If form through consciousness are all devoid of intrinsic nature, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Son of good family!
Because form has no intrinsic nature, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no intrinsic nature.
"If form through to consciousness are without intrinsic nature, this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Brahmaviśeṣacintiparipṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"I have taught the aggregates (*skandha*) for the sake of the world; those aggregates are the support for that world."
One who does not rely upon those aggregates attains liberation from all worldly phenomena.
The world is like the characteristic of space, and that characteristic of space is itself non-existent.
Through such understanding, being without reliance, one cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
“Subhūti, a bodhisattva does not dwell on form when practicing giving; he does not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.”
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"The three realms of existence are mere designations, for things lack intrinsic nature;
it is only within these designations that false imagination constructs distinctions."
"When analyzed through discernment, its own essence cannot be found;
because it lacks an own-essence, even that verbal expression does not exist.
Such sūtras as these should be cited here at length.
The commentary on the "Examination of the Five Aggregates" is concluded. 5.

Examination of the Six Elements (*Ṣaḍdhātu-parīkṣā*). In the fifth chapter, the *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, the examination of the six elements: Furthermore, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they are the objects to be countered by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Now, wishing further to clarify the meaning that the various elements such as earth lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this chapter is composed.
What is this meaning?
As stated in the *Examination of the Aggregates* (*Skandha-parīkṣā*): "If one is separated from form (*rūpa*), there is no cause of form."
In this regard, our own school further cites the Buddha’s words as proof, as it is said in a sutra:
The Buddha told the Great King,
“There are six elements:”
Earth, water, fire, wind, as well as space and consciousness, each have their own characteristics: namely, solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, receptivity, and discernment.
"These six elements are designated as the 'person' (puruṣa).

If one were to designate a "person" based on the existence of something like a flower in the sky—which does not exist—such a meaning would be untenable. Therefore, the proponent's previously established thesis that the substance of the causes of form, such as earth and so forth, does not exist, is thereby destroyed; furthermore, it contradicts the Āgamas.
The proponent says:

For the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the Tathāgata spoke of these six elements, such as earth and so forth, as constituting a person (*puruṣa*); this is not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
In the ultimate sense, the elements such as earth and so forth exist. Why?
Because their characteristics exist.
If these elements such as earth were non-existent in reality, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of their characteristics, just like flowers in the sky.
Now, since there exist solidity and so forth as the characteristics of earth and the other elements, and because these characteristics exist, earth and the others are not non-existent.
The proponent says:
Space lacks intrinsic nature and requires little effort [to refute], because it is understood that it is not a real entity.
Once the realm of space has been understood [as such], the remaining realms can easily be negated.
As the verse says:
"Prior to space, there was nothing; not even the slightest mark of space existed.
The commentary explains:
Space and its characteristic of non-obstruction—these two are not distinct; such is the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"I establish this doctrine that non-obstruction is the characteristic of space, because that characteristic exists."
The proponent says:
This establishment of non-obstruction as existence cannot be understood by others.
What is the meaning of this?

For example, "sound is impermanent" is the proposition (*pratijñā*), and "because it is impermanent" is adduced as the reason (*hetu*); likewise, "this space exists" is the proposition, and "because space exists" is the reason.
This constitutes merely a thesis (*pratijñā*) without a reason (*hetu*) or an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); thus, the meaning is not established.

If you intend that space (*ākāśa*) is characterized by non-obstruction, and that this is understood by all people according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) such that it need not be explained to others for their understanding—this is because such a definition is not established from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, one must certainly state the reason for its understanding so that others may comprehend it.
If he were to state such [a reason], it would entail the fallacies of having a reason (*hetu*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because there is only the thesis (*pratijñā*) itself.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"Space truly exists; it is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
To answer that, as the verse says:
"In this context, when examining space, there is not even a hair’s breadth of substantial reality.
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), space is not real.
Why? Because it is unproduced (*anutpanna*), like the horns of a rabbit.
Thus, because the cause lacks intrinsic nature and because the effect does not exist, one should explain at length through various reasons such as "because it does not exist" and so forth.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"Because the two dharmas—the characterized and the characteristic—are distinct."
The proponent says:
If that were so, they would possess a sequence of priority and posteriority, like a jar, a garment, and so forth.
To answer this, as the verse states:
"If space existed prior [to things], then space would be without characteristics.
The commentary states:
Space is without characteristics; such is the meaning of the verse.
Herein, a proof is stated: space is not that which is characterized by those characteristics. Why?
Because it already exists prior [to them], like any given object.
Furthermore, non-obstruction is not the characteristic of space. Why?
Because they are distinct from one another, just like any given object.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that both the characterized (lakṣya) and the characterizer (lakṣaṇa) are without characteristics (alakṣaṇa), this too is not the case. Why?
Because I also abandon the conceptualization of difference.
Furthermore, if you claim that the cause and non-cause as spoken of in conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) are not established, you cannot avoid the fault of contradicting your own tenets.
Therefore, since both the characteristics of being distinct and non-distinct are unestablished, one knows that space is definitively without characteristics (animitta).
If one were to say that there is an essence despite the absence of characteristics, people would be unable to know it.
For this reason, as the verse says:
"There is nowhere a single thing that possesses an essence while lacking characteristics."
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), if this entity were established as either self-constituted or other-constituted, such a proposition would not hold true. Some may say:
If the space that is the characterized object were to exist as a substantial entity such that a characteristic could function upon it, this would also be incorrect. As the verse says:
"Since there is no substance of the uncharacterized, where could a characteristic function?"
The commentary states:

Because that which is supported (the substratum) lacks intrinsic nature, that which supports it (the dependent) also lacks intrinsic nature; since the meaning [of the argument] is not established, this is further a fault in the reason (*hetu-doṣa*).
Furthermore, if the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) were not distinct, how could the characterized itself serve as the characteristic for the characterized?
Because that distinct characteristic lacks intrinsic nature,
for this reason, within the absence of distinct categories, space is without characteristics (*animitta*).

If one were to speak of characteristics through distinct categories, they too would not be characteristics, because the characterized (*lakṣya*) would be distinct [from them], just as in the case of any single object and so forth.
Since such characteristics have no essence, emptiness likewise has no characteristic; thus the verse says, "there is no essence that lacks characteristics," which refers to space (*ākāśa*).
As for the question, "Where do characteristics function?"—it is because they do not function therein.
This meaning should be understood.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The characteristic of the signless does not proceed; the characteristic of that which has signs does not proceed."
The commentary states:
As you have said, the meanings of the characteristic and the characterized are both untenable. Why is this so?
If there were a characteristic without that substance, this would not be established;
the same applies to the existence of the substance itself.
The verse says:
"Devoid of both existence and non-existence, it does not function in another place either.
The commentary states:
It is entirely incorrect to claim that within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is a single entity whose characteristics function therein.
Why is this? Because the analogy lacks substantiality, the meaning intended by the opponent is not established.
Furthermore, just as a flower in the sky and so forth lack characteristics, those characteristics are likewise non-existent.

Because they lack intrinsic nature, their transformation cannot be described; this is understood by all in the world. Therefore, the verse says: "The characteristic does not transform its characteristic," as it is verified through investigation according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That which is unobstructed does not have the characteristic of space. Why?
Because it possesses characteristics, such as the characteristics of solidity and so forth.
Furthermore, some may say:
"The characteristics of existence and non-existence revolve within the nature of things; thus, there is no fault.
To refute this, the verse says: "Apart from existence and non-existence, it does not revolve elsewhere either; neither of these two is tenable."
As for that fixed position [of yours], it shall be extensively refuted later in the "Chapter on the Fuel and the Fire.
First, as for the fault of the two parts [of the argument] which you previously sought to make others understand, it now reverts to you; this is inconsistent because it entails two faults.
Furthermore, some say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), space exists because it possesses its own characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
If it were non-existent, its characteristics would not be predicated, just like a flower in the sky."
As the Sūtra states, the Buddha told the Great King:
"These six elements are called the 'person' (puruṣa).
Therefore, they exist and function as its defining characteristics.
The proponent says:
The establishment of the characterized object has already been refuted by me previously.
As the verse states:
"Because the characterized (*lakṣya*) is not established, the characterizer (*lakṣaṇa*) is also not established.
The commentary states:
Since the characterizer also falls within the category of the characterized, the characteristic itself is not established; thus, the analogy lacks a real entity (*avastu*).
For this reason, when one observes with wisdom the characterized and the characteristic, neither is established.
As the verse says:
"Therefore, there is no characterized, Nor is there any characteristic."
The commentary states:
Because he causes others to understand that there is no essence to be verified, it is known through this verification that they truly lack essence; thus, this meaning is established.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
According to our established tenet, space possesses substantial reality. Why is this so?
Because it has severed the defilements of desire regarding its objects, it is like form (*rūpa*);
because it is the object of samāpatti, it is like consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is like nirvāṇa.
The proponent says:
If you wish to establish that this space exists within the ultimate sense (paramārtha), is it the characterized (lakṣya) or is it the characteristic (lakṣaṇa)?
Both [positions] are incorrect, as has already been explained to bring about understanding.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Distinct from the characterized and the characterizer, this essence does not exist either."
The commentary states:
Such is the position of our own school; for [the arguments] regarding other things such as *nirvāṇa* fail to establish even a single entity, as their analogies are all unproven.
Furthermore, proponents of another school say:
"Space exists because it possesses a self-nature and because it is conditioned.
