Both this thesis and its reason are unestablished; as with the previously cited refutation, one should speak in this manner.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas say:
"According to our established doctrine, that which is truly non-obstructive is designated as 'space. Space has no substantial essence; it is merely a conventional designation. Such is our position."
The proponent says:

As stated by the Vaibhāṣika masters, because it is the object of samāpatti and because desire-taint is abandoned through that objective sphere, they establish that emptiness has a substantial entity in order to lead people to understanding.

Now, the Sautrāntikas maintain that what is called "space" is merely a provisional designation for the absence of actual resistance; it has no substantial reality and serves only to exclude the existence of prior entities.
Such a position makes my analogy even more evident.
Now, this meaning is explained as follows in verse:
"If form existed apart from the causes of form, This principle would not be so;
Since form originally has no intrinsic nature, How could that which lacks intrinsic nature be established?"
The commentary states:

As previously explained in the "Examination of the Aggregates" (*Skandhaparīkṣā*), it is logically untenable for there to be an obstructive name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Just as the sūtras analyze space as being without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*) to bring about understanding through investigation, this [proposed] meaning is not established.
Some say: "The fact that space has an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not understood by people because there is no analogy for it.
I shall now establish a thesis so that people may easily understand; it should be stated thus: Form and the other [aggregates] have an intrinsic nature, because their non-existence is observed."
If this [subject] exists, one observes that its essence is non-existent, just as, for example, the two—form and taste—lack an essence.
If a dharma lacks an essence, it is not observed when absent, just as, for example, a horse’s horn.
The proponent says:
I have already refuted the notion that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
I do not wish for you to accept their lack of intrinsic nature either; as the verse says:
"It has no essence.
The commentary states:
This refers to the name "form" (*rūpa*).
The verse says:
"Where? The commentary says:
Because of its nature as a flavor.
The verse says:
"How could that which lacks intrinsic substance be apprehended?"
The commentary states:
Since that form does not exist, the analogy lacks substance; thus, the intended meaning is undermined—this should be understood.
The opponent says:
Both existence and non-existence are existent, because that which understands them exists.
If that which understands exists, then those things exist.
The proponent says:
You claim that the one who understands understands both existence and non-existence; yet, is this one who understands possessed of an essence, or is he without an essence?
Both positions have already been refuted; thus, the proposition that the one who understands possesses an essence is not established.
Furthermore, because it is dissimilar to both that which has an entity and that which lacks an entity,
any conceptual interpretation other than this is incorrect.
As the verse says:
"If it differs from both existence and non-existence, where could there be a knower?
The commentary states:
"The knower has no substantial existence; such is the meaning of the verse."
The opponent speaks again:
"I have another approach for making this distinction; one who understands it in this way [does so] because it is not similar to that which possesses an essence or lacks an essence."
The proponent says:

It is not the case that those dissimilar entities constitute a single thing possessing two parts, because they are contradictory; thus, even observation cannot be established, and there is nothing that can be verified to lead one to believe it.
Thus, when space is examined with discernment, it is found to be unreasonable [as a substantial entity]. As the verse says:
"Therefore, know that space Is neither an entity nor a non-entity;
It is neither the characterized nor the characterizer; The other five [elements] are the same as space."
The commentary states:
Just as one causes others to believe and accept that not even a hair’s breadth of space exists by means of negation, the same applies to the other five [elements].
As the verse says:
"Prior to the earth and so forth, not even a hair’s breadth of a characteristic can be found.
The commentary states:
The elements of water and so forth should likewise be explained in detail through such analysis.
Even as the verse says: "Neither an entity nor a non-entity, neither the characterized nor the characteristic; this should be understood in the same way as the negation of space.
What is meant by "element" (*dhātu*)?
The meaning of "store" (*garbha*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*), just as in the case of a gold mine.
This is because that space and so forth can serve as the store for sorrow, suffering, and the like.

Furthermore, the meaning of "element" is the sense of maintaining its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) without effort. These elements are taught for the purpose of converting sentient beings; out of compassion, the Buddha’s words speak of them, yet they are subsumed within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the element has no intrinsic nature, and thus even the "entrances" (*āyatana*) are not established.
Because the elements (*dhātu*) exist, what you desire is not refuted.
Furthermore, some say:

"If, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all meanings of terms are denied as non-existent, this is the teaching of the Lokāyata heresy; though it resembles the Buddha’s words, it should be rejected because it is not the Buddha’s word."
The proponent says:
You have given rise to an increase in the cataracts of error, for you falsely attempt to negate things such as unreal hairs, mosquitoes, and flies.
What is the meaning of this?
When I speak of negating entry into existence, I negate the intrinsic nature of existence, not its lack of nature.
As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Existence and non-existence are both extremes, And so on, up to the range of the mind’s activity;..."
"When that mental activity has ceased, it is called the cessation of the correct mind. Commentary:
Thus, one does not cling to existence as a substance, nor does one cling to non-existence as a substance.
If phenomena have no intrinsic nature, then nothing at all can be produced.
As the verse says:
"To negate existence by saying 'it is non-existent' is not to grasp at non-existence."
"Just as one negates that blue is non-blue, one does not intend to describe it as white.
Commentary: These two types of views are called unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Therefore, those possessed of wisdom who wish to bring an end to conceptual proliferation and attain the bliss of nirvana without remainder must suppress these two kinds of evil views. How, then, is this to be done?

Whether they are comprised within the three realms or are supramundane, whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—just as various activities are undertaken according to conventional truth—if those [activities] possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then the diligent application of effort to perform these various deeds, such as wholesome and unwholesome acts, would be empty and fruitless.
Why is this? Because it exists prior [to its production].
For example, it is like a jar, a garment, or other such things that exist prior [to their manifestation].

Thus, those who possess pleasure always possess pleasure, and those who possess suffering always possess suffering; just as the forms, dimensions, postures, and features of figures painted on a wall remain unchanging, so too should it be for all sentient beings.

Furthermore, if there were no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the diligent application of effort toward the arising of wholesome or unwholesome supramundane dharmas—which are subsumed within the three realms—would be empty and fruitless, because they would not exist. In this way, the world would fall into nihilism; it would be like trying to polish and sharpen a rabbit’s horn until it becomes sharp—it can never be achieved.
Therefore, the verse says:
"One of little wisdom who views all phenomena As either existent or non-existent and so forth—
Such a person does not see The cessation of views, the ultimate truth."
Furthermore, as the Buddha told Kāśyapa in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*:
"Existence is one extreme; non-existence is another extreme.
In this way, both the internal earth element and the external earth element are devoid of duality."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, realize this through their true wisdom; they attain perfect enlightenment as the non-dual, single characteristic, which is to say, the "characteristicless.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī asked a virtuous woman:
"Sister!..."
“How does one contemplate the elements?
The woman replied, “Mañjuśrī!
"Just as when the world is consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, the world becomes empty and void, with not a single thing visible.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"The world has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics."
"If one can know in this way, one will attain liberation from the world.
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail here.
This concludes the commentary on the "Examination of the Six Elements" chapter.
