Verse Text by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñāmitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Six: An Examination of Defilement and the One Who is Defiled. Furthermore, all phenomena are empty.
Why is this? Because that which is defiled and the defiler, as well as that which is hateful and the hater, are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This chapter is composed so that one may thoroughly understand the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Some say: Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there exist the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Why is this so?
The Blessed One has taught that it is the cause of defiled faults;
if this did not exist, the Buddha would not have taught it to be the cause of defilement, just as, for example, one cannot speak of the hair of a tortoise.
How is this known through scriptural evidence?
A verse in the Sūtra says:
"The defiled one does not know the Dharma; the defiled one does not see the Dharma."
"If a person accepts this with complacency, they are called utterly blind and dark.
The commentary states:
Just as it is with the defilement and the defiled one, so it is with ignorance and the other [afflictions] that constitute blindness and darkness.
Therefore, one should know that those aggregates and so forth exist.
The proponent says:

Those aggregates and so forth manifest as a collection of formations, an increase of causes for defilement, and faults; likewise, the defiled subject and those defilements are, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), like a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas, and are not [existent] in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

Contemplate this truthfully: regarding this discrimination of yours, does the defilement exist prior to the defiled one, or does the defiled one exist prior to the defilement, or do both the defilement and the defiled one exist simultaneously?
All three [positions] are incorrect, as the verse states:
"If the defiled one existed prior [to defilement], The defiled one would be established apart from defilement.
The commentary explains:
"Attachment" is a synonym for "craving.
If one who is attached were to be separated from attachment yet still be called "one who is attached," this would not be the case. Why is that?
If there is no fruit when it is ripe, how can it be called ripe?
As the verse says:
"Because of passion, the impassioned one is obtained; yet the impassioned one and passion are not [established as such]."
The commentary states:
If these were distinct and separate—such that "this is the defiled phenomenon" and "this is the defiler"—then even one who is free from defilement would still be called a defiler.
Furthermore, for a defiler to give rise to defilement would ultimately be impossible.
How is this known through verification?
A defiled entity cannot be designated as "the defiler" if it lacks a defiled essence, because it is observed [as such], just like the essence of defilement itself.
Furthermore, the Abhidharmikas say:
As my verse states: "Defilement is called the pervasive cause; it first arises within its own level.
Therefore, that which is defiled can serve as the cause of defilement; such is the meaning of the characteristics of the Abhidharma.
The proponent states in verse:
"Since the defiler already exists beforehand, where could defilement arise again?
The commentary explains:

Just as one who is not defiled is only called a "defiler" when defilement arises at a later time, if that defiler were already established by name beforehand, it would be illogical to say that this defiler again gives rise to defilement; for such a case lacks any essential nature, as it cannot be verified.
The meaning is as follows.
Furthermore, it is just as when there is defilement within the continuum of Devadatta, that defiled Devadatta does not act as a cause for its own realization. Why is this?
Because it is that which is stained, like, for example, Yajñadatta.
The opponent says:

Because neither a distinct nor a non-distinct continuum can be the cause of staining, the formulation regarding "that which is stained" commits the fault of proving what is already established; furthermore, the analogy lacks a real entity and contradicts the intended meaning.
The proponent says: That argument is incorrect.

Because the defilement of a distinct continuum is not the cause [of that defilement], the agent of defilement acts through the gateway of the defiled; thus, there is no fault of "establishing what has already been established."
The defilements and the defiled person belonging to that distinct continuum should likewise be refuted.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the analogy lacks substance; for the similarity of what is to be established and the method of exclusion do not contradict the intended meaning.
The opponent says:
There exists a cause for that which is produced, namely, one who is defiled within another's continuum; since this too serves as a cause for defilement, the analogy lacks substance.
The proponent replies:
This is inconsistent, for it precludes a non-common cause; thus, this fault is not real.
Furthermore, if you insist that the defiled phenomenon exists prior to the defiled person, that too is not so.
As the verse says:
"If there is defilement, whether existent or non-existent, the defiler likewise incurs the same fault.
If the defiler exists prior to defilement, then defilement would be established apart from the defiler."
The commentary states:
What does this mean?
If the defiled subject existed prior to that defiling dharma, this would entail a logical error.

It is because one says "this is defilement" and "this is the defiled one" that there is something which is defiled; thus it is called "defilement. It does not mean that the basis exists prior [to the defilement], just as in the case of "cooked rice."
If you wish to maintain that there is a defiled phenomenon without reference to a defiled person, this is also not the case.
As the verse says:
"A defilement could be established apart from a defiled person; yet such a thing is not desired."
The commentary states:
For example, a cooked object does not arise from observing a cooked object.
How is this verified?
It is not the case that there is a defiling factor while the defiler lacks intrinsic nature. Why?
Because it is observed, just as in the case of the defiler's own intrinsic nature.
The opponent says:
Just as with the two entities of father and son, because they are not invariably [identical], this point is established.
The proponent says:
This is also without fault because it is negated in the same manner.
The opponent says:
Just as a preceding moment that has already arisen and ceased acts as the cause for a future defiled moment that is about to arise, there is therefore no fault.
The proponent states in verse:
"Where could one ever find both defilement and a defiled subject?
The commentary explains:
In this way, it is impossible for a moment of defilement to arise at a later time, followed immediately by a moment of a defiled agent, because such a defiled agent is not established.

Just as that which is a maturation is not itself the entity "maturation," so too it is not logically tenable that a past moment of defilement arising is established as the cause for a present defiled agent.
Why is it not so? For example, Devadatta’s defilement is not the cause for one who is defiled by Devadatta. Why is this?
Because it is defiled, just as, for example, a separate continuum is defiled.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"The thesis we establish is free from the aforementioned faults."
Why is this so? Because that defilement and the defiled one arise simultaneously, there is no fault.
The proponent says:
This too has a fault; you should now listen.
As the verse says:
"It is not possible for the two—the defilement and the defiled one—to arise simultaneously."
"In this way, defilement and the defiled do not exist in mutual dependence.
The commentary asks:
For what reason does this conceptualization arise?

If one were to analyze based on the premise that there is no cause, one could distinguish that "this is the defiled subject" and "that is the defiling factor," or "this is the defiling factor" and "that is the defiled subject"; yet, such [distinctions] are not desired.
What, then, is this? It is because there is observation of desire.
Herein is established the proof: that defilement and the defiled one do not have the sense of arising simultaneously.
Why is this? Because there is observation, just as in the case of a seed and a sprout.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
What is the meaning of this reason you have put forward?
Is it called "with observation" because it observes arising,
or is it called "with observation" because it observes distinct terminology?

If it is argued that they are "with observation" (sāvalambana) because they observe arising, then the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) would also be constantly accompanied by one another and arise simultaneously, because they share a common cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Furthermore, it is like the wick and the light of a lamp, which also arise simultaneously; [the reason] is not one-sided.

If you claim that something is "contingent" (sāpekṣa) because it is designated by distinct terms— just as the two horns of an ox arise simultaneously, one on the left and one on the right, due to having distinct designations— this is not invariably so,
for we observe such cases [where distinct terms are used despite simultaneity].
The proponent says:

This mind and its mental factors, as well as the lamp and its light, arise simultaneously through their harmonious conjunction and sovereign power; this is intended to be so within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), like the observation of the distinctness of two ox horns or the use of language, because none of these are established in the ultimate sense (paramārtha).
The fault you have pointed out does not apply to me.

Furthermore, regarding passion (*rāga*) and the one who is impassioned (*rakta*), whether they are considered identical or distinct, both alternatives are untenable when analyzed in terms of simultaneity.
As the verse says:
"If the defilement and the defiled were one, then being one, they could not exist simultaneously.
The commentary explains:
If one says they are simultaneous, then there would be two distinct entities; such is the meaning of the verse.
Herein a proof is established: defilement and the defiled do not arise at the same time. Why is this?
Because they would be a single entity, like the self-nature of the stained one.
If you intend for the stain and the stained one to be a single entity and simultaneous, this is logically impossible, because they are mutually contradictory.
If you argue that the passion and the impassioned one are distinct entities existing simultaneously, and thus do not incur the aforementioned faults, this too is incorrect.
As the verse says:
"Passion and the impassioned one are distinct; Even their simultaneity cannot be established."
The commentary states:
It is impossible for distinct entities to exist simultaneously, as this has been refuted by logical analysis.
Furthermore, regarding the opponent’s attempt to establish that distinct entities exist simultaneously in order to convince others, this is untenable because such entities lack any ontological basis.
Herein is established the proof: the two, namely passion (*rāga*) and the impassioned (*rakta*), cannot exist simultaneously.
Why? Because they involve mutual dependence (*apekṣā*), just as the intrinsic nature of passion itself [does not exist independently].
Furthermore, we shall now further refute the notion of distinct entities existing simultaneously, as the verse says:
"If they were distinct yet simultaneous, They should also be simultaneous when separated from their companions."
The commentary states:

If you intend that the defilement and the defiled one exist simultaneously, yet do not wish for either to be separated from its companion, then we establish this proof: in the ultimate sense, it is not intended that the defilement and the defiled one exist as distinct entities simultaneously, because they are mutually dependent, just like cause and effect.
Furthermore, other masters of the treatises say:

"If you wish to establish that distinct entities exist simultaneously, then wherever there are distinct entities, they would each be simultaneous—just as when a cow is beside a horse, they are said to be simultaneous, so too a solitary cow without a companion would also be simultaneous."
This is as previously answered; the meaning does not differ in the slightest.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If they were distinct yet arose simultaneously, what need would there be for the defilement and the defiler?"
The commentary states:

It is not logical that the defilement and the defiled one arise simultaneously, because they are distinct from one another, just as, for example, defilement and the state of being free from defilement are distinct.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If both passion and the impassioned one were each established by their own intrinsic nature,
for what purpose would you insist on distinguishing that these two arise simultaneously?"
The commentary states:

If the defilement (*kleśa*) and the defiled one (*kliṣṭa*)—the self-substance (*ātma-bhāva*)—were distinct from one another, then because their substances are distinct, they would not be mutually dependent.

Furthermore, if there were a functional application such that "this is the defiler" and "this is the defilement," then based on the characteristic of mutual dependence, it is said that they arise simultaneously.
Is this your intention?
This statement is flawed. Why is that?
As the verse says: "It is not possible for the defilement and the defiled one to arise simultaneously.
In this way, simultaneous arising is untenable because there is dependence.
It is not said that these very dharmas arise simultaneously, because they are not distinct.
If one intends for them to have separate entities yet arise simultaneously, this is also not the case.
As the verse says:
"If they are thus not established as distinct, you seek their simultaneous arising;
yet if they are established as simultaneous, do you still wish for them to have distinct natures?
The commentary states:
Regarding this meaning, the Elder should speak.
As the verse says:
"What distinct entity exists that could arise simultaneously with desire?"
The commentary says:
What is the meaning of "arising simultaneously"?
Is it said that they arise simultaneously because they possess distinct entities that arise in succession?
Do they arise simultaneously without having distinct entities?
If you say they arise either successively or simultaneously, that is not so; for the faults regarding defilement and the departure from defilement have already been explained previously.
If they were to arise simultaneously, this too is not the case, because there would be mutual dependence, just as was previously explained regarding cause and effect.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Because of the two—the defilement and the defiled one—neither identity nor difference is established."
"All phenomena are like passion; neither identity nor difference is established.
The commentary states:

Whether internal or external, those factors such as hatred and delusion—whether identical or different—are all unestablished. This is because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), those passions and so forth are not established.
As the opponent stated at the beginning of this chapter—that the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth exist because they possess the faults of defilement—his reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.
Furthermore, it contradicts the meaning established by conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), due to the aforementioned defects of his reason.
The meaning that the defilements and the defiled person explained within this chapter lack intrinsic nature, and which has been made understood by others, is thus established.
As the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Good son!..."

Form is neither the essence of defilement nor the essence of freedom from defilement; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither the essence of defilement nor the essence of freedom from defilement.

Furthermore, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the essence of defilement and empty of the essence of freedom from defilement—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

In this way, form is neither the essence of hatred nor the essence of non-hatred; it is neither the essence of delusion nor the essence of non-delusion. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
O Paramavīra!
Form is neither defiled nor pure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither defiled nor pure.
Furthermore, form is neither the nature of defilement nor the nature of purity; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail herein.
The commentary on the "Examination of the Afflicted and the Affliction" is completed.
Chapter Seven: Examination of the Characteristics of the Conditioned (*Saṃskṛtalakṣaṇaparīkṣā*) Furthermore, what are the characteristics by which this chapter is established?

All phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); yet, those who are deluded do not know this and instead grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination.
Now, with the desire to reveal and cause them to recognize the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature, this chapter is composed.
The opponent says:
In the ultimate sense, there exists the intrinsic nature of these conditioned phenomena, such as the aggregates. Why is this so?
Because those conditioned characteristics, such as arising and so forth, mutually support one another,
if this [nature] were non-existent, those conditioned characteristics would lack the sense of mutual support, being like the horns of a rabbit.

Because the characteristics such as arising support the characteristics of the aggregates and so forth through their causal power, those phenomena do not fail to exist—namely, the conditioned aggregates and so on.
The proponent says:
Regarding your statement that arising and so forth are the characteristics of the conditioned, are those characteristics of arising and so forth themselves conditioned?
Is this conditioned or unconditioned?
The opponent says:
It is conditioned.
The proponent says:
We shall now analyze this meaning in successive order.
First, to establish origination, as the verse says:
"If arising were conditioned, it too would possess the three characteristics.
Commentary: In the ultimate sense, we do not intend for those characteristics such as arising and so forth to be the characteristics of the conditioned.
Why is this? Because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
The opponent says:

The natures of arising, abiding, and ceasing each possess their own functions; therefore, one wishes to establish that these characteristics, such as arising and so forth, are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The proponent says:
This proof lacks a factual basis (*svabhāva*); there is only a mere thesis (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, the outsider says:
"Arising, abiding, and ceasing each possess their own functional capacity.
Your denial of these is logically untenable."
The proponent says:
Because characteristics such as arising cannot be apprehended,
and furthermore, even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), arising is not a characteristic of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Why is this? Because it involves the act of origination, just as a father begets a son.
Furthermore, "abiding" is not a characteristic of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Why is this? Because it functions through abiding, just as food sustains the body.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the conditioned is not that abiding which functions.
Why is this? Because it functions as abiding; for example, like a woman placing a jar on the ground.
Furthermore, cessation is not a characteristic of those conditioned phenomena.
Why is this? Because they are subject to destruction, just as a club destroys an object.
Thus, the thesis that those conditioned characteristics such as arising exist is not established.
Because there are these faults—namely, that the reason is unestablished and that it contradicts the meaning—the arising [of phenomena] is not conditioned.
Therefore, the claim that "arising" is a characteristic of the conditioned is logically untenable.
Furthermore, if you wish to avoid the faults previously mentioned by establishing that arising and so forth are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this interpretation is also incorrect.
As the verse says:
"If arising were unconditioned, How could it be called a characteristic of the conditioned?"
The commentary states:

If this arising were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) yet possessed the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), such a principle would not exist; for the very essence of the unconditioned is non-existent. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is illogical to claim that arising—which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—acts as the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Why is this so?
Because it is unconditioned, just like space (*ākāśa*).
The same applies to abiding and cessation; they will not be refuted in further detail.
Furthermore, if you distinguish that arising, abiding, and cessation are conditioned characteristics that perform functions, do these occur sequentially?
Or do they occur simultaneously?
Both positions entail faults. Why is this so?
If they were successive, as the verse says:
"The three stages of arising and so forth / Lack the characteristic of performing an action.
The commentary states:
Against what is it powerless?
It is powerless against the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, regarding the desire to establish [the sequence] of arising and so forth in their proper order: just as when the essence of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) has not yet arisen, the two states of abiding and ceasing are characterized by powerlessness, because the essence of the phenomenon does not exist.
Furthermore, when a phenomenon that has already ceased ceases, it lacks substantiality; thus, the two states of arising and abiding have no power over its cessation.
Moreover, for a phenomenon that has already arisen, the act of arising itself lacks power.
Furthermore, if the essence of a dharma were to abide, then cessation would lack power.
If it is argued that impermanence follows along during the time of abiding, this meaning is not tenable.
As a verse in the *Śata-śāstra* says:
"Without separation from abiding, there is no essence of phenomena; how could impermanence exist if there were abiding?
If there were abiding at the beginning, it would not be possible later on.
If impermanence were constant, there would be no abiding at any time."
If that which was previously permanent could later become impermanent,
then permanence and impermanence would coexist within the same substantial entity at the same time; yet, where there is permanence,
there is no impermanence, and where there is impermanence, there is no permanence.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that the conditioned characteristics such as arising and so forth exist simultaneously, this too is not the case.
As the verse says:
"How can there be three characteristics simultaneously in a single entity?"
The commentary states:
These characteristics do not exist simultaneously; such is the meaning of the words.
Why do they not exist?
That is to say, it is not logically tenable for a single entity to undergo arising, abiding, and ceasing simultaneously, because these states are ultimately contradictory.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika masters state:

"All phenomena possess their own distinct, determinate causes and conditions that continue in a sovereign succession. That which is about to arise at a certain time attains its own essence; this is called 'arising. The stage of the first moment in the continuum is called 'abiding. The dissimilarity with the preceding moment is called 'aging. The destruction of what has already arisen is called 'ceasing.'"
Such things as these definitely exist, because they are observed to exist simultaneously within a single moment.
As for your attempt to find fault with me through such expedients, I am free from this reproach.
The proponent says:
This continuity is also not substantially real, because it is subject to observation.
That which abides in conceptual discrimination consists of the three characteristics of conventional truth; it is not the ultimate truth.
Your claim that the time of abiding contradicts abiding and ceasing is not tenable, because it does not avoid the faults previously stated.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika says:
Just as a substance that has not yet arisen later attains its own nature, this is called "arising."
That which arises and is established is called "abiding.
That which abides and becomes decayed is called "aging.
That which ages and perishes is called "destruction."
Since arising and the others are obtained in succession without being separate from the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), for this reason their characteristics and essence are established.
As previously stated, the claim that the three—arising and so forth—in succession lack the power to perform the function of characteristics is incorrect.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect.
What is meant by "name" and "characteristic"?

This means that they are never separated from their characterized bases (*lakṣya*), just as the characteristic of solidity is not separate from earth, or as the various marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) are not separate from the Great Man himself.
If it is claimed that arising and so forth are the characteristics of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), this is not the case.
Why is this? Because there is a sequential order.
What is this sequence?

It is like placing a lump of clay upon a wheel; once it has been rotated by the movement of the hands into the shape of a small stupa, one strikes it to flatten it, then turns it into the shape of a lid, and finally gathers it together into the shape of a basket.
These various distinct states are not the conditioned essence or characteristics of that jar; yet the characteristics such as arising and so forth are likewise not separate from it.
That which is called a "conditioned phenomenon" (saṃskṛtadharma) is merely a conventional designation.
Regarding "arising from reality," it is negated herein.
How is it negated?
Because that which has not yet arisen lacks the substance of abiding or ceasing.

If one were to claim that when [a phenomenon] arises in the future, it must possess both abiding and ceasing, such conceptualization is merely conventional discourse and cannot avoid the faults previously mentioned.

In this way, the conditioned characteristics such as arising and so forth—whether taken sequentially or simultaneously—are not established in their own essence, because there are logical fallacies in the reasons.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If arising, abiding, and ceasing Were distinct from the conditioned characteristics..."
"If it exists, it would lead to infinite regress.
The commentary states:
"If that which is different from it were itself to have something different from it, then there would be an infinite regress, and this is not what is intended."
Furthermore, if characteristics such as arising were themselves devoid of further characteristics, one would again incur the same fault previously mentioned.
As the verse says:
"That which lacks [characteristics] is not conditioned."
The commentary states:
What is the meaning of this?
It is as you intend: that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not possess the characteristics of being conditioned, precisely because they are conditioned.

In this way, arising and the other [characteristics] are likewise not conditioned characteristics. For this reason, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should not differentiate between characteristics such as arising and so forth as being conditioned.
If it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
then the faults previously mentioned now revert to you.
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīyas say:
Arising is conditioned and not infinite.
How is this known?
Because it arises through the collective occurrence of fifteen factors within the conjunction of its own constituent entities.
What are the fifteen?
First, the essence of this dharma;
second, its arising.
Third, the characteristic of change;
fourth, the characteristic of cessation;
fifth, if it is a wholesome dharma (*śukla-dharma*), then right liberation arises.
Sixth, if it is a dark phenomenon (*kṛṣṇadharma*), then false liberation arises;
seventh, if it is a phenomenon of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadharma*), then the essence of renunciation arises;
eighth, if it is not a phenomenon of renunciation, then the essence of non-renunciation arises.
The preceding seven types are the primary entities (dharma-svabhāva) and their attendants (parivāra).

Within these seven attendants, each has one attendant that follows it; namely, the "arising of arising" up to "non-exit from non-exit. This non-exit from non-exit is the entity of the attendant, and such is the nature of attendant dharmas.

In the synthesis of the essential nature of dharmas, there arise fifteen dharmas in total. Among them, the primary arising (mūla-utpāda), excluding its own self-nature, can give rise to fourteen other dharmas; the "arising of arising" (utpādotpāda) can, in turn, give rise to that primary arising.
The same applies to abiding (sthiti) and the other characteristics.
For this reason, there is no fault of infinite regress.
As my verse says:
"When that arising arises, it gives rise alone to the fundamental root."
"When the fundamental arising arises, it in turn gives rise to the 'arising of arising.
The Ācārya said: "Though you speak many various words, they do not accord with the truth."
Why is this not so? As the verse says:
"If it is claimed that when origination is originating, it can originate the primary origination;..."
"If you arise from what has already arisen, how can you cause that which has already arisen to arise?
The commentary states:
It does not arise in such a manner, because it has not yet arisen, just as it was when it had not arisen at all previously.
The opponent says:
"The primary arising can give rise to the 'arising of arising.
In this way, the 'arising of arising' can give rise to the primary arising; the meaning is precisely as such."
The proponent says in verse:

"If you claim that the fundamental arising can give rise to that 'arising of arising,' Since that [fundamental arising] is produced from the 'arising of arising,' How can it give rise to the 'arising of arising'?"
The commentary states:
It does not arise in such a manner because it has not yet originated; this is the intended meaning.
The opponent says:
Since that fundamental arising and the arising-of-arising each perform their own respective functions at the time they arise, there is no fault.
The commentator states in verse:
"You claim that when this arises, it arises according to its intended function; [yet you have not explained how this occurs]."
"If this arising has not yet arisen, how can that which has not yet arisen cause arising?
The commentary states:

The first phrase refers to fundamental arising; the second phrase refers to the arising of arising; the third phrase refers to the time when arising has not yet occurred; and the fourth phrase refers to the fact that fundamental arising lacks the functional capacity to arise.

Why is this? Because it has not yet arisen, and because it is at the very moment of arising; for example, like the time before it had arisen, or like the essential nature of a phenomenon that is about to arise.
The opponent says:

Just as with the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), when a dharma arises or has already arisen, it possesses the functional capacity to cause the simultaneous arising of various dharmas; therefore, it is not said to be unilaterally so.
Your claim that the reason [is established] because it occurs at the time of arising, and because it is yet to be born, does not establish this point.
The proponent says:
In the previous discussion regarding the defilement and the defiled one, we have already refuted their simultaneous arising and also refuted their cause.
Your claim that [the reason] is not conclusive (anaikāntika) serves only to demonstrate your own error.
Furthermore, as for the claim that there is no fault of infinite regress, this cannot be avoided.
Again, some say: there is another principle by which one may avoid the fault of infinite regress.
What is the reasoning?
As a verse says:
"Just as a lamp illuminates its own substance, it is also able to illuminate others."
The arising of phenomena is likewise so: it arises from itself and also causes others to arise.
The commentary states:
For this reason, there is no fault of infinite regress.
The proponent says in verse:
"In the lamp itself there is no darkness, nor is there darkness in its location.
What, then, does that lamp illuminate, such that you say it illuminates both itself and others?"
The commentary states:
Thus, the lamp lacks even the slightest capacity for illumination; this is the intended meaning of the statement.
Furthermore, here we establish a proof regarding the essence of the lamp: within that ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it cannot illuminate itself, nor can it illuminate others.
Why is this? Because darkness does not exist, just as, for example, with the light of a fiercely blazing sun.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a lamp does not destroy darkness.
Why is this? Because it is vast, like that earth.
For this reason, the analogy lacks substantiality.
The opponent says:

"A lamp is able to destroy darkness at the very moment it first arises. As the verse states, 'Just as a lamp can destroy darkness,' this means that its own nature produces light which is capable of removing external darkness; such is the intended meaning."

Regarding what was previously stated—that darkness does not exist because it is absent—this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the analogy is also devoid of substance, because the meanings of "lamp" and "light" are indeed perceivable.
The author of the treatise says in verse:
"How can a lamp, at the very moment it arises, be able to destroy darkness?"
The commentary states:
What is meant by "refutation"?
It means that it is incapable of refuting; such is the meaning of the words.
The verse says:
"When this lamp first arises, it does not reach that darkness.
The commentary explains:
Because they arise at the same time, it is like a lamp and its darkness.
The opponent says:
"Knowledge and non-knowledge, etc., are not invariably [related]."
The proponent says:
Your adherence to this position falls within the scope of what was previously established; thus, it is likewise refuted that [the reason] is not non-exclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, because [the action] has not yet arisen at the time of its origination, it is like a son who has not yet been born and thus performs no activity.
A lamp is likewise incapable of producing illumination.
Furthermore, as stated in the preceding verse: "How can a lamp, at the very moment it arises, destroy darkness?

Regarding the claim that this lamp, upon its initial arising, does not reach the darkness, here we establish a formal proof: from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that lamp, at the time of its arising, cannot destroy darkness.
Why is this? Because it does not reach [the object], just as, for example, there is darkness between worlds in the absence of light.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a lamp does not destroy darkness.
Why is this? Because that which is to be counteracted cannot be apprehended, just as, for example, with darkness.
The opponent says:
Since it is directly observed that a lamp can illuminate darkness without reaching it, the proponent says:
"Your establishment of this position increases the force of my refutation and makes my analogy even more evident; therefore, I am without fault."
If that were so, one should now examine whether it is as it appears, or otherwise;
for I do not see how a lamp can dispel darkness without reaching it.
If it were the case that a lamp could dispel darkness without reaching it, this principle would not hold true.
As the verse says:
"If a lamp, without reaching the darkness, Were to destroy that darkness;..."
"The lamp abides within this [space], and thus it should destroy all darkness.
Commentary:
You do not admit that the lamp destroys distant darkness.
The case of "near" is likewise; how then could it be destroyed?
Furthermore, as the verse says:
"If a lamp can illuminate itself, and can also illuminate others;"
"Darkness should likewise be thus: it would both obscure itself and obscure others.
[The commentary] says:
If one does not desire darkness to be both for itself and for others, how could one possibly desire a lamp to be so for both itself and others?
Furthermore, a formal proof is established herein: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a lamp does not destroy its own or another's object of negation.
Why? Because there exists that which counteracts it, just as, for example, darkness [is countered by light].
Since it has already been refuted that the substance of a lamp illuminates both itself and others, the analogy lacks validity.

Therefore, when an opponent cites the example of that lamp to establish the thesis that an arising agent can produce both itself and others, this is not the case, because it cannot avoid the aforementioned fault of infinite regress.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that what arises from itself also causes others to arise, by what means does it cause them to arise?
Does it cause them to arise when it has already arisen,
or when it has not yet arisen?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If that which has not yet arisen were to arise, as the verse says:
"If this arising has not yet arisen, how can it produce itself or another?"
The commentary states:
That which has not yet arisen is non-arising, because it has not been produced, just as in the prior state of non-arising.
This point has already been analyzed above.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If this arising has already arisen, what further thing is there for the arising to arise?
The commentary states:
Since that which has already arisen gives rise to its own arising, there would be no need for effort.
Observing it in this way, your claim that an arising can give rise to both itself and others is incorrect, because it cannot avoid the aforementioned fault of infinite regress.

Furthermore, those [characteristics] such as arising establish their own unconditioned nature; because they are unconditioned, those various characteristics like arising are not characteristics of the conditioned.
Thus, your argument that "because they are characteristics" fails to establish its logical reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, one should ask:
regarding that which is said to arise, how does it arise?
Does it arise at the very moment of arising?
Does it arise from that which has already arisen?
Neither of these is tenable.
As the verse says:
"Arising, that which has already arisen, and that which has not yet arisen—none of these have arising;
going, that which has not yet been gone over, and the time of going—these have already been explained therein.
The commentary states:
As has already been demonstrated, this should also be explained in detail here: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no arising at the time of arising.
Why? Because it would involve moving toward a different time, just as in the case of that which is about to cease.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that when a phenomenon has partially arisen and partially not yet arisen, it is said to be "in the process of arising," this too is not correct.
Why? Because if it has already partially arisen, it does not arise further, as further arising would be purposeless.
If that which has not yet arisen were to arise, it would still not arise because it has not yet arisen, just as, for example, the future does not arise.
The opponent says: "That which is certain to arise moves toward the present; this is called the time of arising."
The proponent says:
This meaning should also be examined.
As the verse states:
"It is not correct that it is called 'arising' by virtue of the time of arising;
how can that which is at the time of arising be said to be dependent origination?
The commentary states:
Regarding that which arises: is it conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), or both conditioned and unconditioned?
These faults have already been refuted above.
The opponent says:

For example, it is like a person skilled in the art of swordsmanship who, giving rise to an unwholesome mind and performing an evil and perverse act, harms his own mother, thinking he is acting in accordance with her wishes.
You are just like that.

Why is this? Great Seer, you have taught the profound dependent origination for the sake of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; yet because you have long practiced conceptualization and unrighteous conduct, you have undermined your own aspirations and harmed the correct principle—this adherence of yours is not tenable.
The proponent said: "Do you not know?
There are those with evil views who deny cause and effect, destroy the pure dharmas, and refuse to have faith or accept them."
In order to transform those people of evil views and to cleanse them of the defilements of unwholesome conduct, the Buddha Bhagavān made this statement:

"Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. That is to say, "ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth. This is for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Such being my intention, this is what I desire.
Your statement—that [my position] contradicts its own desire and undermines correct reasoning—is incorrect.
As the verse says:
"Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, And their own-being does not exist;
That 'this exists because that exists'— Such a thing is not so.

Furthermore, as the Buddha said in verse: "If born from conditions, it is unborn; That which arises dependently has no intrinsic being. If it belongs to causes and conditions, it is empty; One who understands emptiness is called heedful."
Such passages from various sūtras should be explained here in detail.

By observing in this way, whether [phenomena] have arisen or have not yet arisen, they are all like illusions; therefore, at the time of their arising, they are quiescent and thus lack the characteristic of arising.

As for what those outsiders say—that that which arises at the time [of conditions] constitutes dependent origination—this is incorrect because, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), their proof is not established.
Furthermore, some may say:
"In the world, we directly perceive various causes and conditions giving rise to their respective effects, such as jars and garments; there is no other proof superior to this direct perception."

Regarding the statement in the preceding verse, "At the time of arising, that which has already arisen, and that which has not yet arisen, all lack arising," this is inconsistent because [arising] occurs through the cultivation of the precepts and so forth.
The commentator says:
Who could oppose those aggregates of precepts and the like, which accord with meritorious qualities?
However, these are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Such treatises arise for the purpose of abandoning attachment and for the sake of the true meaning; therefore, there is no fault.
If you think that jars and garments have arising, this too is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and not ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What I maintain is that if jars or garments are currently arising, they can be apprehended; it is not the case that they arise when they have not yet arisen.
If that which has already arisen were to arise, such arising would be impossible; for the arising of things such as jars and garments occurs while they are as yet unarisen.
To hold such a position is logically untenable.
Why is this? If the jar has not yet arisen, how can one establish a false cognition?
It is by depending on the name "jar" that one says, "a jar arises."
Such a position merely establishes false cognition within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because a jar that has not yet arisen cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"Because [dharmas] exist in the three periods of time, those jars and so forth arise; such is my doctrine."
The proponent says:
This is also not the case.
As a verse states:
"If there were even a single thing anywhere that existed as a substantial entity prior to its arising.
Commentary: "A single thing" refers, for instance, to a jar, a garment, or the like.
If an entity already exists within its conditions, within their conjunction, or elsewhere, the verse says:
"If it already exists, what need is there for it to arise?"
The commentary states:
If that [arising] already existed, then its production would be purposeless.
For this reason, the verse says:
"Because the entity exists when arising does not.
The commentary states:
For this reason, that which previously arose as an existing entity is proven, upon examination, to be non-existent.
Regarding the claim that "entities arise," there is a flaw in the thesis.
Furthermore, those who maintain that time is distinct say this:
"All phenomena possess intrinsic nature."
How is this known through verification?
Because it appears in the present world.
This position is not tenable.
Why is this? If it were to come into the present, it would destroy the present.
Thus, regarding the distinctions of essence, characteristics, and temporal state, all previous fallacies are answered by this same principle.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena exists because it can be manifested; therefore, I am without fault.
The opponent replies:
Since that which is manifest has already been refuted, this [position] is inconsistent.
Furthermore, how can the existence of an entity that has not yet arisen be credible?
The Sāṃkhya replies again:
Because it is subsumed within the worldly [convention], it is like a presently existing thing.
The proponent says:
Since a presently existing thing lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), your example is unestablished, and the point you intend to prove is destroyed.

Furthermore, although they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one does not thereby destroy conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because at the present time, phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) can still be perceived, much like illusions and the like. One should understand that within that conventional truth, phenomena such as form are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

The verse says: "At the time of arising, that which has already arisen, and that which has not yet arisen—none of these have arising," and so forth. Although this has already been answered previously, it shall now be explained further.
As the verse says:
"If one claims that at the time of arising, this arising has something that arises,"
The commentary states:
If their intention is to claim that arising can bring about what is to arise at the very moment it arises, this position is incorrect because it entails logical fallacies.
As the verse says:
"If that arising gives rise to the act of arising, what is it that further gives rise to this [arising]?
The commentary states:
That arising is not tenable because it is an act of arising; for example, the arising of father and son lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Such is the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, if it is asserted that there is another arising capable of producing this [primary] arising, this too entails a fault.
What kind of fault?
The verse says:
"If there is an arising of an arising, this would entail the fault of infinite regress.
The opponent says:
"Because it is an arising that does not itself arise, there is no fault of infinite regress; I intend it to be thus."
The proponent states in verse:
"If arising arises from non-arising, then all phenomena arise in this same way.
The commentary explains:
Since phenomena (*dharma*) are not thus, their arising (*utpāda*) must likewise be so; therefore, one should not insist on making such distinctions.

Furthermore, regarding this "arising," whether it possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), lacks an intrinsic nature, or both possesses and lacks an intrinsic nature, arising is in every case subject to logical faults.
As the verse says:
"If an entity already exists, its arising is useless; If an entity does not exist, its arising has no basis.
The same applies to that which both exists and does not exist; This point has already been explained previously."
The commentary says:
Where was this previously stated?
As it is said in a verse in the "Examination of Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*) chapter: "Neither existent nor non-existent; such should be the meaning of conditions."
Furthermore, as a verse says: "Neither existent nor non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent does a phenomenon arise.
This has already been refuted previously and need not be explained further.
Moreover, as a verse says:
"If there were arising at the time of cessation, this principle would not be so. Commentary:
Because it is the time of cessation; for example, like the time of death.
The opponent says:
It arises before it has ceased; therefore, there is no fault.
The proponent states in verse:
"If a phenomenon has no time of cessation, its essence cannot be apprehended.
The commentary states:
Because its essence and characteristics are incompatible, it is like a flower in the sky; such is the meaning of the verse.
The opponent says:
"Because abiding is not uniform.
The proponent replies:
Since that [self] also follows impermanence, it is not established even before its cessation; thus, I am without fault.
This has been explained at length previously.
The opponent says:
There is such an arising because the phenomena that arise exist. If this [arising] were non-existent,
those phenomena that arise could not exist, just as one cannot make a garment from the hair of a tortoise.
Both [arising and abiding] lack intrinsic nature because they are established through origination; however, the dharma that abides does exist.
Therefore, as it has been stated, arising is not without intrinsic nature.
The proponent says:

Since that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, the act of arising is not established. Although it is said in the conventional sense (saṃvṛti-satya) that this arising exists, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-satya) there is no characteristic of abiding.
Now we ask: does this entity abide as an entity that has not yet abided?
Does that which has already abided abide?
Does that which is currently abiding abide?
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), none of these three cases are tenable.
As the verse says:
"The entity that has not yet abided does not abide; the entity that is abiding also does not abide;
even at the time of abiding, it does not abide. Since there is no arising, who is it that could abide?"
The commentary states:
Regarding the first phrase, because there is no abiding, it is like cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding the second phrase, since the two times—the present and the past—cannot be obtained simultaneously, the meaning of "abiding" is empty.

Regarding the third phrase: apart from that which has already abided and that which has not yet abided, there is no further time of abiding; if one were to claim there is, it is incorrect, as has been extensively refuted above.
Regarding the fourth phrase: there is not a single thing that arises, nor is there a single thing that abides; such is the meaning of the verse.

Furthermore, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), not even a single entity can be found to possess the characteristic of arising. As has been extensively demonstrated through reasoning since the beginning, once arising is established as impossible, who could there be to abide?
For this reason, your previous statement that phenomena which have arisen possess a cause for their arising is entirely untenable.
Furthermore, as the verse says:
"If there were abiding at the time of cessation, this meaning would not be so."
The commentary states:
Because they are contradictory.
If things are contradictory, they do not exist simultaneously; just as the intense rays of the sun do not coexist with darkness, such is the meaning of the verse.
The opponent says:
Because its essence is perceivable while it has not yet ceased.
The proponent states in verse:
"If a phenomenon has no time of cessation, its essence cannot be apprehended.
Commentary: This is because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are pursued by impermanence.
Furthermore, that essence cannot be apprehended.
Why? Because there is no time of cessation, like a flower in the sky; such is the meaning of the verse.

Furthermore, if you think that the characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) has power once it has arisen, such that at that time the essence of the phenomenon (dharma-svabhāva) neither perishes nor is eternal—because immediately following abiding, aging and impermanence (jarā-anityatā) follow in succession.
This position is incorrect.

Why? If this characteristic of duration (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) were present when form and other phenomena exist, and impermanence were absent at that time, then impermanence could not subsequently follow them either—just as there can be no water where fire exists, and fire cannot later become water; the same principle applies to the nature of duration.
The opponent says:
"In the world, we directly perceive that the nature of phenomena undergoes cessation; how can you say they do not exist?
The proponent replies:
This should be examined:
as for this cessation that you perceive, does this cessation always accompany the entity,
or do they exist in separate locations?
If it were to accompany [the entity], there would be no sense of abiding.
If it were in a separate location, its substance would never undergo cessation; since there would be no time of cessation, its substance could not be apprehended.
Both [positions] are incorrect.
Furthermore, some who are clever and arrogant may say:

"For example, just as a person might not have possessed the nature of a Buddha previously but later attains Buddhahood, so too it is with abiding; even if there was no cessation previously, what fault is there in its ceasing at a later time?"
This position is incorrect.

Why? Because one who lacks the essence of a Buddha—that is, one who lacks the characteristics and functions of omniscience and possesses only the wisdom of an ordinary person—cannot later attain Buddhahood; such a meaning does not exist. Even in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this expedient expression is not established.

Thus, when the final momentary wisdom arises, having severed both the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations regarding their objects, it is called "attaining Buddhahood"; that wisdom and the Buddha are non-different in essence.
What you have said lacks any basis in reality.
The same fault applies whether aging and abiding are identical or distinct.
Since this [position] is thus untenable, the Ācārya states in verse:
"All those phenomena are subject to aging and death at all times;
what kind of phenomenon could there be that possesses the nature of abiding yet lacks the characteristic of aging and death?
The commentary states:
If there were such a thing as arising, then, in accordance with the locus of that essence, a state of abiding would be observable and arising could be established.
However, this is not the case; therefore, the meaning of the reason they have posited is unestablished.
Furthermore, you who wish to establish that "abiding" as something that abides: does this abiding abide by itself, or does it abide by means of another distinct abiding?
Neither of these two positions is tenable.
As a verse says:
"Abiding, changing abiding, and un-abiding— these meanings are not so;
just as arising does not arise by itself, nor does it arise from another."
The commentary states:
Why is it that arising from itself is not tenable?
As stated in the preceding verse: "If this arising has not yet arisen, how can it produce itself?"
If that which has already arisen is capable of producing [another], what further thing would that production produce?
Therefore, it is asked: why does it not arise from another?
As the previous verse stated: "If arising were to have another arising, this would entail the fault of infinite regress."
Therefore, abiding is also like this.
The verse says:
"If this abiding has not yet abided, how can it abide by its own nature?"
If this abiding has already abided, what need is there for it to abide once it has abided?
If abiding were to abide by means of a different abiding, that abiding would be infinite;
if abiding were to abide without abiding, then all phenomena would abide in this same way.
The commentary states:
These two verses are explanatory verses (*arthavivaraṇa-gāthā*), not the root verses of the treatise.
They negate the abiding of that which abides in itself, just as the arising of an intrinsic nature was previously negated.
The subsequent refutation of the endurance of endurance by means of another is to be understood in the same manner as the refutation of arising from another. Therefore,
one should know that endurance lacks intrinsic nature.
As you previously stated, "Such an arising exists because it possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Regarding the claim that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The opponent says:
In the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is this arising and abiding. Why?
Because those dharmas that function concomitantly possess that very nature.
If this [arising] did not exist, the nature of those concomitant factors (sahabhū-dharma) would not exist, just as, for example, a horse's horn [does not exist].
Since those concomitants possess cessation, therefore, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), arising and abiding exist by virtue of the power of causes.
The proponent says:

Cessation is also like this; that is to say, it is in every way untenable to claim that there is a cessation of this entity when it has already ceased, when it has not yet ceased, or at the very moment of ceasing.
As the verse says:
"A phenomenon that has not yet ceased does not cease; a phenomenon that has already ceased does not cease;
even at the time of ceasing, it does not cease. If there is no arising, what is there to cease?"
The commentary states:
Regarding the first phrase, because cessation is empty, it is like abiding.
Regarding the second phrase, it is like a person who has already died and does not die again.

Regarding the third alternative: apart from those dharmas that have already ceased and those that have not yet ceased, there is no further time of cessation, as this would entail both faults. Therefore, it is certain that what is in the process of ceasing does not cease.

Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which is in the process of ceasing does not cease, because it follows the worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), just like a phenomenon that is about to arise and comes into the present.
As for the fourth alternative (*koṭi*), what is its meaning?
Because all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising.
To speak of "non-arising" means that the characteristic of arising is absent.
It is logically untenable for there to be cessation where there is no arising, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman.
Thus, for that which is about to arise and that which does not arise, it is not the case that there is cessation at any time.
Furthermore, regarding the abiding or non-abiding of phenomena, the conceptualization of their cessation is in both cases untenable.
As the verse says:
"If the essence of phenomena were to abide, the characteristic of cessation could not be found.
The commentary explains:
Because it abides, there is no cessation; this is understood by all in the world.
If you claim that there is no fault in the view that there is cessation without abiding, that too is not so.
As the verse says:
"If the essence of phenomena has no abiding, then cessation also cannot be found.
The commentary states:
Because there is no abiding, it is like that characteristic of cessation.
Furthermore, does this phenomenon perish while remaining in its current state,
or does it perish after having moved to a different state?
The opponent says:
What does this statement mean?
The proponent says in verse:
"At the time of that state, it does not cease within that very state."
"At another stage, it is also not extinguished at that other stage. Commentary:
That it is not extinguished at this very stage is because it does not abandon its own essence, just as, for example, milk remains in the state of being milk.
Nor does it perish at the time of that other state. Why?
Herein is stated the proof:
in the ultimate sense, milk does not perish at the time of the state of curd, because they are different, just like a different jar or the like.
Furthermore, some say:
"There is such a cessation because it depends upon a substantial entity, just as, for example, that [process of] cooking.
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"If the characteristic of arising cannot be found in any phenomena;
because there is no characteristic of arising, existence through cessation is likewise not tenable. Commentary:
That all phenomena do not arise has already been explained previously.
Whether they are unripened or already ripened, this [position of yours] cannot be established, as the analogy lacks any substantial basis.
Furthermore, regarding what you call "cessation," does it refer to the cessation of something that possesses substantial existence?
Is it the cessation of that which lacks intrinsic nature?
Neither of these two positions is tenable.
As the verse says:
"If a phenomenon (dharma) possessed an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then that which exists would lack the characteristic of cessation.
Commentary: Because they are mutually contradictory, it is like water and fire.
For this reason, the verse says:
"That a single dharma both exists and does not exist is logically untenable.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If dharmas have no intrinsic nature, then their cessation is likewise untenable;
just as with a second head that does not exist, one cannot speak of its being severed. Commentary:
Regarding the verse’s analogy, it is because [the object] does not exist.
To claim that existence is extinguished by means of this non-existence is incorrect, for it would entail the destruction of the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).

Furthermore, if you assert that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) there exists that characteristic of extinction as well as that which undergoes extinction, is this extinction self-extinguishing?
Is it destroyed by another?
Neither of these two positions is correct.
As the verse says:
"A phenomenon does not cease through its own nature, nor does it cease through another nature;
just as it does not arise through its own nature, it does not arise through another nature either.
Explanation:
As for the notion that it arises from itself, this is inconsistent, as has already been explained previously.
If this arising has not yet arisen, how can it produce itself?
If this arising has already arisen, what further thing is there for it to arise?
Regarding arising from another entity, as the verse says: "If this arising were to arise from something else, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
Since arising is thus, cessation is likewise.
The verse concerning cessation (*nirodha*) states: "If this cessation has not yet ceased, how can it cause itself to cease?
If this cessation has already perished, what further thing is there for it to perish?
If this cessation were distinct from the act of ceasing, then cessation would entail the fault of infinite regress."
"If cessation were without cessation, all phenomena would likewise perish.
This verse explaining the meaning should be understood.
Just as the arising [of things] from self or other was extensively refuted previously, the cessation of things from self or other is analogous to the refutation of their arising.

Some say: "When the cause of destruction is obtained, the phenomenon that is to be destroyed then perishes. To this, one should answer as follows: Your positing of a cause for destruction is not tenable. Why is this so?
That phenomenon is not the cause for the destruction of this phenomenon, because they are distinct, just like other objects.

From the beginning of this chapter, such arising and abiding have been extensively refuted; for in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the cause of arising is not established, and the example likewise lacks substantial reality.

If one were to state reasons and analogies within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it would contradict your own tenets; this has already been extensively analyzed in the previous establishment of the proof (*sādhana*), because the underlying principle is autonomous.
As the verse says:
"Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, conditioned phenomena do not exist.
The commentary states:

As for what the outsiders (bāhyaka) have asserted—that those conditioned phenomena such as the aggregates exist because they are conjoined with the characteristics of the conditioned—that has already been refuted.
Furthermore, some say:
"In the ultimate sense (paramārtha), those conditioned phenomena such as oxen and so forth exist."
Why is this? Because characteristics such as horns, humps, and dewlaps exist.
This too should be refuted: regarding these conditioned characteristics you have established, do they themselves possess further characteristics?
Is it because there are no further characteristics?
If there were further characteristics, then these horns, humps, and so forth would not be the conditioned characteristics inherent in the essence of the cow. Why is this?
Because they possess characteristics, it is like the case of a real ox, as extensively refuted previously.

Furthermore, if there were no characteristics, then because of this absence of characteristics, these various characteristics would naturally fail to be established; since the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) lacks power, that which is defined (lakṣya) also does not exist.
Furthermore, there are those who hold [the view of] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
their position entails infinite fallacies. All such [views] have already been extensively refuted as before.
Again, some people say:
In the ultimate sense, conditioned phenomena exist.
Why? Because they exist in dependence upon their counterparts.
If this did not exist, there would be no correlative counterpart, like the son of a barren woman.
Since those two categories—the conditioned and the unconditioned—exist in mutual dependence, for this reason, the conditioned exists in the ultimate sense.
The proponent says: If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) were established, then one could speak of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) by way of excluding those conditioned phenomena.
However, when those conditioned phenomena are examined according to reality, their essence cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, the verse says:
"Since the conditioned is not established, how can the unconditioned exist?
The commentary states:
Just as a rabbit's horn has no arising, one should understand that even within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not to be understood as real.
For this reason, causes and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If that is so, how is it that various characteristics and so forth are conceptually distinguished?
It is for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As the verse says:
"Like a dream and like an illusion, like a city of the gandharvas, it is said that there is arising, abiding, and ceasing; their characteristics are likewise so.
The commentary states:
The various sages know that arising and so forth are the causes for generating cognition regarding conditioned phenomena; they open up the vision of true knowledge.
Just as arising and so forth are described by those wise ones, such is what I desire.

Because the eye of wisdom is obscured by ignorance, one gives rise to overweening pride regarding unreal objects, speaking of those phenomena—such as their arising, abiding, and ceasing—as if they were things in a dream.
This arises from the habitual tendencies of defilement; each adheres to different causes and discriminates three kinds [of natures], asserting that they possess real meaning.
To demonstrate this, it should be understood that three types of analogies—such as dreams and illusions—are taught.
Some say: Arising and so forth exist. Why is this?
Because it is apprehended through manifest cognition, just as form (rūpa) is;
and because there exists an agent, and because it is likewise apprehended as a continuity.
To speak in this manner, such a position is incorrect.
Why is this? Because it is not universal.
To reveal this, one should understand that analogies such as dreams are taught according to their specific measure.

Furthermore, the Buddha Bhagavān, who perceives reality, spoke thus for the sake of counteracting the afflictive obscurations of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle: "Form is like a mass of foam; feeling is compared to a bubble on water; perception is the same as a mirage; mental formations resemble a plantain tree; and consciousness is likened to a magical illusion."
This intention is to make known that "self" and "what belongs to self" are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature, being like reflections or shadows.

Furthermore, in order to serve as the antidote for the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations within the Mahāyāna, it is taught that conditioned phenomena are fundamentally without self-essence.
As stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a visual impairment, a lamp, a magical illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud; one should contemplate them in this way."
The purpose of this chapter is to enable others to understand that conditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature; therefore, its objective is established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
Form is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conditioned nor unconditioned, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

It is only that foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), through deluded attachment and conceptual discrimination, perceive them as distinct, just like a barren woman dreaming of embracing a child."
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: “Subhūti,
all marks whatsoever are false and illusory.”
"If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Such sūtras as these should be explained at length here.
The commentary on the "Chapter Examining Conditioned Marks" is concluded.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Five.
