This cycle of birth and death has no limit; its beginning and end cannot be found.
Commentary:

Until the noble path that serves as an antidote has arisen, because birth, aging, and death continue in succession without ceasing, acting as causes for one another in a revolving cycle, their initial origin is indeterminate; therefore, they are established as being without beginning and without end. This is spoken of within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Those who possess faith believe in the non-erroneous speech of the Bhagavān; they are not those lacking faith.
Why is this? Because those with perverted minds put forward fallacious proofs, it is for the sake of countering them that such a statement is made:

The physical faculties, perceptions, and aggregates of those sentient beings at the beginning of the kalpa are all produced by the accumulated causes of virtuous and non-virtuous karma from previous lives.
Why is this? Because they serve as the causal basis for the arising of suffering, pleasure, and other such phenomena.

Now, the present collection of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth are such because they are the cause for the non-common apprehension of objects; because they can provide benefit and nourishment; because they can provide benefit to others; because they are the cause for the anger or joy of others; because they are phenomena subject to disintegration; and because they are the cause for the common apprehension of objects.
Based on such reasons, the formal proposition and the illustrative example should be understood as previously explained in detail.
The opponent says:
"Birth and death have a beginning."
Why is this? Because it has a limit.
If a phenomenon has a limit, it cannot be said to be beginningless, just like a jar or similar objects.
When right knowledge arises, one perceives the limits of birth and death; as I have stated, because causes possess efficacy, it is therefore certain that birth and death have a beginning.
The author of the treatise says in verse:
"Not only regarding birth and death, Is a prior limit unattainable."
"All phenomena are likewise; they all lack a beginning.
Commentary: Vases and so forth have no beginning.
Why is this? Because they arise through mutual dependence.
Since the initial [thesis] is not established, the analogy fails, due to the fault in the formal proposition (*pratijñā-doṣa*).
Your claim that "having limits" serves as the reason is also incorrect.
Why is this? Because the Buddha did not provide a definitive teaching regarding the existence of causes for the false discrimination of birth and death.
This point will be explained later.
The opponent says:
"If you wish to establish that birth and death are beginningless, then birth and death must likewise be endless."
Why is this? Because they are beginningless, just like a person and space.
The proponent says:
Your statement that the person (*puruṣa*) and other phenomena are without arising is also untenable within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Why? Because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena is not established, as there is no supporting analogy.
Although those rice grains and so forth have no beginning within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are nonetheless seen to perish and decay.
Thus, your objection contradicts the actual meaning.
Furthermore, another person, arrogant in their intelligence, says:
"O Blessed One, you do not possess omniscience. Why?
Because by asserting that saṃsāra has no beginning, you merely reveal your own lack of wisdom, like a corpse that possesses no consciousness."
The proponent says:
Such a statement is made in order to eliminate attachment.
What is the meaning of this?
The various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceptually construct birth and death as having a beginning; therefore, the Buddha said that there is no beginning.
That which has no beginning is precisely what is meant by saying that birth and death are without origin.
Why is it beginningless?
Because it does not exist [as a first point].
Since birth and death are thus beginningless, their initial limit cannot be perceived; it is not that the Bhagavān lacks knowledge regarding them.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "birth and death are without limit," a proof is established herein: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the aggregates (*skandha*) do not exist as they previously appeared. Why is this so?
Because there is no prior limit, it is like a magician creating an illusory person.
The opponent says:

Since the non-conceptualizing consciousness takes as its object the forms and so forth produced by that magician’s illusion, those various forms and so forth exist in exactly the same way at a later time; therefore, the analogy lacks substance.
The proponent says:
The illusory person created by a master of illusions has no intrinsic reality of its own.

Perception is likewise; because the illusory person is produced within the objective sphere of form by non-conceptual consciousness, its own essence is empty. Thus, the analogy is established, and there is no fault of [the subject] lacking an essence.
Therefore, your claim that birth and death exist, as well as your citation of the Buddha’s teaching as a reason for their cessation, are both unestablished.
The opponent says:
"In the ultimate sense, there is a continuity of the aggregates (skandhas), and this is called birth and death."
Why is this? Because it exists therein.
If this were non-existent, that would also be non-existent, just like the horns of a rabbit.
Because there is both defilement and purity within saṃsāra, saṃsāra exists.
Since the point I intend to establish is thus proven, your claim that my reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) and contradictory to the intended meaning is incorrect.
The proponent says in verse:
"Since this has neither before nor after, how can that be obtained therein?
The commentary says:
Because an intrinsic essence cannot be found therein, such is the meaning of the words.
For example, it is like a magician who conjures up a man by illusion; if one seeks an intrinsic essence within that continuum, no such thing exists.
Why is this? Because the prior and posterior do not establish themselves and the middle lacks intrinsic nature, your example is invalid.
As for the faults you have pointed out, they now return to you.
Thus, one should contemplate that birth and death have no intrinsic nature. The verse says:
"Therefore, in the beginning, middle, and end, this sequence is not tenable.
The commentary explains:
The "prior, middle, and posterior" refer to birth, aging, and death.
An opponent might say:
"Birth and death possess an intrinsic nature."
Why is this? Because birth, aging, death, and existence [must] exist; for example, just as a barren woman has no child, it cannot be said that she has birth, aging, or death.
This position is incorrect.

Why is this? Because the son of a barren woman is not established in terms of birth, old age, death, beginning, middle, or end, the meaning of the cause is not established; thus, the analogy lacks substance, for in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the arising and so forth of any single entity is not established.
Furthermore, why is the sequential order of birth and so forth—beginning, middle, and end—not established?
This should be examined carefully, as the verse says:
"If one claims that birth comes first, And old age and death come after;..."
"If there were birth without old age and death, there would be birth without dying.
The commentary states:
If you intend for birth to come first, then birth should occur independently, separated from old age and death.

If there were truly an entity that existed apart from those [causes] from which it arises, such a substance could never be found, just as a fire-horse has no arising by way of its own nature. Why is this?
A horse is not fire; such is the meaning of the statement.

That which previously did not exist and now arises is called "birth"; the constant transformation from moment to moment is called "aging"; and the severance and destruction of the life-faculty is called "death."
Furthermore, regarding the claim that there is birth without death, this means that one is born in such a manner without having died in a previous life;
however, this is not what is intended.
Furthermore, an argument is established here: prior to old age and death, birth cannot exist.
Why is this? Because it is its own intrinsic nature, just as heat exists prior to fire.
Furthermore, if you wish to avoid such a fault, you might say:
That old age and death exist first, and birth exists later, is also not the case. As the verse says:
"If old age and death existed first, and birth existed later..."
"If it has not yet arisen, there is no cause; how then could there be old age and death?
The commentary states:
There is no such thing as old age and death existing when a phenomenon has not yet arisen, because they lack a basis for existence; such is the meaning of the statement.
Furthermore, an argument is established herein: it is not the case that old age and death arise prior [to birth]. Why?
Because they constitute its essence, just as, for example, abiding does.
The opponent says:
"Since old age and death follow upon birth, there is no such fault.
The proponent states in verse:
"Birth and old age-and-death do not exist simultaneously;
for if birth were itself death, both would be without cause.
Commentary:
Why is this not so? Because there is no such principle as dying at the very moment of birth. Why is that?
Because arising has no intrinsic nature.
This principle does not exist in the world.
What fault is incurred if arising has no intrinsic nature?
Both [positions] incur the fallacy of being causeless; "both" refers to the fact that old age and death would be simultaneous, because they would arise together.
Just as old age and death are not the cause of birth, so too birth is not the cause of old age and death.
Therefore, the claim that old age and death arise simultaneously is not tenable.
By virtue of this analysis, the verse says:
"If they were prior, posterior, or simultaneous, In each case, it would be untenable."
"Why do you give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), claiming that there is birth, aging, and death?
The commentary states:
For this reason, one should not give rise to conceptual proliferation within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

As stated at the beginning of this chapter, the argument that birth and death are established by taking birth, old age, and death as their own causes is untenable; for it does not avoid the faults previously mentioned, just as in the case of birth, old age, and so forth.
When examined through the perspectives of beginning, middle, and end, [the self] is not established; all other phenomena are likewise refuted by analogy. How is this so?
It shall now be demonstrated.
As the verse says: "Thus,
all these causes and effects, as well as their essential natures and characteristics,
the sensation and the feeler, and so forth— all such phenomena whatsoever,"
"Not only is the prior limit of birth and death unattainable,
but likewise all phenomena are entirely without a prior limit. Commentary:

Regarding "all phenomena" (sarvadharma), this refers to the means of cognition and the objects of cognition, the knower and the known, those who attain liberation and the practices for liberation, and so forth; as for their established causal natures and characteristics, none of these are tenable.
What is the meaning of this?
I shall now explain it in brief:
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that sprout of rice and so forth did not previously exist.
Why is this? Because it is an effect, just like the essence of a sprout.
If you wish to maintain that the cause precedes the effect, that too is not so.
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no effect prior to the cause, as there would be no cause.
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"There is such a cause that can cognize that effect.
The proponent says:
"Your claim that there is a cause capable of cognizing an effect is likewise incorrect."
Why is this? Because their causes are diverse, their effects are likewise distinct; for example, it is like a lump of clay producing various objects such as jars.

Furthermore, there is a distinction between the cognizing subject and the cognized object, whereas here there is no such distinction. This is because light from the sun, jewels, lamps, and medicinal herbs possesses differences, while jars and the like do not.

If it is claimed that cause and effect are simultaneous, this is also not the case; for in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the two—the rice seed and the sprout—cannot exist simultaneously. Why is this so?
Because they arise simultaneously, like the two horns of an ox.
Furthermore, there is no such principle as the characteristics of the dewlap and so forth existing prior to the body of the ox. Why is this?
Because there is no substance upon which it depends, just as a painting requires a wall;
likewise, the claim that the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) exists prior to the characterized entity (lakṣya) is also incorrect. Why is this so?

Because of its nature as a substance (*tattva*), it is like the substance of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), which does not exist prior to the marks of a great man; or again, like the earth, which does not exist prior to solidity.
Furthermore, the claim that the two factors of substance and characteristic arise simultaneously is also incorrect.
Why is this? Because they arise simultaneously, just like fragrance and taste; as was extensively refuted previously.

What is elucidated in this chapter is that which was established at the beginning of the chapter and its corresponding fallacies—the teaching of suffering and emptiness, intended to bring about thorough understanding in others.
For this reason, this proof is established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra, saying:
"Good son!..."
Form is neither born nor does it die; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither born nor do they die.
If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without birth and without death, this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, O Paramavikrāmin!
Just as nirvāṇa is boundless, so too are all dharmas boundless.
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail herein.
The commentary on the "Chapter on Contemplating Birth and Death" is completed.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Seven.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Eight.
Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Prajñākaramati.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty. Chapter Twelve:

Examination of Suffering (*Duḥkha-parīkṣā*) Furthermore, this chapter arises because suffering lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and since it is the object to be countered by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it serves to negate fixed attachments. Thus, this chapter is commenced.
The opponent says:
In the ultimate sense, these aggregates exist. Why? Because...
Because it is suffering.
If this [self] did not exist, then that suffering would not exist, just like a second head.
That the aggregates (*skandha*) are suffering is as stated in a verse from a sutra:
"The origin of suffering is also the world, the locus of views, and existence.
For this reason, these aggregates exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
The proponent says:
False conceptualization does not apply to suffering.
As the verse states:
"If someone desires suffering, whether it be self-made,
made by another, made by both, or produced without cause— none of those results are tenable. Commentary:
When one examines them through various and immeasurable modes of reasoning within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), none of those [positions] hold true.
How is it that suffering is not self-made?
As the verse says:
"If suffering were self-made, it would not arise from conditions.
The commentary states:
Because it is self-made, it does not depend upon causes and conditions.
Therefore, the notion that suffering arises from conditions would be untenable;
yet this is not the case, for one still desires to obtain it.
What is the meaning of this?
This means arising from conditions.
As a verse says:
"With the present aggregates as cause, the future aggregates arise."
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which is called Devadatta as a continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*) is not created by Devadatta. Why is this?
Because it relies upon dependent origination.
For example, just as one existence arises from the present aggregates acting as the cause to draw forth the subsequent aggregates, the principle is exactly like this.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:

Although the collection of faculties such as the body and so forth are distinct, the "I" within them is not different; since that single, pervasive abiding is also the agent, and it creates this suffering, it is therefore self-created.
If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise and perish moment by moment and are impermanent, this statement is flawed.
What kind of flaw is it?
This suffering that arises simultaneously with the mind in each moment is not produced by that very same momentary mind; therefore, it is neither self-made nor made by another.
Why is this? It is not the case that one person performs an action while another receives its fruit.
If you intend for another to be the agent, it contradicts your own established tenet (*siddhānta*).
The proponent says:
Herein I establish a proof; your assertion that the "person" (puruṣa) is the agent is incorrect. Why is this so?
Because it is eternal, it is like space.
Since its eternity is thus verified, one knows that it is not an agent.
If a "Great Man" (Puruṣa) were the agent, the intrinsic nature of phenomena would be undermined, as this would constitute a fault in the established thesis.
Furthermore, if you insist that "I" create this suffering, it would follow that it does not arise from conditions; such is the fault.
What is the meaning of this?
In our system, the term "suffering" is designated as "self," and the intended sense is precisely this.

Furthermore, if it is claimed that the action performed by a person is "self-made" and does not arise subsequently as a result of acting in conjunction with other causes and conditions, this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? One should understand that suffering is produced by me through the convergence of immeasurable causes;
the meaning is exactly like that of dry grass, cow dung, and so forth acting as conditions for fire.
Furthermore, the suffering of Devadatta was not created by my self as Devadatta. Why is this?
Because it is suffering, just like the suffering of Yajñadatta.
You previously stated:
"If there is no distinct agent for the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise moment by moment, then the action performed by them is itself their own agent.
Now, I shall answer you:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), suffering is inexpressible; therefore, I am without fault.
In the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), because the characteristics of cause and effect are continuous and not distinct, the world universally perceives them as such and speaks accordingly.

Just as one might say, "The lamp has come from that place," or "This mango tree was planted by me," so too is it here: at a later time, there is a characteristic that continues the sequence of that prior thought; thus, cause and effect are not distinct.

The preceding volition (*cetanā*) is what constitutes "one's own action" (*svayaṃkṛta*); through that preceding moment of volition, wholesome and unwholesome karma is accumulated, and at the time that karma ceases, it serves as the cause for what follows.

Just as the flame of a lamp serves as the cause for that which follows it, so too does this successive continuity proceed until the fruit is attained; therefore, it is not the case that the fruit is obtained without having been produced, nor is it the case that what has been produced is lost and extinguished.
If you think that the various formations (saṃskāra) do not experience the later fruit of the karma previously accumulated because they are momentary and distinct—
just as in the case of separate continuums (saṃtāna)— then [the following applies].
This meaning is not so, as the verse says:
"Everywhere, the phenomena of dependent origination Are neither identical to those conditions, Nor are they different from those conditions;
They are neither eternal nor subject to annihilation."
The commentary states:
Such is my own tenet (*siddhānta*).
If you establish "being different" as the reason (*hetu*), this argument is not established.

Why is this? Because the karma transmitted from preceding moments of mind possesses a superior functional capacity that counteracts [the afflictions] before they have arisen, maintains the continuity [of the antidote], and brings about its fruit.

For example, if one soaks *mātuluṅga* seeds with the juice of purple lac and plants them, the flowers produced later will possess the color of purple lac; this does not contradict conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, those who assert the existence of a "person" (*pudgala*) claim that while one part performs the action, another part experiences the fruit, and thus there is no fault as described above.
The proponent says:

On that one side, [the result] is obtained without having performed the action; on this other side, what has already been performed is lost and destroyed. Thus, there is the fault that the side consisting of performed action never attains its fruit.
The opponent says:
"I am one; therefore, there is no fault.
How is it known that [the self] is one?"
Because it would be associated with the number one.
The proponent says:
It is not the case that there is such a principle as my being associated with the number one.
Why is this? Because it exists, just as, for example, the number one exists.
For this reason, suffering is neither self-made nor made by another.
What is the meaning of this?
As the verse says:
"If the preceding aggregates were different from the succeeding ones, and the succeeding aggregates were different from the preceding ones;..."
"If these aggregates arise from those, one could say that suffering is created by another. Commentary:
If a person wishes to maintain that suffering is created by another, the nature of phenomena (dharmas) is not established; thus, there is a fault in their proposition.
But in reality, this is not so.

Why is it not so? Herein we establish a proof: from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the later aggregates (*skandha*) of Devadatta are not other than his earlier aggregates.
Why is this? Because Devadatta is a collection of aggregates (*skandha*), just like one's own subsequent collection of aggregates.
Furthermore, because the nature of that suffering is a continuous succession without distinction, the thesis and the analogy should be understood as before.
Furthermore, those who maintain the existence of a person (pudgala) say:
"The karma created by one is experienced as its fruit by another.
This argument is not tenable.
Why is this? Because all distinctions of status are created by humans, they are called "self-made suffering" and also "made by another.
Regarding what is established by these two schools, I am free from such faults.
The proponent says:
You merely utter these words, yet even this is not so.
As the verse says:
"If a person creates suffering for themselves, and there is no other person apart from that suffering,
who is this 'person' of whom it is said that they create their own suffering?
The commentary states:
What is suffering? It refers to the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Apart from those aggregates of suffering, there is no separate person; how then can it be said that a person creates suffering?
Furthermore, if you maintain that the person and the five aggregates are neither identical nor different, this argument is incorrect.
Why? Because the name "Devadatta" is merely applied to the five aggregates; no person can be found, because [the person] is dependently originated, just like a jar or other such things.
Thus, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that person is not established; since the person is not established, there is no one who creates suffering.
Furthermore, the claim that another person creates suffering is incorrect, as the verse says:
"If another were to create suffering and deliver it to this person;
since there is no 'other' apart from suffering, how can one say that another creates suffering?
The commentary states:
There is no person apart from suffering, as this has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, there is no evidence to establish that the person possesses a distinct essence that can be perceived.
Thus, the notion that suffering is self-created is untenable; this has already been established through proof to clarify those who have not yet understood.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If self-creation is not established, where could there be creation by another?
If suffering were created by another, that would still be self-creation."
The commentary states:
To claim that suffering is not self-created and yet point to it as being created by another is incorrect.
Just as with the karmic actions that result in a fixed retribution within a distinct continuum, there is no such principle whereby one could say that [suffering] is created by another.
Therefore, the verse says, "Where could there be the action of another? The meaning of these words is as follows:
your claim that while there are distinctions in states, the person remains without difference, is a false statement.
For this reason, it is not the case that suffering is either self-created or created by another.
Furthermore, the Nirgrantha put forth this argument:
"A person creates their own suffering; therefore, suffering is self-created."
Furthermore, if suffering does not coincide with the person, it is called "created by another.
Thus, both the positions of self-creation and creation by another are established.
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"Self-made suffering is not so.
The commentary says:
No person creates suffering; such is the meaning.
Because suffering lacks intrinsic nature, the person likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
If it is claimed that the essence of suffering is the person, this is also not logically tenable. Why is this so?
The verse says:
"Suffering does not produce suffering again.
The commentary explains:
As stated in the previous verse: "If suffering were produced by itself, it would not arise from conditions.
These two lines have already been refuted therein; such is the meaning of the words.
Furthermore, if suffering were to produce further suffering, it would mean that a fruit produces another fruit; moreover, suffering would arise of itself without depending on causes and conditions.
These two possibilities are not observed in the world.
As for what you previously stated—that suffering is not identical to the person, yet this person creates suffering, which is called "created by another"—this statement is incorrect.
As the verse says:
"If suffering were created by another..."
The commentary states:
The opponent intends for the person (*pudgala*) to be the "other"; however, this person lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and thus cannot produce suffering.
Why does it not produce it?
Because it is empty. That which is empty is devoid of substance; how, then, could there be arising or activity?
That there should be an essence without arising is not what the wise desire.
Therefore, the verse says:
"If there is no other, who creates suffering?
The commentary explains:
There is no such meaning of "other"; this is the intended sense of the statement.
For this reason, both "self-caused" and "caused by another" are untenable.
As for those who claim [it is] "caused by both":
There is no fault because [the self] performs both [actions].
To refute this, the Ācārya says in verse:
"If each [action] were performed separately, one could say that the two perform suffering."
The commentary states:
Each [of these] does not act, as has already been refuted above.
Suffering is neither self-created nor created by another; therefore, your claim that suffering is created by both is incorrect.
Nor is it without cause.
Why? Because this adherence to causelessness has already been refuted in the "Examination of Arising" (Anutpāda-parivarta).
In this regard, the verse says:
"Since neither self nor other performs [it], how could suffering exist without a cause?
The commentary explains:

What has been stated previously in this chapter—that if suffering were without a cause, then suffering would not exist—is intended to show that there is no such principle as the existence of suffering without a cause.
This is because, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), suffering cannot be apprehended; such is the meaning of the statement.
Through such various investigations, that suffering is found to have no intrinsic nature.

As for the opponent’s statement at the beginning of this chapter—that the existence of the aggregates is established by taking suffering as the reason—this position is not tenable from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As the verse says:
"If one does not observe suffering alone, the fourfold meaning is not established;
regarding all external phenomena, the fourfold [analysis] likewise does not exist."
The commentary states:
According to the reasoning previously explained, the analysis of external form and so forth also lacks this meaning.
How is it that form is not self-made?
Why is this? Because the causes for existence or non-existence are not tenable, as has already been explained above.
Furthermore, because things arise from conditions, just as the essence of a sprout is not said to be self-made.
If it is claimed that the name "other-maker" (para-kartṛ) is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta), this meaning is not tenable.
Why is it not tenable?
Because the primary elements are not designated as "other" with respect to form (rūpa).
Why is this? Because it is external, like the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, because its substantial existence is negated, form lacks an intrinsic nature; thus, the opponent's position is not established.
Nor is it produced by both together, because each individual factor is not established [as a cause].
Nor is it without a cause. Why is this?
Since this adherence to the doctrine of causelessness has already been refuted previously,
the same logic should be applied to refute [the claim regarding] sound and so forth as well. Therefore,
because the reason stated at the beginning of this chapter— that "because it is suffering"— is faulty, this argument is not established.
In this present chapter, because it is intended to demonstrate that suffering has the meaning of emptiness, this [point] is established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra, saying:
"Good son!..."
Form is neither suffering nor pleasure; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither suffering nor pleasure.
If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither suffering nor pleasure, this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"What is called the Noble Truth?
If it were suffering, or origin, or cessation, or path, it would not be called the Noble Truth."
"The non-arising of that suffering and so forth is what is called a Noble Truth," and so on.
Furthermore, within the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Bhagavān spoke as follows: A bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
"Gotama! Is suffering created by oneself?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Was it created by another?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Then do they both act together?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is it produced without a cause?
The Buddha said:
"No. Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail here.
The explanation of the "Examination of Suffering" chapter is complete.

13. Examination of Formations (*Saṃskāra-parīkṣā*). In the *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, this thirteenth chapter, "Examination of Formations," is further introduced in order to cause others to understand that all various distinctions among formations (*saṃskāra*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
In this context, an outsider cites a sūtra to establish their thesis, as stated in a verse:
"The Bhagavat has taught that it is a false and deceptive dharma.
The commentary states:
How is it known that those phenomena, such as the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), are false?
Because those conditioned formations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and because they deceive ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*).
Through the discrimination of false cognition, they are conceived as being obtainable; therefore, they are false.

Furthermore, because it serves as the cause for the loss of mindfulness and other faculties regarding the sphere of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is a false and deceptive phenomenon (*abhūta-dharma*).
When the Bhagavat says this, he addresses the bhikṣus within the various sūtras, speaking thus.
Those phenomena that are false and deceptive are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The supreme reality is the true dharma of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, it is taught in the Śrāvaka-dharma that all such formations (*saṃskāra*) are deceptive phenomena and phenomena subject to destruction.
The Mahāyāna sūtras also state this: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are false, and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not false.
These two Āgamas both clarify that all formations (*saṃskāra*) are false phenomena; thus, this meaning is established.
The proponent says:
Herein is established a proof that, in the ultimate sense, internal phenomena are empty. Why is this so?
Because it subverts the nature of phenomena, it is like a person created by illusion or transformation.
An opponent says:
"There is no distinction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the logical reason (*hetu*)."
As for your statement that in the ultimate sense all phenomena are empty, this means they are non-existent;
likewise, that which robs or destroys phenomena is also non-existent.
Because the reason (*hetu*) adduced is deficient, the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not established, as it is subject to fault.
The proponent states in verse:
"If the phenomenon to be wrongly taken away does not exist, what is there to be called 'robbery'?
The commentary explains:
You claim that both the thesis and the reason are non-existent.
If that were so, since these are non-existent, what thing could possibly be called "robbed"?
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are like the horns of a rabbit.
Therefore, these two terms, "falsehood" and "plundering," are not without meaning.
What further meaning do they convey?
To discriminate objective spheres while their own intrinsic nature is empty is the meaning of "falsehood"; they do not exist as they truly are, being like reflections or shadows.

This is the meaning of "deprivation" (*apahāra*); since this differs from the "proving reason" (*hetu*) and the "thesis" (*pakṣa*), I am free from the fault of lacking a proving reason within my thesis.
Because these two faults are absent, the intended meaning is established.

Furthermore, regarding the words "plundering" (*apahāra*): the Buddha, the Bhagavān, has uprooted the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), exhausting them forever without remainder; therefore, he spoke these words.
As the verse says:
"The Bhagavān spoke this To reveal the meaning of emptiness."
The commentary states:
The term "deprivation" (apahāra) is not distinct in essence from emptiness (śūnyatā), just as when one says, "There is smoke there," it implies that "there is fire there.
The opponent says:
This statement of falsehood is not without meaning.
What is its meaning?
It means that the Tathāgata does not say that all phenomena are without self.
If that is so, how can one speak of false speech?
As the verse says:
"Because one perceives the transformation of phenomena, All phenomena lack intrinsic nature."
The commentary states:
What is the meaning of this verse?
It means that because one perceives the transformation of all phenomena, one knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is it without substance?
Because it is not permanent.
Such is the principle regarding the Blessed One’s statement that [all things] are false speech.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"That which has an essence is not without essence.
The commentary explains:
What is meant by "existence"?
It is because things possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to your reasoning, all phenomena would then be devoid of intrinsic nature; however, this is not the case.
The verse says:
"Because all phenomena are empty.
The commentary says:
Since all phenomena (dharmas) are devoid of self and what belongs to a self, your position is as follows;
therefore, you ought to believe that phenomena possess intrinsic substance (svabhāva). If it were not so, the verse says:
"If intrinsic substance does not exist, what phenomenon could undergo transformation?"
The commentary states:
Since we directly perceive that this entity undergoes transformation, we know with certainty that there exists a phenomenon characterized by transformation.
Herein is established the proof: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this? Because its essence undergoes transformation.
If this [essence] were non-existent, there would be no transformation, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman.
Because there is the transformation of an existent entity—namely, the internal sense bases and so forth—it follows that, in the ultimate sense, phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"If a phenomenon possesses intrinsic nature, How could it undergo transformation?"
The commentary states:
It is not tenable that a phenomenon possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and yet undergoes transformation. Why is this so?

Because that which possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be destroyed, yet we now clearly perceive its nature undergoing transformation; therefore, one should know that this transforming nature and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) are inseparable. Thus, the reason (*hetu*) you have established is self-contradictory.

Some say that the meaning of "false and illusory phenomena" refers to not seeing phenomena as they truly are—namely, that they lack intrinsic nature; this is what is meant by the teaching of non-self (*anātman*). Why is this so?
What is called "self-entity" is simply the designation "self.
To perceive the transformation of phenomena means to see that all phenomena undergo change, decay, and destruction.
Therefore, false speech cannot be separated from non-self.
This false speech refers to the teaching of non-self (*anātman*), not the teaching of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Therefore, as long as the Noble Path has not arisen and the mountain of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has not collapsed, the shadows and reflections of "self" and "what belongs to self" appear within all internal and external phenomena;
when the Noble Path arises, one no longer discriminates between "self" and "what belongs to self" regarding these phenomena.
If one says that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then this is like the "self" (ātman) as conceived by the non-Buddhists; such a self has no reality.
To establish this point would be to prove what is already established for me.
Regarding such causes, they establish the absence of self (*anātman*), but do not establish emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The proponent says:
"When you conceptualize phenomena as being without substance, you mean that they are non-existent like the horns of a rabbit; it is because of this [conceptualization] that fear arises."
It is like a small child who, seeing his own reflection at night, mistakes it for a non-human spirit and cries out in terror.
You are just like this.
As you have said, while the outsiders cling to a self, establishing this "non-self" actually results in what we ourselves have established.

Listen attentively now: if one establishes the non-existence of a self by means of false speech, and likewise understands that even the "self" asserted by the non-Buddhists lacks intrinsic nature, it is exactly so, it is exactly so.

The reason I have now established the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) as the cause and revealed it to you is that this also establishes the meaning of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*). Why is this?
Because this selflessness of persons is not separate from that emptiness of phenomena.
In this way, this reason causes one to have faith and understanding.
For example, as when one establishes the thesis: "Sound is impermanent.
How does one state the reason?
This is because they are produced.
By the statement that they are "produced," it is also established that suffering, emptiness, and selflessness are proven.

When such illusory phenomena are thus established as lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the principle of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is likewise established, because they are inseparable, as the outsiders (*bāhyaka*) have stated.
Regarding the meaning of "falsehood," this clarifies that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena does not abide.
Now, this point is answered:
if a phenomenon were graspable, the verse says:
"His essence does not undergo change, nor do others undergo change;
as youth does not become old age, so too old age does not become youth.
Commentary:
These two analogies correspond respectively to the sequence of the [preceding] enumeration.
Herein a formal argument is established: it is not the case that a phenomenon (dharma) abides in its own essence while undergoing transformation. Why is this?
Because its own essence is not abandoned, it is like youth and old age.
If it is argued that the abiding of a preceding moment characterized by a different state of aging is what constitutes "transformation," this is also not the case.
Why is this? Because distinct characteristics have already departed, just as in the case of old age.

If an outsider were to say that just as milk transforms into curd without abandoning its own essence, and for this reason the logical reason (*hetu*) is not "one-sided" (*anaikāntika*), this argument is incorrect.
Now I shall question you:
what is curd?
He replied, "It is milk."
If milk were already curd without abandoning its own nature, how could one distinguish it by calling this "curd"?
If they were definitively distinct, the verse says:
"If this very substance were different, then milk would be identical to curd."
The commentary states:
Because milk does not relinquish its color, taste, potency, function, and benefits, it does not become curd.
Nor is it the case that they are different [entities].
Why is this? As a verse says:
"Apart from milk, what thing exists that can produce that curd?"
The commentary states:
Since there is no curd that can arise, other entities likewise undergo no transformation.
Your claim that the reason is not invariably concomitant is incorrect.
Another person said:
"I also do not say that milk does not produce curd.
Although the characteristic of curd is different from milk, yet by the power of their harmonious conjunction, milk produces curd."
The proponent says:
Regarding your statement concerning the power of the sovereign force of combination, does this milk abandon its own nature in order to produce curd,
or does it produce curd without abandoning its own nature?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it were to abandon its own essence, one could not say that milk gives rise to curd.
If it were not to abandon its own essence, this would be contradictory.
How are they contradictory?
If it is milk, how can it be called curd?
If it is curd, how can it be milk?
In that world, everyone understands it in this way:
if someone says, "Milk does not produce curd; it merely transforms into curd."
This point is likewise refuted as previously stated.
When examined in this manner, the notion that phenomena are distinct within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is entirely untenable.
As for your claim that phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), using this as a reason, that reason is unestablished.
The opponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are not empty. Why is this?
Because these opposing factors exist, they are like inverted cognition and non-inverted cognition.
If these did not exist, there would be no opposing factor, just as with a flower in the sky; for it is by virtue of opposing non-emptiness that the phenomenon of emptiness exists.
For this reason, according to the arguments as stated, all phenomena are not empty.
The proponent says:

If the aggregates and so forth existed in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then one could establish the dharma of emptiness by excluding those existing things; however, in the ultimate sense, there is not a single phenomenon that is not empty.
As the verse says:
"If there were even one phenomenon that was not empty, By observing this, emptiness would exist;
Since there is not a single phenomenon that is not empty, Where could emptiness be found?"
The commentary states:
Regarding "empty" and "not empty," such distinctions are made based on the nature of phenomena within the context of conventional truth.
What is the meaning of this?
For example, if there is a house, it is called "not empty" because someone dwells in it; if no one dwells in it, it is called "empty.
Now, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is not a single dharma that is not empty. Where, then, could an empty dharma be found that is capable of being apprehended?

As for your previous statement that the conceptualization of mutually contradictory phenomena serves as the cause [for emptiness], this reason is unestablished; it is merely a provisional expression of "emptiness" intended to negate attachment.
Furthermore, the proponents of the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra* say:
"Because the self-nature of that which is conceptually constructed does not exist, the nature of conceptual construction is empty.
This emptiness of all phenomena is truly existent."
What is reality?
It is because one does not perceive a creator.
The proponent says:
"This view of yours is called the 'view of clinging to emptiness' (śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi).
The opponent says:
"For what reason do you designate me as one who clings to emptiness?"
The proponent says:
Since all phenomena are empty because they lack intrinsic nature, emptiness is not a real entity and should not be clung to.
To refute this, as stated in the previous verse: "If there were even a single phenomenon that was not empty, would this not be an object of conceptualizing cognition?"
Is this the domain of non-conceptual wisdom?
If there were even a single thing that was empty, this would be called the domain of the wisdom of emptiness; yet no such thing exists.
Since there is not a single thing that is not empty, it is said that all phenomena are empty.
Therefore, the verse says: "Where can emptiness be found?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is not a single dharma that is not empty—what does this mean?
Those who hold the view of non-emptiness are consumed by the fire of emptiness.
Those who conceptualize emptiness are likewise consumed by it.
Therefore, the verse asks: "Where can emptiness be found?

Furthermore, those who practice dualistic conduct engage in such conceptualization: they perceive that things like illusory horses are empty because they lack intrinsic nature, while things like real horses are not empty because they possess intrinsic nature; this is a distinction of cognition.

When one who practices non-duality practices the perfection of wisdom through non-conceptualization, they contemplate all phenomena within the realm of the ultimate truth as being truly like space—of a single mark which is markless—and thus see that there is nothing to be seen.
The verse says: "There is not a single dharma that is not empty; where, then, could emptiness be found?
For this reason, the opponent's logical reason is unestablished.
The outsider says:
Even if [the reason] were unestablished or contradictory, you would still be constantly negating emptiness at all times;
such is also my intention. For this reason, that which is desired is established.
The proponent says:

It is not that phenomena become empty through the arising of the wisdom of emptiness; rather, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is itself empty. Wisdom merely realizes this emptiness, just as a lamp illuminates and makes known [an object].
A non-existent jar is not something produced.
Why is this? Because that jar has no intrinsic nature and cannot be made to exist.
Therefore, what you have said is the result of poor reflection.
Furthermore, some may say:
"You who propound emptiness are attributing faults to others.

Yet, while relying upon emptiness, you see that emptiness lacks power; consequently, you further claim that there is no emptiness. Therefore, the doctrine you intend to establish is refuted, and it also contradicts your own *siddhānta*."
How is it that one contradicts oneself?
As a verse in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If there are those who understand emptiness, They all perceive the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"If separated from combination, No such entity exists;
Therefore, emptiness is without arising, And I say it is without intrinsic nature."
"In this way, you contradict your own Āgama.
The proponent says:
"Have you not heard?"
As it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Those who understand my Dharma-gate as being like the parable of the raft should abandon even this Dharma, let alone what is not Dharma."
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
"One does not contemplate form as empty, nor does one contemplate form as non-empty; this so-called 'view of emptiness' is also a form of attachment, and therefore it must be prevented."
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who makes the conceptual distinction that [emptiness] is not empty, this too should be abandoned.
This is because these two types of grasping entail great faults; it is not the case that one who abandons emptiness is at fault.

When such various views and afflictions disturb and disorder the mind, the Tathāgata gives rise to his foremost great compassion in order to sever the seeds of suffering for those sentient beings who have not yet escaped it.
As the verse says:
"The Tathāgata taught the dharma of emptiness for the purpose of escaping all views.
The commentary states:
"Views" refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; "emptiness" refers to the internal sense-bases being empty (*adhyātma-āyatana-śūnyatā*) as their antidote.
If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are not yet mature and who have not attained the profound *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, they will not understand the right path.
As the verse says:
"Those who perceive emptiness.
The commentary explains:
What is meant by "one who views emptiness"?
It refers to one who clings to emptiness, asserting that "this emptiness exists.
What is the fault in clinging to emptiness?
As the verse says:
"It is said that he cannot be cured.
The commentary explains:
The Tathāgata has said that sentient beings who hold the view of emptiness are incurable.
What is the meaning of this?
It is like taking a purgative medicine that rouses all manner of illnesses, yet instead of being expelled, they are retained and result in a grave illness.
Thus, the teaching of emptiness is for the purpose of abandoning all false views;
yet if one should instead cling to emptiness itself, it is said that such a person is incurable.
For this reason, there is no fault in abandoning [clinging to] emptiness.
Furthermore, it is like a person whose cart has sunk into the mud; in order to extract the cart, he says to another person:
"Give me nothing at all, and I will pull out the cart.
Yet, after that other person has pulled out the cart, he asks the owner of the cart for that which was promised: "nothing at all."
Because they do not understand the intended meaning of these words, they are held in derision by the wise.
Therefore, you should not cling to emptiness and take it to be an existent thing.
For this reason, your reason is not established, and the fault does not depart from you.
Since the meaning of the reason you have stated is unestablished, my own reason is free from the aforementioned faults and possesses logical force.
What is meant by "possessing power"?
It refers to teaching that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty, thereby causing people to believe and understand.
Since the meaning of this chapter is thus, it is established as valid.
As the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Paramavīra in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "Good son!
All those dharmas arise from inversion; they are unreal, non-existent, false, and not as they truly are."
"O Paramavīra!
If there is a person who practices even a single dharma, this inverted practice is not a practice of reality.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"The foolish people of the world cling to various truths, yet these dharmas are neither real nor false.
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail herein.
The commentary on the "Chapter on Examining Formations" is concluded. 14.

The Commentary on the *Prajñāpradīpa*, "Chapter Fourteen: Examining Combination. Furthermore, this chapter is composed in order to inspire conviction and understanding that all composite phenomena, which are the objects of negation by emptiness, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The opponent says:
You claim that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.
To speak in this way contradicts correct reasoning.
What is the reasoning?
As the Buddha has taught, the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—is termed "contact.
For this reason, what you previously stated is contradictory.
According to my established position, all phenomena possess intrinsic nature within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because it is on the basis of this reason that they are said to be "conjoined."
If this [conjunction] did not exist, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of this cause as "conjunction" (saṃyoga); it is, for example, like not speaking of clothing based on the hair of a tortoise.
Because the Buddha taught that there are the three fetters—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion—he designated them as "conjunction."
Because my statement of the reason accords with correct reasoning, it follows that all phenomena do not lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The opponent says:
Although you have made this statement, the meaning is not so.
As the verse says:
"The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing— These three occupy distinct locations;
When compared two by two, None of them are joined."
The commentary states:
The seeing, the object seen, and the seer—each pair of these, when compared with one another, do not cohere; furthermore, all of them together do not cohere.
Because of this, the verse says:
"One should know that the defilement, the defiler, and the phenomena defiled by them—
along with other afflictions and other bases— the three types are all devoid of conjunction. Commentary:
"Defilement" (*rañjana*) refers to the characteristic of desire.
As for "afflictions" (*kleśa*), they are so called because they are able to defile the continuity (*saṃtati*) of sentient beings; thus, defilement and the like are designated as afflictions.
The "remainder" refers to hatred and so forth.
This also consists of three types: namely, hatred, the hater, and the object of hatred.
As for the remaining sense bases (*āyatana*), they have already been explained above in the context of the eye.
Among these, the "others" refer to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Why are they called "entrances" (āyatana)?
Because they are the gateways through which the mind and mental factors arise; therefore, they are called entrances.
This also consists of three types: namely, hearing, that which is heard, and the hearer; and so on, up to knowing, that which is known, and the knower.
Those afflicted by defilements and the other sense bases (āyatana) do not mutually correspond when paired two by two, nor do they correspond at all.
Just as with "visible" and so forth, one should understand that there is no conjunction.
Now, in order to cause others to understand this without doubt, the verse says:
"If difference were to conjoin with difference, This difference could not be apprehended."
"And with all that is visible and so forth, / All distinct characteristics are incompatible.
The commentary states:
"The visible and so forth" refers to seeing, the object seen, and the seer.
In this way, passion, the impassioned one, and the object of passion are all mutually uncombined.
To provide a proof for this: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the seer does not combine with the seen or with the act of seeing.
Why is this? Because they are not different.
If things are not different, they can never be conjoined, just as, for example, a thing cannot be conjoined with its own self-nature.
Some say that as for the claim that distinct things combine with what is distinct: herein, if the continuity of defilements and so forth were located in separate places, they would not combine.
Because they proceed without interruption from those separate locations and distinct continuities, they are termed "conjoined" (*saṃprayukta*); thus, this reason is established.
The proponent says:
If that which is visible and so forth first exists in separate locations and subsequently exists in a single location, it is called "conjunction.
This reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) and lacks any proof; therefore, your statement is incorrect.
Because it is thus, the verse says:
"Not only is difference unattainable in the visible and so forth,
But difference is also unattainable in all other phenomena."
The commentary states:

According to the reasoning previously explained, there is no sense of conjunction between hearing, the object heard, and the hearer; nor between anger, the object of anger, and the one who is angry, and so forth.
The opponent says:
"Your statement that the self, the visible object, the eye, and so forth are not distinct is unestablished, because the reason [you provide] is unestablished.
The proponent replies:
The reason is not unestablished. Why?
As the verse says:
"Otherness takes otherness as its condition.
The commentary states:
It is called "otherness" because it depends upon otherness.
The verse says:
"Without separation, there is no difference.
The commentary explains:
Regarding that which arises with the seed as its condition: because it depends upon this seed, the sprout is said to be "different" [from it].
The verse says:
"If that which arises from conditions Is not different from those conditions."
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it cannot be seen that there is anything distinct from the eye. Why is this?
Because distinct terminology is based on conceptual observation, it is like the visible nature of a thing itself.
If a phenomenon arises from conditions, it is not different from those conditions.
If one were to say they are different, then the sprout should emerge from something other than this seed.
Just as fire does not observe a separate entity, for its own nature is heat;
so too, one who sees does not observe the visible, one who hears does not observe the audible, and one who is defiled does not observe defilement and the like.
If fire did not depend on cold but were inherently hot by its own nature, this distinction would not be established.
Why? Because such a principle does not exist within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The opponent says:
The seer is distinct from the eye and so forth; they do not need to be observed in relation to one another. Why is this?
Because they are distinguished by their characteristics, they are like an ox and a horse.
In this context, that which appears as the objective field is called the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*); this is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*).

The collection of formations (*saṃskāra-kalāpa*) belonging to this seer, which takes as its object the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness, is called the eye (*cakṣus*).
Shape and color—these are called the visible.
As I have stated, because the cause possesses efficacy, the distinct meanings of the "seer," such as the eye and so forth, are established.
The proponent says:
This statement is not correct,
because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the two entities of "cow" and "horse" cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, some say:

If it is argued that the distinction between the seer and the eyes and so forth is established because of the differentiation of perceptions and because of the distinction between cause and fruit, this is answered as before.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
there exists a distinct substantial entity [of the self] which enters into conjunction with objects.
The proponent says:

If you intend for there to be a distinct entity of difference that conjoins with an object, then a second object should also naturally possess difference without [an external cause], because you establish that difference has a separate essence.
Herein, the proof is established: there is no distinct entity that combines with an object.
Why? Because it is an objective entity (*vastu*), just like an objective entity prior to the occurrence of verbal expression.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), difference has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why?
Because it consists of both the general and the particular, just like the essence of form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), difference is not the cause for verbal expression or cognitive awareness.
Why? Because it is the cause for the verbal expression and cognitive awareness of distinction, just as, for example, the essence of form (*rūpa*) is.
Furthermore, does this difference exist within that which is different,
or within that which is not different?
What fault is there in either case?
If [difference] were to exist within difference, as the verse says:
"Within difference, there is no difference.
The commentary explains:

If that distinct entity is already distinct prior to its existence, then to say that this distinctness moves toward that other distinct entity is meaningless; because the distinct entity is empty, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of distinctness is not established.
If it were to exist within that which is non-different, this too would not be the case.
As the verse says:
"It does not exist even within that which is non-different."
The commentary states:
This refers to the fault that there would be a difference within the intrinsic nature itself.
As has been explained, because the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is refuted, a distinct phenomenon (*bhinnadharma*) cannot be established.
The opponent says:
"Unity and difference are two extremes. You now negate difference; thus, the phenomenon of difference would be non-existent.
If this difference does not exist, one must accept non-difference; therefore, you incur the fault of contradicting your own established tenet (*siddhānta*)."
The proponent says:
Just as the non-existence of "otherness" has already been made understood by others, so too is the non-existence of "non-otherness. As the verse says:
"Because there is no distinct phenomenon, non-distinct phenomena also do not exist.
Commentary: Non-distinctness exists in dependence upon observing distinctness; since distinctness has already been refuted, [non-distinctness] does not exist.
Since they neither differ nor exist [as separate entities], how can they be negated?
Now, I shall present the proof: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the seer and the seen cannot be established as different. Why is this so?
Because it is observed through distinct linguistic expressions, just as, for example, the nature of the visible [object] is perceived.
Likewise, because it exists, because it is an effect, because it is a cause, and because it is the object of both doubt and knowledge—these various reasons should be explained in detail.
In this way, both identity and difference are negated, because [the notion of] oneness and so forth is not established.
As the verse says:
"One phenomenon is not tenable; A different phenomenon is also not tenable."
If someone were to say:
"There is such a defilement that conjoins with the defiled one. Why is this so?"
Because they exist at the same time, like water and milk.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is a conjunction with the one who is defiled. Why is this so?
Because it is observed through conventional designations of differentiation, it is like the union of an eater and food.
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"At the time of conjunction, after conjunction, and even the conjoiner—none of these exist."
The commentary states:
As previously explained, there is no such principle as the conjunction of distinct entities through expedient means (*upāya*).
Since the opponent’s initial reason was already refuted at the beginning of this chapter, this is done to lead others to understand that conjunction lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning within this chapter is therefore established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra, saying:
"Good son!..."
Form is neither conjoined nor dispersed; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
That form through to consciousness is neither conjoined nor dispersed—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Such sūtras as these should be explained in detail herein.
The commentary on the "Examination of Union" (Saṃyoga-parīkṣā) is concluded.
*Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Nine.
Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prabhākaramitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.

Chapter Fifteen: Contemplating Existence and Non-existence. Furthermore, this chapter is composed so that others may understand that all dependently originated phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal, by means of the negation of existence and non-existence, which are the opposites of emptiness.
The opponent says:
Your claim that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is incorrect. Why is this so?
This contradicts your own statement and constitutes a fault in establishing your thesis.
How does it contradict your statement?
It is like someone saying, "My mother is a barren woman, yet my father practices celibacy."
An opponent objects:
"If your parents were truly as you say, how could you exist?
If you arose from birth, then the principles of the barren woman and the brahmacārin would both be untenable."
It is the same for you: if there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva), how can they be called "all phenomena" (dharmas)?
Since you call them "all phenomena," how can they lack intrinsic nature?
Therefore, this is a contradiction of your own words and a fault in your formal proposition.
The proponent says:
As for your claim that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), what kind of thing could this be within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)?
Since there is no supporting analogy, your statement is incorrect.
Furthermore, if I had previously asserted in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) that various phenomena exist, and later established their non-existence, it would contradict my own words.
But in reality this is not the case; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of all phenomena as being like illusions and so forth within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), I do not deny this, and thus there is no fault in the thesis.
However, some who are clever yet possessed of false pride may ask:
"Which phenomena are those that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?"
If, as you claim, these phenomena have no intrinsic nature despite the fact that they possess an essence according to false conceptualization, then you are merely proving what I already maintain.

Furthermore, if these phenomena arise from causes and conditions yet you intend to assert they lack an essence, this contradicts direct perception and conflicts with what is commonly understood by the world.
The proponent says:
Within ultimate reality, a non-conceptualizing consciousness that arises taking form as its object cannot be found;
as for the claim that "this thing exists," it has already been refuted previously.
Since I do not negate what is spoken according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it does not contradict what is perceived by direct observation or what is understood by the world.
Therefore, the meaning of what you have stated is not correct.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), if there were even a single phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the principle of arising would not exist.
As the verse says:
"If a phenomenon possessed an intrinsic nature, Arising from conditions would be impossible."
The commentary states:
If one asserts that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such faults ensue.
If you insist that seeing the arising of phenomena cannot refute my position, then this must be asked:
Regarding your statement that you see phenomena as having an arising: does this depend on other causes and conditions?
As the verse says:
"If [a thing] arises from causes and conditions, Its intrinsic nature is a produced phenomenon."
The commentary states:
If it were a producing agent (*kāraka*), it would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); how then could there be the characteristics of causes and conditions?

If a phenomenon arises from its own immediate antecedent part (*samanantarapratyaya*) and is uniquely capable of giving rise to its own effect, this is the characteristic of a cause. That which is the opposite of this is called a condition (*pratyaya*). How, then, can it be called a "producer"?
If phenomena possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would not require to be produced.
However, since there is now production, we know they lack intrinsic nature.
Herein is established the proof: from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) lack intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because they arise from causes and conditions, just as a magician conjures illusory phenomena such as oxen.
If things possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would not arise from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there are some who do not understand the analogy herein and speak as follows:
"The illusory spells, medicinal herbs, clay, grass, wood, and so forth are existent and not non-existent; because these exist, the forms of elephants, horses, and the like manifest."
For this reason, your analogy lacks the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*).
The proponent says:
You have not stated it well.

Regarding my employment of analogies, I take the lack of intrinsic substance in elephants, horses, and the like as my examples, rather than taking the possession of intrinsic substance by grasses, trees, and the earth as examples.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that grasses, trees, the earth, and so forth possess arising and substantial reality, this has already been refuted previously.

Some say: "All phenomena that arise from conditions possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for instance, space and the like do not arise from conditions yet are existent things. Therefore, the reason you have put forward is not conclusive."
The proponent says:
You have not explained it well.
Phenomena born of causes and conditions are like illusions, dreams, and mirages; they exist within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
What is the meaning of this?
As the verse says:
"If there were an intrinsic nature, how could it ever be produced?"
The commentary states:
If it were a constructed phenomenon (*kṛtaka*), it would not be apart from the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Since the very essence of that which is to be countered does not exist, the reason (*hetu*) adduced is therefore not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), even things such as space are unarisen, just like a rabbit’s horn; how could they possibly exist?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this has already been examined previously so that others may gain faith and understanding.
Now, another proof is established: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why? Because they are produced (*kṛtakatvāt*).
Furthermore, because they are observed through conventional designations of differentiation, they are like illusory persons and the like.
If any single entity possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would contradict the aforementioned [argument].
Moreover, herein an opponent establishes a proof: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), those internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth all possess intrinsic substance."

Why is this? Because it serves as the cause for the conventional designation of the distinction between self and other; just as there is shortness because of length, where length is the cause of shortness, so too, what is here called "self" serves as the cause for the conventional designation of the distinction from "other."
The proponent says:
It has already been established through proof that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
however, because you maintain [a contrary view], I shall now state it once more.
As the verse says:
"Since phenomena have no intrinsic nature, how could they have an extrinsic nature?
The commentary states:
If phenomena possessed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then by observing that intrinsic nature, one could speak of extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).
Since intrinsic nature does not exist, observing what could one speak of the extrinsic?
Your claim that intrinsic nature serves as the cause for the extrinsic is untenable, both because the reason is unestablished and because it contradicts the meaning.
Furthermore, because shortness and length do not exist within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the analogy is unestablished.
The opponent says:
"In the ultimate sense, the eye and so forth possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
Why is this? Because of its essential nature, just as fire has heat.
The proponent says:

Fire has no intrinsic nature; as was already refuted in the "Examination of the Aggregates" regarding existence and arising-and-ceasing, it was also previously negated in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Since fire is not established, the analogy lacks substantiality.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"When the intrinsic nature of self and other has been refuted, where could any phenomenon (dharma) possibly exist?
The commentary states:
Since the meaning of "entity" has already been refuted, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because phenomena do not exist, the meaning of a "cause" is not established; such is the intended sense of the statement.
The opponent states a verse:
"If one perceives self and other, Or existence and non-existence;
Such a person cannot perceive The Tathāgata’s true Dharma.
As you have stated, once the nature of self and other has been dispelled, where could any further phenomenon exist?
As stated in the verse, this statement is contradictory.
Furthermore, such an entity exists because of its opposition [to others], like the crow and the owl.
The proponent says:
Since arising has already been refuted within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), as the verse says:
"If an existent entity is not established, how can a non-existent entity be established?
The commentary states:
To refute the attachment to existence, it is therefore said that "it does not exist.
Since non-existence itself has no substantial essence, even if one were not to say "it does not exist," non-existence would still not be what I intend. Why is this so?
Because there is no separate dharma that can be grasped, the reason is likewise not unestablished.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because the nature of this dharma is different, people of the world call it 'without nature'."
The commentary states:

Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are termed "non-existent. Yet, there is not a single phenomenon that can be named "the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Therefore, the meaning of your proposed reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, and it contradicts the intended meaning.
What constitutes a contradiction with the meaning?

You establish a contradictory property as the reason; because it is refuted by its own contradiction, the subject (dharmin) you have established is likewise not proven, and thus this is a contradiction.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the crow and the owl lack intrinsic nature; therefore, the analogy is not established.
By this analysis, all three—the self, the other, and the absence of intrinsic nature—are unestablished.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of unattached wisdom, does not perceive any phenomena—whether self or other, existence or non-existence, and so forth.
Why are they not perceived?
Because he has ascended the vehicle of non-conceptualizing wisdom.

Furthermore, those of shallow wisdom have not previously aroused the profound Dharma-patience; because they are permeated by the habitual tendencies of verbal expression regarding phenomena such as self and other, or existence and non-existence, their true wisdom is obscured and obstructed.
As stated in the preceding verse: "If a person perceives self and other, as well as existence and non-existence, they are unable to see the true Dharma of the Tathāgata.
What is the meaning of this?
The meaning of the verse is as follows: because the [notion] that self and others are identical contradicts both correct reasoning (*yukti*) and the scriptures (*āgama*).
Regarding the contradiction with correct reasoning, it has already been explained above.
Regarding the contradiction with the scriptures, you should now listen.
As a verse says:
“The Buddha, able to contemplate according to reality, Does not cling to existence or non-existence;
He instructs Kātyāyana To leave behind both existence and non-existence.”
The commentary states:
