What is the instruction?
It is as the Buddha told Kātyāyana:
"The world for the most part relies upon two extremes, namely 'existence' and 'non-existence.
Those with profound wisdom do not cling to existence or non-existence. And so forth.
Furthermore, as the Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one says 'it exists,' this is the adherence to the extreme of eternalism.
If one says 'it does not exist,' this is the adherence to the extreme of nihilism."
Furthermore, some may say:
"If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely non-existent, how can there be the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*)?

It is because, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), phenomena arise from conditions; when observed through wisdom, these dependently arisen phenomena are without self, without other, and are neither existent nor non-existent."
To negate such views is called "seeing the truths" (*satyadarśana*).
How does one see the truths?
Because this principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the cause for seeing reality.
Who perceives reality?
It is those sons of the Buddha who are illumined by the sunlight of the wisdom of dependent origination;
it is because this serves as their cause.
The proponent says:
Those who fear emptiness speak in this manner.

It is just as people in the world, fearing empty space, cling to the existence of resistant, substantial entities as their basis; consequently, they give rise to the thought of desiring to distance themselves from empty space.
Those who distance themselves from emptiness do so by relying on views of self, other, and so forth; as the verse says:
"If a person perceives self and other, as well as existence and non-existence, they will not be able to see the Tathāgata’s true Dharma."
What is the meaning of this?
To view things in such a manner is called wrong view.
Therefore, within the Buddha’s teaching to Kātyāyana, both extremes of "existence" and "non-existence" are negated; this is the correct principle.
By this principle, one should not perceive those phenomena of self, other, and so forth. How is this so?
As the verse says:
"If a phenomenon (*dharma*) possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it could not be said to be non-existent. Commentary:
This is because it lacks an intrinsic nature both prior to its arising and after its destruction.
Furthermore, if all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the verse states:
"If phenomena possess an intrinsic nature, subsequent alteration would be impossible.
The commentary explains:
Just as fire has heat as its characteristic, it is not the case that it becomes cold at a later time; for this reason, it is said that the analogy is dissimilar.
Likewise, the proposition that phenomena are eternal yet undergo origination and cessation is logically untenable.

Herein is established a formal argument: just as when a real dharma is realized, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth does not manifest. Why is this?
Because the internal sense-bases and so forth undergo change at a later time; for example, when water encounters fire, it becomes warm, yet warmth is not the intrinsic nature of water.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master says:
"Just as in my Āgama it is stated that there are various elements (*dhātu*) within wood, by this same principle water also possesses heat.
Your claim that heat is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of water is therefore invalid as an analogy."
The proponent says:

Regarding that statement made in the Āgamas, it refers to a bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over the mind; whenever he wishes to transform objects such as grass or wood into gold, water, fire, or the like, according to his intention, it is accomplished. Therefore, it is said that within wood there are various elements (*dhātu*).
Regarding "various realms" (*nānā-dhātu*): this refers to the presence of multiple functional capacities within a single substance, such as wood.
If a certain capacity exists within a given object, that capacity is not the substantial entity (*dravya*) of that object itself.

If these various functions were the very substance of that [entity], then just as there are four functions within the earth element, it would likewise have to take moisture, heat, and motion as its substance, rather than taking solidity alone.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters say:
Although the temporal states are distinct, their substance is not different; this is how it should be understood. Why is this so?
Because this is an object of consciousness, it is like that which exists in the present.
For this reason, your previously stated reason—that the substance [of the past] is different—is not accepted by me.
If you wish for them not to be different, then your own thesis is not established.
The proponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), even the existence of present things is not established; therefore, your example is invalid.
If it is claimed that there exists a phenomenon which persists through the time periods and various states, this is not the case. Why?
Because arising has already been refuted.
Furthermore, within the past and the future there is no present phenomenon, because it is not present, just like a flower in the sky.
Moreover, even in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the past and the future is not established.
If a Sāṃkhya proponent were to say:
"Your previous statement of the reason—that they are of different entities—is not correct. Why is that?"
I establish that all phenomena possess two meanings:
first, they are concealed; second, they enter into the treasury of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-garbha*).
To establish this meaning, further proof must be provided: it is certain that such non-extinguished phenomena exist.
Why is this? Because it is obscured, just as the radiance of the sun eclipses the light of the stars.
Furthermore, because it is an object of consciousness and because it is spoken of in terms of temporal sequence, it is like the present world.
Therefore, the meaning of the reason you have established is unproven.
You should answer as follows:
"A presently existing entity is also unproven in terms of ultimate reality."
Why is this? Because there is no analogy.
As for your establishing "obscuration" as the reason (*hetu*), that argument is also unestablished; this must be explained here.
How is this verified?
That which was not understood previously remains ultimately ununderstood. Why is this so?
Because they are not understood, they are like flowers in the sky.
Furthermore, for one who does not enter the treasury of self-nature, there is ultimately no sense of "entering. Why is this?
Because it does not enter [into reality], it is like a mental construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, it is like a storehouse of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-garbha*); because there is the fault of clinging to this as a substantial entity, as the verse says:
"If there were such an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then one could not say it does not exist;
if the intrinsic nature were to differ, it ultimately would not be so.
Commentary:
Because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is thus immutable, there can be no analogy [for it].
If it were a non-existent thing, there would likewise be no mutation, just as the son of a barren woman does not grow from childhood to adulthood.
It is ultimately impossible to cause people to believe in change by means of such [illusory] transformations.
As a verse says:
"If there is no intrinsic nature, How can there be change?"
The commentary states:
Both extremes entail faults; therefore, the wise do not accept them.
The outsider says:
Do you intend to say that self-nature, whether it possesses an essence or lacks one, is entirely devoid of transformation?
Therefore, the thesis you previously established is refuted, and your reason is also unestablished.
How is it not established?
If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that underwent transformation, this would be impossible.
The proponent says:
This statement is not correct.
Why? Because when I say "non-existent," I clarify that intrinsic nature is empty; I do not intend to assert that such dharmas of intrinsic nature exist.
As the verse says:
"In reality, there is not a single dharma whose intrinsic nature can be apprehended.
The commentary explains:
It is not the case that there is an intrinsic nature; rather, you have made this conceptual distinction due to the sovereign power of the habitual tendencies of those afflictions.
As stated in the previous verse: "If there is no intrinsic nature, how can there be alteration?"
This fault of transformation has already been explained previously.
Both the refutation of the two extremes and their establishment exist only in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, my previously established thesis remains unrefuted, because within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) there is indeed transformation; furthermore, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) presented is not unestablished.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣika says:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*) such as the eye definitely possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
Why is this? Because these [factors] can serve as causes for the arising of cognition, just like nirvāṇa.
The proponent says:
As for your statement that there is a cause for cognition, this reason is unestablished. Why?
Because, for example, water in a mirage also serves as a cause for cognition; therefore, the reason is not conclusive.
Now it shall be explained further, as the verse says:
"To exist" is the clinging to permanence; "To not exist" is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, the wise person Should not rely on existence or non-existence.
The commentary states:
What fault is there in the attachment to the views of eternalism and nihilism?

If phenomena were eternal, pleasure would be eternally pleasant and suffering would be eternally painful; consequently, there would be no weariness with suffering nor seeking for pleasure, and one would not give rise to the Noble Path.
If something already existed beforehand, it would not require causes.

If dharmas were subject to annihilation, there would be no defilement or purity, nor suffering or pleasure; even if one were to observe the prohibitive precepts, they would be empty and without fruit. Therefore, none of these [positions] are tenable.
To hold that both existence and non-existence coexist is called a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Because this false view can block the gates to the realms of gods and humans as well as the gate to *nirvāṇa*, those who wish to emerge from the wilderness of birth and death, those who wish to sport and enjoy pleasure with celestial maidens, those who wish to sever all [craving for] enjoyment, and those who wish to experience the bliss of the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) should not rely upon the two views of existence and non-existence.
Why is this? Because those who rely upon them incur the faults of nihilism and eternalism.
In what way do these two views constitute the faults of nihilism and eternalism?
As the verse says:
"If a phenomenon possesses intrinsic nature, its non-existence would imply permanence;
that which previously existed but now no longer exists entails the fault of nihilism."
The commentary states:

Because of such faults as those of eternalism and nihilism, one who proclaims the Middle Way should engage in correct reflection: based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the arising of dharmas such as form is the cause for the cognition of existence;
if form has not yet arisen or has already ceased, it is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one realizes that the self-nature is empty; because it is without arising, it is not the view of existence.
Because it is like a magical illusion, one does not cling to the view of non-existence.
Because of this, one does not fall into the two extremes.
Herein, in order to negate the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, it causes people to believe and understand that dependently arisen phenomena are neither annihilated nor eternal.
The meaning of this chapter is thus established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Pramudita-vīra, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
Form is neither annihilated nor eternal; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither annihilated nor eternal.
That form through to consciousness is neither annihilated nor eternal—this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* says:
"Existence and non-existence are two extremes; Purity and impurity are likewise so.
Therefore, the wise person Leaves the extremes and does not dwell in the middle."
Such sūtras as these should be explained at length here.
The commentary on the "Examination of Being and Non-being" (Sadasatparīkṣā) is concluded. Chapter 16:

Examination of Bondage and Liberation (*Bandhanamokṣaparīkṣā*) Furthermore, having already refuted existence and non-existence to avoid the faults of nihilism and eternalism, this chapter follows in order to clarify the meaning that bondage and liberation—the objects of negation by emptiness—are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus, this chapter arises next.
Some say: Within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth must possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why is this?
Because bondage and liberation exist by means of those sense-bases (*āyatana*) and so forth,
if these were non-existent, there would be neither bondage nor liberation, just as one cannot speak of the son of a barren woman.
Therefore, it is certain that, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the various sense-bases possess substantial reality.
The proponent says:

All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are bound by characteristics like illusions, mirages, and dreams; yet those who lack wisdom and are utterly blind and dark have, since beginningless time, been swallowed up by the grasping at "I" and "mine," and are fettered by the shackles of afflictions such as craving.

Therefore, in order to enable beings to escape from the prison of birth and death and the shackles of craving and views, the Tathāgata provisionally teaches by means of names and signs within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When right knowledge arises, one becomes detached from those most heavy fetters such as greed; thus it is called "liberation. This designation is not established from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because it is not logically tenable that there be one who is bound or liberated within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That which the Tathāgata speaks of as "birth and death" is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*); therein, there is no actual transmigrator.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: it is merely a conventional designation, and there is no one who attains parinirvāṇa therein.
Having seen this sūtra, the Ācārya said:
"If one definitively distinguishes between bondage and liberation, then as for this present bondage, is it these conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)?"
Are these sentient beings?
If they are those who practice, are they permanent or are they impermanent?
Both [positions] are incorrect. Why?
If it were permanent, as the verse says:
"If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were eternal, they would not undergo cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Commentary:
To cause others to believe that conditioned phenomena are eternal is logically untenable, as such a thesis lacks any basis in reality.
If one posits that things are eternal, then there would be neither bondage nor liberation.
Since bondage and liberation would not exist, the nature of phenomena would be inverted, and the established thesis would be flawed.
Furthermore, as for the claim that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are eternal and do not undergo transmigration—how can this be so?
The continuous succession of coming and going through the various realms of existence is called birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If these were permanent, then conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would have no distinction of priority and sequence.
To speak of "transmigration" under such conditions would be logically untenable.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas and those of our own school say:

If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were eternal, there would be no distinction between their arising and ceasing, nor between priority and posteriority; consequently, there would be no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Now, if all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were impermanent, there would necessarily be transmigration. This, however, is not so. Why is that?
As the verse says:
"The impermanent does not transmigrate.
The commentary explains:
If things were impermanent, they would cease and not arise again.
Therefore, it is not the case that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) undergo fivefold coming and going.
Furthermore, that which is impermanent does not transmigrate, just like external conditioned phenomena.
Herein is established a proof: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is not the case that internal conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) undergo transmigration. Why?
Because they are impermanent (*anitya*), just like external objects such as jars.

Just as it is not the case that either conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—whether permanent or impermanent—undergo transmigration, so too is it if you conceptually construct that there is a sentient being who transmigrates; this has already been answered as before.
Do these sentient beings transmigrate eternally,
or do they transmigrate impermanently?
If both were established, the faults previously mentioned would likewise apply.
What is the meaning of this?
If sentient beings were permanent, there would be no cyclic existence (saṃsāra). Why is that?
Because they are unchanging and because there is no distinction between before and after,
sentient beings are neither impermanent nor subject to saṃsāra. Why is this?
Because that which has already ceased lacks the nature of arising.
As a verse says:
"Sentient beings would likewise share this same fault."
The commentary states:

Therefore, if sentient beings were to undergo transmigration as either permanent or impermanent, they would likewise incur the same logical fallacies as those previously established regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, among the followers of the Buddha who wish to maintain that both conditioned phenomena and the person (*pudgala*) are impermanent, they speak as follows:

For those who have not yet given rise to the path of antidote, the various formations that ceased previously take this as their cause, and the subsequent formations that arise in succession constitute the fruit.
It is the same for sentient beings.
Thus, since the meaning of the continuous flow of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is established, I am without fault.
The opponent says: That statement is incorrect.

If it is argued that the various formations (*saṃskāra*) and sentient beings, having already ceased, act as conditions for subsequent moments, this has already been refuted in the previous discussion on the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because both the thesis and the analogy are flawed.
This case is likewise, and therefore I am without fault.
Furthermore, the Lokāyata proponent says:
"Your statement that conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), whether permanent or impermanent, do not undergo transmigration, establishes my own position."
How is this known?
As it is said in a verse from my own treatise:
"Śamatha is seen only by the eye; That which is of one kind is called a 'great man' (puruṣa)."
The learned speak of future lives as a man speaks of animal tracks;
you are now exceedingly handsome, so eat to your heart's content and go wherever you please.
Past karma is entirely non-existent; this body is merely a collection of conditioned formations.
"The deceased never returns; you should believe this.
Therefore, one should know that not a single dharma passes from this world to the next, nor does any person come from the next world to enter the womb.
If someone were to say:
"Prior to this womb, there was yet another previous life," how could this be verified?
This means that the consciousness immediately preceding the initial awareness upon entering the womb serves as its immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Why is this?
Because it is an awareness, just like the awarenesses that arise subsequently.
This analogy is not tenable. Why?
Because there is only a single awakening.
Because this single awakening remains constantly in this manner until the very end, there is no prior existence.
Furthermore, there is also no future existence.
By what reasoning is this stated?
For example, when Devadatta dies, his mind does not become the mind that first enters the womb for a future life.
Why is this? Because it is a mind at the moment of death, just like the mind of an Arhat at the moment of death.
The proponent says:
The流转 (pravṛtti) of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is not denied within the context of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
However, the notion that these conditioned phenomena are eternal while undergoing such流转 is likewise denied; therefore, this does not establish what you seek to prove.
Furthermore, the perception of Devadatta’s form and the perception of Devadatta’s sound are not non-different.
Why? Because their objects are distinct, just like the perception of the bodily continuum of another person.
By such reasoning, because there exists an analogy, it is not the case that a prior life is unestablished within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, a future life is not non-existent.
How is this proven?
This means that the final conscious moment of one's impure existence (*sāsrava*) is able to continue into the initial consciousness of conception in a future life. Why?
Because it is impure.
Because the minds [of those] at the moment of death differ, there is no contradiction in meaning within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, the Lokāyatikas say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), Devadatta’s cognition is not different from the cognition of all other people."
Why is this? Because it is an awakening, just like the awakening of Devadatta.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect.
That cognition of Devadatta has already been refuted previously within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, your claim that, in the ultimate truth, it is not different from the cognition of all other persons is an untenable position.
To establish that there is no difference within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) would contradict worldly consensus.

Furthermore, regarding whether the final mind of an Arhat at the end of life has a subsequent thought or not, none of these are established from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because there is no supporting analogy; thus, their establishment involves error.
If one establishes that the untainted mind does not continue into future lives, then within the realm of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), what I have set out to prove is established.
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīyas say:

"According to our tenet, regarding the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), whether they are identical or different, permanent or impermanent, all such things are inexpressible."
The person is also like this; the two kinds of faults you previously mentioned cannot refute my position. Why is this?
Because such a person undergoes transmigration.
The proponent says in verse:
"If a person were to transmigrate, they would be sought in five ways among the aggregates, bases, and elements, yet they are utterly non-existent; who, then, undergoes transmigration?"
The commentary states:
Because there is no cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
How is this known through verification?
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), no person can be apprehended.
Why? Because apart from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is no separate entity, just like the horns of a rabbit.

Although in reality there is no person, you nevertheless claim that there is; this grasping at a self-identity obscures and obstructs true wisdom, just as a person with cataracts sees floating hairs and the like.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"If [the self] were to go from one grasping to another grasping, Then it would incur the fault of non-existence."
"If there is no grasping and no existence, who would come and go?
The commentary states:
If one were to take up a subsequent grasping from this present grasping, then the essence of grasping would be empty.

Existence (*bhava*) is designated by virtue of grasping (*upādāna*); since the essence of grasping is empty, existence has no locus to rest upon. Where there is neither grasping nor existence, there is no substantial obstruction; because there is no substantial obstruction, there is nothing that can undergo transmigration. Yet you insist that there is coming and going—this is not so.
The opponent says:
"Because there are the aggregates of grasping within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the meaning of 'grasping' is established, and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply.
A different school refutes this, saying:
When you abandon the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and there is the time of rebirth in another realm, between these two there is neither grasping (*upādāna*) nor existence (*bhava*).
As with the aforementioned fault, you cannot escape it.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas and others say:
What you have said does not understand my meaning.
Why is this? Because these moments of relinquishing and grasping are simultaneous within the same moment.
As for the claim that there is neither grasping nor existence, this meaning is not so.
Regarding your previous statement that, when sought in five ways, nothing exists and thus no one transmigrates—I shall now answer you: such a person does indeed exist.
Why is this? Because it would subsequently abide within grasping.
If this [self] did not exist, one could not say that it abides within subsequent grasping, just like the son of a barren woman.
Because this person exists, one proceeds from a prior appropriation toward a subsequent appropriation and abides therein; how is this known through verification?
As the Buddha said:
"In the past, I was King Mūrdhaja and King Sudarśana."
Therefore, it is known that there is a person who goes from here to there.
The proponent says:
As stated in the previous verse, "If one goes from grasping to grasping, then the fault of non-existence is incurred."
What is the meaning of this?
Appropriation belonging to the first existence does not act as the cause for the support of a subsequent existence. Why is that?
Because there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from existence and non-existence, it is like Devadatta going from this room to that room.
As for your claim that those various appropriations exist and can constitute a person, that argument is not tenable.
Why is this? Because of grasping, just as other people grasp.
Therefore, the verse says: "Without grasping and without existence, who could come and go?"
Thus, it is in every way incorrect that there are formations (*saṃskāra*) or sentient beings (*sattva*) who transmigrate within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, regarding the adherence to the existence of one who attains liberation, one should also examine whether this liberated one is these very formations.
Are these sentient beings,
or are they this person?
If you say that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) attain liberation, are these present conditioned phenomena permanent?
Is it impermanent?
If you wish to maintain that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that is not so.
As the verse says:
"That conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are nirvāṇa—this can never be so.
The commentary states:

Since, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no arising, [the claim that] conditioned phenomena are eternal is not established even within the context of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
If it were the case that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) attain nirvāṇa through impermanence within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), this too would not be so. Why?
Because they are impermanent, just like external objects such as the earth and so forth.
If it is claimed that sentient beings attain liberation, this too is not so.
As the verse says:
"Sentient beings attaining nirvāṇa— this matter is likewise not so."
The commentary states:
If one were to attain nirvāṇa through permanence or impermanence, or through conceptualization or non-conceptualization, none of these would be correct.
Why is it that sentient beings do not attain nirvāṇa through permanence?
Because it lacks the visual, auditory, and other sense faculties, it is like space.
If something were non-obstructive, devoid of sight and hearing, yet existent, it would not be believed by the world, being like the son of a barren woman.
If it is claimed that one attains nirvana through impermanence, this is also not the case.
Why? Because if something is impermanent, it lacks the sense of liberation, just like external objects such as the earth and so forth.

It has already been demonstrated that liberation cannot be attained through impermanence; as for the opponent’s established doctrine that liberation is attained through a specific distinction in the nature of entities, none of these are established, because they suffer from faults in their formal propositions.
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīya says:

According to my established doctrine, when it is said that there is a person (*pudgala*), it cannot be described as either permanent or impermanent. Because this is so, the meaning of liberation is established, and the aforementioned faults do not apply.
The proponent says:
Your claim that, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a person exists as a real entity and attains liberation by being inexpressible as either permanent or impermanent, is likewise incorrect.
Why is this? Because it is designated in dependence upon causes,
just like a jar and other such things.
In this way, [your position] is refuted.
If a real entity (*dravyadharma*) were also impermanent— just like form (*rūpa*) and so forth—
then by virtue of this proof, the "real person" (*pudgala*) you establish would be describable as having an impermanent essence.
Your statement that the differentiation of the essence of dharmas is inexpressible is undermined, for it involves a fault in your formal proposition.

Furthermore, at the single moment of parinirvāṇa without remainder, if the person (pudgala) possesses an essence, it entails the fault of eternalism; if the person lacks an essence, it entails the fault of nihilism.
If one says that at the moment of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it cannot be said whether a person has an essence or lacks an essence, this is identical in meaning to my *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
As a verse in a sutra says:
"If liberation possessed a self, then having a self would mean it is permanent;
if liberation were without a self, then being without a self would mean it is impermanent."
Furthermore, an argument is established herein: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the cognition that takes a person as its object has no real objective referent.
Why? Because it is a cognition;
for example, like the cognition that takes a jar or similar objects as its referent.
Because that person is verified to be devoid of even a single entity, there is no liberation in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
If you insist that the person is a real dharma (*dravyadharma*),
for what reason?
As for the argument that "because it is cognizable, like form and so forth," this meaning is not tenable.
Since impermanent things and the like are equally cognizable and possess no distinct ontological essence, reasons such as "like a rabbit's horn" are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the members of our own school say:
"Due to causes and conditions, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) increase through successive continuity.
If they arise together with afflictions such as greed, they obstruct the happy realms."
Because greed and the other afflictions exist, the meaning of "bondage" is established.

If those who are bound hear the true Dharma and contemplate it with right mindfulness, they give rise to clear wisdom that eliminates the darkness of ignorance; thus, becoming free from greed and the rest is called "liberation."
For this reason, bondage and liberation are established.
How can you say that there is neither bondage nor liberation?
The proponent of the treatise says in verse:
"All conditioned phenomena have the characteristic of arising and ceasing; they are neither bound nor liberated.
Sentient beings, as previously explained, are neither bound nor liberated. Commentary:
As previously stated, whether conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent or impermanent, there is no transmigration in either case, just as with external objects and the like.

Now it is likewise: if sentient beings, who are conditioned phenomena, were either permanent or impermanent, there could be neither bondage nor liberation; all such views are untenable, just as with external objects and the like.

Therefore, regarding the various schools' conceptualizations concerning the flow of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and nirvāṇa within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), none of these are tenable.
How do they hold such views?

They claim that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) perish anew at every moment; or that they abide thus initially and only undergo disintegration at a later time; or that they are inexpressible as either permanent or impermanent. According to these views, such conditioned phenomena would possess neither cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) nor parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because they arise and cease, just like a jar or similar objects.
As stated in a previous verse: "Those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that arise and cease are neither bound nor liberated."
Sentient beings are as previously described:
neither bound nor liberated.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have no abiding.
Why is this? Because [the moments] arise at distinct times, moment by moment.
It is not the case that there is bondage or liberation within these states and phases, as has already been explained previously.
As for your statement that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise together with craving, this is because [craving] has already ceased.
That one who possesses a dharma already ceased attains liberation is not so.

Nor is it the case that one attains liberation at the very moment future conditioned phenomena are about to arise, because these are contradictory; as the verse says: "Regarding the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena, there is neither bondage nor liberation."
Furthermore, the Abhidharmika says:
As stated in a verse from my *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
"When the mind of one beyond training arises, it is liberated from all obstacles."
"How can you say that there is neither bondage nor liberation at all?
The proponent replies:
"Regarding that which arises—whether it be defiled or undefiled—there is no liberation in either case, because both positions entail logical fallacies."

Regarding that which is inexpressible: even at the time of defilement, it is as in the case of arising; whether there is defilement or no defilement, there is no liberation, because it is inexpressible.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika says:
"Because bondage and liberation exist within the continuum of the stream [of consciousness], there is no fault.
The proponent of the treatise says:
That continuum lacks any substantial reality.
Within the process of the continuum, whether it be defiled or undefiled, there is likewise no liberation, as has already been refuted previously.
Since bondage and liberation are established within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no fault of nihilism.
If you maintain that sentient beings possess bondage and liberation, we now respond to this point:
as stated in the preceding verse, "Because sentient beings have no intrinsic nature, the phenomena of bondage and liberation also do not exist."
Furthermore, as a verse says: "All conditioned phenomena, whether permanent or impermanent, are neither bound nor liberated;
sentient beings, whether permanent or impermanent, are likewise neither bound nor liberated."
The meaning is precisely this.
Furthermore, some say:

because those sentient beings are submerged in various forms of grasping (*upādāna*), they are called "bound"; because these bonds cease, they are said to "attain liberation. However, it cannot be said that these sentient beings are either permanent or impermanent.
Regarding the previous statement that there are faults in both the permanence and impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), I am not at fault.
The commentator states in verse:
"If one is bound by the various graspings (*upādāna*), The one who is bound has no liberation."
The commentary states:

To say that one is called a "grasper" because of various graspings, and yet that this person is truly liberated because they are bound by those very graspings, is logically untenable; for the natures and characteristics of bondage and liberation are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, Devadatta’s appropriation does not constitute that Devadatta.
Why? Because it is [merely] by virtue of appropriation, as in the case of a "false" [Devadatta].
If it were the case that there is grasping or fixation, yet that [grasped object] exists prior to such grasping, this would not be logically tenable.
As the verse says:
"Because there is no grasping, there is no bondage; At what stage could a person be bound?"
The commentary states:
If there were no state of a person apart from the state of grasping, then for this reason, there would be no person who could be bound; such is the meaning of the verse.
Furthermore, some say:
There must certainly exist sentient beings who are capable of being bound. Why?
Because there exists bondage; just as a person is imprisoned by means of such instruments as handcuffs, fetters, and shackles.
Because these various graspings (*upādāna*) act as the means of binding, it is known that there exists a sentient being who is the object to be bound.
The author of the treatise states in verse:
"If the binder were to exist prior to the binding, One could say that the binding is capable of binding."
"Yet prior to that, bondage does not exist; this has already been refuted regarding the past and the future.
The commentary states:
You claim that because the instruments of bondage existed previously, there could be a sentient being to be bound; however, prior to the binder, the instruments of bondage did not actually exist.
How is this verified?
Because Devadatta is without bondage. Why is that?
Because they are simultaneous, it is like the person of Devadatta.
Furthermore, that which is already bound is not being bound. Why is this?
Because they have already been bound.
One who has already been bound is not bound again, just as one who is not liberated [is not bound].
Nor is one who is unbound bound.
Why is this? Because there is no bondage, just as with one who is liberated;
even at the time of being bound, one is not bound.
Why is this? At the time of being bound, one part would already be bound while another part would not yet be bound; thus, there would be two faults.
Furthermore, that which cannot be described likewise lacks the meaning of being bound.
Why is this? Because it is inexpressible.
If one were already liberated at the very moment of liberation, that would not be the case.

Furthermore, in the "Examination of Going and Coming" (*Gatāgata-parīkṣā*), it has already been extensively analyzed that the three propositions—that there is an initial setting out in what has already gone, what has not yet gone, and the present going—are all untenable.

This case is also like that: whether one is already bound, not yet bound, or in the process of being bound, the notion that there is an initial arising of bondage does not hold in any of these three instances. Why is this so?
It is not logically tenable that one who is already bound could undergo the initial arising of further bondage. Why?
Because they are already bound, just like one who has been bound for a long time.
That there is an initial arising of bondage for one who is not yet bound is also not the case. Why?
Because they are not yet bound, just like those who have been liberated for a long time.
If it is claimed that when one is bound, there is an initial arising of the bond, this too is not so.
Why? Because both positions entail faults and because [the nature of the bond] is inexpressible, just as in the case of liberation.
Question:
It is my firm conviction that such a bondage exists. Why is this?
Because there is contradiction, just as wisdom is the antidote to ignorance.
As for the antidote to bondage, it is liberation; by virtue of liberation, bondage is not non-existent.
The answer is:
If you insist that there is liberation, does it exist for one who is already bound, for one who is not yet bound, or for one who is in the process of being bound?
All three [positions] are incorrect.
As the verse says:
"If there is one who is bound, there can be no liberation."
The commentary states:
When the path that serves as the antidote to bondage has not yet arisen, this is called "bondage" and cannot be called "liberation. Why is this?
Because there is no counteragent, they are like those bound by all fetters.
The verse says:
"For one who is not bound, there is no liberation."
The commentary states:
This is because bondage is empty.
Bondage is empty because, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), bondage lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like one who has been liberated for a long time.
If you claim that the moment of liberation is called "liberation," you must specify definitively: who is it that exists at that moment of liberation?
If you say that one who is already bound is called "at the moment of liberation," that too is not correct.
The verse says:
"If there were one who was liberated at the very time of being bound, then bondage and liberation would occur simultaneously.
The commentary states:
One does not desire that bondage and liberation occur simultaneously.
Therefore, such a person would again wish to take up bondage and again wish to take up liberation;
if it were thus, there would be the fault of both bondage and liberation existing at once, which cannot be avoided.
For this reason, it is not tenable that there is a liberated being in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

As you previously stated—that there is a contradiction and an antidote—both this logical reason (*hetu*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are unestablished; thus, your thesis (*pratijñā*) is flawed.
The opponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), liberation exists. Why is this?
Those who seek liberation do so because they possess hope.
If the fruit did not exist, they would never give rise to a hopeful mind for it, just as, for example, with the jewel atop the head of the *tuṇḍubha* snake.
Because it definitely exists, those seeking liberation give rise to a heart of aspiration.
As a verse says:
"When I am extinguished and free from all grasping, I shall attain nirvāṇa."
The commentary says:
How should one know that nirvāṇa exists?
For example, it is like the extinguishing of fire upon fuel; therefore, it is certain that nirvāṇa exists as something attainable.
The proponent says:
Your claim that "when the self ceases and all grasping is absent, I shall attain nirvāṇa" is an untenable attachment.
As the verse says:
"One who holds such a view, this view is unwholesome. Commentary:
If one gives rise to such a thought, grasping at the notion that "I shall attain nirvāṇa," this is not a wholesome grasp.
Why is this so? Because this unwholesome grasping obstructs liberation; such is the intended meaning of the verse.

Furthermore, although appropriation (*upādāna*) lacks intrinsic nature, one conceives of appropriation as an objective condition (*ālambana*); the erroneous discriminative cognition (*mithyā-vikalpa-jñāna*) arising from this is called "unwholesome grasping."
Therefore, your statement that one who seeks liberation possesses hope, and that this serves as the reason [for bondage], is an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).
Thus, when one carefully examines conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and those persons who are bound or liberated, none of these exist in reality.
As the Ācārya instructs those who study, he spoke this verse:
"One should not abandon saṃsāra, Nor should one establish nirvāṇa;
Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa Are non-dual and without distinction."
The commentary states:

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are of one single characteristic without distinction, because they are like the characteristic of space, because they are the object of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and because they are neither accumulated nor dispersed, being non-substantial phenomena.

Therefore, one should not engage in such conceptual discrimination—such as abandoning saṃsāra and establishing oneself in nirvāṇa—for whether one posits or denies [these states], both are objects within the domain of attainable things through the power of conceptualizing cognition.
If these were objects that could be apprehended as substantial entities, they would all be phenomena subject to aggregation and dispersal.
Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who can be taught through the means of nirvana; for the sake of attracting them, one speaks of the existence of nirvana.
How is it established?

It is simply that, regarding future unwholesome formations, the cessation of the signs of conceptualization and the arising of afflictions is termed "nirvāṇa as quiescence"; therefore, it is called "establishment."
Furthermore, in order to cause them to become weary of and detached from birth and death, he spoke these words:
"The sufferings of birth and death are many; you should abandon and leave them behind. Why is this?"
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), arising successively from conditions, lack intrinsic reality and are like illusions, dreams, or mirages.
These very things are called birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); by abandoning them, one is said to attain nirvāṇa.
Such a statement is made from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this?
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty within the context of ultimate truth.
As for the claim that the characteristic of the subsiding of afflictions is called nirvāṇa, such things do not exist either; one should not posit a separate nirvāṇa.
Since those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have no intrinsic arising and are primordially quiescent like nirvāṇa itself, the attempt to establish them as nirvāṇa is incorrect.
Those who would abandon birth and death should likewise not do so.
As the preceding verse states: "One should not abandon birth and death, nor should one establish nirvāṇa;
birth and death and nirvāṇa are non-dual and without distinction."
One should understand it thus: because there is no distinction within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
If one were to claim that these two realms are distinct, and that because the objects differ, the wisdom [engaged with them] must also differ—both of these positions are incorrect.

As stated at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Forders," the argument that there is birth-and-death and the existence of bondage and liberation within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) is therefore invalid as a reason.

Regarding the establishment of the thesis through the proof stated by that [opponent], the proponent has already refuted those errors previously; furthermore, the meaning of this chapter is to lead others to understand that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are empty and non-existent, and thus this objective is achieved.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Paramavīra, saying:
"Good son, form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated."
"If form through consciousness are neither bound nor liberated, this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, as stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "O Brahmā!"
I do not perceive birth-and-death, nor do I perceive nirvāṇa. Why is this?
That which is called "birth-and-death" is merely a provisional designation of the Tathāgata; there is not a single person who transmigrates therein.
"To speak of nirvāṇa is also a mere conventional designation, yet there is not a single person who attains parinirvāṇa.
Such sūtras as these should be explained here in detail.
The commentary on the "Chapter on Examining Bondage and Liberation" is completed.

Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Vidyāmati.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñāmitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: Examination of Karma. Explanation: [The commentary on] the seventeenth chapter, "Examination of Karma," states:

This present chapter is also taught in order to refute that which is counteracted by emptiness, so as to lead to an understanding of the meaning that karma and its fruits lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Abhidharmikas say:

"It is not correct that, as stated in the previous chapter, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) undergo transmigration, and that sentient beings (*sattva*), persons (*pudgala*), and so forth, also all undergo transmigration."

Furthermore, regarding the thesis established in that proof, [the opponent claims] that if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were either permanent or impermanent, it would entail the faults of eternalism or nihilism.
Thus, they argue that while there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), this is not the case [for them], and they assert that conditioned phenomena ultimately have no cyclic existence at all.

Because he previously made that statement, there is no such fault in my current explanation of the permanent and the impermanent herein; rather, there is the continuous flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

One who speaks thus intends to lead others to understand that, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there definitely exist these internal sense-bases (*āyatana*) and conditioned phenomena, which undergo birth and death and are conjoined with karma and its results.
If this [self] did not exist, one would not perceive the conjunction of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) with the fruits of karma, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman.

Now, because conditioned phenomena do conjoin with the fruits of karma, there is birth and death; therefore, I now examine the fruits of karma, the meaning of which is explained in detail in the Abhidharma.

Therefore, that verse says: "The volition (*cetanā*) that guards one's own body and speech, as well as that which gathers others, has the Dharma of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as its seed; it is able to attain results in both the present and the future.

As for what is called "volition," it refers to the volition associated with this mind that is capable of self-discipline and the distancing from what is unrighteous (*adharma*); thus, it is termed "volition."

"Gathering others" refers to gathering them through giving, kind speech, and protecting those from fear; because one is able to gather others by means of such practices, it is called "gathering others.
"Loving-kindness" (maitrī) refers to the mind; the mind is itself called the dharma and is also the seed, and the seed is also called the cause.
For whom is it the cause?
It is the cause of the fruit.
What kind of fruit is it?
This refers to the results of the present and the future.
Why is the mind called the seed?
It is called the seed because it is capable of giving rise to the actions of body and speech.
What is meant by "unrighteous" (*adharma*)?
It is called unrighteous because it violates the Dharma.
That which is unrighteous refers to evil, the unwholesome, and so forth.
What is meant by "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*)?
That which neither accords with nor contradicts the Dharma is called indeterminate.
There are four types of indeterminate karma:
First, those born of retribution; second, those of deportment; third, those of craftsmanship; and fourth, those of transformation.
Furthermore, regarding the "indeterminate" (avyākṛta): it is called indeterminate because it is not defined as either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, that which is "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) is also called indeterminate because it does not give rise to the fruits of the wholesome or the unwholesome.
There are such distinctions as these;
there are also two types [of the indeterminate] in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
What is the meaning of this?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"The karma taught by the Great Sage Is volition and that which arises from volition."
"Thus, within these two types of karma, / An immeasurable variety is taught.
Commentary: Why is he called the Great Sage (Maharṣi)?
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are also called "sages" (ṛṣi); however, because the Buddha is the most honored and supreme among them, he is called the "Great Sage" (maharṣi).
Because he has reached the further shore of all the perfections (*pāramitā*), merits, and roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), he is called the Great Sage (*maharṣi*).
Furthermore, the names were listed in the preceding verse; they shall now be explained individually.
What is the meaning of this?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"As previously explained, volition (cetanā) is designated solely as mental action (manas-karma)."
"That which arises from volition (*cetanā*) is precisely bodily and vocal action.
The commentary asks:
Why is it said that volition is exclusively mental action (*manas-karman*)?
That is to say, volition associated with the mind is called mental action (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, because this volition reaches its culmination within the mental door (*mano-dvāra*), it is called mental action, not bodily or vocal action.
What is meant by "arising from volition"?
It refers to acting after having known; that which is performed after knowing is called "action arising from volition.
This action is of two kinds: namely, bodily and verbal.
If [an action] is consummated through the gateway of the body or consummated through the gateway of speech, it is termed bodily action (kāyakarman) or vocal action (vākkarman).
Having explained these two types of action, the various distinctions thereof will now be explained.
What is meant by "immeasurable varieties of distinctions"?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"Physical action and verbal action, The fourfold consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest."
"Speech arises from detachment and so forth; all possess both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The commentary states:
"Speech arises" means that when words are articulated clearly through written characters, it is called the arising of speech.
What is meant by "distancing oneself"?
It refers to the movement of the hands, body, and so forth.
As for "movement," it means giving rise to the thought and saying:
"I shall perform this wholesome karma.
From the initial volition of performing wholesome karma until the subsequent volition of performing wholesome karma,
for a person who has arisen, whether they perform wholesome karma or refrain from performing it, the substance of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is constantly produced.
Regarding "non-restraint" (*avirati*), it is likewise thought:
"I shall perform this unwholesome action, whether by body, speech, or mind.

From the very first moment an unwholesome action arises, whether one subsequently performs an evil deed or not, one is termed "non-restrained" due to that unwholesome cause; thus, a substance of non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is constantly produced.
What is meant by "active" and "non-active" form (*rūpa*)?
That which causes others to understand through bodily or vocal forms is called active form; that which does not cause others to understand through bodily or vocal forms is called non-active form.
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"The merit of enjoying one's own body, And likewise the arising of demerit,
Along with volition— these are the seven karmas, Which can discern the characteristics of all actions."
The commentary states:
What is meant by "the basis of enjoyment"?
It refers to the dwellings, gardens, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and other articles for sustaining the body that have been offered by donors.
What is meant by "merit" (*puṇya*)?
It means the sense of "fishing out.

Seeing all sentient beings drowning in the river of afflictions (*kleśa*), one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and fishes them out to place them on the shore of nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called merit.
As for non-merit, it refers to performing various unwholesome deeds that cause sentient beings to enter the evil realms.
How, then, can this also be the experience of its own substance?
It is called "non-merit" because it is contrary to merit.
Having explained merit and non-merit, one next explains the meaning of volition (*cetanā*).
By what dharma is it designated as "volition"?
That is to say, the mental action (manas-karman) arising from the mind with respect to virtue and non-virtue, as well as non-virtue and non-virtue, is called "intention" (cetanā).
That treatise thus explains the characteristic of karma through these seven types of karma.

Even practices such as sitting in meditation, reciting scriptures, listening to the Dharma, and maintaining mindfulness are also termed "karma"; however, because they are all subsumed within the seven types [of karma], they are not mentioned separately.
Because this karma exists, one perceives the union of karma and its fruit.

This "union with the fruit" refers to the manifestation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) within the five destinies (*gati*). Therefore, when it was stated at the beginning of this chapter that the union of karma and its fruit serves as the causal basis for emergence, the principle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is established from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because there is bondage and liberation, and thus the substance of birth and death exists.
The proponent says:
Now, as for this karma, does it persist constantly from the moment it first arises until the time it receives its fruit?
Or does it perish immediately after arising for a single moment?
None of these views are correct.
The fault in them is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If [the action] were to persist until the fruit is received, then this karma would be eternal."
"If karma were to perish, once it has perished, who would produce the fruit?
[The commentary] says:
If the intrinsic nature of karma, having arisen, does not disintegrate immediately but only later disintegrates, this is not so, for it would entail the fallacy of permanence.
The Abhidharmikas say:
"Just as with the plantain, bamboo, reed, and so forth, which perish immediately after yielding their fruit, there is therefore no fault.
The Proponent says:

Bamboo, reeds, and the like perish in each and every moment and do not abide; that they subsequently undergo a similar continuity until their cessation is merely said to be "perishing" within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

However, it is not so if one claims, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), that karma continues through a succession like that of bamboo or reeds until the point of receiving its fruit.

If one were to say that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of karmic phenomena remains indestructible—whether prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with [the action]—it would be difficult to cause others to understand, and you would not be without fault.
The Abhidharmikas say:
"In the beginning, it is not yet destroyed; because its causes are present, it is not destroyed."
If it were to perish at a later time, such that it perishes only when a cause arrives,
what fault would there be?
The proponent of the treatise says:
This argument is not tenable.
Regarding your assertion that there exists a cause of destruction, that [alleged] cause is not the cause of the destruction of that object, because it is distinct from that object.
Since it is a cause, it is like any other object.
As it is said in the Āgamas, the body and the various faculties arise for a single moment and do not persist; thus, your position contradicts the Sūtras.
If you wish to avoid this fault by asserting that they perish immediately after arising, that too is erroneous.
If karma were to cease, it would lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If you intend that karma can grant its fruit at the very moment it is ceasing, this is not so; for that moment of cessation would be called "half-ceased and half-unceased" as it grants the fruit, which entails the same fault as previously answered.
If you say that it cannot be said whether [the action] gives its fruit after having ceased or without having ceased, this is called "indescribable karma.

If it is indescribable karma, it is not possible for it to give its fruit within the ultimate sense (paramārtha), because it is indescribable, just like, for example, the time when one is about to be born.
What you have perceived is not firm; the reason you have put forward is unestablished and also contradicts your own tenet.
The Abhidharmikas say:
"Because there is continuity, our tenet is not contradicted."
How is this known?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"Just as the continuity of sprouts and so forth arises from a seed,"
"From this, the fruit arises; apart from the seed, there is no continuity.
The commentary states:
This means that from the sprout, the stem arises, and so on, up to the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, each having its own characteristic.
Although the seed perishes, it gives rise to a continuity that proceeds successively until the fruit is reached.
If apart from the seed, the continuity of the sprout and so forth would have no circulation.
For this reason, what is the meaning?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"The seed has a continuity, From that continuity the fruit arises;
The seed comes first and the fruit later, Neither interrupted nor eternal."
The commentary says:
How is it not severed?
It is because the continuity of the seeds persists.
Why is it not eternal?
Because once the sprout has arisen, the seed perishes.
It is the same for internal phenomena, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Thus, from the initial mind, the mental phenomena arise in succession;
from this, the fruit arises; apart from the mind, there is no succession.
Commentary:
This means that a mind of loving-kindness and a mind lacking loving-kindness are what is termed "karma"; although this mind ceases, it arises in a continuous succession.
As for the arising of the fruit of this succession, it refers to the pleasant and the unpleasant, because they possess feeling and perception.
If one were separated from the mind, the fruit would not arise.
Now, the dharma of continuity shall be explained.
What is its meaning?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"From the mind there is continuity; from continuity there is fruit.
Thus, karma precedes the fruit; it is neither annihilated nor eternal."
The commentary states:
How is it not severed?
It means that the continuity is capable of producing its fruit.
Why is it not eternal?
Because it does not persist into a second moment. Herein is the proof:

in the ultimate sense, there exists such karma and fruit that accords with the names and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of sentient beings; for the Tathāgata has taught the means for those sentient beings who desire to attain superior fruits so that they may achieve those fruits.
If this did not exist, the Tathāgata would not have taught the means for attaining the fruit of happiness, just like a garland of flowers in the sky.
Now that he teaches that such means do exist, what is their meaning?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
“The skillful means for seeking the Dharma Are the ten paths of white karma;
The five kinds of superior desire and joy Are attained in both the present and future lives.”
The commentary states:
"Dharma" refers to the resultant dharma;
"expedient means" refers to that which attains the resultant dharma.
As for the causes, they refer to wholesome karma (*śukla-karman*).
As for the fruits, they refer to obtaining the pleasures of the five sensory desires in the present and future.
What kind of fruits are obtained?
This refers to the attainment of both retributive fruits (*vipākaphala*) and dependent fruits (*niṣyandaphala*).
"White" means pure and wholesome.
That which can accomplish the causes and conditions for merit arises from these ten white paths of action (*śuklakarmapatha*).

The ten refer to not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not using divisive speech, not using harsh speech, not engaging in idle chatter, not being envious, not being resentful, and not holding wrong views; these are called the ten white karmas, also known as the ten paths of wholesome action, all of which arise from body, speech, and mind.
What is meant by "supreme fruit"?
It refers to attaining the most excellent status among humans and devas within the realms of humans and devas.
What is the meaning of this?
Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
"If a person can subdue their own mind And bring benefit to sentient beings,
This is called the practice of loving-kindness and compassion, And one shall obtain the retributive fruits of both worlds."
The commentary states:
For this reason, the Buddha taught that there exists this skillful means for attaining the fruit; thus, the meaning of what was said is established.
The proponent says:
Regarding your statement that because there is a continuity of karmic fruit, you employ the seed as a metaphor, this entails a great error.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"One who makes such a distinction incurs great and manifold faults."
"As you have stated, this is not so in terms of its meaning.
The commentary asks: Why is it not so?
This means that your previous distinction—that there is a continuity of seeds consisting of a similar dharma-substance—is not tenable. Why?
Because seeds possess form, color, and resistance; they are visible phenomena and thus can have a continuity.

If even this matter cannot be apprehended when one reflects upon it now, how much less so can the mind and karma, which are formless, colorless, non-resistant, and invisible, arising and ceasing moment by moment without abiding? Should one wish to provide proof for them, such proof cannot be established.

Furthermore, regarding the transition from the seed to the sprout: does it proceed to the sprout as a continuity after having ceased, or does it proceed to the sprout as a continuity without having ceased?
If it proceeds to the sprout after having ceased, then the sprout would be without a cause.
If the sprout were to arise without the seed ceasing, then the sprout would constantly arise from the original seed.
If that were the case, all various sprouts would arise from within a single seed.
This is not so, for it entails a great error.
A person belonging to the Saṃmitīya school says to a follower of the Abhidharma:
"As you have stated—that there is a personal continuum capable of giving rise to karma that produces a continuum such as that of a deity—this meaning is not correct."
Why is this? Because their natures are distinct; for example, a *riṇva* seed does not produce the fruit of a mango tree, and so forth.

If it were the case that a wholesome mind could successively give rise to wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral minds; that a neutral mind could successively give rise to wholesome or unwholesome minds; or that an unwholesome mind could successively give rise to wholesome or neutral minds—none of these propositions would be tenable.

Even up to the point where a mind bound to the desire realm can successively give rise to minds bound to the form realm and the formless realm, as well as an untainted (anāsrava) mind; and where an untainted mind, in turn, successively gives rise to minds bound to the desire, form, and formless realms—what was previously stated regarding the arising of a sprout is, in all these cases, not so.
Since this has already been refuted in general within the proofs established previously,
the claim that there are those who perform wholesome deeds is likewise incorrect.
I shall now explain the correct analytical meaning of the ripening of karmic results in accordance with their actions.
What is this discrimination?

As for the aforementioned discrimination regarding the similarity of the continuity of seeds, because it is as I have explained, it is free from those faults; thus, the stains of error cannot defile it.
What is being taught?
It is the teaching on the meaning of correct discernment (*samyak-pravicaya*). By whom is it taught?
As stated in a verse from the Āgama: "That which has been spoken by the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas, and that which is collectively discerned by all the assemblies of noble ones."
What is being distinguished?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"The non-perishing dharma (*avipraṇāśa*) is like a promissory note; karma is like the wealth owed."
"And this is of an indeterminate nature; in terms of the realms, there are four kinds.
The commentary explains:

This refers to the existence of the *avipraṇāśadharma* (the law of non-disappearance), which is like a creditor who possesses a promissory note; although the wealth has been given away, it is not lost, and at a later time, both the interest and the principal are recovered.

Karma is likewise: it can bring about a subsequent fruit. Although the karma itself has already perished, because the "law of non-disappearance" remains, it enables the practitioner to obtain a superior karmic retribution.
Just as a creditor, having received the wealth, destroys the original bond in the presence of the debtor, so too,
once the *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing factor) has bestowed the fruit upon the agent, its own substance is also destroyed.
How many kinds of non-loss (avipraṇāśa) are there?
There are four according to the realms (dhātu). What are these four?
They are the realm of desire, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
As for the nature of the dharma of non-loss (*avipraṇāśa*),
it is of the nature of being non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
That which is unobscured is also called non-obscured.
It is indeterminate (avyākṛta) because it is said to be neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
By what path is this dharma of non-disappearance abandoned?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"It is not abandoned by the path of seeing, But is abandoned by the path of cultivation;
Because of this non-perishing dharma, All karmas have their retributive fruits."
The commentary states:
This refers to that which is not abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
When, then, is it abandoned?
This means it is abandoned when one progresses toward a subsequent fruit through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, although unwholesome karma to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) has been abandoned, because this "dharma of non-loss" (*avipraṇāśadharma*) remains, it is not abandoned at the time of seeing suffering; for this dharma of non-loss is capable of yielding its fruit. This is illustrated by the case of Maudgalyāyana being humiliated by a non-Buddhist, and the Bhikṣu Lāṭūpāda being imprisoned for twelve years by King Brahmadatta.

Although Maudgalyāyana and others had attained the fruits of sainthood, because they had not yet lost the *avipraṇāśa-dharma* (the dharma of non-perishing), they experienced the retribution for their past unwholesome karma.
Thus, a verse in the treatise says:
"If that which is abandoned by the Path of Seeing, That karma reaches a similar [result];"
"Then one would incur such faults as the destruction of karma and so forth.
The commentary states:
If this *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing phenomenon) were to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), or if it were to accompany the karma to a future life, then there would be these faults.
What fault would there be?

If the non-disappearance of dharmas were to be abandoned in the same way as the afflictions abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), such that the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) and karma were also simultaneously abandoned, then the relationship between karma and its fruit would be destroyed.
What kind of fruit is destroyed?
It refers to the destruction of the fruit of unwholesome karma abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); this meaning should be understood.

If [unwholesome karma] were not abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), then noble ones (*ārya*) would still possess all the karma of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). For this reason, afflictions and karma are abandoned through the path of seeing.

The non-loss dharma (*avipraṇāśa*) is not abandoned by the path of seeing; therefore, it is said that while karma is abandoned by the path of seeing, the non-loss dharma is abandoned at the time of progressing toward a subsequent fruit through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
When one transcends the desire realm toward the form realm, and when one transcends the form realm toward the formless realm, the same applies to that which is abandoned.
Thus, a verse in the treatise says:
"All karmic actions, Whether similar or dissimilar,"
"At the present time, before it has ended, a single karma and a single dharma arise.
The commentary states:
"Similar" refers to karma of the same kind.
At the time of death in the present life, there arises a single "non-perishing phenomenon" (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*) which retains all karmas.

As for those that are dissimilar, this refers to the distinctions among the types of karma; for example, there are immeasurable varieties of karma belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, how many kinds of karma are sustained by the principle of non-loss (*avipraṇāśadharma*)?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"Thus, these two kinds of karma, which receive their retribution in the present..."
Or it is said: "Even after the retribution has been received, this karma still persists.
The commentary states:
"The two types of karma refer to volition (*cetanā*) and that which arises from volition."
Some may say: "If karma remains even after its retribution has been experienced, it is because it does not perish moment by moment.
Furthermore, as previously stated regarding the various distinctions of immeasurable kinds, each one also possesses a 'non-perishing dharma' (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*) that arises to maintain it."
For what reason does the *avyākṛta-dharma* (the non-perishing phenomenon) not repeatedly bestow its fruit after it has already done so while still remaining?
It is because it has already bestowed its fruit.
It is like a promissory note that has already been settled: once the debt has been repaid, even though the note remains, one can no longer claim the funds.
The non-perishing dharma (*avipraṇāśa*) is likewise: because it has already yielded its fruit, it does not repeatedly produce fruit again.
At what time, then, does this non-perishing dharma cease?
Thus, the verse of the treatise says:
"Upon attaining the fruit [of arhatship] and at the end of life, it ceases upon reaching this point;
one should know that the distinctions lie between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*). Commentary:
This refers to that which is abandoned at the time of cultivating the path.
It is as previously described: at the time of death, both similar and dissimilar karmas are held together by a single non-perishing phenomenon (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*).
Just as the fruit of stream-entry and so forth ceases once it has been attained, and as arhats and ordinary persons cease after death,
this dharma of non-disappearance likewise possesses further distinctions.
What is the distinction?
Because there is a distinction between outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) karma, the *avipraṇāśa* (non-perishing phenomenon) is likewise both outflowing and non-outflowing;

it is because of this that it is so. Furthermore, the *avipraṇāśa* arises from various types of karma and enables sentient beings to experience differentiated fruits, such as receiving a particular region or realm of existence (*gati*), receiving color or form, and receiving faith or precepts. Only after it has bestowed these fruits does it subsequently perish.
For this reason, what is the meaning?
Thus, the verse of the treatise says:
"Though empty, it is not annihilated; though existent, it is not eternal."
"The law that no karma is lost—this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
The commentary says:
Of what is emptiness empty?
This means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty;
there are no phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as conceptualized by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Yet, karma is not interrupted because there exists the principle of non-wastage (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*).
What is existence?
Existence refers to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Birth-and-death means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) circulate through various realms of rebirth; therefore, it is called birth-and-death.
Why is it not eternal?
Because karma undergoes destruction.
What is meant by the "law of non-loss" (*avipraṇāśadharma*)?
It is said that in various sūtras the Buddha has stated that such a distinction must be made.
For this reason, what I previously asserted—that karma and its fruit conjoin as the cause for emergence—is not logically untenable.
The proponent says:
What you have stated is entirely incorrect; I shall now explain for you the causal conditions of right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
What is their meaning?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Karma is fundamentally unarisen, because it lacks intrinsic nature;
Karma is fundamentally undestroyed, because it is unarisen."
The commentary states:
In our school, karma has no arising.
Likewise, that which is a continuity of seeds has no arising from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the analogy you have established lacks a real basis and suffers from the fallacy of an incomplete analogy.
