It serves as the means for the practitioner to understand the truth of self-awakening; such language is the expedient means for attaining the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding what you have said: "If one does not state the characteristic of reality, one fails to establish one's own thesis and merely attributes faults to others; this is your error, but I do not have this error. [I reply: I do not have this error.
Having answered with this verse, one has thus explained the characteristic of reality.
This was done by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Now, it shall further be explained by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
What is the meaning of this?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"An entity that arises from conditions is not, in its essence, those conditions."
"Nor is it separate from those conditions; it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Commentary: This clarifies that the fruit arises from conditions, yet this fruit is not identical to the cause.
In this context, it is stated that cause and effect do not arise simultaneously because they are distinct objects of cognition, just as, for example, the cognition and its object are distinct.
Furthermore, an effect arising from conditions does not exist apart from those conditions; if it were to exist apart from them, the arising of the effect would fall into the error of being causeless.

Furthermore, herein we establish a proof that cause and effect are not distinct, because they arise only by depending upon conditions, just as, for example, the self-nature of a cause [is not distinct from itself].
Since cause and effect are thus neither identical nor different, there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
Furthermore, although the fruit arises at a time when the cause has already perished, it does so because the continuity of the causal type persists.

Nevertheless, the fruit does not perish simply because the cause has perished; for since they are not different, the substance is not severed. And because the cause has already perished by the time of the fruit, the fruit is not eternal.
As a verse in the sutra says: "Because there is the arising of an entity, its cessation cannot be found;
because there is the extinction of an entity, its permanence cannot be found.
How, then, can it be neither interrupted nor permanent?
It is said that the nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is such that it arises in a continuous succession from moment to moment; therefore, it is not discontinuous.
Because the essence of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) perishes moment by moment, it is not eternal. Now, I shall expound this meaning for you.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
“Neither identical nor different, Neither annihilated nor eternal—
This is called the supreme nectar-dharma Of all the World-Honored Ones.”
The commentary states:
"Ambrosia" refers to obtaining the cause of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Just as the Buddhas, by means of the wisdom they have themselves attained, employ the light of the Buddha-sun’s speech throughout the realm of all sentient beings, causing the flowers of wisdom to bloom according to the capacities of those beings.

Furthermore, those śrāvakas, by practicing the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, attain the true nectar of the Dharma and realize nirvāṇa in the present life, bringing all suffering to rest.
Alternatively, because their accumulations of merit and wisdom are not yet fulfilled, although they do not realize liberation now, they will certainly attain it in a future life.
What is its meaning?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Those who cultivate reality, though they have not yet attained the fruit in this present life,"
"In the future it will certainly be attained, Just as the karma [yields its fruit] without requiring further effort.
The commentary states:

For those who practice the path of reality, even if they do not attain the fruit in this life or in a subsequent life, by virtue of the perfuming of their various practices (*saṃskāra*), they will naturally attain true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) in a future existence.
Nor does it have anything else as its condition, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"When the Buddhas have not yet appeared in the world, and the śrāvakas have already ceased to exist,
there are nevertheless pratyekabuddhas who give rise to wisdom by relying on tranquility."
The commentary states:

As explained in the *Tri-rahasya-sūtra*, when a pratyekabuddha gives rise to true wisdom by relying on tranquility, it is because physical and mental tranquility serve as the cause for the arising of that wisdom; this is called the "Dharma of Ambrosia."
Whether in this life or in future lives, those who are able to cultivate the true reality will certainly attain the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta).
Therefore, those who desire liberation should practice this Dharma of true reality.

In this chapter, the arguments established by opponents are refuted, and it is also explained that our own arguments are free from fault; the intended meaning of this chapter is to lead others to believe and understand that the aggregates, the self, and what belongs to the self are empty. For this reason, my thesis is established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "O Suvega!
Form is neither self nor non-self; likewise, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither self nor non-self."
"If form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither the essence of a self nor the essence of a non-self, this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
As a verse in the sutra says: "There is no self, no sentient being, no person, and no experiencer; it is merely a body designated by various conditions—thus has the Buddha attained understanding."
In this context, it clarifies that the self, persons, sentient beings, and the aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are all empty and lack any causal origination.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Śūnyatāpraśnavyākaraṇa-sūtra*:
"All sentient beings raise the banner of the view of self, unfurl the sail of ignorance (*avidyā*), encounter the winds of affliction (*kleśa*), and enter the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)."
"The great compassion of all Buddhas spreads the vast net of the Teaching to scoop up and rescue devas and humans, placing them on the shore of Nirvana.
As stated in the verse above: "The non-dual gate of peace and security can shatter all false views."
"The sphere of activity of all Buddhas is called the dharma of selflessness.
This concludes the commentary on the "Examination of Dharmas" (*Dharmaparīkṣā*).
Chapter 19: Examination of Time (*Kālāparīkṣā*) The *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā* explains the nineteenth chapter, "Examination of Time," as follows: [text continues]
This present chapter is also spoken in order to refute that which is counteracted by emptiness—that is, to demonstrate that all entities lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there exists an intrinsic nature of temporal phenomena (*kāla-dharma*), because it serves as a cause of manifestation (*vyañjaka-hetu*), just like a lamp."
If time did not exist, how could there be a revealing cause?
It would be like the hair on a tortoise's coat.
Because physical entities exist, time serves as their revealing cause; therefore, time exists.
The proponent says:

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they are termed "activity" (*kriyā*). This arising is merely the arising of the entities themselves; there is no separate arising apart from them.

When these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have already arisen as cause and effect, it is called the past time; when the cause has ceased and the effect has arisen, it is called the present time; and when both cause and effect have not yet arisen, it is called the future time, because they establish a definite limit of activity.
Time is designated based on things; there is no separate time existing independently.
Even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), time is spoken of as a mere designation, such as when one says, "He came at the time of milking.
However, the non-Buddhist outsiders (*bāhyaka*) conceptually cling to the existence of time; this is how one should investigate it from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
"Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), time exists as a distinct entity and is eternal.
The opponent replies:

Now, in order to refute this [notion of time], [it is argued that] in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no separate time existing apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), because it possesses a substantial nature (*svabhāva*), just like the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena themselves. Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, no eternal time can be cognized, just as, for example, a jar [cannot be found apart from its constituent parts].
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
"Like space and so forth, [things] are not invariably impermanent.
The proponent of the treatise says:
Since that [notion of] space as a distinct entity lacks substantiality, it is likewise refuted.
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
Time exists externally to the substance of form and is conjoined with form, because consciousness arises when time is present, just as, for example, a person is conjoined with a staff.
Just as consciousness perceives the object Devadatta and unites with it, so too does it arise in relation to form within present consciousness.
That which exists as a distinct entity external to this form is called "time"; therefore, time exists as a separate reality.
The proponent says:

Regarding your statement that the arising of consciousness has [time] as its cause, since the consciousness that apprehends a staff arises with respect to an object characterized by non-time, then time is destroyed.
Because the wielder of the staff is impermanent, the principle of permanence is subverted.

Since the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*svabhāva-dharma*) and their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-dharma*), and so forth, are all thus refuted, this constitutes the fault of your thesis, reason, and other logical members.
The conjunction of the person with the staff is a metaphor for that which lacks intrinsic nature.
Since, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the possessor of the staff cannot be established, the metaphor is invalid.
The cognition that apprehends form conjoins with time; yet this cognition cannot manifest [time], and therefore time does not exist.
Furthermore, regarding the distinct establishment of the three times: is it established through mutual dependence, or without mutual dependence?
If one posits that time is established through dependence, the fault is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If the present and the future depend upon past time,
then the present and the future would already exist within past time.
Commentary:
This means that time depends on something else.
Because time depends on something else, it is like past time.
Furthermore, if present and future time existed by depending on past time, then present and future time would have to exist within past time.
Why is this? Because it is by means of the past time that the present and future times are established.
Furthermore, the present and future times should also abide within the past time; in this way, the entirety of the present and future would be designated as the past time.
If all time were exclusively called the past, then there would be no present or future, because everything would have been exhausted as the past.
If there were no present or future, there likewise should be no past.
Why is this? Because the present and future times are already contained within the past time.
Furthermore, if a time were dependent [upon another], it would either exist simultaneously with it, since dependence is not contradictory to simultaneity; for example, father and son are distinct.
If time were established as something dependent [on other factors], there would be the fallacy of the present and future arising separately.
The meaning of this is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"The present and the future do not exist within the past time;..."
"How can the present and the future exist in dependence upon anything?
The commentary states:
This means that within the time of the past, there is no time of the present or the future.
If one claims that within the past time there is no present or future time, yet the present and future times are established by means of the past time, how could these two possibly be established?
If the present and future times do not exist, what fault would there be?
Below, the proof is stated: in the ultimate sense, the present and future times do not exist, because time exists only in dependence upon its own intrinsic nature, just like the past time.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas say:
"Because the present and the future are obtained simultaneously within the past, there is mutual dependence.
The Proponent says:
There is also a mutual dependence regarding different times, as in the case of brothers; it is not unilaterally fixed, so your statement is incorrect.
Thus, a mutual dependence across different times is not established.
Furthermore, if time were not established through mutual dependence, the fault would be as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"Without depending on past time, those two—present and future—would not be established; thus, there would be no time at all."
The commentary states:
"Those two" refers to the present and the future as a pair.
Without depending upon past time, the present and future times would not be established.
Why is this? If the present and future times existed without depending on past time, in what location would the present and future times exist?
Since they lack mutual dependence, the present and future times are likewise not established.
What is the meaning of this?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Being no different from the past, The other two proceed in succession."
"And as for the superior, middling, and inferior grades, one should contemplate them as being identical in essence.
The commentary states:
By means of this expedient, one should explain this through successive application.
What is the meaning of this?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the future and the past depend upon the present time,"
If the future and the past exist within the present time,
And if the future and the past do not exist within the present time,
Upon what could the future and the past depend to exist?
Without depending on the present time, those two—future and past—would not be established; thus, there would be no such thing as time.
If the present and the past were to depend on the future time, [the same fault would follow].
If the present and the past exist within the future time,
Or if the present and the past do not exist within the future time,
Upon what could the present and the past depend to come into being?
Without depending on future time, those two [present and past] are not established;
thus, present and past would be without time.
Commentary:
This is the verse from the commentary which, as established previously, refutes the opponent's position.
How are the stages of superior, middling, and inferior, up to the state of being a single essence (ekatva), defined?

For example, although all human beings are equally called "humans," there are distinctions among them: those who are fully endowed with merit are called superior persons; those with slightly less are called middling persons; and those who possess none at all are called inferior persons.
Are such things established through dependence,
or are they established without dependence?
For now, that which is "superior" is not [inherently] superior, because its own essence involves mutual dependence, just like the essence of the "middle."
Likewise, the middle is also not the middle itself, because its own nature exists in mutual dependence, just as with the nature of the lower.
The lower is also not the lower itself, because it exists in mutual dependence, just as with the nature of the upper.

Furthermore, using the fact that things exist in mutual dependence as the reason, I wish to make you understand that the categories of superior, middling, and inferior lack intrinsic nature; do you not accept this absence of intrinsic nature?
If one wishes to maintain that there is a self-nature [of "superiority"], claiming it is called "superior" in dependence upon the "middle," this is also not the case.
Likewise, the self-nature of the number "one" and the numbers "one," "two," and so forth, are also refuted as before.
The first [category], number, shall now be explained.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the "one" is not the essence of the number one. Why is this?
Because these numbers exist in dependence [upon their objects], they are like the number two and so forth.
Thus, the number two is not the essence of "two," and the number many is not the essence of "many"; this should be explained in the same way as the number one.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one does not desire for those numbers to exist apart from the essence of phenomena;

how then could they be obtained? That which is "one" is so called because it lacks a second and lacks differentiation; that which is "two" is so called because it lacks a first and lacks differentiation; that which is "three" is so called because it lacks a second and lacks differentiation; and from three onwards, they are collectively termed "many. This should also be understood through the previous refutations to bring about clear realization.
Now I shall further explain: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), even "one" is not one, because it is something that can be counted, just like "otherness.
Likewise, "two" is not two, and "many" is not many; these are also explained by the same reasoning as the number one, and one should apply this same logical analysis accordingly.
What is meant by "and so forth"?
It means that a single atom is not a single atom, because it is something that can be counted, just as with distinct [objects].
Likewise, two atoms are not two atoms, and many atoms are not many atoms; this is also as explained above.

As well as long and short, far and near, before and after, cause and effect, and that which is not long and short, far and near, before and after, cause and effect; even so it is said for the conditioned and the unconditioned, and that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
"In the ultimate sense, such a time exists. Why is this?"
Because it possesses measure.
If time did not exist, there would be no measure; just as a horse that lacks horns cannot be said to have measure.
Because time exists, there are measures such as the *kṣaṇa*, *lava*, *muhūrta*, day and night, the half-month and the month, the seasons, the year, and the two-year cycle.
If there were a finite measure, then time would exist, just as, for example, rice grains and the like do.
Because it exists, it has a finite measure; therefore, one knows that time exists.
The proponent says:
The meaning of what you have stated is inconsistent. Why is this?
As the verse in the treatise says:
"When there is no grasping and no abiding, even the time of abiding does not exist;
since there is neither that which can be grasped nor that which cannot be grasped, how can anything be designated?
The commentary states:
"Non-abiding" refers to the fact that the aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are subject to arising and ceasing; this is called non-abiding.
Within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), when the aggregates of conditioned phenomena and so forth are designated as "time," this time is called ungraspable.
Regarding the time of abiding (*sthiti-kāla*), there is no non-material time to be apprehended apart from the essence of the dharma; this is what is called the time of abiding.
How can it be apprehended or not apprehended?
How is it designated?
When a time can be apprehended, it can be designated; when a time cannot be apprehended, it cannot be designated.

For this reason, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are thus: they are called "conditioned" because they function with temporal limits. Since conditioned phenomena arise, abide, and cease, and because dharmas such as *muhūrta* have measurable portions, they are termed "time."
The meaning of the reason you have stated is not established. Why?
Because it lacks a basis, just like that which has no substance.
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:
There is eternal time, because there exist various distinctions such as kṣaṇa, lava, muhūrta, past, future, and so forth.
For example, just as a pure maṇi jewel manifests various appearances depending on those surrounding colors, the proponent says:
"This entity acquires designations such as 'momentary' by depending upon that other entity; such is my position."
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"This and that exist in mutual dependence; such is the nature of phenomena in conventional truth.
In the ultimate sense, there is no intrinsic nature; apart from nature, how could time exist?"
The commentary states:
Regarding "mutual dependence," this means that the opponent establishes mutual dependence within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
My position is likewise: in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no eternal time; thus, you cannot escape the faults I have pointed out.
The Vaiśeṣika proponent says:

In the ultimate sense, there exists a real substance of time (*kāla*), just as "non-otherness" and "otherness," "simultaneity" and "non-simultaneity," "slowness" and "quickness," and so forth, are the characteristics of time; it is not the case that there are characteristics without a substance.
The proponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is not even the slightest essence.

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there are various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) characterized by differentiation, mutual dependence, and continuity. As for the claim that cognitions such as "not other" and "other" arise simultaneously, this refers to the fact that conditioned phenomena lack differentiation at the momentary level; they are mutually dependent, and what is not simultaneous possesses either slowness or speed.
"Slow" refers to the subsequent continuity proceeding at a later time; "rapid" refers to the lower continuity proceeding immediately.
That which is not the arising of another consciousness consists merely of these conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); there is no separate time.
The reason (*hetu*) you have established lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); where, then, could the nature of time ever be found?

If the opponent intends to say that the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) which serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousnesses in others are not time, then where could time be found?
The proponent says:
Your attempt to cause others to understand that time is eternal and unitary lacks any validating proof (*sādhana*).

I shall now state the proof: In the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), an eternal and unitary time does not give rise to cognitions such as those of "otherness," because it is a cognition, just like the cognition of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
The Vaiśeṣika further says:
"There must truly exist time, because it possesses a conventional entity.
The proponent asks:
"Resembling what kind of thing?
The Vaiśeṣika replied:
"It is like form (rūpa) and so forth."
The proponent says:

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the substance of form and so forth is not established, as has already been explained previously; this enables one to understand that the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) lacks substantiality.
Because the characteristic of form lacks substantiality, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) also lacks substantiality.
Because the metaphor lacks substantial reality, time also cannot be established.

Furthermore, although the self does not exist, it is spoken of as existing; for example, like a chariot, an army, or a forest, these are designated despite lacking substantial reality. Therefore, [the argument] is not absolute.
Should someone think:
"Time is designated based on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), just as it is said that 'daytime abides' or 'a muhūrta abides,'" one should answer such a person as follows.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Time exists because of things; Apart from things, time does not exist.
Furthermore, there is no essence of even the slightest thing; Where, then, can time be found?"
The commentary states:
This means that because it arises dependent upon phenomena (*dharma*), it is designated as "time" (*kāla*); apart from these functioning phenomena, there is no separate essence of time.
Those who maintain that time exists assert that time definitely exists, because it serves as the cause for the arising of various conventional designations.
One does not perceive any phenomenon that can give rise to verbal expression; because one perceives that jars have been made, are being made, or will be made, one thereby knows that time exists.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect.
That which has already produced jars and the like, serving as the cause for verbal designation, is likewise not "time" among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, your reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), and it commits the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*).
That which can give rise to verbal expression is a phenomenon of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for when you state it in various ways, it is in every case unestablished.
As previously explained regarding the "reason of proof" (*siddha-hetu*), its meaning likewise remains unestablished.
From the beginning of this chapter, faults have been established against the opponent, while our own position has been established without fault.
This is the intended meaning of this chapter: to inspire conviction that time, which is the object to be negated by emptiness, lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

For this reason, what follows cites the sūtras to demonstrate and establish this point. As the Buddha said in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed Subhūti: "Time is not a dharma of form, nor is it a dharma of non-form;

it is not a dharma of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it a dharma of non-sensation, non-perception, non-formation, or non-consciousness. It is not a dharma of arising, nor a dharma of non-arising; not a dharma of abiding, nor a dharma of non-abiding; not a dharma of change, nor a dharma of non-change; not a dharma of destruction, nor a dharma of non-destruction. It is not a dharma of grasping, not a dharma of abiding, and not a dharma of emerging, nor is it a dharma of non-grasping, non-abiding, and non-emerging. It extends even to being not the mark of aging, not the mark of illness, not the mark of death, not the mark of bluishness, not the mark of being devoured, not the mark of decay, and not the mark of dispersion; nor is it the mark of non-aging, non-illness, non-death, non-bluishness, non-devouring, non-decaying, and non-dispersal."
Subhūti! That which is neither form, nor arising, nor abiding, nor changing, nor perishing in character—this is called the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If it is neither form nor non-form, and so on, up to neither feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor non-feeling, non-perception, non-mental-formations, or non-consciousness, then time is neither time nor non-time.
"If that which is neither time, nor non-time, nor 'not non-time' is inexpressible, this is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*:

"The bodhisattva mahāsattva thoroughly understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) throughout the three periods of time: because they have already arisen, they are called the past; because they have not yet arisen, they are called the future; and because they are arising at the present moment, they are called the present."
Regarding these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that abide in the present world, one understands them to be non-abiding. Why?
Because they do not abide for even a single moment.

Within this single moment, there are distinctions between the time of arising and the time of abiding; because a moment does not endure but perishes swiftly, there is certainly no such thing as "time.
The commentary on the "Examination of Time" is hereby concluded.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Ten.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Twelve.
Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prabhākaramitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: Examining the Conjunction of Cause and Effect. Commentary:

This chapter is also intended to refute emptiness, which is its primary object of negation. It is taught because the Vaiśeṣikas and others failed to establish the existence of "time" in the preceding chapter.
The Vaibhāṣikas and the Sāṃkhyas and others say:
"In the ultimate sense, time exists as such, because effects undergo arising and ceasing.
Just as when a seed is combined with water and soil, the sprout is able to arise because time possesses substantial reality."
If there were no cause, the effect would not arise.
For this reason, as previously stated, because the cause possesses power, one should know that time exists.
The proponent says:
If someone should say that a fruit arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions, we shall now respond to them.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If it is claimed that from a multitude of causes and conditions, A fruit arises through their conjunction;"
"If this effect already exists beforehand, why would it need to arise through conjunction?
The commentary states:
If the effect were present within the conjunction, such a fault would ensue.
Why is this? Because existence does not arise.
If existence were to arise from a combination of conditions, how could existence possibly arise?
If one says that "arising" exists, it does not exist within the combination.
Why? Because the two dharmas of "existence" and "arising" are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, if an effect already exists, it does not arise, because it already exists.
If an effect already exists, there is no need for it to arise again. Why is this?
Arising and non-arising are mutually contradictory.
If someone were to say that within the conjunction of causes and conditions there is no fruit, yet it is able to produce a fruit, we shall now respond to this.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If you claim that from a combination of various causes and conditions a fruit arises,
yet there is no fruit within that combination, why must it arise through such a combination?"
The commentary states:
This means that the effect is not produced because there is no production, just like a rabbit’s horn.
If there were no production, the essence of the phenomenon of production would be destroyed; this constitutes a fault such as the contradiction of your own thesis.
If one posits that the effect exists within the combination of causes and conditions, this shall now be further refuted.
As the verse of the treatise says:
"If it is claimed that from a multitude of causes and conditions, An effect arises through their combination,"
"This fruit should be graspable, yet in reality it cannot be grasped.
Commentary: This means that the fruit is ungraspable.
Why is this? Although one desires with a single mind to grasp it, one cannot grasp it because the effect does not exist.
Hereafter, a proof is established: within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that which is called the sprout—the effect—likewise cannot be grasped.
Why is this? Because there is no effect within the combination, it cannot be apprehended.
If it cannot be apprehended, then it does not exist therein; for example, there is no jar or silk cloth within a seed.
Thus, within the composite whole (*saṃghāta*), there is no such thing as a sprout that can be designated as an "effect," and therefore it cannot be apprehended.
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:

There is indeed a sense in which it is said that [the effect] cannot be apprehended within the composite; namely, that factors such as extreme distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense faculties, mental confusion, and intervening obstructions are capable of obstructing its apprehension.
Although it possesses a substantial entity, it cannot be grasped; it is not that it cannot be grasped because it is entirely non-existent.
To claim that it is non-existent would be a fault in their formulation of the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, there are other Sāṃkhyas who say:
"As for the faults previously mentioned, we shall now state them further.
Regarding that reason you previously stated—that [the self] cannot be apprehended—what is the meaning of this reason?"
Is it because it cannot be apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
For instance, although the various sense-faculties and consciousnesses truly exist, they likewise are not apprehended by direct perception.
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) they have established is not invariably certain (*anaikāntika*).

If that which is to be established cannot be apprehended through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is not established; this is because, as in the case of the reason "the effect exists within the cause," it is apprehensible and measurable.
If it is measurable, then the cause is not empty, just like the substantial entity of an effect.

In this way, the two types—suffering and pleasure—are capable of serving as the causes for the three afflictions of greed, hatred, and various views; likewise, the five types of form and sound are also capable of serving as the causes for the three afflictions such as greed and hatred. Because these causes possess valid evidence (*pramāṇa*), the effect is apprehended within the cause.

Although you claim that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) cannot apprehend [the object], since it can indeed be apprehended by means of inference (*anumāna*), the meaning of your stated reason (*hetu*) is unestablished.
If both direct perception and inference were unable to apprehend it, this would contradict my own position and your reason would remain unestablished.
The proponent says:
When I state that my path is "ungraspable," it means that because there is ultimately no fruit within the combination of causes and conditions, it is ungraspable.

Your claim that things such as the "extremely distant" are also ungraspable yet not entirely non-existent has no basis even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), let alone in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there are likewise no such things as "extreme distance" and so forth; just as suffering, pleasure, form, sound, and the like do not exist in the ultimate sense, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is thus unestablished.
As for what is called the "fruit," the fruit is also empty of intrinsic nature.
If the fruit does not exist within the cause, then even in conventional truth the fruit would not arise; just as a fist cannot produce another fist, so too a cause cannot produce itself.
As for your statement that a cause can produce an effect, this has already been refuted even within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"If the causal substance does not exist prior to the production of the effect, then the effect likewise does not exist beforehand and only arises subsequently."
The proponent says:
Now I shall state the proof.

If there were no cause beforehand, it would not arise later either, because it does not exist; for example, like a flower in the sky or a barren woman’s son, as extensively explained in the proof previously stated.
Now, to provide a general response to the Sautrāntikas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and others who maintain that the effect does not exist within the cause, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If it is claimed that although the various causes and conditions Are combined, the effect does not exist;
Then these various causes and conditions Would be the same as those that are not causes and conditions."
The commentary states:
This statement that "there is no fruit" means that the fruit is empty.
What, then, is the distinction between cause and fruit?

The characteristic of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) refers to specific distinctions such as the production of its own fruit, immediate production, and production from its own part; these constitute the characteristic of cause.

The characteristic of condition (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which universally produces various fruits, is able to nourish others, causes others to continue in succession, and even reaches distant places to universally produce all fruits; it is not produced from its own part, yet is capable of providing extensive benefit.
Such as these are called the characteristics of the distinctions among causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). As for that which is not a causal condition, it does not produce a fruit. Why is this?
Because the effect is empty.
For this reason, causal conditions and non-causal conditions are the same.

Furthermore, we shall now provide a proof for those who maintain that the effect does not exist within the cause: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), seeds and other such causal conditions cannot produce an effect.
Why is this? Because the effect is empty, like that which is not a causal condition.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas say:
Conditions are able to produce effects.
Why is this? Because there exist determinate conditions that are capable of producing effects.
If the effect were empty, the meaning would be inconsistent.
The proponent says:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), such a proof does not exist; it remains subject to the same fault as the previous argument regarding non-causality.
If you wish to cause others to believe and understand, your proof lacks power.
The Sautrāntikas further state:
since we observe that a barley seed can produce a barley sprout, the reason you have put forward is devoid of logical validity.
The proponent says:
Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is indeed seen that a barley seed can produce a barley sprout;
this is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If, within the ultimate truth, a barley seed were to produce a sprout, that would not be the case.
Thus, it is incorrect to observe that an effect arises, as was previously answered.
If you establish the arising and ceasing of an effect as the cause, the logical sense of an effect arising is untenable.
Furthermore, I now ask those who maintain that the effect does not exist within the cause:
Does the cause perish after having produced the effect?
Or does it perish before the effect has been produced?
The proponent replied:
"What fault is there in me that you ask these two questions?
The opponent said:
This is logically inconsistent.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the cause, having already performed its function of producing the fruit, were only then to perish;"
"If there were both the cause and the cessation of the cause, then there would be two entities.
The commentary states:
This means that even within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one does not wish to allow the fault of a single phenomenon having two entities—that which gives and that which ceases.
Furthermore, if [a cause] were to perish prior to exercising its capacity to produce an effect, we shall now provide the response.
As stated in a verse of the Treatise:
"If the cause has not yet exercised its capacity, And the cause perishes beforehand;..."
"If the cause ceases and the effect arises, then this effect would be without a cause.
The commentary states:
This means that one does not desire for an effect to exist without a cause; therefore, it is not the case that the effect only arises after the cause has already ceased.
Why is this? Because it has already ceased, just like that which has long since ceased.
This meaning is commonly understood by all the world, and thus there is no need to cause others to understand it further.
The Sautrāntikas further state:
"The arising of the harmonious factors (sāmagrī) can simultaneously produce an effect; it is like a lamp and its light, which arise at the same time—this principle must be so."
The proponent says:
If it is claimed that the effect arises simultaneously [with its cause], this too is not so.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If cause and conditions were to coalesce simultaneously and thereby produce an effect,
then the producer and the produced would both fall within the same moment.
Commentary:

This means that there would be the fault of simultaneity; yet one does not wish for the two dharmas—the producer and the produced—to arise simultaneously like a father and son, as that would entail the aforementioned fault.
Furthermore, how do they arise at different times?
It refers to the duality of the produced effect and the producing cause.
Now, we shall establish a proof: the effect and the cause do not arise simultaneously in conjunction.
Why is this? Because there is a duality between that which is produced and that which produces, just as there is a duality between father and son.

As previously stated, because of the power of the combination of the vessel, wick, oil, and so forth, in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the lamp and its light arise simultaneously; it is not the case that the lamp and the light stand in a causal relationship toward one another. Therefore, what you have said is incorrect.
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"The effect already arises prior to its conjunction; it is only at the time of subsequent conjunction that it becomes manifest.
The respondent replies:
This is not the case.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the effect were to arise already existing prior to the coming together [of causes and conditions];"
"Once separated from those causes and conditions, the arising of the effect would be without a cause.
Commentary:
This means that if an effect were to exist prior to the conjunction of causes and conditions, such a thing is not observed even in the context of conventional truth.
For this reason, within my Buddha-dharma, there is no fruit that arises prior [to its cause].
As for your claim that it is manifested later, this has already been answered.
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
Although the causal dharma has already ceased, its causal substance (kāraṇa-bhāva) still persists until the time the fruit arises.
The proponent says:
If the substance were not discarded once the cause has ceased, such that it remains as the substance of the fruit, this would be logically untenable.
Why is this? As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the cause transforms into the effect, then the cause would have departed."
"If that which already exists were to arise again, it would fall into the error of re-arising.
The commentary states:
This means that the substance of the cause becomes the fruit without relinquishing its own substance, just as Devadatta does not abandon this house when he goes to that house.
Why is this? If the essence of the cause already exists and yet arises again, it would constitute a "re-birth.
Since it does not produce a fruit, it performs no function whatsoever.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that the cause itself transforms into the effect, then this cannot be called "transformation.
Since it is not called transformation, it would be like a lump of clay, which is not identical to the jar.

Once the lump of clay has ceased, the jar arises; therefore, it cannot be called "transformation" (pariṇāma), because it does not remain unchanged, just as, for example, the substance of the clay itself [remains].
The Sāṃkhya further says:
"The cause can produce the effect; my doctrine is thus, and it is free from the aforementioned fault."
The proponent says:

If you designate something as a "result" without it relinquishing its causal nature, then there is merely a difference in names while the substance of the result does not exist; thus, you cannot avoid the fault previously stated.
If the cause, having relinquished its own nature, were to remain within the nature of the effect at the time the effect arises, this would be illogical.
You have made such a statement without due reflection.
Furthermore, I now ask those who maintain the existence of distinct categories (vaiśeṣika-sāṃkhya):
regarding your claim that the cause can produce [the effect], does the cause produce the effect after it has already ceased,
or does it produce the effect before it has ceased?
Neither of these two positions is tenable, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Does that which has already ceased produce a fruit?
Or does that which has not yet ceased produce a fruit?"
"If the cause has ceased and is already destroyed, how can it produce an effect?
The commentary states:
This means that what has already ceased is no longer a cause; how, then, could it produce an effect?
If the cause has already arisen and its substance does not perish, how could it produce an effect?
What you have said is logically inconsistent.
Furthermore, another Sāṃkhya proponent says:
Ultimate dharmas abide eternally; yet, while the preceding entity ceases and the subsequent entity arises, there is this transformation.
For this reason, the causal entity does not perish, yet it is able to produce an effect.
The proponent says:
This, too, is erroneous.
When the preceding entity ceases, the substantial dharma also ceases.
Why is this? Because the real dharma is not different from the substance of the entity, just as, for example, the substance of a dharma that has already ceased.
When the substance of a subsequent dharma arises, the real dharma also arises.
Why is this? Because the true dharma is not different from the entity, just like the nature of a dharma that has already arisen.
What you have said contradicts the principles of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one relies on the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), what entity of a phenomenon ceases and what entity of a phenomenon arises such that one could say there is transformation?
For what reason?
At no time is there any analogy [for this].
What you have stated is not logically tenable.
Furthermore, regarding your claim that the prior substance of a phenomenon perishes: is this substance the causal substance?
Is it not the essence of the cause?
If it were the essence of the cause, then when the essence of the preceding dharma ceases, the essence of the cause would also cease.
As the verse says, "the cause having ceased," this means that a cause already ceased does not possess the power to produce an effect.
Furthermore, if the preceding dharma that has ceased were not the essence of the cause, as the verse in the treatise says:
"When cause and effect abide in conjunction, how could the effect be produced?"
"If it does not unite with the fruit, what thing could produce the fruit?
The commentary states:
This means that the cause does not produce the fruit.
Why is this? Because the essence of cause and effect is not different; for example, a cause does not produce itself from its own essence.

If the cause and the effect were to coexist in union and yet the cause did not produce the effect, then the cause would be useless, as the nature of phenomena would be inverted. This is a fault in your proposed thesis.
If someone should say:
"The cause does not combine with the effect," this is also answered as above:
a thing does not produce an effect.
Why is this? Because the effect is empty, just like any other effect.
Thus, the cause’s capacity to produce an effect has already been refuted in general.
Now we shall explain this separately to refute those [views] regarding the results such as visual consciousness.
If this visual consciousness has the eye as its cause, does this eye see and then grasp the object?
Is it that the object is apprehended without being seen?
Neither case is tenable.
If consciousness were to arise only after the eye has seen and apprehended, then consciousness would be useless.
If the eye were to grasp an object without seeing it, then the objective field of form would be useless.
Furthermore, some say:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a cause is able to produce an effect."
Why is this? Because the cause acts as the cause for the effect.
If the cause did not produce the effect, then milk would not be the cause of curd, just as milk is not the cause of a jar.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect. Why is this so?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"There is no past effect that is conjoined with a past cause;
Nor is there a future effect that is conjoined with a produced cause."
The commentary states:
This means that because both cause and effect are non-existent, they are like the horns of a rabbit.
Furthermore, because the past cause belongs to a different time, it does not unite with the effect.
Furthermore, regarding the non-conjunction of arisen and unarisen effects with arisen and unarisen causes, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"An arisen effect and an unarisen cause Ultimately do not conjoin;
An unarisen effect and an arisen cause Likewise do not conjoin."
The commentary states:
This refers to the distinction of time, because cause and effect are two distinct entities.

That which has already arisen as an effect does not conjoin with a cause that has already arisen or one yet to arise; likewise, a destroyed effect does not conjoin with a cause that has already been destroyed or one not yet destroyed. As stated in the verse of the treatise:
“There is no already-arisen effect that is conjoined with an already or not-yet arisen cause;
nor is there an already-perished effect that is conjoined with an already or not-yet arisen cause.
Commentary:
This refers to the claim that cause and effect are simultaneous; however, this has already been refuted previously.
Because their times differ, your position is untenable.
Upon such examination, it is clear that cause and effect can never be conjoined.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If causes are not in conjunction, how can they produce an effect?
If causes are in conjunction, how can they produce an effect?"
The commentary states:

The following constitutes the proof: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), a cause does not produce an effect because they do not coalesce; for example, when a seed is in the ground, a sprout does not emerge from a high mountain.
Furthermore, there is now a logical argument that exposes the faults of those who maintain that the fruit is either non-existent or existent within the rice seed.
As the verse of the treatise says:
"If the fruit is empty within the cause, How can it produce the fruit?"
If the effect is not empty within the cause, how could it produce an effect?
Commentary: This means that the seed does not produce an effect because the effect is empty; as previously answered, it is like other effects.
Regarding the claim that the effect is not empty within the cause: this means that because the effect already exists, the cause does not produce it.
For example, the cause does not produce [the effect], as has already been answered previously.
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
Before the fruit has arisen, this fruit already exists.
The proponent says:
Such a principle does not exist.
Now, in order to refute this error, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"The unarisen fruit is not empty; If it were not empty, it would not cease.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, The fruit incurs the fault of being non-empty."
The commentary states:
This means that the effect does not arise from conditions, because the effect possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If it were to arise while already existing, such a principle would not hold; since it already exists, there is no need for it to arise again.
If it is claimed that an effect arises without [an action], then the essence of that effect would necessarily be permanent and indestructible.
For this reason, the effect would incur the fault of being non-empty.
Yet, the proponent does not wish for the effect to incur the fault of being non-empty; as the verse of the treatise says:
"If the fruit is not empty, it does not arise; if the fruit is not empty, it does not cease.
Because the fruit is not empty, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Commentary:
If the fruit were empty, there would be no arising or ceasing; if it were definitively existent, it would not need to arise again.
Since there is no arising, there is no ceasing. For this reason, if the fruit were not empty, how could there be arising and ceasing?
Furthermore, why is this?
One who wishes to obtain such a fruit [does so] because it is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
If the fruit already existed, one would not perceive it as a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, just like the characteristic of the present.
Furthermore, a Lokāyata proponent says:
Prior to the arising of an effect, the effect has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Why is this?
Because the essence of the fruit is empty,
even that which has already arisen as a fruit lacks the essence of any other dharma.
The proponent says:
This statement is false and devoid of logical principle.
I shall now answer you. Why is this so?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the effect is empty, how can it arise?
If the effect is empty, how can it cease?"
"Because the fruit is empty, there is neither arising nor cessation.
The commentary states:
This means that within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is not the case that the fruit is empty and yet undergoes arising.
Why is this? Because the effect has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), like a flower in the sky.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the absence of the intrinsic nature of a barley sprout within a rice sprout is not established by the cessation of that [rice sprout's] nature; for it lacks intrinsic nature, just as, for example, the cessation of what is not a rice sprout [does not establish the absence of a barley sprout].
Furthermore, that which arises from conditions is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for this is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within my Dharma.

If one were to claim that there exists even the slightest thing that is not empty, such a thing would not arise from causes and conditions; yet even in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), such a thing does not exist, being like a flower in the sky.
As stated in the verse above: "If the unarisen effect were not empty, one would incur the fault of the effect being non-empty.
This means that if the effect were not empty, one would incur the fault of it being without arising and ceasing.
I now cause you to understand that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the effect is empty yet arises, just like a magical illusion and so forth.
Within the ultimate truth, the effect is empty because it undergoes cessation, and thus it is also like a magical illusion; the effect is likewise so.
If an effect were to have as its essence the absence of another entity, then this effect would neither arise nor cease.
Furthermore, since there would be no effect even within the realm of conventional truth, it would be like a flower in the sky.
This is also as explained above: "How can an empty fruit arise?
How can an empty fruit cease?
This means that both arising and ceasing lack any substantial entity.
Since this fruit is empty, it is without arising or cessation.

However, because outsiders do not wish to allow that the fruit lacks arising and cessation, [the author] here establishes a proof: the fruits such as the internal sense bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) do not lack intrinsic nature, because they possess arising, just like illusions and the like.
By this evidence that there is neither arising nor ceasing, you are refuted regarding the existence of arising and ceasing in your result.
Since your distinct phenomena are thus refuted, this constitutes a fault in your formal proposition.
Furthermore, regarding the productive cause: is this cause identical to its effect, or is it different?
The fault in either case is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If cause and effect were one, this principle would never exist;
if cause and effect were different, this principle would likewise not exist.
The commentary states:
Why is it that cause and effect cannot be identical or different?
The fault in this regard is as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If cause and effect were one, then the agent and the object would be one."
"If cause and effect were different, then the cause would be no different from a non-cause.
The commentary states:
This means that you do not accept the relationship between producer and produced as being like that of a father and a son; how then could they be one?
Furthermore, it is like fire and fuel; how could these be one?
These two analogies are commonly seen in the world.
For this reason, I shall now state a formal proof: cause and effect cannot be identical.
Why is this? Because there is a distinction between that which produces and that which is produced, just as in the case of father and son.
This refers to the fault of those who reckon them as one.
Furthermore, what is meant by "adhering to difference"?
It means that because the cause and the effect are different, they are like all non-causal phenomena (*ahetudharma*).
Yet you do not wish for the cause to be the same as a non-cause; rather, your intention is to establish that the two phenomena of cause and effect are a continuous succession without difference.
Furthermore, I now ask those who maintain that the effect pre-exists within the cause:
does this effect arise having already existed,
or does it arise having not yet existed?
None of these are tenable.
The fault is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If the effect already exists, What need is there for it to arise from causes?"
"If the fruit does not yet exist, how can the cause further produce it?
The commentary states:
This means that if the fruit possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why would it depend on a cause for its production?
Even within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it cannot cause people to believe and understand.
If effects lacked intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would be like flowers in the sky; even within conventional truth, they could not be made understood by people.
As stated in the verse above: "How can an empty effect arise?
Through this observation, it is not the case that a cause can produce an effect within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*); if a cause does not produce an effect, then it is not a cause.
Regarding the "ability to produce an effect" established by the opponent as before, the cause would have to function as a cause in every instance.

Now, in order to refute this, it is shown that the meaning of the cause is not established; furthermore, you contradict your own previous statement by attempting to establish the doctrine that a cause produces an effect within the context of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, as for what is now called "contradiction," it means that while in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) causes do not produce effects, in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) there is production, such as that of illusions and the like.
The Vaiśeṣika further says:
In the ultimate sense, the cause is able to produce the effect. Why is this so?
The people of the world all say, "This is the cause of this fruit"; therefore, one should know that the cause is capable of producing the fruit.

If the cause did not produce the fruit, one would never point it out and say, "This is the cause of this fruit," just as, for example, one does not speak of a camel-horn bow because it does not exist.
Now, it is spoken of by virtue of existence; for example, it is said that the eye is the cause and consciousness is the effect, or that the rice seed is the cause and the sprout is the effect.
It is spoken of because they exist. If the analogies of consciousness and the sprout can be established, then the thesis I have proposed is established; such is the proof.
The proponent says:
If even a slight amount of an effect had arisen as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one could say "this is the cause" and "this is the effect," and such a demonstration could be made.

Now, since the cause capable of producing [the effect] is absent, that which you cited above—the claim that worldly people all say this is the cause of that effect—is unestablished and also contradicts your own tenet.
Furthermore, there are Sāṃkhyas who say:
"The fruit arises because it attains the conditions of conjunction; this conjunction, by attaining the proper season, is able to produce the fruit.

Now, at the beginning of this chapter, they refuted my statement that "the cause is not established because the fruit has arising and ceasing as its cause," but this is not unestablished. Nor is it the case that the fruit is produced by the cause alone; rather, the fruit is produced through both conjunction and the attainment of the proper season.
As for their claim that causes do not produce effects, this actually establishes my own position.
The commentator says:
that which is a combination of causes and conditions is not a real entity (*dharma*) capable of producing [an effect] by its own nature.
If it were possible for an entity to produce an effect once it has already arisen, that is not the case now.
Why? Because the fault is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
“The intrinsic nature and the various conditions, even when combined, cannot produce [an effect];
since the intrinsic nature itself does not arise, how could it produce an effect?
Commentary:
This means that a combination does not produce an effect.
Why? Because it is not a real entity (*dravyadharma*), just like a magical illusion (*māyā*) and so forth.
It is also as stated in Āryadeva’s *Śata-śāstra*, in the verse refuting conjunction (*saṃyoga*): "A single conjunction does not exist, nor do multiple conjunctions exist.
If one were to say it is a single [entity], it would have to exist apart from causes and conditions."
Now, I shall analyze the correct meaning for you.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Therefore, the effect does not arise from conditions, whether they are combined or uncombined."
"Because the fruit does not exist, the composite entity also does not exist.
Commentary: This means that apart from the various conditions, there is no composite entity.
Furthermore, as previously refuted that a cause does not produce an effect, we now refute that a combination also does not produce an effect.
How so? It means that this combination neither produces [the effect] through immediate proximity nor through distance.

Regarding that which is unarisen in the ultimate sense, as was already established through conviction in the previous refutation of causes and conditions, likewise, neither a composite phenomenon nor a non-composite phenomenon produces a fruit.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Śata-śāstra*:
"Worldly names exist through combination, yet the essence of dharmas does not exist.
Because the essence does not exist, there is also no combination."

For this reason, the purpose of this chapter is to refute the reasons stated by the opponent at the beginning of the chapter by exposing their logical fallacies, thereby negating the existence of temporal phenomena (kāladharma) so that one may gain conviction in the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) of cause and effect. This is the intended meaning of this chapter.
For this reason, my thesis is established.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"O Parākrama!..."
Form is neither cause nor effect.
If form is neither cause nor effect, then even feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither cause nor effect. Why is this?
Because form is without conjunction.

If form is without conjunction, then even feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without conjunction. Not seeing form, not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and having nothing to practice—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

As the Buddha said in a verse in the *Vijñānagatiparaloka-sūtra*: "When one speaks of the locus of conjunction, this is spoken of as a gateway of skillful means; for the sake of attaining the ultimate truth, the wise understand it thus."
The commentary on the "Examination of Cause and Effect" chapter is concluded.
21. Commentary on the "Examination of Formation and Destruction" (Chapter Twenty-one) of the *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*. It is said:
This present chapter is also intended to refute that which is the antithesis of emptiness.

As in the preceding chapter, having already caused [the audience] to gain faith and understanding through the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in cause and effect, it is now taught in order to demonstrate that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without arising or ceasing.
The Sāṃkhya proponent says:
"Time exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)."
Why is this? Because time is the cause of formation and destruction.
If time did not exist, it would not be a cause, just like the extra foot of a snake.
Because time exists, the two phenomena of formation and destruction proceed according to time; therefore, time is said to be the cause.
Since the cause is established, my own thesis is thereby established.
The proponent says:
Regarding the two phenomena of arising and ceasing, does cessation exist apart from arising,
or does cessation exist without being apart from arising?
Is it simultaneous with its destruction?
Neither of these is tenable.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
"Without arising, there is no destruction; even together with it, there is no destruction.
Without destruction, there is no arising; even together with it, there is no arising. Commentary:
Such is the meaning of my Buddha-dharma.
As for your statement that time is the cause, that meaning is not established. Why is this?

If destruction existed apart from formation, then destruction would not be dependent upon formation; thus, destruction would be without cause, and furthermore, there would be no formed phenomenon to be destroyed.
What, then, constitutes formation?
It means the convergence of various conditions.
What is its destruction?
It means the dispersal of various conditions.

Furthermore, if destruction were to exist apart from formation, there would be no formation; since there is none, who then could be destroyed? For example, it is like a non-existent jar. Therefore, apart from formation, there is no destruction.
If it is argued that destruction exists simultaneously with [formation], this too is not the case.
Why is this? Because phenomena first become distinct and only then undergo conjunction; thus, these conjoined phenomena are not separate from difference.
If they were separate from difference, then destruction would be without cause; therefore, even when coexisting with it, there is no destruction.
Thus, if there were arising apart from destruction or simultaneous with destruction, there would be no such thing as arising. Why is this?
If there were arising apart from destruction, then arising would be permanent; permanence is the characteristic of non-destruction, yet in reality, no phenomenon is seen to be permanent.
For this reason, apart from disintegration, there is no formation.
If it is claimed that they exist simultaneously, that too is not so; since formation and disintegration are mutually contradictory, how could they exist at one and the same time?
The Sāṃkhya says:
How can one establish one's own doctrine while attributing faults to another?
If your own doctrine is indeed established, you should state the reasoning for it.
The proponent replies:
Your position is incorrect.
Its fallacy is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If there is no disintegration apart from formation, how could there be disintegration?
If there is no birth apart from death, how could there be formation without disintegration? Commentary:
This means that apart from arising, there is no phenomenon of destruction; since this is understood by all people in the world, it need not be explained in detail.
The explanation of how there is no destruction apart from arising is complete.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as destruction occurring simultaneously with existence, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If existence and destruction were simultaneous, How could they possibly be apprehended?
Just as birth and death, They cannot occur at the same time."
The commentary states:
Herein, a proof is set forth: destruction and formation do not exist simultaneously. Why is this so?
Because arising is the condition for destruction, they cannot coexist, just as death and birth cannot be found together.
Having explained that they do not coexist,
next is the second analysis concerning the impossibility of arising in the absence of destruction, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If destruction were to exist apart from formation, how could it ever be apprehended?
Impermanence exists at all times within all entities.
Commentary:
This means that there is no establishment [of existence] apart from disintegration. Why?

Because, as in the formal proposition, those entities which are impermanent—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—are impermanent by their very nature (*svabhāva*), just as, for example, impermanence itself is impermanent by its own nature.
Furthermore, a person from the Saṃmitīya school says:
"Although phenomena are impermanent, it is only when a cause of destruction arrives that the substance of the phenomenon perishes; impermanence does not exist at all times."
The proponent says:
If that were so, it would be like a person who, having taken a purgative and subsequently purged, says to others,
"It is this deity who has made me purge."
It is not said that medicine causes evacuation.
You are just like this: since the nature of impermanence can destroy the essence of a phenomenon at all times, it is incorrect to say that it must wait for a cause of destruction to arrive.

If it were only upon obtaining the cause of destruction that impermanence could then destroy the essence of a phenomenon, then it would be the cause of destruction itself that destroys the essence of the phenomenon; why then can you further claim that impermanence is what destroys it?
Now I ask the outsider:
Is the nature of a phenomenon already of a disintegrating character and then meets with a cause of disintegration to undergo destruction?
Or is it not of a disintegrating character and then meets with a cause of disintegration to undergo destruction?
If this dharma-essence were of a nature subject to disintegration such that it could be destroyed when a cause of destruction arrives, that would not be the case. Why is this so?

Because the dharma-essence disintegrates immediately upon its arising; it perishes as soon as it arises and does not reach a second moment. How, then, could it wait for a cause of destruction to arrive before being destroyed?
If a phenomenon has an intrinsic nature that is not subject to destruction, it is like *nirvāṇa*, which does not await the arrival of a cause of destruction to be destroyed.
Furthermore, destruction has no cause; because destruction is without cause, a phenomenon is not destroyed, just like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
By this evidence, that cause of destruction is refuted.

Once that cause is refuted, the substantial entity itself is refuted; thus, there is a fault in your thesis, for it is not the case that the two phenomena of arising and destruction exist sequentially.
Having already refuted the possibility of arising and ceasing being established separately,
furthermore, the position that arising and ceasing exist simultaneously is also untenable. Why is this so?
As the verse of the treatise says:
"How can formation and destruction be simultaneous?
It is just as birth and death— To be simultaneous is not possible."
The commentary states:
This means that when performing this contemplation, the meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
Furthermore, regarding their mutual non-establishment, it is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If formation and destruction were established through mutual dependence, these two would not be established;
apart from this mutual establishment of the two, how could these two phenomena be established? Commentary:
This means that the two phenomena of formation and destruction cannot be established.
As the opponent previously asserted that time serves as the cause for formation and destruction, such a cause is not established.
The Sarvāstivādins further state:

This phenomenon of intrinsic nature that undergoes destruction does not perish immediately upon arising; because there is a period of abiding immediately following its arising, and it is only after this abiding that destruction occurs.
The proponent says: This is not so.
The meaning is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"That which is exhausted has no arising; that which is not exhausted also has no arising.
That which is exhausted has no destruction; that which is not exhausted also has no destruction. Commentary:

This means that if a phenomenon possesses impermanence, it is called "exhaustion"; that which is exhausted does not arise. This is because the two phenomena of arising and exhaustion are mutually contradictory, just as, for example, birth and death are.
If one were to say that once arisen, it does not cease without interval, this would not be the dharma of exhaustion.

For this reason, as previously stated regarding the dharma of arising and exhaustion, since it is not established within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is no need for further conceptualization or discrimination concerning the dharma of exhaustion.
That which is inexhaustible does not undergo destruction of its own essence, just as, for example, liberation (vimukti) does not.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
There must be both arising and destruction, because there exists the substantial entity (dravya).
If there were neither arising nor ceasing, there would likewise be no substantial nature of phenomena; it would be like the arising and ceasing of a toad’s fur.
This is because that which possesses the nature of a substance must necessarily possess arising and ceasing.
The proponent says:

If, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there were even a single entity that truly underwent arising and ceasing, one should speak of the phenomena of arising and ceasing; however, since no such arising or ceasing can be spoken of, [it does not exist].
The meaning of this is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If one is apart from arising and ceasing, Then there is no substantial entity;
These two dharmas of arising and ceasing Also do not exist apart from a substantial entity."
The commentary states:
Regarding "entity" (*vastu*), it is so called because its nature consists in being established.
Since that which is established lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), your previous argument—that the existence of the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) serves as the reason—is unestablished.
Why is this? Because that which is depended upon has no substance, that which depends upon it is likewise not established.
Furthermore, regarding your assertion that a substantial entity serves as the cause, I shall now state its fault.
The Sautrāntikas say:
"The substance of things has no reality; their intrinsic nature is empty, yet upon these things there exist the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
The Sarvāstivādins further state:
If things possessed substantial reality and their intrinsic nature were not empty, then arising and ceasing would occur within those things.
Now, to answer both schools regarding arising and ceasing in general, as the verse of the treatise says:
"If there were two dharmas of arising and ceasing, The substance of things being empty would not be so."
"There exist the two phenomena of arising and perishing; it is not the case that their essence is empty.
The commentary states:
In this context, the proof is established as above, because the phenomena of essence exist.

If you claim that they exist by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then they should not undergo destruction; for this reason, the logical reason (*hetu*) you have established is unproven.
Furthermore, there is another principle for exposing a fault:
Are these phenomena of formation and destruction identical?
Are they different?
Neither of these two positions is correct.
What, then, is the meaning?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"It is not tenable that these two phenomena of arising and ceasing are of one essence;
it is also not tenable that these two phenomena of arising and ceasing are of different essences."
The commentary states:
This refers to their mutual contradiction, just as, for example, ignorance and wisdom [are contradictory].
However, these two dharmas depend upon the same single entity, just as other physical objects do; thus, this reason also commits the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
The Vaiśeṣika proponent speaks in verse:
"I always perceive that entities Are subject to both arising and destruction;
Therefore, one knows that the nature of things Must exist and is not empty."
The proponent says:
Your actual seeing is merely identical to the cognition of ordinary worldlings; it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Now, I shall analyze its meaning for you.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Arising has already been refuted, And the dharma of non-arising is also refuted;
To see [things] as established is folly, And to see them as destroyed is likewise."
The commentary states:
This refers to the absence of an essence that undergoes arising and ceasing.
If an opponent were to say, "I perceive arising and ceasing," how could one know that this is merely delusion and not the ultimate truth?
The proponent says:
This has already been answered previously.
If your mind is still not satisfied, I shall explain it further for you now.
If, within the ultimate sense, one perceives a substantial entity, then arising and perishing could depend upon that entity.
However, does this entity produce an entity by virtue of having an essence?
Does that which lacks an essence produce an essence?
Neither of these is tenable. Why is this so?
The meaning of this is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"An existent entity does not produce an entity, Nor does it produce a non-existent entity;
A non-existent entity does not produce an entity, Nor does it produce a non-existent entity."
The commentary states:
"That which has an existent nature does not arise from an existent nature," because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it lacks an existent nature, just like an already arisen nature.
If an outsider should say:
