What is the meaning of "inversion" (*viparyāsa*)?
A member of our own school replies:
That which is actually impermanent, yet is claimed to be permanent, may be called a perversion.
The proponent says:
This statement is incorrect.
The fault is as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"To regard the impermanent as permanent Is called a perverted clinging;
Since the impermanent is also a clinging, Why is emptiness not likewise a clinging?"
The commentary states:
This means that because the objects apprehended by that cognition are inverted, this very statement constitutes the meaning of "inversion.
For example, it is like someone asking: "If one has already become free from desire for the three realms, why is one not called 'liberated'?"
Such words as these are themselves liberation.
A member of our own school asks:
"You have now further stated that impermanence is also empty; why is this not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?"
The proponent says:
Because there is no arising.
This meaning of non-arising has already been refuted by reason as previously explained; for example, nirvāṇa neither arises nor is it impermanent.

Furthermore, this essence of impermanence can give rise to the cognition that discriminates permanence; if one claims that this is a perverted attachment to the perception of permanence, then the objective referent would have no essence.
Therefore, regarding what was stated in the previous verse—“If impermanence is also a grasping, why is emptiness not an inversion?”—it is indeed an inversion. Why is this so?
Because it involves conceptual construction, it is like the adherence to permanence.

Herein is established the proof: in the ultimate sense, the claim that form is impermanent is itself a perversion, because it is a conceptual construction, just like the adherence to form as permanent.
The follower of our own school says:
"When wisdom discriminates, saying that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty, that wisdom is not exclusively inverted.
The proponent replies:
This is also a perversion, yet I say there is no fault in it.
A proponent of our own school says:

"If this is so, then this knowledge of emptiness is not the cause for attaining liberation because it is a perversion, just as, for example, the internal sense-bases are the objects of the cognitions of suffering, pleasure, and so forth."
The proponent asks:
"What is the meaning within your established thesis?
The member of our own school replies:
"Is the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the eye not the cause for attaining liberation?
The proponent says:
"If that were so, it would conversely establish my own position."
How does this establish my position?
Because liberation is attained through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
If one were to say that the eye is empty, the wisdom that cognizes the emptiness of the eye would itself be conceptual.

Setting aside these words for now, I shall now explain my own fundamental doctrine to you once more: just as it is an inversion to grasp at what is impermanent as permanent, so too is it said that to grasp at what is non-self as self, what is without bliss as bliss, and what is impure as pure is likewise an inversion.
There are members of our own school who establish a thesis through analysis, stating:
"Such an adherence exists, because there is that which adheres and that which is adhered to.
However, the arising of such adherence is of three kinds, and it is not non-existent.
The proponent says:
Your position is not tenable.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"The grasper, the act of grasping, and the object grasped— All these are of the nature of total quiescence; Therefore, there is no grasping.
Commentary:
Apprehension is of three kinds: namely, the instrument, the arising, and the object, etc.
The instrument of apprehension refers to the subject that apprehends, which is the cognition that takes the substance as its general object.
The arising of apprehension refers to the mind that performs the act of apprehending, such as through false attribution or denial, and so forth.
Furthermore, "one who clings" refers to the person who gives rise to clinging.
"The object of clinging" refers to the objects of conceptualization, such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

These three factors are all empty of intrinsic nature; according to the principles I have explained, I intend to bring about an understanding that the instruments of clinging and all else are characterized by total quiescence. Therefore, there is no clinging.
Furthermore, for those who hold such views and seek to cause others to understand through the expression "existence exists," there is no illustrative analogy.
For this reason, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Because the nature of grasping does not exist, Neither the false nor the correct can exist either."
"Who now is subject to inversion?
Who is not subject to inversion?
The commentary states:
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), who is subject to inversion and who is not?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, abiding in non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), does not engage in any conceptualization; there is neither right nor wrong, neither inversion nor non-inversion.

Furthermore, if someone were to say that inversion definitely exists because there are those who possess inversion—just as when there is a parasol, there must be one who holds it—so too is it with the inversions of ordinary persons:
because there are those who possess inversion, therefore inversion exists.
The proponent says:
This argument is not tenable.
As stated in the verse above: "Because the nature of grasping does not exist, neither the false nor the correct exists."
Because these two principles have already been explained for the sake of clarification, the existence of an "ariser" is also not established;
in this way and that way, both the inversion and the one who undergoes inversion are likewise not established.
As stated in the verse above, who is inverted and who is not inverted?
This statement means that there is no inversion; because there is no inversion, those who are inverted likewise do not exist.

Furthermore, if there is perversion, then there must be non-perversion; for this reason, your logical reason is unestablished. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), your example lacks substantiality and also contradicts your own position.
Furthermore, people of the world say:
"One who is conjoined with inversion is called an inverted person.
Regarding this inversion, does it conjoin with one in whom inversion has already arisen?
Is it joined with one who has not yet given rise to perversion?
Or is it joined with one at the very moment perversion arises?
Now, the answer is: in all three cases, its conjunction with perversion is untenable.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"That which has already arisen does not undergo conjunction; that which has not yet arisen likewise does not undergo conjunction.
Apart from what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen, there is no third alternative; thus, the time of conjunction does not exist."
The commentary states:
This means that for one who already possesses inversion, to further conjoin them with inversion would be useless. Why is this so?
Because that which is inverted is empty, it is like other things that are not inverted.
If one says that there is an inversion which conjoins with time, this involves a double fault.
It is not the case that something apart from both the inverted and the non-inverted conjoins with time; when one examines it in this way, none of these positions hold.
If you claim that it exists, you must now answer: with what does this inversion conjoin?
Therefore, there is no one who conjoins with inversion.
For this reason, you incur the same fault as previously stated.
Furthermore, just as in the ultimate sense all entities lack intrinsic nature, this principle has already been explained to bring about understanding.
For this reason, as the verse of the treatise says:
"Since there is no arising and nothing yet to arise, how could there be perversion?"
"All inversions are entirely without arising; where, then, could inversion originate?
The commentary states:
This means that because the verse’s intent reveals the absence of arising, there are no inversions; thus, the reasons and other elements you have put forward are all fallacious.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Those who claim that permanence, bliss, self, and purity truly exist—
those [very] notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, when reversed, become inversions."
The commentary states:
This means that the notion of a permanent self (*ātman*) and so forth within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) should also be understood as a misconception (*viparyāsa*).
As the verse of the treatise says:
"If the self, permanence, bliss, and so forth, were non-existent,
then non-self, suffering, and impurity would necessarily be perceivable. Commentary:
This means that the self-nature of non-self and so forth can eliminate the inversion of self and so forth; because they exist in mutual dependence, even "non-self" does not become a non-entity.
Since there is no self, where could a self possibly exist?
Because this is an inverted view, it is like the case where, in the absence of a person, one would never give rise to the inverted perception of a person in a tree stump.
Thus, the fault regarding the causes and so forth is unavoidable.
By observing in this way that [notions] such as permanence and impermanence—whether inverted or non-inverted—are devoid of a cause.
Regarding their being causeless, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Because they lack a cause, ignorance and volitional formations cease."
"Up to birth, old age, and death—all these are likewise extinguished.
The commentary states:

This means that because ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) lack inverted causes, one realizes their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are stilled, and the meaning [of liberation] is established.
Regarding those who assert that things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): as for these various afflictions, do they have a real entity or do they lack a real entity?
What is it that you are now asking?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If a person's various afflictions Possess a single intrinsic essence,
How could they ever be severed?"
"Who can sever that which has intrinsic nature?
The commentary states:
This means that that which possesses intrinsic nature cannot be destroyed.
If the various afflictions were unreal, like the horns of a rabbit, they would also be subject to the fault stated in this verse:
how could they not be abandoned?
This is because that which does not exist cannot be discarded; just as a flower in the sky cannot be discarded because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as a horse has no body, one cannot be made to abandon this non-existence.
Furthermore, if one holds the view that there are actual afflictions which can be severed when the Noble Path arises:
Regarding the claim that this explanation is faultless: what kind of appearance do these actual afflictions have such that the path of antidote arises and is able to sever them?
Your proposed thesis is difficult for others to understand.
For this reason, it is not the case that one can eliminate the conceptual discrimination of afflictions regarding whether they possess substantial reality or lack it. To establish a proof for this:

in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), afflictions have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they are subject to cessation. For example, when an illusory woman is conjured, although she is a mere magical creation, ordinary people give rise to a mind of defiled desire; later, upon realizing she is not real, their defiled mind naturally subsides.
The lack of substantial reality in the afflictions is likewise so.

Herein, having already explained the faults in the proofs established by the opponent and demonstrated that my own established proofs are without fault, the intended meaning of this chapter is to cause an understanding that [afflictions] are inverted and lack intrinsic nature.
For this reason, the following passage cites a sutra to demonstrate and establish this point.
As a verse in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (The Golden Light Sutra) states: "Speech is not form; it does not exist anywhere, because it is ultimately non-existent."

Afflictions are also like this: just as speech has no substantial reality and does not abide either internally or externally, the essence of afflictions lacks substantial reality and likewise does not abide internally or externally.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If one understands that defilement is itself the meaning of reality as it is (yathābhūta), not a single defiled inversion can be found.
If the defilements that sentient beings give rise to have no reality, they are themselves inversions.”
If that inversion is without reality, it is because within it there is no mark of true reality. Śāriputra,
one who understands in this way is said to be pure, for afflictions have no substantial entity.

When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he taught that the afflictions are neither form nor formless; they are neither feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor are they the absence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they are neither non-consciousness nor the absence of non-consciousness, because they cannot be seen and cannot be grasped.

The one who understands has nothing to be severed or eliminated; at the time of realization, there is likewise nothing to be attained. It is not by means of realization, nor by means of attainment; there is neither realization nor attainment, neither marks nor unconditioned phenomena—these are merely provisional names, like illusions and transformations.

Regarding all phenomena, their unchanging nature is neither grasped nor not grasped; they are like shadows and echoes, free from characteristics and free from conceptualization, without arising and without ceasing.
**Commentary on the Examination of the Noble Truths, Chapter Twenty-Four of the Prajñāpradīpa:** The commentary states:
This chapter is also taught in order to negate the objects of negation of emptiness and to cause an understanding that the Four Noble Truths lack intrinsic nature.
The proponents of our own school say:
"If it is claimed that the Noble Truths are empty and lack intrinsic nature, this is not the case.
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:"
"If all phenomena are empty, There is neither arising nor ceasing;
To say that the Noble Truths lack intrinsic nature Brings you such a fault.
The commentary states:
As for the claim that the principles he has set forth cause beings to attain faith and understanding, this is not the case; because they are empty, they are like flowers in the sky.
For this reason, he incurs this fault.
Because arising and ceasing lack intrinsic nature, the essence of the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) is non-existent.
Because the Truth of Suffering lacks intrinsic nature, that which can give rise to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) also lacks intrinsic nature.
Because the Truth of Origination lacks intrinsic nature, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) likewise lacks intrinsic nature.

Because the truth of cessation has no intrinsic nature, the path leading to the cessation of suffering—namely, the truth of the path cultivated with right view as its primary element—is likewise without intrinsic nature.
As stated in the verse above, that [position] incurs this fault.

For this reason, those sentient beings who fear birth and death should diligently apply themselves with vigor toward the realm of the Four Noble Truths: suffering is to be known, its origin is to be abandoned, its cessation is to be realized, and the path is to be cultivated.
None of these exist.
How do they not exist?
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"Whether it be knowing or abandoning, The practices, realizations, activities, and so forth—
Because the Noble Truths lack intrinsic nature, None of these are to be found.
Commentary:
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: they are called "Noble Truths" because they constitute the continuous essence of the noble ones.
Furthermore, "truth" (satya) signifies the meaning of reality.
If one says that they do not exist, this meaning is not tenable.
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"Because the Noble Truths lack intrinsic nature, the four fruits likewise do not exist."
"Because the fruit has no intrinsic nature, those who abide in the fruit likewise do not exist. Commentary:

This means that the various faults—such as the view of a self, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—serve as the fuel, while the Noble Truths serve as the fire. For the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, the fire of the vision of the Noble Truths is able to burn away the afflictions (*kleśa*).
One who abides in the fruit refers to one who has attained the path of *srotāpanna*.
The fruit of *srotāpanna* is also called "not being subject to the conjunction of other conditions," because no celestial Māras can destroy it.

Furthermore, because they are in harmony with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are called the Saṃgha; this Saṃgha is known as the unsurpassed field of merit.
If that [Saṃgha] did not exist, its meaning would not be so.
Therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"If the Jewel of the Saṃgha did not exist, then the eight types of persons would not exist."
"If the Noble Truths have no essence, there would likewise be no Jewel of the Dharma. Commentary:
If the Jewel of the Sangha did not exist, there would be no distinction between the four paths and the four fruits.
Furthermore, because the Jewel of the Sangha does not exist, the Jewel of the Dharma also does not exist.
Because the Jewel of the Dharma does not exist, the Jewel of the Buddha likewise does not exist.
Thus, a verse in the treatise says:
"If there were no Dharma and Sangha, how could there be the Buddha Jewel?
If the Three Jewels are all empty, then all existence is destroyed. Commentary:
A Buddha is one who has personally awakened to the noble truths and is further able to awaken others; therefore, he is called a Buddha.
Why is he a treasure?
Because he is difficult to encounter.

As a verse in the Sūtra says: "That which should be understood has been understood by me; that which should be cultivated has been cultivated by me; that which should be abandoned has been abandoned by me; for this reason, I am called a Buddha.
This means that because one has attained equal awakening regarding all phenomena that possess intrinsic nature, one is therefore called a Buddha.

As stated in a verse within a Sūtra: "In phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, one awakens to them exhaustively and without remainder; through awakening to the equality of all dharmas, one is therefore called a Buddha."
This refers to the realm realized by all Buddhas; it is not the case that they lack intrinsic nature.
As stated in the verse above: "If the Three Jewels were all empty, then all existence would be destroyed."
This position contains a fault; therefore, the verse of the treatise says:
"If the essence of cause and effect were empty, Then dharma and adharma would also be empty;
Worldly conventions and the like— All such things would be utterly destroyed."
The commentary states:
This refers to one who makes such a statement while not wishing to incur a fault.
How can this fault be avoided?
If one does not establish emptiness and instead asserts that all entities possess intrinsic nature (svabhāva) through their arising and ceasing, then such a position would be free from fault.
To prove this point: all entities possess intrinsic nature, because they undergo arising and ceasing.
If it is said that all entities lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then their arising and ceasing should not be perceived, just like flowers in the sky.
The proponent of the treatise says:
The meanings of what you have cited are in every way incorrect.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"You yourself do not understand emptiness and the meaning of emptiness, which can extinguish all conceptual proliferation; yet you wish to refute emptiness?"
The commentary states:
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is so named because it can extinguish all attachments and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
As for the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatārtha*), it refers to the wisdom that takes emptiness as its object; this is called the meaning of emptiness.

If you now wish to destroy the true nature of reality, it is like a person extending their fist to strike at empty space; you will only exhaust yourself in vain, for in the end, nothing will be damaged.
If you should say as the preceding verse states: "If all phenomena are empty, there is neither arising nor ceasing."
Since you speak in this manner, you too are merely exhausting yourself without understanding the meaning within.
Why is this? As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"The Buddhas rely upon two truths To teach the Dharma to sentient beings:
The first is called conventional truth, The second is called ultimate truth. Commentary:

Conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to worldly discourse, such as speaking of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing of form and so forth; or speaking of Devadatta going and coming, Viśvantara eating, Sumati practicing meditation, or Brahmāda being liberated. Such instances are called worldly discourse and are termed conventional truth; these are not said to be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
It is called the ultimate truth because it is the foremost and possesses meaning.
Furthermore, it is called the ultimate truth because it is the true object of the supreme non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Reality is characterized by being devoid of other conditions and so forth.
Non-conceptual wisdom that abides in the objective sphere of this reality is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

In order to preclude [the notions of] arising and so forth, the non-arising and so forth that accord with what has been taught, as well as the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, are all the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What, then, is this wisdom?

This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for it serves as the causal condition for the skillful means that effect the non-perverted [realization] of the supreme; therefore, it is further named the ultimate truth.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If a person cannot understand The distinct characteristics of the two truths..."
"One does not understand the true reality, the meaning of the profound Dharma of the Buddha.
The commentary states:

This means that if a person does not understand the distinction between the two truths (*satyadvaya*), is confused regarding the characteristics of objects (*viṣayalakṣaṇa*), and possesses much improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), such a person does not understand the profound Dharma of the Buddha, and gives rise to the conceptualization of grasping at existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-abhiniveśabuddhi*).
What is meant by "profound"?
It is difficult to traverse and cross over.
As for the Buddha, he has already been explained as before.
The Dharma is for the purpose of enabling devas and humans to realize the nectar-like Dharma.
Regarding such profound realms as these, the practitioner should know them, abandon them, realize them, and cultivate them.
Furthermore, that which is called the teaching free from inversion is termed the "Nectar Dharma.

Because such persons do not understand the principle of the foremost, profound, non-conceptual wisdom, although they practice without inversion and abide within the realm of the true Dharma, they speak of sentient beings regarding the essence of phenomena—which is neither arising nor ceasing—and they give rise to the view of a "realm" where no realm exists.

Those who speak in this manner do not understand the principles of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. To claim that, within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all phenomena such as arising and ceasing are entirely non-existent, and to engage in such conceptualization, incurs the same fault as stated in the verse above: "If all phenomena are empty, there is neither arising nor ceasing."

Those who harbor such discriminations do not understand that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in accordance with conventional truth, speak of the existence of the essence of various dharmas—such as the observance of precepts, the cultivation of meditative concentration, and arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Ignorant people claim that such things also exist within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); those who engage in such false conceptualizations fall into the wilderness of the various realms of existence (*bhava*) from which there is no time of escape.
The proponent of our own school says:
"If liberation were attained through the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), then one should not proclaim the two truths.
The respondent says:
For this reason, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If one does not rely on conventional truth, one cannot attain the ultimate truth;
if one does not rely on the ultimate truth, one will never attain nirvana."
The commentary states:
Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all phenomena are by nature unborn and empty.
Yet, because sentient beings are subject to inversion, they give rise to false attachments; thus, [these phenomena] are considered real within the world.

Because the various noble ones have thoroughly realized the nature of inversion in the world, they know that all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature; for these noble ones, this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and it is also called "real."
The Buddha teaches for the sake of sentient beings by means of the two truths.
What is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
It is that which universally transcends all paths of verbal expression.
This is because it causes one to abandon all causes of conceptualization as distinguished by all the Hīnayāna schools.

Furthermore, if there were no conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one could not realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); for this reason, the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth is the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
If one does not rely on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the path to nirvāṇa can never be attained.
Furthermore, among the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), those who are clever and arrogant may make such distinctions as:
"there is emptiness" and "there is non-emptiness."
What is emptiness?
It refers to seeing that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are empty, because those views of grasping have no substantial essence.
What is non-emptiness?
This means that one perceives the aggregates (*skandhas*) as not empty, yet says, "I have seen the self.
Now, one sees the self and should see that these aggregates are empty; there is no emptiness apart from the aggregates.
Within emptiness one sees the aggregates, and within the aggregates one sees emptiness.
To hold such a view is improper reflection; it is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
As a verse in the treatise says:
"The person of little wisdom and delusion Destroys emptiness with evil views."
"It is like improperly grasping a snake, or not maintaining the mantra according to the Dharma.
The commentary states:
This means that because it creates obstacles for the life-force of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), such [persons] are destroyed by evil views.

Furthermore, to give rise to the view that things possess substantiality where there is no substantiality is also called "destroying emptiness. This is like a person who does not handle a snake skillfully and brings about his own death.
One who clings to substantiality within emptiness can likewise destroy the life of liberation, just as a mantra-practitioner harms himself by failing to rely on the ritual methods of the mantra.
For this reason, those who do not properly understand emptiness can perform various kinds of unbeneficial actions.
As a verse in the treatise says:
"For this reason, the Buddhas turned their minds away and did not preach the Dharma."
The profound Dharma realized by the Buddha is something sentient beings cannot enter.
If you now act in this way, you will slander emptiness,
claiming that dharmas neither arise nor cease, and even go so far as to destroy the Triple Gem.
The commentary states:
As for "denigrating," it refers to saying that all things are empty.
If you, out of anger and resentment, wish to find fault with emptiness, emptiness will ultimately not be subject to your fault.
Why is this? Because all entities lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are empty and thus without entity from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As for the meaning of "without entity," I do not even accept it, because it involves the characteristic of clinging.

Furthermore, in order to refute the emptiness as conceptualized by those of our own school, we now negate this very emptiness; thus, while stating that [phenomena] are empty and lack intrinsic nature, we do not cling to emptiness either.
One who makes such conceptual distinctions regarding emptiness must now abandon them.
As stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness through the arrogance of overestimation."
For this reason, one does not perceive form as empty, nor does one perceive form as non-empty.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If that which is empty were thus, then everything would be thus."
"If it were not so with emptiness, then nothing would be so.
The commentary states:
This asks, for one who correctly perceives emptiness, what is meant by "everything being so"?
This refers to arising and so forth.

How is this so? It means that existence, non-existence, and so on, as well as the eye and other faculties, are all empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), just as a magical man (*māyā-puruṣa*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of a man.
Why is this? Because all things have as their essence the gathering together of various conditions.
What constitutes this essence?
"Entity" refers to suffering.
What is suffering? That which arises is called suffering.
The contemplation of suffering and so forth is called the Truth of Suffering.
What is the Origin? That which gives rise to the causes of suffering is called the Origin.
Furthermore, as for "origination" (*samudaya*): it is called origination because suffering arises from this.
When one perceives the aspects of origination and so forth, it is termed the Truth of Origination.
That which extinguishes the cause of suffering is termed cessation (*nirodha*).
The contemplation of the aspects such as cessation is called the Truth of Cessation.
The means for attaining the cause of the cessation of suffering is called the Path.
If one contemplates the aspects such as the path, it is called the Truth of the Path.
Because those Noble Truths exist in this way, their dharma is established.
One who awakens to all conditioned phenomena through self-arisen wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna) is therefore called a Buddha.
Regarding the teaching that accords with the Śrāvakas, as it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Regarding such suffering, in the past I did not hear that within all phenomena there arises the eye, the wisdom, the clarity, and the awakening; for the intrinsic nature of these various entities is entirely like an illusion."
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), seeing that there is no arising and so forth is called seeing the Noble Truths. As stated in the *Mañjuśrī-caryā-pratipadā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
'If one sees that all phenomena are without arising, one understands the Truth of Suffering.'"
If one sees that all phenomena are without abiding, one is able to sever the origin [of suffering].
If one sees that all phenomena are ultimately nirvana, one is able to realize cessation.
“Mañjuśrī! To see that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is itself the cultivation of the path.
For this reason, the principle of the Noble Truths is established within the Mahāyāna.
Because the principle is established, wisdom is established.
Because wisdom is established, everything is possible.
If one slanders emptiness, as the verse above states: "If emptiness were not possible, then nothing would be possible."
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Do you now wish to transfer your own faults to me?
It is like a person riding a horse who has forgotten the very mount he is upon."
The commentary states:
If you do not wish for emptiness to incur these faults, they shall now be explained.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If you see all phenomena as having intrinsic natures,
then since those natures would lack causes and conditions, you would instead fall into the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva-dṛṣṭi*). Explanation:

If one perceives that all entities possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then there would be no entities arising from causes and conditions, because they would possess their own nature independently of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, if one perceives that all entities possess an intrinsic nature, the following fault shall now be stated.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If cause and effect were independent, then the agent and the action,
as well as arising, ceasing, and so forth— all phenomena would be destroyed."
The commentary states:
This means that for one who does not depend upon causes and conditions, the principles of cause, effect, and so forth are all unestablished.
How can you thus give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the meaning of emptiness?
For example, when a small child sees a painted yakṣa, fear arises in him and he lets out a loud cry.
If form and the other aggregates were empty and lacked intrinsic nature, they would be like flowers in the sky.
For one who makes such a distinction, there should be no fear regarding this.
For this reason, as the verse of the treatise says:
"Phenomena arising from a multitude of conditions—I declare them to be emptiness."
"It is merely a provisional name, and it is also the meaning of the Middle Way.
The commentary states:

Regarding the fact that the entities of the eye and so forth arise from conditions, within those various conditions, the eye and so forth are neither existent nor non-existent; neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent; neither different nor identical; neither self nor other; and neither both nor neither.

All things that arise from conditions have no arising by way of their own-being (*svabhāva*) in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*); it is only in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) that the arising of the eye and so forth exists.
When I say that this arising is empty, I mean that it is empty of own-being.
As a verse in the Sūtra says: "That which arises from conditions is not called 'arising,' for the nature of arising has no intrinsic essence.
That which depends upon conditions is precisely what is termed 'emptiness.
Both the mundane and the supramundane are merely provisional designations."
"Those who understand emptiness are called heedful.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that the self-nature is unarisen:
regarding this unarisen nature, as the Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I teach that all phenomena are empty.
If one says they arise from conditions, this too is merely another name for emptiness. Why is this so?"
"Because they are established through designation,
both mundane and supramundane dharmas are products of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Such designation by name is itself the Middle Way, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"What is called the Middle Way?
It is so named because it is free from the extremes of arising and non-arising, as well as existence and non-existence. That is to say:
all entities are neither arising nor non-arising; they are neither existent nor non-existent; neither eternal nor non-eternal; neither empty nor non-empty."

When one who practices the Middle Way observes, they do not perceive the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor do they perceive it as lacking an intrinsic nature; likewise, up to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they do not perceive them as having an intrinsic nature, nor do they perceive them as lacking an intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Existence is one extreme; non-existence is another extreme. Apart from these two, in the middle, there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Thus, this Middle Way is called the skillful means for realizing the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
For this reason, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"There has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions."
"In this way, all phenomena are none other than empty. Commentary:
This means that things arising from conditions—such as, for example, a person created by magic—ultimately lack any intrinsic nature.
The Sāṃkhya says:

"If [you argue that] things produced from conditions serve as the reason for excluding [others], such as space and so forth which are not produced from conditions, then this meaning is not established within one part of your own school; this is a fault in your probans (*hetu*)."
The proponent says:
The faults of space have already been explained as before.
As for the great transgression, it now gathers upon your person and is difficult to evade.
What is the fault?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If all things were not empty, There would be neither arising nor ceasing."
"The substance of the Four Noble Truths does not exist; the fault remains with you.
The commentary asks:
What is the meaning of this?
If suffering were not empty and possessed an intrinsic nature, then there would be no agent.
Because there would be no agent, it would not arise from conditions.
To maintain that it exists [with such a nature] is not even accepted within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), let alone in the ultimate sense (paramārtha).
For this reason, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If it does not arise from conditions, Where could suffering possibly exist?
The meaning of impermanence is suffering; That suffering has no intrinsic nature."
The commentary states:
This means that if something were not produced from causes and conditions, it would be eternal; and what is eternal is not suffering.
The Sautrāntikas say:
If that which is impermanent is suffering, and that which is suffering is non-self, then that which is non-self lacks intrinsic nature.
For this reason, suffering lacks intrinsic nature.
The proponent says:
What you have stated is logically inconsistent.
As it is said in a verse of the treatise:
"If suffering has no intrinsic nature, where could there be an origin?
Since the origin does not exist, this would then refute emptiness. Commentary:
This means that the essence of suffering does not arise.
Why? Because if it possessed an intrinsic nature, it would exist without depending on causes and conditions.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If suffering possessed a fixed intrinsic nature, Which was previously unperceived,
how could it be perceived now?"
"Because its nature does not differ.
The commentary states:
If one did not previously perceive the nature of suffering, then one should likewise not perceive it at the time of attaining the fruit of sainthood.
Why is this? If intrinsic nature were fixed, how could it be perceived?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If suffering had an intrinsic nature, it could not have the quality of cessation;
since you cling to its having an intrinsic nature, you thereby negate the very essence of cessation.
If suffering had a fixed nature, there would be no cultivation of the Path."
"If the Path were something that could be cultivated, it would have no fixed nature.

Commentary: This means that if there were an essence of cessation, there would likewise be an essence of suffering. How then could a cultivator be said to "cultivate" by repeatedly giving rise to right view and so forth? Thus it is called cultivation.
If the essence of this path were already established prior to its arising, then for it to arise would be impossible.
If one wishes to avoid such faults and maintain that the path can be cultivated, as the verse of the treatise says:
"If the path is something to be cultivated, Then it possesses no intrinsic nature."
"Suffering, its origin, and even its cessation—these are all entirely non-existent.
Commentary: This means that even if the sense of the arising of the Path were established, it would still not be apart from the absence of intrinsic nature.
For this reason, according to the principle stated in the verse above, there is no one who gives rise to suffering; since suffering does not exist, its cessation likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
If one asks what the path for the cessation of suffering is, as the treatise’s verse says:
“The path for the sake of ceasing suffering— what path can be found?”
"One does not understand the intrinsic nature of suffering, nor does one understand the cause of suffering.
The commentary states:

This means that according to the logic you have presented, if suffering possesses an intrinsic nature, then that which possesses an intrinsic nature cannot be understood; furthermore, there is the fault that the cause of suffering cannot be understood, and thus the meaning of cessation is not established.
Because the substance of the cause of non-interruption exists, cessation itself lacks substance.
If the substance of craving were inexhaustible, the meaning of exhaustion could not be established; thus, "extinction" would be a name for non-substance.
Because it is non-substantial, the meaning of realizing extinction cannot be established.
If there were a self-essence in the path that leads to the realization and attainment of cessation, then there would be no cultivation.
If there is no path of cultivation, then there would likewise be no one who realizes the four fruits of spiritual attainment.
If one wishes to have a person who has realized the fruit [of the path], yet clings to the view that there is a self-essence and does not relinquish it, I now ask:
why does one not relinquish it? If the fruit to be realized possessed a self-essence, how could one further speak of a person capable of realizing it?
For this reason, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"Since the intrinsic nature of the fruit does not exist, Neither those abiding in the fruit nor those progressing toward it exist;
Because the eight types of noble persons do not exist, The Jewel of the Sangha does not exist."
The commentary states:
"The eight persons" refers to the four paths and four fruits, as there are distinctions among persons.
What is meant by "persons"?
This refers to those who are superior among humans, such as the "great person" (puruṣa) and so forth.
If the Four Noble Truths lacked intrinsic nature, it would not only mean that the Saṅgha does not exist; as the verse of the treatise says:
"If the Four Noble Truths do not exist, There is likewise no Jewel of the Dharma."
"Since there is no Dharma or Saṃgha, how could there be a Buddha?
The commentary states:
A Buddha is so called because he is able to awaken his disciples through the Dharma; therefore, [if these do not exist], how could there be a Buddha?

Furthermore, we now ask those who maintain that things possess intrinsic nature (svabhāva): Is the Buddha, the Blessed One (Bhagavān), possessed of intrinsic nature, or is he without intrinsic nature?
It is asked:
What fault is there in this question?
The answer is:
If you wish to maintain that a Buddha possesses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then one would not be called a Buddha by virtue of realizing suchness (tathatā).
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If awakening were not the condition for the Buddha, the Buddha would fall into the error of being unconditioned;
if the Buddha were not the condition for awakening, awakening would fall into the error of being unconditioned."
If the Buddha possessed a self-essence, then the bodhisattvas who practice and exert diligent effort for the sake of Buddhahood would not be able to attain it.
Since there is no person capable of creating these dharmas or non-dharmas, [the Buddha cannot possess a self-essence].
"If it is non-empty, why must it act?
If it possesses an intrinsic nature, its acting is not possible. Commentary:
This means that it is not tenable for a phenomenon that possesses intrinsic nature to arise as an agent.
Furthermore, your intention—that it neither enlarges the small to make it large nor dispels darkness to make it light—has already been addressed with the aforementioned refutation.
The proponent of our own school says:
"In what way do all agents lack intrinsic nature?
The respondent says:

In every case, the agent is seen to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like the things produced by an illusion; the same applies to the activity of the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth.

Furthermore, these internal sense-bases themselves lack intrinsic nature. If there were any entity possessing intrinsic nature, it would contradict the previous principle; this is because there is no such thing as an entity that is produced.
You maintain that there is the meaning of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if such a nature exists, you should explain it clearly to me.
If you say that there is both activity and an intrinsic nature, what kind of thing is it like?
Therefore, what you have stated is entirely a false view.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If there is no cause consisting of either dharma or adharma, The result would incur the fallacy of being causeless."
"If one is apart from both dharma and adharma, you would obtain a result that is independent.
Commentary: If your intention is to avoid contradicting worldly discourse and you speak thus because you wish to maintain the existence of dharma and adharma, it is as the verse of the treatise says:
"If you wish for there to exist dharma and non-dharma, as well as their causes and effects,
which arise from dharma and non-dharma— how could these not be empty?
Commentary:
This means that because whatever arises is empty, it is like a magical illusion;
not only does this contradict your own school's tenets, but there are further faults as well.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"All matters expressed through speech are undermined by the world;
if the principle of dependent origination is destroyed, the meaning of emptiness cannot be established."
The commentary states:
"Speech" refers to making such utterances as "make a jar," "make a garment," or Devadatta saying, "Bring the white ox; I wish to drink its milk."
If things such as jars possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would not require an agent;

this is not the case. If one does not accept that they arise from conditions, then as stated in the verse above: "If the principle of dependent origination is destroyed, the meaning of emptiness cannot be established."
"What fault do you incur by subverting the meaning of emptiness?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
'Not even a single thing need be produced, nor does anyone initiate activity.'"
If that which does not act is called an agent, then the meaning of emptiness is destroyed.
There is neither arising nor ceasing; this is what is called "permanence.
All various categories of things would then abide in their own intrinsic nature.
The commentary states:
What is meant by "categories of things"?
For example, on a painted wall there are various colors, various shapes, various natures, various dimensions, and so forth, each with its own distinctions.
What is meant by "abiding in its own nature"?
It means that being without an agent is called abiding in its own nature; because it is indestructible, it is termed "permanent.
Regarding this permanence, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"What has not yet been attained should be attained, and the task of reaching the end of suffering should be completed;
all afflictions are severed because of the meaning of emptiness.
The commentary states:
This means that for those who have realized the supreme dharma—both mundane and supramundane—and who have reached the end of suffering, there is no need to cultivate remedial dharmas (*pratipakṣa*).

One does not desire the characteristics described [by others]; rather, one desires to realize the dharma of dependent origination as being like a magical illusion or a mirage, lacking any intrinsic arising, because [intrinsic existence] entails faults such as the existence or non-existence of a self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Those whose eye of wisdom is obscured falsely perceive that all phenomena do not arise from conditions; this perception is a conventional (saṃvṛti) view, yet they falsely cling to it as the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
What is this view?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"What are called suffering and its origin, And even up to cessation and the path?
To see that there is arising and ceasing— Such a view is called not seeing."
The commentary states:
Why is it that they do not see?
It is because they do not see the dharma of dependent origination as it truly is.
The proponents of our own school say:
"Apart from the various formations such as the vision of suffering, there is no separate dharma of seeing the truths.
The proponent of the treatise says:
What is the meaning of "one who has seen the truths" (*dṛṣṭasatya*)?
A member of our own school says:
it means that one sees the internal sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because this is non-erroneous (*aviparīta*).
The proponent says:
The reasoning you have presented regarding arising and so forth has already been refuted previously.
As for the claim that "seeing that suffering and the other truths are without arising is the meaning of seeing the truths"—this which you have just stated may indeed be established.
To claim that one perceives the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) without error is a distortion of speech;
the meaning you intend is not established.
You should examine this closely: in what way do you perceive suffering?
This is not like a child asking his mother for a *modaka* (joy-pill) and pointing at his hand while saying he has received it.

The purpose of this chapter is to refute the errors asserted by our own school regarding the antidote to emptiness, to clarify that the Noble Truths lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thereby to lead beings to faith and understanding; such is the intended meaning of this chapter.
For this reason, what follows cites a sutra to demonstrate and establish this point.
As stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Brahmā:
"By means of this gate, one should know that suffering is not a noble truth; one should know that origin, cessation, and the path are likewise not noble truths."
Furthermore, what are the noble truths?
O Brahmā King!
If suffering does not arise, this is called a noble truth; if the origin cannot arise, this is called a noble truth.
To see that all phenomena are ultimately like nirvana, without arising or ceasing—this is called a noble truth.
To know that all phenomena are equal and non-dual while practicing the Path—this is called a noble truth.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If one perceives the dharma of causes and conditions, that person can see the Buddha, perceive the Noble Truths, attain the fruits of the noble ones, and extinguish all afflictions."
The commentary on the "Examination of the Noble Truths" (Āryasatyaparīkṣā) is concluded.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 14. *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 15.
Verses by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; Commentary by Bodhisattva Bhāviveka.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñāmitra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Five: Examination of Nirvāṇa. Explanation: Chapter Twenty-Five: Examination of Nirvāṇa. The commentary states:
This present chapter is also taught in order to refute that which is the counter-position to emptiness, so as to lead to the understanding that nirvāṇa has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"That which was previously stated—that if all things were not empty, there would be neither arising nor ceasing—refers to the meaning of having no intrinsic nature."
That which lacks intrinsic nature, such as the son of a barren woman, has neither arising nor ceasing.
Because afflictions lack intrinsic nature, they do not arise or cease.

Furthermore, the causes of afflictions and name-and-form likewise do not arise or cease, as stated in the verse above: "If there is no severing of suffering and no realization of cessation, who then attains nirvana?"
Regarding that which he previously stated: "I now desire to attain what is to be severed, thereby realizing nirvāṇa.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Defilement and the defiled one arise together as afflictions."
Because this [defilement] is completely extinguished, it is called nirvāṇa.
Such nirvāṇa is the liberation of the mind, like the extinction of a lamp.
Those who attain nirvāṇa do so because afflictions possess intrinsic nature.
As stated above regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if there were no essence to afflictions, there would likewise be no nirvāṇa, just like the son of a barren woman.

Furthermore, if one uses the absence of intrinsic nature as a proof that no one attains nirvāṇa, this also subverts the meaning of attaining nirvāṇa; it is thus a fault in the thesis and the reason [adduced] for establishing that specific dharma-essence.
The proponent says:
Your statement is incorrect.
That all phenomena lack intrinsic nature is like the extinguishing of a magical lamp; this does not contradict the sphere of conventional worldly knowledge.
That which lacks intrinsic nature arises through the successive progression of beginningless causes and conditions, like a magical illusion or a mirage.
The non-arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*.
The realization of nirvāṇa is likewise thus: it possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since I do not establish a "nature" that is non-existent, there is no fault in my thesis.
As for the example of the barren woman cited above, it is established within the context of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If you maintain that things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then because such a nature is indestructible, it is impossible for anything to be abandoned.
Therefore, if one speaks of an intrinsic nature without perceiving the true principle, the attainment of nirvāṇa cannot be established, for the intrinsic nature of phenomena would be undermined.
How is this so? Because the three factors you previously presented—the reason (*hetu*), the thesis (*pratijñā*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are all unestablished, they are fallacious.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika says:
As that verse says: "If all things were not empty, there would be no arising or ceasing;
there would be no cessation of suffering or realization of extinction—then who could attain nirvana? This is not so.
I now maintain that nirvāṇa exists.
What is this nirvāṇa?

It means that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because one attains nirvāṇa by severing all afflictions (*kleśa*) and extinguishing name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is not like the horns of a camel.
Nirvāṇa is not like that, because it possesses an essence, cessation, extinction, and attainment.
The commentator says:
As stated in the preceding verse, "If all things were not empty, there would be neither arising nor ceasing."

Regarding the question, "If there is no severance of suffering and no realization of cessation, how can one attain nirvāṇa?"—this refers to the fact that if there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would be indestructible.

If this intrinsic nature were to exist, then for our own school’s position, if the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) established were similar [to the thesis], then the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) would possess efficacy.
Now, because you lack this power, both the meaning of your reason and your example are unestablished; furthermore, they contradict the thesis you previously established.
I now ask you: is the nirvāṇa you have established the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)?
Is this the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
If you wish to attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), I shall now answer you.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
“Without falling away and without attainment, Neither annihilated nor eternal,
Neither arising nor ceasing— This is taught as nirvāṇa. Commentary:
This means that such a nirvāṇa is what I seek to attain.

As for your statement—that it is because of abandonment and cessation that it serves as the cause for emergence, and that one attains nirvāṇa by abandoning all afflictions—all these causal meanings are now untenable. Because of a perverted mind, you have made such assertions; in meaning, they are all incorrect.
Furthermore, among those who maintain that nirvāṇa exists, some say that nirvāṇa is a real dharma, while others say that nirvāṇa is a conventional designation (prajñapti-dharma).
Neither of these two positions is correct.
For this reason, one must next conduct an investigation.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If nirvāṇa possessed a self-nature, it would fall under the characteristics of aging and death."
"If nirvāṇa were an entity, it would be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The commentary states:
This means that if nirvāṇa possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be no proof by which it could be made intelligible or accepted through faith.
If one were to grant that nirvāṇa has an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it would fall into the characteristics of aging and death. Why?
Because there is no intrinsic nature that is separate from the characteristics of aging and death, nor are the characteristics of aging and death separate from an intrinsic nature.

Those of the Hīnayāna do not desire a nirvāṇa that possesses the characteristics of old age and death. For this reason, as I have established through proof: in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), nirvāṇa is not a substantial entity, because it lacks the characteristics of old age and death; it is, for example, like the son of a barren woman.
Therefore, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) in your thesis is unestablished.
Because the reason is unestablished, it also contradicts the correct meaning.
Furthermore, we shall now present another fault.

If you do not accept that nirvāṇa is conditioned, yet wish to maintain that nirvāṇa is unconditioned, this is not so; for there is no place where a single entity can possess both substantiality and the quality of being unconditioned.
Now, an argument shall be established: Nirvana is not an entity because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), like a flower in the sky.
Furthermore, its faults will be further explained, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If Nirvana were an entity, How could it be without a cause?"
"Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that can exist apart from a cause.
The commentary states:
This means that all entities (bhāva) are established by depending upon causes; Nirvana is an entity and cannot be without a cause.
For this reason, a proof is established herein: nirvana is not an entity, because it cannot be designated by means of a cause, just like a rabbit’s horn or a tamālapatra leaf.
Furthermore, the Sūtra-followers and others say that *tāmaravarta* means "copper-colored leaf" in the language of Tang;
as the Vibhāṣā masters state, nirvāṇa is like the extinguishing of a lamp.

When I now speak of nirvāṇa, it is merely the absence of arising; because it is provisionally established within the context of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the meaning of what I have posited is consistent with reason.
The proponent says:
To answer this now, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If your nirvāṇa is not an entity, how can it be a non-entity?"
"If nirvāṇa has no substance, how can it be causeless?
The commentary states:
The Vibhāṣā and other treatises distinguish nirvāṇa as the ultimate good (paramārtha-kuśala), taking the cessation of afflictions as its cause.
Now, since your thesis does not possess such a nature, when you claim that nirvana is without nature, do you mean it lacks goodness and so forth?
Neither interpretation is tenable; it is like a flower in the sky.
If you claim that nirvana is without reality and lacks intrinsic nature, there is no such evidence capable of bringing about understanding.
As for your assertion that nirvana is not without substance, it is difficult for others to comprehend.

Furthermore, the Vibhāṣā distinguishes that nirvāṇa has an existent nature prior to [attainment] and a non-existent nature thereafter; its use of the lamp as an analogy is intended to demonstrate what is understood by the world, namely that while the lamp exists before it is extinguished, it is non-existent once extinguished.
If you maintain that it lacks intrinsic nature, just like a lamp that has already been extinguished, as stated in the preceding verse: "If nirvāṇa lacks intrinsic nature, how could it be causeless?"
This means that just as a lamp exists without an intrinsic substance, yet is designated as a "lamp" based on its causal conditions,
so too do the aggregates and afflictions exist without an intrinsic substance, yet are designated as "nirvāṇa" based on their causal conditions.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Nirvāṇa is not non-existent, yet it does not depend on causes;
If it is without cause and without condition, This is what is called nirvāṇa."
The commentary states:

As you have said, nirvāṇa is without intrinsic nature and is the ultimate truth; for this reason, it is only through the presence of the characteristics of coming, going, and cyclic existence that saṃsāra is conventionally designated.
Whether Nirvana has an essence or lacks an essence is what is spoken of within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
As a verse in the treatise says:
"What the Great Teacher has taught Is the severing of existence and the severing of non-existence."
"Therefore, know that nirvāṇa is neither non-existent nor existent.
The commentary states:
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Some people seek to emerge from existence by means of existence, while others seek to emerge from existence without relying on existence; neither of these is correct.
If one says that Nirvana is a substantial entity, this is not so.
The Vātsīputrīyas say:
"The nirvāṇa we now establish is not the same as theirs; it possesses both the sense of being an entity and the sense of not being an entity.
Because these two senses exist, the aforementioned faults do not apply, and this principle is indeed correct."
The proponent says:
That which you have established is not logically tenable.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If you say that nirvāṇa is both an entity and a non-entity;
because nirvāṇa is an entity, it is not the case that the liberated one [is so].
Explanation:
This means that existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory.
If something is existence, it cannot be non-existence; if it is non-existence, it is not existence.
If they were dependent upon one another, then there would be the characteristics of both existence and non-existence.
To speak in this manner is inconsistent with the meaning.
Why? Because it entails the fault of conceptual discrimination and attachment.
The Vātsīputrīyas say:
Why is nirvāṇa not a substantial entity?
It is called "non-substantial" because the body and the various sense faculties lack substantiality.
What is its essence?
Because it possesses ultimate, unsurpassed bliss, it is called "the essence.
The commentator says:
This statement is incorrect.
Since the bodily faculties, as well as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, have already been refuted, the refutation of arising and so on is likewise established.
As for "ultimate unsurpassed bliss," just as the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) was refuted, that bliss is also refuted.

If you wish to cause sentient beings to understand by means of the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no such entity to serve as proof; thus, the thesis you have established is inconsistent.
Furthermore, if you claim that *nirvāṇa* possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as the verse in the treatise says:
"If you say that *nirvāṇa*, Both [it and saṃsāra] possess an intrinsic nature;..."
"Nirvāṇa is unconditioned; the two bodies are conditioned.
The commentary asks:
What meaning does this verse reveal?
This means it is shown that there is no characteristic of nirvāṇa existing separately outside of existence and non-existence.
It is not the case that if a phenomenon has a characteristic distinct from another phenomenon yet constitutes the essence of that phenomenon; for example, like water and fire.
Thus, it is not the case that the characteristics of nirvāṇa consist of being an entity or a non-entity.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntikas say:
because nirvāṇa is neither an entity nor a non-entity, it cannot be described as either.
As for the previous statement that there would be the fault of having two entities and being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), that is not so.
The proponent says:
"Nor is such a thing the case."
Now, in response to this statement, as it is said in a verse of the treatise:
"If you say that nirvāṇa Is neither an entity nor a non-entity;
If both 'entity' and 'non-entity' were established, Then their two negations would also be established."
The commentary states:
This means that just as with light and darkness— wherein because light exists, darkness can be spoken of— likewise,
because existence and non-existence exist, that which is neither existence nor non-existence is established.
Furthermore, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If that which is neither an entity nor a non-entity were nirvāṇa,
By what dharma could these two absences of entity be cognized?"
The commentary states:
This means that if one says it is apprehended by cognition, such cognition has already been refuted.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, one does not say 'it exists' nor 'it does not exist,' nor does one say 'it both exists and does not exist,' nor 'it neither exists nor does not exist.
While the Tathāgata is present in the world, one likewise does not say 'it exists' nor 'it does not exist.'"
"Nor does it speak of existence or non-existence, nor of neither existence nor non-existence.
The commentary states:

This refers to [the Buddha's] not declaring whether there is a self within the body, whether the self and the body are one, whether the self and the body are different, whether there is a self apart from the body, or whether the body itself is the self. Since none of these were declared among the "unanswered questions," nirvāṇa is not established in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Thus, your proposed reason is also unestablished; the fault lies with you.
The Vaibhāṣikas further state:

Nirvāṇa exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), for those who fear saṃsāra exert diligent effort in order to seek it; nor do they exert diligent effort because they see that the seeker is obtaining a non-existent thing.
The proponent says:
According to our school, no person is seen to attain that nirvāṇa, because in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"The limit of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa Are not the slightest bit different;
The limit of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra Are likewise not the slightest bit different."
The commentary states:
This means that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally non-apprehendable, because neither of these two can be apprehended.

Furthermore, just as the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are unapprehendable; this has already been made understood through faith and realization.
Therefore, the claim you have made—that the cause for attaining nirvāṇa is the exertion of diligence—is logically untenable and contradicts the true meaning.
To clarify this through the relationship between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as the verse of the treatise says:
"The limit of saṃsāra is nirvāṇa; The limit of nirvāṇa is saṃsāra."
"Between these two, there is not even the slightest dharma.
The commentary states:

Nirvāṇa is an alternative name for True Suchness (tathatā), the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and emptiness (śūnyatā). Because True Suchness has no differentiation, it is like space: although there are distinctions of direction, there are no distinct characteristics.
The Vaibhāṣikas say: That [opponent] claims that all evil views are abandoned through emptiness, and that nirvāṇa is itself emptiness.

However, it is not the case that nirvāṇa is non-existent and thus incapable of counteracting those views; therefore, nirvāṇa exists because it serves as an antidote, just as light is the antidote to darkness.
The proponent says:
Since it is not established that the light of a lamp here can illuminate and possesses substantial existence, your example lacks substantial existence; this is the fault of the probans (*sādhana*).
When I speak of emptiness, I mean that all phenomena are unapprehendable; this is precisely the teaching of the antidote to apprehending something as real.

However, that realm of apprehension is empty because it is unapprehendable at all times; it does not possess an intrinsic essence, for it is unarisen. Nor is it non-existent, for I have already previously refuted such a position.
To cling to emptiness is also a false view; therefore, the wise should abandon this clinging.
If those lacking wisdom cling to emptiness as having an intrinsic nature, then because emptiness would possess an intrinsic nature, it would be devoid of benefit.
As stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If there is someone who says they can see emptiness, I declare that person to be incurable."
For this reason, the meaning of emptiness is not established.
As for your claim that the antidote serves as the cause, the logical status of that cause is not established.
Furthermore, if such a view existed within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then the existence of its antidote would be tenable.
Now, observing that these various views do not exist, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"Views such as existence or non-existence after cessation, as well as permanence and so forth,
and [views regarding] nirvana and its prior or posterior limits— these are the bases upon which all views depend."
The commentary states:
This refers to whether, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata exists or whether the Tathāgata does not exist.
Is there a Tathāgata, or is there no Tathāgata?
Is it that there is neither a Tathāgata nor is there no Tathāgata?

Is the world finite, or is the world infinite, or is it both finite and infinite, or is it neither finite nor infinite? Likewise, is the world eternal, or is the world non-eternal, or is it both eternal and non-eternal, or is it neither eternal nor non-eternal?

These four views comprise twelve types: those concerning whether the Tathāgata exists after his parinirvāṇa arise based on nirvāṇa; those concerning the finitude of the world and so forth arise based on the future; and those concerning the eternity of the world and so forth arise based on the past. How do such views as these arise?
This is due to the fault of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
However, it has already been explained that this conceptualization lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"All entities are entirely empty; how can there be the finite, the infinite, both the finite and the infinite, or neither the finite nor the infinite?
How can there be this or that thing, or what can there be that is permanent or impermanent?"
"Is it both eternal and non-eternal? Is it neither eternal nor non-eternal?
The commentary states:
The objective realm upon which such conceptual distinctions depend has no intrinsic reality.
Because that which serves as their basis lacks intrinsic substance, the conceptualizing mind also lacks intrinsic substance. Why is this so?
Because all phenomena, at all times and in all ways, arise from the conjunction of various conditions; they are ultimately empty and lack self-nature.
Within such a Dharma, what has limits? Who is "with limits"?
What is both "with limits" and "without limits"? What is neither "with limits" nor "without limits"? And furthermore, what is the body?
Who is it that possesses a body? Is the body one and the self one, or is the body different and the self different?
Such views as these—namely, the sixty-two views—are all unattainable within ultimate emptiness.
For this reason, as it is said in a verse within a sutra: "Since that which is discriminated does not exist, where could discrimination arise?
Because the discriminator is extinguished, that which is discriminated also perishes."

From the beginning of this treatise, we have investigated all phenomena (*dharmas*): existence is non-existent, non-existence is non-existent, both existence and non-existence are non-existent, and neither existence nor non-existence is non-existent. This is called the true mark of all phenomena—the equality of emptiness—which extinguishes all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and attains the path of peace.
If one were to put forward a reason based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it has already been refuted as before.
The Sautrāntikas say:

"Nirvāṇa exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-satya*); for the sake of enabling sentient beings to realize it, the Buddha observes their faculties, their minds, the dharmas, the time, and the place, and thereby teaches the Dharma."

If there were no nirvana, the Buddha would not have delivered this teaching, including the eighty-four thousand gateways of remedial practices for the afflictions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Because he taught these things for the sake of attaining nirvana, nirvana exists.
The proponent says:
If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), you wish to establish [the self] by taking the teaching of the Dharma as the reason, is that what you intend?
As the verse in the treatise says:
"All that is attained is relinquished; when conceptual proliferation ceases, there is auspiciousness.
The Tathāgata has no fixed location, and he has not taught a single dharma.
The commentary states:
That "all that is apprehended is discarded" means that because the objects of apprehension lack intrinsic nature, the mind that apprehends them also lacks intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, because the objects of apprehension are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the mind that apprehends them does not arise; thus, all such apprehensions are discarded.

The cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) means that the objects of apprehension lack intrinsic substance; since the verbal designations of those objects do not arise either, it is therefore called the cessation of conceptual proliferation.
"Śrī" (Auspiciousness) means that because all calamities and misfortunes are entirely without intrinsic nature, it is called "Śrī.
This is because, through the nature of conceptualization arising from them, all phenomena are unestablished and all phenomena are inexpressible.
Regarding the use of teaching the Dharma as a cause within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), as stated in the verse above: "The Tathāgata has no locus; there is not a single dharma that he teaches.
Furthermore, the true dharma attained through self-awakening (*svasaṃvedya*) is inexpressible; however, this verbal expression is identical to the realm of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The true Dharma that is realized is inexpressible, as stated in the verse above: "The Tathāgata has no locus; there is not a single dharma for him to teach.
Furthermore, how does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?

In order to encompass all states of existence, he has accumulated a mass of merit and wisdom over immeasurable thousands of kalpas; the Buddha-body arises from this accumulation of merit and wisdom, just as a wish-fulfilling gem can manifest all forms and images.
By the power of the vows of all sentient beings' mastery over their minds, the Tathāgata, through effortless spontaneity, emits sounds that encompass the three vehicles.
Due to the power of the Buddha’s body and because those who hear it are deluded, they say, "The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma for me."
As for the one who preaches the Dharma, they exist as a conventional designation within the realm of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, the aggregates (*skandha*) are not the Tathāgata, nor is there a Tathāgata apart from the aggregates, as this has already been examined previously.

Regarding the name "Tathāgata," there is not a single thing that can be spoken of, nor is there anyone who speaks, nor anyone who listens, nor any place of speaking, because it lacks any substantial reality.
As stated in the verse above: "The Tathāgata has no location; there is not a single dharma for him to teach.

Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without volitional construction, and this aggregate of conditioned phenomena is untainted (*anāsrava*). Having severed both obstacles, it serves as the basis for the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) and so forth. Because he possesses these four dharmas, he is named the Tathāgata.
Because those aggregates of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are without any creative agency, it is not the case that there is a speaker of the Dharma.

Even up to the listener of the Dharma, these are aggregates of outflowing formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra-rāśi*); to speak of a "listener" or a "receiver" is merely conventional expression, for they possess no substantial reality.
Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all things are like illusions and transformations; who is there to speak, and who is there to listen?
For this reason, the Tathāgata has no fixed location and does not preach even a single dharma.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, he established the power of his past vows and attained mastery, gathering all sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
