By the power of the causes and conditions of the roots of goodness resulting from their fixed karmic retribution, and through the mastery of their faculties, inclinations, and mental vows, [the Tathāgata] preaches the Dharma endowed with sixty aspects effortlessly in order to bring joy to all sentient beings.
Although this sound arises in dependence upon the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata remains eternally in meditative concentration.
That the mind exerts effort without functional power, that there is no essence of vitarka or vicāra, yet sounds emerge, is entirely incorrect.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has no locus and has not preached a single dharma.
Furthermore, because he has personally understood and realized for himself the Dharma taught by previous Buddhas:
all dharmas have already been taught by previous Buddhas; the present Buddha teaches them in accordance with them, without adding a single word.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has no fixed location and does not preach a single dharma.

Furthermore, because all dharmas are ultimately empty within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended as either a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) or a specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) by means of wisdom.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has no fixed location and has not preached a single dharma.
As it is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"When the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, there was not a single dharma he could receive from Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
Why is this? Because it is neither graspable nor expressible.

All those of the non-Buddhist schools are truly to be pitied; I shall now, by means of the principles taught in this Supreme Vehicle—the emptiness of intrinsic nature through the absence of essence—shatter their false sophistry.
However, those non-Buddhists, relying on the logic of their own evil views, conceal the faults of their own tenets and, clinging to their own perspectives, spoke this verse:
"In that ultimate truth, the Buddha never taught the Dharma;
since the Buddha is free from conceptual construction, it is not correct to say he taught the Mahāyāna."
As for the emanated Buddha preaching the Dharma, this matter is not so;
the Buddha has no mind that preaches the Dharma, and the emanation is not the Buddha.
Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), he likewise does not preach the Dharma.
Non-conceptual emptiness exists, yet compassionate mind does not;
because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, the Buddha likewise lacks intrinsic nature;
since that Buddha lacks intrinsic nature, there is also no compassionate mind.
The non-Buddhists said to the proponent:
"In that Buddhist Dharma, if it is claimed that there is compassion within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is like a barren woman weeping for her child."
The proponent says:
That which is clarified here as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is characterized by a single mark, namely, the markless (*animitta*); therein there is neither Buddha nor Mahāyāna.
This ultimate truth is the sphere of non-dual wisdom (*advayajñāna*).
What you have spoken in verse is precisely the principle of my Buddha-dharma.
Now I shall explain for you the body of the Tathāgata.

Although the body of the Tathāgata is free from discrimination, because it has been cultivated through the adornment of great vows—the power of previously planted aspirations to benefit others—it is able to gather in all sentient beings.

At all times, he manifests the body of a transformation Buddha; from this transformation body, there issue forth sounds in the sequence of written characters and phrases, which are not shared with any non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. He expounds the two kinds of selflessness for the sake of accomplishing the paramita of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and for the sake of those who wish to accomplish the vehicle of the Supreme Vehicle; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Because there exists the Buddha of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-buddha*), the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises based upon that Buddha, and from this transformation body, the teaching of the Dharma arises.
Since the Buddha of ultimate truth serves as the cause for the teaching of the Dharma, my established thesis is not undermined, nor is the world's conventional desire contradicted.
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins say:

"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is all taught through conceptual differentiation; it arises as a cause for teaching the Dharma through the power of the sovereign vows of the minds of other sentient beings, just as, for example, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas and others."
The proponent says:
This argument is not correct.
A transformation Buddha who preaches the Dharma is free from conceptual discrimination; it is not as you say, characterized by one-sided conceptualization.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
"It is not the case that the Buddha teaches the Dharma without conceptual discrimination; because he lacks conceptual discrimination, he would be like a clod of earth.
The proponent says:

Because it cannot be said that the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) is different from the Buddha of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-buddha), the existence of a Buddha within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) does not preclude that Buddha of the ultimate truth acting as the cause for preaching the Dharma within the conventional truth; nor does it preclude that the Tathāgata is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) within the ultimate truth.

To differentiate whether the Tathāgata possesses compassion or lacks compassion is entirely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); such conceptual proliferations are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Both the sentient beings who are objects of compassion and the one who gives rise to compassion likewise lack intrinsic nature.
As you previously stated, if there were compassion within conventional truth, such that it could be said to be like a barren woman weeping for her child, that analogy would be incorrect.
What are the characteristics of compassion?

It refers to the arising of a mind of sorrow and distress upon seeing others suffer; this is called the characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*). It is, for example, like an affectionate mother who cherishes her most beloved child.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to a heart of pity and sympathy toward all sentient beings in exactly the same way.
Even if a barren woman possessed a heart of compassion, what harm would that do me?
Yet such is not the case; for example, the hair of a tortoise is as utterly non-existent as empty space, and thus cannot be compared to the great void.
Therefore, even if there were those who possess compassion, the compassionate mind of the Buddhas is not at all like the compassion of a barren woman.
The compassion of the Buddhas has been accumulated, cultivated, and brought to ultimate fulfillment over immeasurable eons, pervading the entire realm of all sentient beings.
If a barren woman lacks this compassion, then do not further claim that the compassion existing in conventional truth is similar to the compassion of a barren woman.

Regarding the proofs established by the Vibhāṣā masters and others at the beginning of this chapter, the Master has already stated their fallacies, demonstrating that nirvāṇa possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For this reason, the following passage from a sutra is cited to demonstrate this point.
As a verse in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "In reality there is no nirvāṇa; it is the Tathāgata who speaks of nirvāṇa."
"It is as if space were to bind itself, and as if space were to release itself.
Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying,
"If there are discriminating sentient beings who wish for all phenomena to have arising and ceasing, the Buddha does not appear in the world for such people."
If one gives rise to conceptualized marks regarding nirvāṇa, saying that it possesses a substantial entity, then those sentient beings will certainly be unable to escape from saṃsāra,
World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*?
The complete stilling of all signs is *nirvāṇa*.
The cessation of all conditioned activities is *nirvāṇa*.
World-Honored One!

Although ignorant sentient beings have left the household life within the Buddha-dharma, they fall into the views of external paths in their quest for the essence of nirvāṇa. This is no different from seeking oil from sesame seeds by pointing at one's hand and claiming it has been obtained, or searching for fresh butter within milk.

If one seeks nirvana within the ultimate quiescence of all phenomena—even among those who are heterodox, arrogant outsiders or those who are śrāvakas outside the Buddha-dharma—if such a practitioner has achieved right view, they do not conceive of a single dharma as arising or ceasing, nor do they desire to realize or attain a single dharma, nor do they perceive the principle of the Noble Truths.
As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"Nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an image in a mirror, like the moon reflected in water, and like a city of the Gandharvas."
The commentary on the "Examination of Nirvāṇa" chapter is concluded.
Chapter 26: Examination of the Dependent Origination of Conventional Truth (*Saṃvṛti-pratītyasamutpāda-parīkṣā*). The commentary states:
This present chapter also serves to refute that which is the counteragent to emptiness, by means of the dependent origination of conventional truth.
A member of our own school says to me:
"The previous statement that the Tathāgata has no location and does not teach a single dharma is incorrect.
The proponent replies:
I shall now explain.

The Tathāgata, wishing to terrify all non-Buddhists, humans, devas, and other sentient beings, and to cause them to cease their various evil views and afflictions, has taught the Dharma of dependent origination.
Because the Buddha has fully awakened to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), his fame is exalted and pervades all worlds; for this reason, he is called "Buddha.
You, however, by now attributing fault to the principle of dependent origination, contradict your own desire.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Enveloped by ignorance, one performs those three kinds of karmic actions that lead to future existence;
by means of these, one goes to the various realms of rebirth."
The commentary states:
That which is the direct opposite of clarity is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
This ignorance is able to obscure and obstruct the wisdom of sentient beings, thereby producing the various formations (*saṃskāra*) that lead to future existence.
What is meant by "subsequent existence" (*punarbhava*)?
It refers to that which has not yet received birth; because it proceeds toward subsequent existence through the inseparable conjunction of causes and effects, it is called "subsequent existence."
What is meant by "all conditioned phenomena" (saṃskāra)?
There are three kinds of conditioned phenomena:
first, the dharma of selflessness; second, momentariness; and third, the three types of karma.
What are the three types of karma?
They are merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable.
Furthermore, there are three kinds, namely: body, speech, and mind.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not only the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), but can also serve as a reciprocal condition for subsequent members such as consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, its essence does not consist solely in obscuring sentient beings; there are other afflictions as well. Regarding "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*): they are so called because they constitute the performance of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"By means of the causes and conditions of the saṃskāras, consciousness takes up residence in the various realms of existence;
once consciousness has taken up its abode through continuity, at that time, name-and-form arise."
The commentary states:
What is consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
It is called consciousness because it discriminates and grasps objects one by one.

"Entrusting" refers to birth. Regarding "conditioned by formations" (*saṃskārapratyaya*): it means that formations serve as the condition for consciousness; thus, it is called "conditioned by formations.

Furthermore, it is not only the formations alone that serve as the condition for consciousness. At the time that consciousness arises, there are also various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that arise simultaneously with it. For this reason, those mental factors also serve as conditions.

Furthermore, regarding "conditioned by formations, consciousness arises": although Arhats also possess formations, why do they not serve as a condition for consciousness that links to a future existence?
Because the rope of craving has been severed, they do not serve as a condition for consciousness that links to a future existence.
Therefore, since afflictions such as craving also serve as conditions for the consciousness of future lives, why is it stated that "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) alone do so?
It is because formative forces possess a superior power.

For example, when a king is victorious in battle, it is not only the king who is victorious; the entire host of troops is also said to be victorious. Because the king is the leader, one says "the king is victorious."
Furthermore, some may give rise to this thought:
"It may be that ignorance is the cause of unwholesome volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), since delusion itself is unwholesome; but how can it serve as the cause for wholesome volitional formations?"

This means that for one who has not yet severed ignorance, in order to experience the pleasure of being attended by celestial maidens, they perform various meritorious deeds; therefore, ignorance also serves as a reciprocal cause for meritorious deeds.

Furthermore, regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*), all meritorious formations (*puṇya-saṃskāra*) that are ultimately (*paramārthatas*) unwholesome (*akuśala*) and are bound to birth and death are designated as unwholesome. For this reason, ignorance (*avidyā*) can serve as a condition for all formations in their entirety.

Furthermore, regarding the three types of karma—those leading to happy destinies, those leading to unhappy destinies, and those leading to the immovable—each has distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior; these various formations are called the karma that leads to the various destinies.
Regarding those who go to the various realms of existence, the various masters hold differing views.
For instance, the Sarvāstivādins say:
"The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists, because there is a continuity of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that proceeds to take rebirth."
The Saṃmitīyas, the Dharmaguptakas, and others assert: "There is no such intermediate state (antarābhava);
rather, consciousness arises with volitional formations (saṃskāra) as its condition, and at that moment it is called 'taking rebirth' (pratisaṃdhi)."
Furthermore, those who maintain the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) say:

when sentient beings possessing form perish in one place, those same sentient beings possessing form arise again in a continuous succession; arising without interval between the preceding and succeeding moments until they reach another realm of existence is called "taking rebirth" (*pratisaṃdhi*), because it arises as a continuous succession, just like a lamp.

For this reason, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exists in dependence upon the aggregates (skandha) and continues in succession; because it arises without interruption from the moment of death until the moment of rebirth, it is called "rebirth" (upapatti), just as a person in the present goes from here to there.
Furthermore, those who deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) say:

between the death-existence (*cyuty-bhava*) and the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no further intermediate existence; because it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is like the death-existence and birth-existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which lacks an intermediate existence.

Why is this? That which arises as the body of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) at the moment of death is not the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because that body is a result of maturation (*vipākaja*), just like the body currently being experienced.

Furthermore, as for those who maintain that there is an arising of a body: because this is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering, it is like taking the mental substance (*manomaya*) as a body; since it proceeds to another place through a continuous succession moment by moment, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), nor does it consist of a single, uniform set of aggregates (*skandha*).
Your proposed doctrine of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not established.
Furthermore, those who maintain that there is an intermediate state ask:
"If there were no intermediate state, how could one reach the place of future rebirth?"
Furthermore, those who deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) say:

from the moment of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) until the moment of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), the continuity proceeds like the transmission of a scripture, like the passing of a lamp, like the impression of a seal, like the appearance of a reflection in a mirror, like an echo in the sky, like the shadow of the sun or moon in water, like a seed producing a sprout, or like the saliva produced in the mouth when a person sees vinegar; thus, when the subsequent aggregates arise in succession, there is no intermediate state that travels back and forth to transmit this [existence] to that.
Therefore, the wise should understand it in this way, as stated in the verse above: "Once consciousness has entered into continuity, at that time name-and-form arise.
What, then, constitutes name-and-form?
There are two kinds of "name" (*nāman*):
first, that which goes of its own accord toward the various realms of existence; second, that which is driven by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and forcibly compelled to enter those realms.
Furthermore, "name" refers to the four formless aggregates (*skandha*), which are collectively termed "name."
What is form (*rūpa*)?
It is called "form" because it is subject to transformation; this refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four sense objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth.
Not only consciousness (*vijñāna*) serves as a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, also serve as its conditions.
Furthermore, regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*): consciousness, ignorance, and so forth are not invariably the conditions for name-and-form.
In certain cases, where there are beings of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), they also serve as conditions for those six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
For those born in the formless realm, this consciousness serves as a condition for name alone.
As a verse in the treatise says:
"From the substance of name-and-form, the six sense bases arise in succession."
"The conjunction of the mental objects (*viṣaya*) and so forth gives rise to the six types of contact (*sparśa*). Commentary:
What are the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*)?
This refers to the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base.
As for the eye-base, it takes visible form as its objective sphere.
Because that translucent matter (rūpa-prasāda) is the basis for visual consciousness, it is called the "eye-base" (cakṣur-āyatana).
Likewise, with respect to sounds and other objects, because that translucent matter is the basis for auditory consciousness and the others, it is called the "ear-base" and so forth.
Regarding the mind-base (manāyatana): that which ceases in immediate succession is designated as the mind-base.
Why is it called a "base"?
It is because consciousness and the mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise from pure matter; therefore, it is termed a "base."
Why is it called "contact" (sparśa)?
It is so named because it is the conjunction with each of the painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Due to those three factors— the eye, visible forms, and mental attention—
serving as conditions for name-and-form, consciousness then arises.
Commentary:
Regarding the arising of consciousness: just as the eye takes form as its condition, and consciousness arises by depending upon form;
so too the ear takes sound as its condition, and auditory consciousness arises, and so on until the mind takes mental phenomena as its condition, and mental consciousness arises.
What is meant by "contact" (sparśa)?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"The eye and so forth, form, and consciousness— These three come together in harmony."
"This is what is called contact; from contact, sensation arises.
The commentary states:
Because the three factors—the object, the sense faculty, and the mind—unify as one, it is termed "contact."
With contact as a condition, three kinds of feeling arise, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Feeling is the condition for the arising of craving; for the sake of feeling, craving arises.
Craving, in turn, is the condition for grasping; grasping is of four kinds."
The commentary states:
This refers to the characteristic of seeking desire, which is termed "craving.

An unlearned worldling, for the sake of pleasant sensation, gives rise to a mind of greedy seeking; like licking honey from a blade, they fail to perceive the subsequent harm and affliction to the tongue.
If it were the case that craving arises only toward pleasant feelings, that might be so; but how can craving arise toward painful feelings or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings?

This is because painful feelings and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings also serve as conditions for craving. When experiencing a painful feeling, there also arises a mind seeking to be free from it, which is itself a form of craving. Therefore, there is no fault.

The four graspings (upādāna) are: the grasping for sense-pleasures (kāmopādāna), the grasping for views (dṛṣṭyupādāna), the grasping for precepts and observances (śīlavratopādāna), and the grasping for the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
What is meant by "grasping"?
It means the sense of accumulation.
Furthermore, because craving increases, it is also grasping (*upādāna*).
Because one gives rise to a mind of pursuit in order to obtain the pleasures of the five desires, this is also called grasping.
As a verse in the treatise says:
"Because one grasps at existence, the grasper arises from existence;
because there is no grasper, one is liberated from suffering and severs all existence. Commentary:
"Existence" (bhava) is a characteristic of karma.
Furthermore, "existence" is another name for birth, and the dharmas that are the causes of birth are also called "existence.
If this is so, how can the cause itself be the fruit?
Now, we currently observe that causes receive the name of their effects; for example, when a Buddha appears in the world.

Since the five resultant members, such as consciousness and so forth, which constitute pleasure, are subsumed within the present life, they are nevertheless said to arise from ignorance and formations.

If one encounters a virtuous friend, hears the true Dharma, and gives rise to right reflection, one will be able to perceive the modes of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self within all conditioned phenomena, such as pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without arising and are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). When one gives rise to true knowledge regarding them, craving no longer arises. Because craving does not arise, there is no further pursuit. As stated in the verse above: "If there is no grasping (*upādāna*), one is liberated from suffering and severs all states of existence (*bhava*)."
What is the meaning of this?
It means that because there is grasping (*upādāna*), there is becoming (*bhava*); if there were no grasping, there would be no becoming.
What are the characteristics of becoming?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
“The five aggregates possess substantial existence;
From existence, birth subsequently arises, Along with old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, Weeping, grief, and suffering.”
The commentary states:
This means that it is also taught that the cause of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitutes the limb of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

Furthermore, regarding the cause of the five aggregates being called "existence," it is not only the cause of the five aggregates that is termed "existence"; the cause of the four aggregates in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) is also termed "existence."
"Birth" refers to the present arising of the aggregates where none previously existed.
"Aging" refers to the characteristic of transformation and decay.
"Death" refers to the non-existence of the aggregates.
"Sickness" refers to the body being oppressed by suffering.
"Sorrow and lamentation" refer to the arising of internal burning sensations caused by separation from what is beloved, encountering what is hateful, and so forth.
"Lamenting" refers to the loss of loved ones or virtuous kinsmen, whereby one utters sounds to praise their virtues and weeps for them.
"Suffering" refers to physical sensation; "grief" refers to mental sensation; and "exhaustion" refers to the utter fatigue of both body and mind.
Regarding the detailed explanation that birth and so forth are all termed "suffering," how is this so?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Sorrow, fatigue, and the like, All have birth as their cause."
"Only this aggregate of suffering arises; ultimately, it possesses no characteristic of pleasure.
The commentary states:
"Only the aggregate of suffering arises" means that it is not conjoined with pleasure.
"Aggregates" (skandha) refers to a collection; "arising" refers to the birth of aggregates; and "continuity" refers to dependent origination as subsumed under conventional truth, not ultimate truth.
Since it was already explained in the previous chapter that there is no arising in order to induce conviction and understanding, that which I have established remains unrefuted.
If it is said that the flow of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) revolves within birth and death, how can they be non-arising?
I shall now answer this, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"This is called birth and death, The root of all conditioned phenomena."
"What is done by the ignorant is not done by those who see reality.
The commentary states:

"The various formations (*saṃskāra*) are the root of birth and death, and are produced by the ignorant. This means that the ignorant do not perceive that the various formations have, since beginningless time, arisen through successive conditions like an illusion or a mirage; because they do not see their faults, they seek pleasure. In order to seek pleasure, they perform various formations such as meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma.

"Seeing reality and not acting" means that because the Noble Path has already arisen, one sees the truth; and because the ignorance that constitutes the essence of the cognitive obscurations and afflictions has already been severed.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If ignorance is already severed, The formative forces will no longer arise."
"By cultivating wisdom, ignorance is thereby severed. Commentary:
This means that because the conditions are lacking, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not arise; it is like a sprout that does not grow because the seed lacks substance.

Now, by cultivating what wisdom does one attain the severance of ignorance? It is the wisdom that illuminates dependent origination as explained in this treatise; it negates the inherent existence of all entities and brings about the realization of the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena.
The cultivation of the wisdom of emptiness refers to repeated practice.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"When each individual factor ceases, its corresponding factor does not arise."
"Only this mass of suffering is said to be truly and eternally extinguished. Commentary:

This means that because the path of counteraction arises for each individual link of existence, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), these links of existence are extinguished and will not arise again; this is due to the cessation of volitional formations.
With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases, and so on, up to the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so forth.
That the aggregate of suffering alone is eternally extinguished is because it is subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), these factors such as ignorance neither arise nor cease, how can they still be called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
The Buddha taught the ultimate sense by relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); such is my position.
As stated in the preceding verse: "Without relying upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one cannot explain the ultimate (paramārtha).
For this reason, there is no subversion of the thesis I have established.

At the beginning of this chapter, members of our own school (svayūthya) claimed that my thesis was flawed; however, since I have now demonstrated that such a flaw does not exist, the intended meaning of this chapter is to cause beings to gain faith and understanding through the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) of conventional truth.
As the Buddha taught that "non-arising" is called dependent origination, this means that what does not arise is described as dependent origination.
If there is no arising, how could there be cessation?
If one can realize non-extinction within that which is without extinction, this is called "understanding the dharma of dependent origination," and so forth.
The commentary on the "Chapter Examining Conventional Dependent Origination" is hereby complete. 27.
Examination of False Views (*Mithyādṛṣṭi-parīkṣā*). Commentary on the *Prajñāpradīpa* (Lamp of Wisdom), Chapter Twenty-Seven: Examination of False Views. The commentary states:
This present chapter is also taught in order to refute that which is the counteragent to emptiness, so as to bring about an understanding that all views are empty.
An adherent of our own school says:
"The five appropriated aggregates possess intrinsic nature because they are the locus of views; it would not be possible for them to be the locus of views if they were non-existent."

Regarding the statement that "the five aggregates are the locus of views," as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, those five aggregates are suffering, they are the origin [of suffering], they are the world, and they are the locus of views; such things exist.
The proponent says: Not so.
We shall now examine the various views; herein, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"In the past, in former lives, did I exist or not?
These views concerning permanence and so forth all arise based on the prior life.
Commentary:
This refers to the views: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist? Did I both exist and not exist? Did I neither exist nor not exist?
Such views arise based on the past life.

The four views—namely, that the world is eternal, that the world is non-eternal, that it is both eternal and non-eternal, and that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal—are taught in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*) of the present life; all views regarding the eternity and so forth of the aggregates of past lives likewise arise based upon these.
"Dependent upon" means "conditioned by. Conditioned by what?
It means conditioned by various views.
What is the meaning of "view"?
This refers to clinging to grasping and so forth.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"Furthermore, there are other views that cling to the non-arising of the future."
"The future [extremes] such as arising and so forth, all depend on the future arising.
Commentary:
These various views arise based on the past world.

The four views—namely, that the world is finite, that the world is infinite, that it is both finite and infinite, and that it is neither finite nor infinite—arise because of the present aggregates (*skandha*).
That which will arise as the aggregates in the future is called the "final limit.
For now, let us examine how various views arise based on reliance upon past lives, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"It is not the case that there was a self in the past; this matter is not so."
"Those sentient beings of the previous life are not those of the present life.
The commentary asks: Why is this not so?
This is because their times differ and they are produced by different karmas, just like other sentient beings; furthermore, their bodies and sense faculties are also distinct.
If it is argued that although the faculties and so forth differ, the "self" is one, this too is not correct.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"That which was formerly called 'self' Is merely the appropriation of a self-nature;
If one is separated from those various appropriations, What further self could there be?"
The commentary states:
This means that it is not the case that the self of Devadatta in past lives is the same as the self of today, because they are apprehended as distinct, just like the self of Yajñadatta.
For this reason, it is not the case that the self born in a previous life is the same as the self born today.

Furthermore, if one wishes to maintain that the characteristic of the self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) is distinct from the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*), it is as stated in the verse above: "If one is separated from all forms of grasping, what self could there possibly be?"
Because there is no such thing as a "self," we have already extensively refuted the notion that a self exists apart from the aggregates (*skandhas*).

If those who postulate a self think, "I do not wish for my self to be without substance," and thus take up-taking (*upādāna*) as the very substance of the self, they are merely making a conceptual distinction similar to those who speak of non-self, who likewise take the substance of up-taking to be the self.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If grasping were the self, where else could there be a self?
Since grasping arises and ceases, how can it be the grasper?"
The commentary states:
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), appropriation (*upādāna*) is not the self (*ātman*).
Since appropriation possesses the two natures of arising and ceasing, it has already been explained that there is no self, in order to bring about faith and understanding.
What is grasping? It refers to both grasping and the grasper.
Grasping is the action, while the grasper is the agent who performs the action, just as there are two things: fuel and fire.
Furthermore, since the self has already been refuted previously, the doctrine of the self is not established.
How is it not established?
As stated in the previous verse: "The appropriated [aggregates] are not the self, because they arise and cease."
The self is neither existent nor non-existent.
Such a self cannot even be made understood by others within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, I shall further respond to those who reckon that there is a self distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*), as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If there were a self distinct from those appropriations, it would not be so;
for it should be apprehendable apart from the aggregates, yet it cannot be apprehended. Commentary:
This means that it is not the case that the self is distinct from appropriation. Why?
If the self were separate from appropriation, how could one say that appropriation is a characteristic of the self?
If there were no characteristic that could be described, then there would be no grasping and no self.
If it is claimed that while there is no self apart from grasping, grasping itself is the self, this is also not the case; for there is no self distinct from grasping, just as with other things.

In this regard, a formal proof is established: the grasping is not distinct from the self that is grasped, because grasping is a phenomenon that is graspable, whereas the self is not graspable; it is, for example, like the nature of grasping itself. Why is this so?
Grasping arises and ceases, but I am not so.
Furthermore, how can grasping itself be the grasper?
If it is claimed that there is a grasper apart from grasping, that too is not the case.
If there were an appropriator who does not appropriate the five aggregates, then that appropriator would have to exist separately from the five aggregates.
Such is their position.
Now, I shall state the reasoning, as it is said in a verse of the treatise:
"I am not different from grasping, nor am I identical to it;
yet I am not without grasping, nor am I definitively non-existent. Commentary:

This means that the self is neither separate from appropriation nor identical with appropriation; yet it is not without appropriation, nor is it non-existent. This has already been made understood by others.
If one says that there is a self in the past, that is not so.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"There is no past in this present life; this matter is likewise not so.
That which was born in a previous life is not different from this present life."
If it were different from what preceded, it would exist independently apart from that predecessor;
thus it should be eternally abiding and not subject to the conditions of the present aggregates.
Commentary:
This means that the questioner does not wish for it to be so.
What does he wish for?
He wishes for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the previous life to serve as the condition (*pratyaya*) for the five aggregates of the present life.

I now establish this proof: the five aggregates of Devadatta in the present life cannot be different from his five aggregates in the past, because they form an uninterrupted continuity and because the past aggregates serve as their cause, just like [the case of] Devadatta himself.

Regarding the past five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), there is not only the fault that they would exist independently prior to their separation from the present, but there are further defects as stated in the verse above: "In this way, they would be eternally abiding, and would not serve as conditions for the present aggregates."
"What is the condition?
It is because the subsequent aggregates do not arise.

If that were so, there would be no birth from death; rather, the aggregates of birth previously received in a prior life would remain in the past, while now there would be a different set of distinct aggregates arising in the present."
For this reason, there would be a great error.
What is this error?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"All karmas are severed and destroyed; yet the person who created the karma shall receive its retribution, thus incurring such a fault.
The commentary states:
If that were so, there would be the fault of nihilism, for one would lose the fruit and retribution of all karmic actions.
Furthermore, it would follow that one person commits the offense while another receives the result.
Moreover, it is not the case that karma and birth arise simultaneously.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"Arising does not occur through common karma, for there would be faults in this;
The self is a creator like a pot, being previously non-existent and subsequently arising."
The commentary states:
In what sense is the "self" (ātman) something conditioned?
It means that which did not previously exist but subsequently comes to be.

If the self were not previously to give rise to afflictions and karma, it should take external phenomena as its cause of arising, rather than taking the karma accumulated in previous lives as its cause of arising.
That which can thus produce the causes for subsequent aggregates would then be without intrinsic nature, being neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, the past life is likewise subject to the same two types of faults as previously mentioned.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" means that no such dharma exists.
Having thus examined the four propositions regarding existence and non-existence in the past,
we shall now examine the four propositions regarding the future, as stated in the verse of the treatise:
"Some hold such a view: 'In a future life, there is an arising of a self;
in a future life, there is no arising of a self'—this is identical to the fault [already] found in the past. Commentary:
This means that just as [the views of] identity, difference, both, or neither regarding future lives are refuted, they are likewise refuted here and now.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If the deity and the person were one, Then the self would fall into eternalism;..."
"Since the heavens are unborn, they are eternally incapable of being born.
The commentary states:
"In this way, the self falls into the error of eternalism."
The proponents of our own school say:
"What fault is there in the meanings of identity, difference, and so forth?
The respondent says:
If one who has not yet been born as a deva were already a deva, then the self would be unarisen; that which is unarisen is eternal.
For this reason, when I had not yet been born as a deva, I should have been able to perform the actions of a deva;
yet such a thing does not occur.
If it is claimed that the self is permanent and was already capable of performing the deeds of a deva even before being born as one, this is not believed by the world.
Furthermore, if the self were impermanent, then when this self in the human realm is born into the deva realm, the former human self would have already perished.
If you think that there may be a difference [between the self and the aggregates] without the aforementioned fault of identity, this is not the case.
For the view that they are different also entails a fault, as the verse of the treatise says:
“If the deity were different from the human, Then the self would fall into impermanence.”
"Because gods and humans are different, that which continues [from one to the other] is not so.
The commentary asks:
What is the fault in this?
This is because they would be distinct entities, just as, for example, Devadatta and Yajñadatta are; thus, there would be a logical fault in the continuity of two selves.
Furthermore, if someone were to say:
"The continuity of the self is one, yet it possesses both the nature of a deity and the nature of a human."
Now I shall answer this.
As stated in the verse of the treatise:
"If the deity occupies one part, and the human occupies another part,"
"It is not possible for the permanent and the impermanent to coexist in one place.
The commentary asks: Why is this not so?
It is said that there is a celestial realm (*devasthāna*); since there are devas therein, they are eternal.
Because there are no humans in that celestial realm, the absence of humans is impermanent.
If there were a realm of humans, then the presence of humans would be eternal.
Because humans lack the celestial nature, being without the celestial nature is itself impermanence.
It is like the claim that a single object in a single location could be both white and black; such a proposition is logically untenable.
If someone were to say:
"I am neither permanent nor impermanent," as the verse in the treatise says:
"If both permanence and impermanence Were to be established as two distinct meanings;..."
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal, your position is likewise established.
[Commentary: This meaning is difficult for people to understand.
Furthermore, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If there were a place from which someone comes, And a dwelling place from which there is going;
Then birth and death would be without beginning— But such a thing does not exist."
The commentary states:
"Locus" refers to either the celestial realm or the human realm.
"Person" refers to either a celestial being or a human being.
"Abiding place" refers to the locations within the worlds of the devas and so forth.
"One who goes" refers to a person who departs toward another realm of existence.
If this were the case, then this self would exist eternally from beginningless time and would therefore be permanent.
Yet such a thing does not exist.
Why does it not exist?
Because sentient beings and persons have already been refuted.
For this reason, there is no permanent self (*nitya-ātman*).
If one were to say that although there is no permanent self, there exists an impermanent self (*anitya-ātman*), this too is not correct.
As it is said in a verse of the treatise:
"If there is no permanent self, who then is impermanent,
both permanent and impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent?
The commentary states:
This means that impermanence is spoken of in dependence upon permanence.
Since permanence itself does not exist fundamentally, in dependence upon what could impermanence be spoken of?
Furthermore, permanence, impermanence, and so forth have all already been established as unproven.
Now, one should examine the four positions regarding finitude and so forth, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If the world were finite, how could there be a future life?
If the world were infinite, how could there be a future life?"
The commentary states:
What is meant by "extreme" (*anta*)?
It refers to the ultimate limit, the point of exhaustion, and so forth; it is like the aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat in nirvāṇa.

That there is a future life existing now means that the aggregates of the previous life serve as the cause and the aggregates of the subsequent life serve as the effect; thus they proceed without end, for it is by depending on the cause of the preceding aggregates that the effect of the succeeding aggregates arises.
Nevertheless, these aggregates now arise in a continuous succession of one another, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"These successions of aggregates Are like the flame of a burning lamp;
For this reason, the world Is neither finite nor infinite."
The commentary states:

Herein a proof is established: there exists the non-exhaustion of the affliction of ignorance, whereby the succession of the aggregates (skandhas) remains uninterrupted, because these aggregates possess a fruit, just as, for example, the succession of a lamp’s flame.
For this reason, it is not the case that the world has an end.

As for the arising of these similar effects without destruction, it is not because the preceding aggregates remain undestroyed while subsequent effects arise; rather, it is like the preceding flame of a lamp.
For this reason, it is not the case that the world is infinite.
To verify the meaning as it has been stated, it should be as the verse in the treatise says:
"If the aggregates of the previous life have already perished, and the aggregates of the subsequent life arise separately,"
"Then it does not depend on the preceding aggregates; this is called 'having an end.
The commentary states:
This means that if the preceding aggregates arise and then immediately perish, such that they do not serve as the cause for the continuity of the subsequent aggregates, this is "having an end."
As the verse in the treatise says:
"If the preceding aggregates did not perish, And the subsequent aggregates did not arise, Then,
since they would not be caused by the preceding aggregates, They would simply be infinite."
The commentary states:
Why is it "boundless"?
Because it is eternally and constantly present at all times.
This interpretation is not tenable, as stated in a verse of the treatise:
"One part is finite, One part is infinite;
Apart from those [states of] finitude and infinity, There is no further possibility of both or neither."
The commentary states:
This refers to the four propositions concerning whether the world has a final limit and so forth. Why is this so?
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"How could it be that for a single appropriator, one part is subject to destruction while another part is not? Such a thing is impossible."
The commentary states: Why is this not so?
Because it has already been refuted in the previous two types of lamp analogies; therefore, it is not so.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
"If both 'having an end' and 'being endless' Could be established as two [distinct] positions,
Then 'neither having an end nor being endless' Would likewise be established as its meaning."
The commentary states:
This means that if one person were established as both finite and infinite, then by virtue of their mutual dependence, it would also be established that they are neither finite nor infinite;
however, such a thing does not exist.
Just as it is stated in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) that all views are untenable, so too does one cause beings to understand this, as the verse in the treatise says:
"In the ultimate sense, because all phenomena are empty,
where, by what causes and conditions, and who could give rise to various views?"
The commentary states:
This means that if, within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all entities are empty, who is there?
And what object is there as a condition?
What is the cause?
What kind of view arises?
Since that person is empty, the object is empty, the cause is empty, and the view is empty, it is not the case that there is a person, an object, a cause, or a view that arises.

For this reason, the statement made by those of our own school at the beginning of this chapter—that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), these five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that constitutes a basis for views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*)—is incorrect as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Why is this not so? Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), we have already caused those who understand to realize that all views are entirely empty; therefore, it is not so.
If you were to establish your reason based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it would contradict your own tenet.

The Buddha Bhagavān, as the Kinsman of the World, perceives that all sentient beings give rise to various seeds of suffering through false discrimination and various views; therefore, he gives rise to compassion for them.
As stated in a verse of the treatise:
“The Buddha, for the sake of severing all suffering, Expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
With compassion as his cause, I now pay homage to Gautama.”
The commentary states:
"The severance of suffering" refers to the severance of all sufferings, such as the birth and death of all sentient beings.
"Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma) means that because it is pure, it is called the Sublime Dharma.
It is called "pure" because it can extinguish the fire of the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Furthermore, it is also called "pure" because all causes of merit increase and reach fulfillment.
The "Sublime Dharma" refers to the Mahāyāna.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
"World-Honored One!..."
"To embrace the sublime Dharma" means to protect and preserve the Mahāyāna. Why is this so,
World-Honored One?
This is because all vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born from within the Mahāyāna;
even all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas are likewise born from within the Mahāyāna.
World-Honored One!
It is just as, for example, the four great rivers issue forth from Lake Anavatapta.
In this very way, World-Honored One!
The Mahāyāna can give birth to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Such a vehicle takes compassion, joy, and equanimity as its causes, rather than worldly fame or profit.
"One who now pays homage to Gautama is so called because he is able to reveal and show the unsurpassed, wondrous treasure of the Dharma;
thus he is named Gautama. Furthermore, he is named Gautama because his clan name is Gautama."
What is ritual (li)?
There are two kinds of ritual:
the first is verbal praise and eulogy.
The second refers to bowing the body so that the head and face touch the ground.
As stated in a verse from the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "One who deeply understands the Dharma of causes and conditions will be free from all false views."
All phenomena belong to causes and conditions; they have no fixed, inherent foundation.
Phenomena born of causes and conditions do not arise, and phenomena born of causes and conditions do not cease. If one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas will always appear before one.

The purport of this chapter is as follows: at its beginning, it demonstrates the fallacies in the proofs established by those of our own school, and furthermore, it brings about understanding by means of the emptiness of all views.
As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vīryavanta-parākrama:

"Know that form (*rūpa*) is not the locus where views arise, nor is it the locus where views are severed; and so on, up to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), which are not the loci where views arise."
Nor is it a locus for the view of annihilationism.

If form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not loci for the arising of views, nor loci for the view of annihilationism, this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Now, to bring about understanding through the distinctions of non-arising and so forth in dependent origination means: namely, the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and the complete pacification of various views such as identity and difference. This is the dharma of self-realization; this is the dharma like space; this is the dharma of non-discrimination; this is the dharma of the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). To bring about understanding by means of such true nectar (*amṛta*) is the fundamental purport of this treatise.
Question:
What the Buddhas have taught is entirely true in its beginning, middle, and end.
Why, then, is it necessary to establish numerous proofs extensively within this treatise?
The answer is:
There are some dull-witted sentient beings who cannot develop correct faith in the Buddha’s Āgamas; therefore, in order to gather in those beings, various proofs are extensively established.
Now, in order to pay homage to the Master Nāgārjuna, I shall compose this verse:
The Prince of the Muni’s Dharma, The Master of Great Wisdom,
Through the subtle principles of Prajñā, Has expounded this *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Skillfully understanding the practice of benefiting others, you are the sun and moon that illuminate the world;
revealing the profound Dharma, you explain the causes for attaining the Buddha-way.
Whatever the Ācārya has composed, I shall now fully expound and interpret.
In order to extinguish all false views, I have composed the Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra.
This Prajñāpradīpa is a most profound and wondrous Dharma beyond compare;
yet, whatever slight merit I may possess from this work now—
By means of this Lamp of Prajñā, may I gather in all classes of sentient beings;
may they behold the Dharmakāya Tathāgata pervading the lands of the ten directions,
attain the Dharma realized within themselves, and bring to rest all views and conceptual proliferations.
Quiescent and non-conceptual, peerless like space;
may the Lamp of Prajñā further shine universally upon the world,
establishing those shrouded by darkness in nirvāṇa.
The twenty-seventh chapter of the *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā* is hereby completed.

The Great Bodhisattva Prajñāpradīpa—who has reached the perfection of all treatises, possesses profound and vast wisdom, and rides upon the Mahāyāna—has finished composing this prose commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*. He then makes this aspiration:
"By virtue of this single thought of goodness, and through sympathetic joy, dedication, and so forth,..."
Together with all sentient beings, at the end of life, one shall behold Maitreya.
*Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Fifteen.
